In Clark v. Rau (A16A0558), the Georgia Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s order modifying child custody. The case involved Kathrine Clark and Ricky G. Rau, parents of three minor children. In October 2013, a Chatham County Superior Court order established joint legal custody, with Clark as primary physical custodian of B.C., Rau as primary custodian of K.C., and shared custody of V.C. In March 2014, Rau petitioned for modification, alleging material changes in circumstances affecting the children’s welfare. Following a bench trial, the trial court awarded Rau sole legal and physical custody of all three children. Clark appealed pro se. The majority affirmed, citing Clark’s failure to comply with appellate rules (her brief lacked a statement of facts, citations, and enumerated errors with supporting argument), the absence of a transcript, and the presumption of regularity in proceedings below. The majority found the trial court’s order sufficient under Weickert v. Weickert, noting it found a material change substantially affecting the children but did not explicitly use “best interest” language, which the majority deemed unnecessary to remand. The dissent argued the trial court’s order was facially deficient for failing to determine that the custody change was in the children’s best interest, a requirement for modification. The dissent contended that despite brief inadequacies, Clark’s notice of appeal and brief sufficiently identified the judgment and error, invoking statutory duties to review appeals on the merits under liberal construction. The dissent would have vacated the judgment and remanded for application of the proper legal standard.

Under a May trade deal, the United States began accepting cooked poultry from China. The agreement was part of a bilateral exchange in which the United States exported beef and liquefied natural gas to China, while allowing China to export cooked poultry meat. The United States permits only cooked poultry because raw poultry could transmit avian influenza; since 2013 China has confirmed 1,557 human cases of AH7N9 flu and 370 deaths. The United States is the world’s largest poultry producer and does not face a shortage, but the deal opens a market for Chinese processed poultry. Critics argue the deal prioritizes commerce over public health, given China’s history of food‑safety problems, including bacterial contamination, antibiotic residues, and heavy metals. Improper cooking or cross‑contamination can allow salmonella and campylobacter to infect humans; in 2014 these bacteria sickened nearly 14,000 Americans, hospitalized 3,221 and killed 41. Chinese poultry may contain antibiotic residues due to inconsistent enforcement of withdrawal periods, and heavy metals from coal‑burning can contaminate feed and meat. The USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) must deem China’s inspection system equivalent to the U.S. system before imports can proceed; FSIS conducts annual on‑site audits of Chinese plants. Processed poultry is exempt from country‑of‑origin labeling, so consumers and restaurants may not know the product’s origin. Although Chinese labor costs are lower, the Chinese poultry industry is less integrated and technologically advanced than the U.S. industry, limiting its competitiveness in the short term.

Blackwell is NVIDIA’s latest GPU architecture, featuring Fifth‑Generation Tensor Cores, Fourth‑Generation RT Cores, and an AI Management Processor (AMP). It powers the GeForce RTX 50‑series: GB202 (92.2 B transistors, 12 GPC, 192 SM, 24 576 CUDA cores, 192 RT cores, 768 Tensor cores, 512‑bit memory) drives the RTX 5090; GB203 (45.6 B transistors, 7 GPC, 84 SM, 10 752 CUDA cores, 84 RT cores, 336 Tensor cores, 256‑bit memory) powers the RTX 5080 and RTX 5070 Ti; GB205 (31 B transistors, 5 GPC, 50 SM, 6 400 CUDA cores, 50 RT cores, 200 Tensor cores, 192‑bit memory) powers the RTX 5070.

RT Core enhancements include double the ray‑triangle intersection throughput, an Opacity Micromap Engine, a Triangle Cluster Intersection Engine, and hardware‑accelerated Linear Swept Spheres (LSS). LSS approximates strand geometry and renders hair about 2× faster than DOTS while using ~5× less VRAM.

Mega Geometry adds cluster‑level acceleration structures (CLAS) of up to 256 triangles, reducing BVH construction cost by two orders of magnitude. It also introduces a Partitioned Top‑Level Acceleration Structure (PTLAS) that updates only changed partitions, enabling large, static scenes to be ray‑traced efficiently. Mega Geometry APIs are available in DirectX 12 (via NVAPI), Vulkan (vendor extensions) and OptiX 9.0, and are supported on all RTX GPUs starting with Turing.

Shader Execution Reordering (SER) 2.0 doubles the efficiency of Ada’s reordering logic, allowing better thread‑coherence extraction and more application‑specific control through a small API.

The AI Management Processor is a programmable RISC‑V scheduler on the GPU that offloads context scheduling from the CPU, lowers latency, and works with Windows Hardware‑Accelerated GPU Scheduling (HAGS) to improve multitasking and game smoothness.

Video features include a ninth‑generation NVENC that improves AV1 and HEVC quality by ~5 % BD‑BR PSNR, adds 4:2:2 chroma‑sampled H.264/HEVC encoding, and a sixth‑generation NVDEC that doubles H.264 decode speed. DisplayPort 2.1b supports UHBR20 (up to 80 Gbps), enabling 8K@165 Hz and 4K@480 Hz (with DSC).

Max‑Q power improvements comprise fine‑grain clock and power gating, separate voltage rails for GPU cores and memory, accelerated frequency switching that changes clocks 1000× faster than previous generations, and a low‑latency sleep state that enters 10× faster than Ada, delivering up to 50 % power savings for small‑language‑model inference.

DLSS 4 introduces Multi Frame Generation that can produce up to three additional frames per traditionally rendered frame, using a 40 % faster AI model that consumes 30 % less VRAM. Blackwell’s display engine, with twice the pixel processing capability, enables enhanced Flip Metering for smoother pacing. A new transformer‑based model powers Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and DLAA, improving temporal stability, reducing ghosting, and increasing detail.

Neural shaders are enabled by the Cooperative Vectors API for DirectX 12 and Vulkan, giving pixel and ray‑tracing shaders access to Tensor Cores. This unlocks RTX Neural Materials, Neural Texture Compression (up to 7:1 compression), Neural Radiance Cache (real‑time global‑illumination inference), RTX Skin (subsurface scattering), and RTX Neural Faces (generative AI that refines rasterized faces). These technologies are powered by Blackwell’s enhanced Tensor Cores and SER 2.0 scheduling.

Bear markets are defined as periods when the market closes below its 200‑day moving average. Historical data on the S&P 500 show that such markets occur roughly twice a year, last about 25 trading days on average and together account for roughly 30 % of the time. Traders are advised to prepare by backtesting their strategies through both bull and bear cycles and by keeping short‑selling setups ready, because short positions tend to become profitable when the market falls. The article also stresses that long‑only strategies can still perform well in bear markets; an example is an ATR‑swing trade on QQQ that posted positive returns in several bear years (2000‑2002, 2008, 2018, 2022) and outperformed buy‑and‑hold over the long term because lower losses in downturns allow better compounding. Cognitive errors such as buying after price rises and selling after declines are highlighted with the case of the CGM Focus Fund, where the fund gained 18.2 % annually but the average investor lost 11 % annually because they bought near the peak and sold near the bottom. For investors, continuing to invest during a bear market is rational because lower prices provide better entry points and equities have historically been an inflation hedge. Research also notes that women tend to be better long‑term investors because they buy consistently at set intervals and avoid reacting to short‑term market noise. The article recommends staying disciplined, ignoring pessimistic news, maintaining a clear‑cut plan and being adaptable rather than holding a fixed bullish or bearish outlook. Overall, the key message is that a well‑backtested short‑term strategy should be executed through a bear market, short trades will often improve, and long‑term net buyers should keep buying, treating the bear market as an opportunity rather than a threat.

The UC1825B‑SP controller operates from a regulated 10 V‑30 V supply; if the supply is several inches away, additional bulk capacitance (typically 100 µF tantalum) may be required. The output diode voltage stress is given by Vout + Vin_max and a 60 V‑rated diode (UC1825‑SP) was selected. Primary switching MOSFETs see roughly twice the input voltage, so MOSFETs for a push‑pull design should be rated 2.5–3 × the input voltage. Output capacitance of about 1145 µF was chosen to limit ripple; an output filter was added, comprising six ceramic capacitors before the filter and larger tantalum capacitors after it, followed by a 500 nH inductor to attenuate ripple. The filter’s resonant pole was placed well below the switching frequency and a 0.5 Ω resistor was placed in parallel with the inductor to damp high‑frequency peaking. Type IIB compensation was used, inserting a zero at least a decade below the 5 kHz crossover frequency and a pole at the ESR zero; component values were optimized during testing. The sense resistor monitors ripple current and shuts down the switching cycle when the CS pin voltage exceeds ~1 V; the maximum current limit is defined by a given equation. Layout recommendations include using a low‑EMI ferrite‑core inductor (toroid or closed E‑core), routing the feedback trace on the opposite side of the PCB from the inductor with a ground‑plane separation, placing input and output filter capacitors and compensation components close to the IC and using surface‑mount parts, keeping high‑current traces short, direct and at least 15 mil per ampere, and connecting all grounds to a ground plane, with a dedicated power‑ground section for high di/dt currents. VCC and VREF should be bypassed to their respective ground planes and the output must be clamped with a high‑current Schottky diode to VCC and PGND. ESD precautions apply, and mechanical, packaging, and orderable information follows the standard data‑sheet format.

Strength training builds muscle mass, strength, and endurance, and helps maintain fitness and independence. To avoid injuries it requires correct technique, adequate warm‑up and cool‑down. Warming up raises heart rate and blood flow, delivering oxygen to muscles and reducing injury risk; a rabbit study showed warm‑up protects muscles from tearing under stretch and force. Cooling down regulates blood flow after exercise.  

Common training injuries include rotator‑cuff tears and tendinopathy (caused by repetitive overhead motions), hamstring strains and tears (often from sudden powerful movements), herniated discs (from poor weight‑lifting form or sudden extreme motion), tendonitis (micro‑tears from repetitive or sudden stress), and lateral or medial epicondylitis (tennis and golfer’s elbow, resulting from repetitive wrist/arm motions). Prevention strategies include maintaining good shoulder posture, adjusting programmes when discomfort occurs, regular stretching and warm‑up, limiting forceful repetitions, progressing workout intensity gradually, using weights appropriate to ability, staying hydrated, and applying ice, compression and elevation after injury. Treatment options range from rest and over‑the‑counter medicines to physiotherapy, steroid injections or surgery if symptoms persist. Seeking advice from a qualified fitness instructor or doctor before starting a new programme and not ignoring pain further reduces injury risk.

SmartReflex modules minimize power consumption by dynamically adjusting voltage based on process, temperature, and performance using DVFS and AVS. Each Core Logic Voltage Domain supports multiple Operating Performance Points (OPPs) defined by maximum frequency and associated voltage range; OPPs can be changed in real‑time without reset, but not all combinations are allowed and voltage difference between domains must stay below 150 mV. SRAM blocks can be placed in SHUTDOWN mode to reduce leakage; voltage is removed and data lost; SRAM in switchable power domains automatically shuts down when its domain is turned OFF. I/O pins are grouped (DVDD, DVDD_GPMC, DVDD_C, DVDD_SD) with each group independently selectable for 1.8 V or 3.3 V; DDR I/O voltage is independently selectable between 1.5 V and 1.8 V. PHY power‑down modes must be configured before turning off a power domain; the device supports a Low‑Power Standby mode where all switchable domains are OFF, the ARM Cortex‑A8 runs an IDLE loop at its lowest frequency, and unnecessary blocks are clock‑gated. Power supplies are organized into four sequencing groups (CVDD, DDR, 1.8 V, 3.3 V) and must follow a specific power‑up and power‑down order; 3.3 V supplies must never exceed 1.8 V supplies by more than 2 V. The device provides several system‑level reset sources: Power‑On Reset (POR), External Warm Reset, Emulation Warm Reset, Watchdog Reset, Software Global Cold Reset, Software Global Warm Reset, Test Reset, and Local Reset; reset priority is defined and isolation is supported for PCIe and EMAC Switch. During reset most I/O pins enter Hi‑Z except emulation pins, EMAC Switch pins (when isolation enabled), RSTOUT_WD_OUT, and DDR address/control pins; the RSTOUT_WD_OUT pin reflects reset status and is asserted on watchdog reset and on other resets when BTMODE[11] is latched as “0”. Clock architecture uses DEV and AUX reference inputs (internal oscillators or external 1.8 V LVCMOS), SERDES differential clock for PCIe, and optional 32 kHz clock; the device contains 12 top‑level PLLs plus PLL_ARM; PLLs start in bypass and require external filtering on supply pins. SYSCLKs generated by the PRCM distribute clocks to modules; module clocks are derived from PLLs, SYSCLKs, or external inputs and are limited by the selected OPP. The ARM Cortex‑A8 AINTC handles up to 128 interrupt requests with programmable priority; the C674x DSP interrupt controller maps up to 128 events into 12 prioritized interrupts, with alternative sources selectable through multiplexed events. Peripheral overview includes two DCAN interfaces (CAN 2.0), an EDMA controller with 64 channels, Advanced Event Triggering (hardware breakpoints, watchpoints, counters, state sequencing), trace logic, IEEE 1149.1 JTAG, an Ethernet MAC Switch supporting MII/GMII/RMII/RGMII with MDIO management, four GPIO modules (up to 128 pins), a GPMC/ELM for NOR/NAND/SRAM with BCH error location, and an HDMI 1.3a transmitter with TMDS, CEC and multichannel audio. Additional details cover power‑domain state transitions, reset timing specifications, PLL frequency limits, clock timing parameters, interrupt mapping tables, and PCB guidelines for HDMI TMDS routing.

This continuation patent application describes systems and methods for data storage involving storage clusters with multiple storage nodes, each containing CPUs, non-volatile solid state storage units, and flash memory. The storage system includes storage array controllers managing data operations, NVRAM for fast write operations with energy backup, and PCIe-based communication links. Data protection is achieved through erasure coding, RAID schemes, and replication across storage devices. Storage nodes contain authorities that control data placement and manage storage partitions. The system supports various network protocols and can integrate with cloud services providers offering IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS models. The architecture enables scalable, fault-tolerant storage with capabilities including hot-swappable nodes, automatic data rebuild on failures, and distributed control across multiple storage nodes and chassis.

Shop & Save Market signed a letter of intent to open a grocery store at Jeffery Plaza, 2101 E. 71st St., the last vacant former Dominick’s in Chicago. Mayor Rahm Emanuel said more than $10 million in tax‑increment financing would support development, with opening in 18–24 months if the deal proceeds. Whitworth University is reducing its annual tuition from $54,000 to $26,900 to improve cost transparency and address sticker shock. The change, based on two years of research, replaces opaque discounting with a publicly available GPA-based scholarship scale. University officials say the reset is not driven by enrollment decline but by families' desire for clearer pricing earlier in the application process. Researchers note that tuition resets correlate with increases in Pell-eligible students but not overall enrollment growth. Economists explain that institutions use high sticker prices to signal quality, creating a "prisoner’s dilemma" where adopting transparent pricing carries antitrust and market risks. Whitworth’s effort has received positive feedback from parents.

A study by University of Guelph professor Nigel Raine finds that the neonicotinoid pesticide thiamethoxam reduces the chance that bumblebee queens start new colonies by 26%, raising extinction risk. Exposed queens laid fewer eggs in laboratory tests using field‑realistic pesticide levels, while a common parasite showed little effect. The research, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, projects substantial long‑term population declines. About a third of human food crops rely on insect pollination, with bees providing roughly 80% of that service. Neonicotinoid use has been linked to worldwide bee declines; Ontario restricts the chemicals and Europe has a moratorium. The authors note the study is conservative, considering only one pesticide and one parasite.

TCGX closed a $1.3 billion fund. Enron transformed from Houston Natural Gas, a pipeline company acquired in 1985, into a major energy trading company by 2000 under Ken Lay and Jeff Skilling. Skilling, hired as a consultant in 1985, created the "Gas Bank" concept that contractually guaranteed gas supply and price, allowing Enron to act as a trader rather than broker. The company dominated North American natural gas trading with 20 percent market share by 1995 and expanded into electricity, broadband, and other commodities.

Skilling built an aggressive culture emphasizing "intellectual capital," hiring graduates from elite schools through intensive "Super Saturdays" interviews. Employees received high salaries, large signing bonuses, and perks including concierge services, gym access, and massages. Enron implemented a forced ranking system called the Performance Review Committee ("rank and yank"), replacing 15 percent of the workforce annually.

Skilling succeeded Lay as CEO in February 2001. Problems emerged quickly: Enron faced blame for California's energy crisis, its Dabhol, India power plant incurred heavy costs, and its telecommunications investments collapsed as the tech bubble burst. Analysts questioned the company's accounting practices, particularly its extensive use of mark-to-market accounting and asset sales to boost profits.

The stock price fell from $80 in January 2001 to approximately $35 by October. Key executives including Rebecca Mark left after failed ventures like Azurix. Skilling resigned after six months as CEO, citing personal reasons and family time. Lay returned as CEO, acknowledging problems with the performance review system and promising to focus on core business.

John Cracknell Youth Enterprise Bank appointed Tony Robinson patron. Grants up to £1,000 support young people in Hull, East Riding, Malton, Norton, Pickering, Scarborough; over 400 benefited. Robinson, Hull-born micro-business champion, co‑founded Enterprise Rockers CIC in 2012, says enterprise requires a different skill set.

Researchers developed TOPIC, a crystal structure prediction algorithm constrained by corner-sharing (CS) bond topology, to efficiently discover oxide solid-state electrolytes. They validated TOPIC by reproducing known oxide systems (up to 192 atoms/unit cell). Using machine-learning potentials (SevenNet-0) and density functional theory, they screened quaternary oxide compositions with lithium ratios ≤1.0 and identified 92 candidate materials with potentially high ionic conductivity. After validation, 15 materials met stability and conductivity criteria (>0.1 mS cm⁻¹ at 300 K). The lithium ratio serves as a key descriptor for CS framework stability, with lower ratios favoring CS frameworks that exhibit higher ionic conductivity. Notable candidates include Li₄Hf₂Si₃O₁₂ with 14.09 mS cm⁻¹ conductivity and a 6.5 eV band gap. Novel structural prototypes were discovered, and aliovalent doping strategies were demonstrated to enhance conductivity.

The NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU delivers 312 TFLOPS of mixed-precision FP16/FP32 performance with 108 SMs and 432 Tensor Cores, providing 2.5x the mixed-precision performance and 20x the standard FP32 throughput of the Tesla V100. The A100 introduces support for TF32, BF16, and FP64 data types while maintaining compatibility with Volta's FP16 and Turing's INT8/INT4/binary formats. TF32 provides the range of FP32 with FP16 precision, enabling automatic AI training acceleration without code changes, while FP16/BF16 mixed-precision training offers up to 16x throughput versus FP32. The A100 introduces fine-grained structured sparsity with a 2:4 pattern that doubles compute throughput for inference. Memory improvements include 40 GB HBM2 with 1555 GB/sec bandwidth, a 40 MB L2 cache (6.7x larger than V100), and L2 cache residency controls for managing persistent versus streaming data. The Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) feature can partition a single A100 into seven isolated GPU instances with dedicated compute, cache, and memory resources. Third-generation NVLink provides 600 GB/sec total bandwidth with 12 links per GPU. CUDA 11 introduces task graphs, asynchronous copy operations, and hardware-accelerated barriers. The DGX A100 system delivers 5 PFLOPS in a 6U form factor using eight A100 GPUs interconnected via NVSwitch.

David Swensen, chief investment officer of the Yale endowment from the mid‑1980s until his death in 2021, co‑created the Yale Model (David Swensen Portfolio), a diversified investment strategy that emphasizes alternative assets such as private equity, real estate, hedge funds and natural resources alongside stocks and bonds. Swensen moved Yale away from the traditional 60% stock/40% bond allocation, focusing on low‑cost index funds, passive investing and risk management through diversification and targeting undervalued, unconventional investments. Under his management the Yale endowment grew into one of the world’s largest and most successful endowments. Historical data shows the Yale Model (1985‑2020) delivered an annualized return of 12.5%, outpacing the S&P 500’s 9.7% over the same period. Backtests using ETF proxies (VTI, VNQ, VEA, EEM, IEI, TIP) report a 6.23% annual return with lower drawdowns, though recent performance lags the S&P 500 because of the portfolio’s bond weighting and emerging‑market exposure. Asset allocation can be adjusted for individual risk tolerance, typically implemented with low‑cost ETFs and regular rebalancing. The Yale Model is widely used by endowments, foundations and high‑net‑worth investors, but it is not a one‑size‑fits‑all solution; investors should evaluate their own goals and risk tolerance and may seek professional advice before adopting the strategy.

A prospective study of 157 patients hospitalized for acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) evaluated bioimpedance spectroscopy (BIS) for predicting outcomes. BIS measured overhydration (OH) and OH/extracellular water (ECW) ratio at admission and discharge. Among participants, 72 (45.9%) had chronic kidney disease (CKD) and 111 (70.7%) had heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). CKD patients showed higher OH and OH/ECW at admission but these metrics did not predict major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) or heart failure hospitalization (HHF). HFrEF patients demonstrated greater reductions in OH/ECW ratio (P=0.036), indicating better response to diuresis. However, over a 10.7±7.1-month follow-up, OH, OH/ECW, and changes in these parameters were not significant predictors of MACE or HHF in any subgroup. BIS effectively monitors fluid status in ADHF patients, particularly HFrEF, but has limited prognostic utility for predicting clinical outcomes in CKD and HFpEF subgroups.

Wireless communication faces challenges like fading due to multipath effects and moving receivers. Electromagnetic waves in free space decay as 1/r with propagation delays, but obstacles create additional paths with varying delays and attenuations. Moving receivers introduce Doppler shifts, and when multiple paths have different shifts, they cause fast fading that severely degrades communication. The channel can be modeled via ray tracing as a sum of attenuation and phase terms per path, resulting in a time-varying system function. The output is a time-varying convolution of the input with delayed, attenuated copies of the signal. Single Doppler shifts are manageable, but Doppler spread (variation across paths) determines how often channel estimates must be updated for reliable communication.

Following the 2013 recognition of an 18th‑century treaty, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy obtained legal hunting rights in southwestern Ontario, allowing members of Six Nations to harvest white‑tailed deer in Short Hills Provincial Park. Chester Gibson, a Mohawk hunter, led a six‑day “harvest” (the community’s term) conducted with bows only, from sunrise to sunset, with no limit on the number of deer taken. Ministry biologists and park officers assisted hunters, and the meat was divided among the six longhouses, elders and individual families, replacing a previous reliance on purchased beef.  

Protesters gathered at the park entrance nightly, displaying anti‑hunt signage and delaying vehicles. Several animal‑rights groups and the Niagara Anti‑Racism Coalition wrote letters supporting the hunters, arguing that the selective protest reflects racism. Vandals placed nails on the access road and other acts of harassment were reported; police are investigating.  

The hunt is portrayed by participants as a means of cultural renewal, nutrition improvement and ecological balance: the community has high rates of obesity and diabetes, and research links consumption of lean wild meat to better health outcomes. A York University biologist noted the deer population in Short Hills (about 400 in 2016) far exceeds the park’s carrying capacity of 50, causing damage to ground cover and trees.  

First‑time hunters such as dietitian Deyowidro’t faced verbal abuse, including the term “lady killer,” while others highlighted the lack of hunting opportunities as a barrier to traditional food consumption.

The lecture continues the study of folding a polygon’s boundary onto itself to produce convex polyhedra.  A gluing tree encodes how edges and vertices are identified; each leaf is either a vertex or a “fold point” (an edge glued to itself).  The example of a cross turning into a cube is used to illustrate an Alexandrov gluing (no crossings, total curvature 720°, each vertex of a cube carries 270°).  

The combinatorial problem is to count how many different gluings a given polygon admits.  Three goals are distinguished: decision (is there any folding?), enumeration (list all foldings), and counting (how many?).  For the most general gluing, the number of combinatorial types is bounded above and below by 2^{Θn}.  The edge‑to‑edge case (whole edges glued to whole edges) also admits an exponential bound, but a decision algorithm can be done in polynomial time (O(n³)) by dynamic programming; enumerating all edge‑to‑edge gluings remains exponential because the output itself may be exponential.  Bounded‑sharpness polygons—those whose reflex angles stay at most 360° − γ for a fixed γ>0—yield only a polynomial number of combinatorial gluings and a polynomial‑time enumeration algorithm.  Whether a polynomial‑time decision algorithm exists for unrestricted gluings remains open; the best known algorithm is exponential.

A combinatorial gluing is defined by an abstract gluing tree together with a specification of which polygon vertices or edges appear at each junction (leaves and branching nodes).  The number of such types is 2^{Θn}, using the fact that a tree can have at most n + 4 leaves and therefore only a linear number of nodes.  A lower bound comes from a highly spiky star polygon where many tiny convex angles fit into larger reflex angles, giving 2^{Ωn} distinct gluings even in the edge‑to‑edge setting.

The edge‑to‑edge algorithm uses sub‑problems consisting of an interval of the polygon boundary between two vertices.  For each possible matching edge, the solutions of two smaller sub‑problems are combined (cross‑product) to enumerate all gluings.  The decision version stores only the solution that minimizes the angle glued at the endpoints, yielding a polynomial running time.  For general gluings, additional sub‑problems arise (vertex glued to an edge) and are handled by “zip” and “tug” operations; enumeration stays exponential, but bounded sharpness makes the number of candidates polynomial, giving a polynomial algorithm.

The lecture ends with examples: the Latin cross yields 85 distinct gluings that produce 23 convex polyhedra; triangles and squares exhibit rolling‑belt families of gluings, and implementations of the algorithms have been produced.

The passage describes a convention for halted virtual CPUs in a virtualized environment where a guest must execute HLT with interrupts disabled, and the host re‑enters the guest if any interrupts or non‑maskable events are pending. The #HV doorbell page is configured through VMGEXIT requests (SW_EXITCODE 0x8000_0014) providing REQ, SET, and QUERY actions; the host may clear the RMP assignment of the page and the guest is expected to PVALIDATE the page before handover. Host behavior requires faithful emulation of APIC interrupt presentation: it writes the highest‑priority ready vector into PendingEvent.Vector, sets NoEoiRequired when no further interrupts are pending, and sets NoFurtherSignal for non‑maskable events; it may overwrite a non‑zero vector with a higher‑priority one without sending another #HV. The guest must acknowledge an interrupt by atomically exchanging PendingEvent to zero, and perform an EOI by atomically exchanging NoEoiRequired; if NoEoiRequired was already zero the guest must also write the APIC register. NMIs are dispatched regardless of EFLAGS.IF, and the guest must validate every observed vector. Non‑cooperative hosts or guests can cause denial‑of‑service but do not corrupt the opposite party’s state.

The Rangers’ search to replace manager Bruce Bochy is focused on internal candidate Skip Schumaker, a former NL Manager of the Year. Martin Braithwaite left Middlesbrough in January seeking regular playing time to secure a spot in Denmark’s World Cup squad. Russia's foreign ministry said the U.S. activation of a missile shield in Romania and planned site in Poland breach the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, calling it a gross violation.

LLMs have potential to contribute to social science by generating novel hypotheses or theories, but concerns about originality and validity remain, and effective human‑AI collaboration is needed. Rapid advancement of LLMs creates legal and ethical challenges such as misinformation, deepfakes, and bias, and existing governance frameworks may be insufficient. Balancing innovation with regulation is difficult, and key challenges include a gap between industry and governments, lack of international consensus, and delayed identification of risks (e.g., jailbreaking prompts). Proposed actions include top‑down partnerships among industry, academia, and policymakers, forward‑looking regulations, and bottom‑up reporting by developers and users, supported by transparent handling of issues and social‑computing monitoring. The passage also contains extensive references and acknowledges contributions from Microsoft Research Asia and collaborators.

ASTROCO is a conformer‑style encoder that combines multi‑head self‑attention, depthwise convolutions with gated linear units, and a gated feed‑forward network to model irregular stellar light curves. Magnitudes, uncertainties and sinusoidal time embeddings are concatenated and projected into a d‑dimensional space, then processed through residual‑connected blocks. A masked‑reconstruction pretraining scheme probes 50 % of time steps (≈30 % masked, 10 % replaced, 10 % unchanged). Two model sizes—ASTROCO‑S (5.9 M parameters) and ASTROCO‑L (15.2 M parameters)—both achieve lower reconstruction error and higher macro‑F1 classification scores than Astromer v1/v2 on the MACHO R‑band dataset, with the smaller model surpassing prior work using less training time and hardware. Soft feature mixing across all layers yields compact sequence embeddings.

The team experienced brief lapses that allowed quick goals, but overall played well and created chances, with the opponent’s goalie making saves. Despite losing the first game, they remain confident, viewing the opponent as one of the league’s best defensive teams that requires hard work to score.

The passage outlines defensive strategies for countering the NBA triangle offense, describing both a basic NBA show‑and‑recover approach and a more aggressive SOS (Spread‑Out‑Strong) pressure system. It details four defensive phases: (1) denying the initial pass and the corner cut while X1 and X3 assume pass‑denial positions; (2) defending the post feed, collapsing weakside defenders, and forcing the post player to shoot a rushed jump shot or pass; (3) reacting to a corner screen‑and‑roll, with X5 showing on the roll and X1 fighting over the screen while weakside defenders pack the lane; (4) handling weakside two‑man actions, using “show” and contact switches to congest the three‑second area. The SOS method includes wing‑entry pressure, fronting the post on split actions, rotating to “I” help positions, and forcing the offense into a “free‑lance” situation. The all‑out SOS disruption centers on a first‑pass trap at three‑quarter court, trapping the wing, rotating defenders into “Triangle‑I” positions, executing quick close‑outs, and initiating “Base‑Go‑Red” trap rotations on kick‑out passes. Throughout, specific responsibilities for defenders X1–X5 and required ball‑side and weakside rotations are defined.

Girlfriends' shop is preparing prom accessories for Liberal High School and other schools, including Southwestern Heights, Forgan High School and Hugoton, helping customers choose flowers, ribbons, stones and corsages. The shop has received close to 100 orders, including tux and corsage orders, and began work around March 1 because flower suppliers in Arkansas require lead time. Staff enjoy seeing customers post photos online and urge students to place orders promptly.

NFDI4DS is a German consortium that supports the research data lifecycle for Data Science and AI, emphasizing FAIR principles, transparency and reproducibility. It organises shared tasks at venues such as NSLP, SDP, CLEF, SemEval and ISWC to engage the community and develop tools for a FAIR research data infrastructure. The paper reports twelve shared tasks: seven completed, one ongoing, and four under development.  

Completed tasks:  
- SOMD 2025 – software mention detection from scholarly articles; six teams, best F1 0.89 (Phase I) and 0.63 (Phase II).  
- SciVQA – visual question answering on scientific figures; 20 registrations, seven submissions, highest ROUGE‑L 0.80 and BertScore 0.98.  
- ClimateCheck – linking climate‑related social‑media claims to scholarly abstracts; 27 participants, top Recall@10 0.66 and F1 0.73.  
- FoRC 2025 – field‑of‑research classification of ACL Anthology papers; one team achieved micro‑F1 0.68, macro‑F1 0.66.  
- LLMs4Subjects@SemEval‑2025 – bilingual subject tagging of the TIBKAT catalog using LLMs; 14 teams, synthetic data generation and multilingual design proved beneficial.  
- LLMs4OL‑2024 – ontology learning with term typing, taxonomy induction and relation extraction; 14 teams, hybrid ML/LLM methods outperformed baselines.  
- Scholarly QALD – QA over DBLP and ORKG knowledge graphs; 7 teams in 2023, 3 teams in 2024, evaluated with F1, Exact Match and METEOR.  

Ongoing task: CheckThat!Lab Task 4 – scientific web discourse detection and claim‑source retrieval, using SciTweets (≈500–1000 tweets) and CORD‑19 tweet‑study pairs (≈15 967), evaluated by macro‑F1 and MRR@5.  

Under development: (i) ML‑model and dataset mention detection using GSAP‑NER corpora; (ii) ReadMe2KG – NER and entity linking on GitHub README files; (iii) CURED – clinical prognosis with calibrated uncertainty estimates, planned for 2026; (iv) Algorithm2Domain – meta‑benchmarking platform for algorithm generalisability and domain adaptation.  

Together these tasks illustrate community‑driven competitions that advance methodological progress and support the NFDI goal of sustainable, interoperable research data practices.

The A100 GPU architecture delivers 2.5× FP64 performance of V100 using third‑generation Tensor Cores that support IEEE‑compliant FP64 and mixed‑precision modes (TF32, FP16, BF16). Mixed‑precision Tensor Core acceleration is exemplified by the cuSOLVER TCAIRS solver, which achieves geomean speedups of 2.0× over FP64 with TF32 and up to 4× for large matrices, while maintaining convergence comparable to FP64. Fine‑grained 2:4 structured sparsity doubles Tensor Core throughput by pruning trained weights and skipping zero computations. Memory hierarchy improvements include a combined L1/shared memory of 192 KB/SM, 40 GB HBM2 DRAM at 1555 GB/s, a 40 MB L2 cache (2.3× the bandwidth of V100) with data‑compression that yields up to 4× DRAM bandwidth gains, and ECC protection on HBM2, L2 and SM registers. Simultaneous FP32 and INT32 execution and an asynchronous copy instruction reduce register‑file traffic and improve data‑movement efficiency.

Third‑generation NVLink provides 600 GB/s bidirectional bandwidth (12 links, 50 Gbit/s per lane) and improved error‑detection/recovery; PCIe Gen 4 with SR‑IOV doubles PCIe bandwidth and enables virtualization. Multi‑Instance GPU (MIG) can partition a single A100 into up to seven isolated GPU Instances, each with dedicated GPCs, L2 slices, memory controllers and QoS, supporting multi‑tenant and single‑tenant workloads while preserving CUDA programming semantics. MIG migration allows vGPUs to move between instances for load‑balancing and servicing.

CUDA 11 adds asynchronous copy, hardware‑accelerated shared‑memory barriers, L2 cache residency controls (persisting/streaming data), task‑graph acceleration for reduced launch latency, cooperative groups with hardware‑accelerated warp reductions, and support for the new Tensor Core formats and sparsity features. The DGX A100 system integrates eight A100 GPUs via NVSwitch, delivering 5 PFLOPS of AI performance, up to 6× faster than V100‑based DGX‑1, and scales to thousands of nodes with Magnum IO SDK; its NGC Private Registry supplies GPU‑optimized containers for deep learning, inference, analytics and HPC. Fine‑grained structured sparsity with a 2:4 pattern yields virtually no accuracy loss across vision, detection, segmentation and language tasks, enabling efficient inference acceleration.

This passage reviews a longitudinal study (2015–2025) analyzing the global ranking performance (Times Higher Education World University Rankings) of the top five higher education institutions (HEIs) from ten Asian countries: Bangladesh, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Pakistan, Philippines, Russia, Thailand, and Vietnam. Chinese universities (e.g., Tsinghua, Peking, Fudan, Zhejiang, Shanghai Jiao Tong) showed consistent improvement, with Tsinghua rising from 49th to 12th and Peking from 48th to 13th by 2025. Japanese universities (e.g., University of Tokyo, Kyoto) maintained top 100 positions with stability, while other Japanese HEIs experienced fluctuations but remained competitive. Russian universities (e.g., Lomonosov Moscow State) consistently ranked in the top 200. Indian universities generally improved, with the Indian Institute of Science ranked between 201–250 in 2025, though other Indian HEIs ranked lower. Indonesian, Pakistani, Philippine, Thai, Bangladeshi, and Vietnamese HEIs generally lagged behind global counterparts or showed declining trends, often ranking below 800 globally, with some entering rankings only recently. The study concludes that most Asian HEIs are behind American/European institutions except in China, Japan, and Russia, and recommends policies such as increasing internationalization, funding, and global marketing to enhance rankings.

The lecture continues the analysis of the heavy‑to‑light current $b\to s\gamma$ in soft‑collinear effective theory. The current is split into a part that reproduces the QCD infrared structure, ultraviolet divergences removed by counterterms, and a remainder that defines the matching. The counterterm contains a $1/\epsilon^{2}$ pole and a logarithmic term; the label $\omega$ in the operator equals $m_{b}$ by kinematics. Writing the renormalized Wilson coefficient as the product of a bare coefficient and a counterterm leads to the renormalization‑group equation $\mu d/d\mu\log C=\gamma$. At one loop the anomalous dimension splits into a regular part (e.g. $5C_{F}$) and a cusp part that multiplies $\log\mu/\omega$. The cusp anomalous dimension generates the leading‑log series; solving the homogeneous RG equation with a tree‑level boundary condition $C=1$ at $\mu_{0}\sim\omega$ yields a Sudakov exponential $\propto\exp[-(\alpha C_{F}/\pi)\log^{2}(\mu/\omega)]$ for fixed coupling (QED) or, with a running coupling, a ratio of $\alpha(\mu)/\alpha(\omega)$ raised to a power, summing logs of $\alpha$ and $\log$. The cusp originates from the kink (cusp) in the Wilson line that combines the static‑source line with the collinear Wilson line; the associated renormalization theory yields a single‑log term in the anomalous dimension to all orders.

The lecture then addresses when the $\omega$ parameters of Wilson coefficients are fixed by external kinematics: if each collinear sector contributes only one building block, external momentum conservation fixes all $\omega$’s, leading to a product form of the coefficient without convolution. When two building blocks belong to the same collinear direction, one linear combination of $\omega$’s remains fixed while the other does not, introducing an integral in the anomalous‑dimension equation; this reproduces evolution equations such as the DGLAP equation for parton distribution functions.

As an example, the operator for deep inelastic scattering is introduced: two quark fields (or gluon fields) in distinct collinear sectors, with a Wilson coefficient depending on the large momentum fractions $\omega_{i}$. In the Breit frame the incoming proton is collinear and the hard virtual photon provides the hard scale; the hadronic tensor can be expressed via the forward matrix element of this operator. The forward kinematics enforce $\omega_{1}=\omega_{2}$, leaving the sum of the $\omega$’s unconstrained and representing the parton momentum fraction; the resulting operator is essentially a momentum‑space number operator for quarks dressed by Wilson lines—i.e. the parton distribution function. The next lecture will combine this operator with the Wilson coefficient to obtain a factorization theorem for DIS and discuss its renormalization‑group evolution (the DGLAP equation).

The passage discusses patterns for distributed systems and container-based architectures. It emphasizes that patterns allow developers to learn from others' mistakes, provide shared vocabulary for discussion, and enable reusable components. The book introduces three single-node container patterns: sidecars, which augment existing applications without modifying them; ambassadors, which broker interactions between application containers and external services; and adapters, which modify application interfaces to conform to standardized expectations. These patterns support modularity, reusability, and separation of concerns. The passage also covers multi-node distributed patterns including replicated load-balanced services, session-tracked services, sharded services, and caching layers, ultimately presenting a complete architecture for stateless replicated serving with caching and SSL termination layers.

The study involved 75 secondary‑school students (ages 11–12) assigned to an experimental group (four hours of PE per week) and a control group (two hours). Attention was assessed with the Bells Test before (October) and after (December) a period of structured PE that included cognitively demanding activities. Experimental class 6 showed a significant improvement in 30‑second speed (p < 0.001) and in 120‑second sustained attention (p = 0.012); experimental class 7 improved only in 30‑second speed (p < 0.001). Control groups in both classes displayed no significant changes. The results indicate that increasing PE time, particularly when combined with cognitively engaging tasks, can enhance short‑term attention and may modestly improve sustained attention in early adolescents.

The UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has designated Google Search with Strategic Market Status (SMS), making it the first company targeted under the new Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act. The designation recognizes Google's substantial market power, holding over 90% of UK general search queries. The CMA proposes measures including offering users choice of rival search engines, fair ranking principles, and increased data portability. The CMA may also require Google to seek permission to use publishers' content in AI Overviews. Over 200,000 UK firms spent more than £10 billion on Google search advertising in 2024. Google responded that these interventions could inhibit innovation and harm businesses. The new regulation affects Google Search's News tab, Top Stories carousel, and Google Discover, but not Google News or Gemini.

Method for configuring hardware for a Deep Neural Network (DNN) activation module using a programmable lookup table (LUT) comprises: providing calibration data to a representation of the hardware; monitoring inputs to the activation module to determine the actual range of input values the module will receive; generating lookup data that approximates the activation function over the determined range; and loading the generated lookup data into the LUT of the hardware. The LUT stores either gradient/offset pairs or discrete output values; interpolation (linear or quadratic) using the most significant bits of the input address and the remaining bits yields the activation output. Input values outside the determined range are clamped to the function value at the nearest bound or extrapolated by a line. The activation module may also include a simple Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) path to reduce power when ReLU is required. The range of inputs is derived from statistics such as max/min values or a histogram covering a programmable proportion of the distribution. The method supports multiple activation functions, switching between two LUT data sets while performing a series of functions, and can be applied after optimisation of the DNN. The hardware may be embodied in an integrated circuit and manufactured using an integrated circuit manufacturing system.

Rockwood School District in Missouri maintains mixed‑ability whole‑class reading instruction and supplements it with flexible, needs‑based small groups. All students receive daily grade‑level phonics and comprehension lessons, after which they move into groups that provide reteaching, enrichment or targeted interventions based on real‑time data. Instruction incorporates movement strategies (gestures, tapping, jumping) to support engagement. The district uses evidence‑based Tier I curricula and does not lock students into static tiers. At the end of the 2024‑25 school year, kindergarten students exceeded national proficiency averages in every skill group, in some cases by more than 17 percentage points; first‑ and second‑grade students also outpaced national averages across nearly every domain. Research cited in the article notes that students placed in the lowest reading groups rarely catch up, and that lower‑track students receive less complex vocabulary and fewer comprehension strategies, reinforcing persistent gaps. Rockwood’s data show growth in skill, confidence, stamina and joy among its readers.

A study of 198 honey samples found 75% contained neonicotinoid pesticides; 45% had two or more compounds and 10% had four or five. Pollinator harm rises; North America (86%), Asia (80%) and Europe (79%) had highest detection.

China announced it will close its domestic ivory market by the end of 2017 to address the decline of African elephants, which has worsened despite a 1989 international ban due to a loophole allowing trade in pre-ban ivory. Conservation experts say this closure, the world's largest legal ivory market, is essential to reducing poaching and could be a pivotal turning point for the species. China plans to retrain artisans and educate the public, while the U.S. has already restricted trade, potentially influencing other countries like Vietnam, the UK, and Japan to follow suit.

Platinum futures are standardized contracts traded on the CME Globex platform for physical delivery of 50 troy ounces of platinum at a predetermined price on a future date. They are used for speculation, portfolio diversification, and hedging. A platinum futures strategy involves technical and fundamental analysis, precise entry and exit signals, and backtesting to achieve optimal market timing and risk management.

Two backtested strategies are presented. The first trades long and short with parameters including a monthly edge, yielding 473 trades with a 64% win rate and 1.7 profit factor. The second is a seasonal strategy trading on a specific day with a volume requirement, yielding 60 trades with a 75% win rate and 2.3 profit factor. Both strategies show uncorrelated returns to the stock market.

Platinum prices are influenced by supply and demand, political and economic conditions, production costs, and automotive and jewelry market demand. Platinum is rarer than gold and more volatile, with an all-time high of $2,308.80 in March 2008 and an all-time low of $267.10 in July 1985. South Africa supplies about 80% of global platinum.

Trading occurs Sunday 5:00 p.m. to Friday 4:00 p.m. CT with a one-hour halt daily. Contract specifications: 50 troy ounces per contract, minimum fluctuation $0.10 per ounce ($5.00 per contract), settled by physical delivery, trading terminates on the third last business day of the contract month.

Risks include leverage amplifying losses; for example, a 1% adverse price move with 20x leverage results in a 20% account loss. Benefits of trading platinum futures include portfolio diversification, uncorrelated returns, and inflation protection. Compared to gold, platinum is more industrial, while gold is a better long-term store of value.

To start trading, one must open an account with a futures broker, fund it, and develop a plan based on backtests. Strategies should have positive statistical expectancy and low correlation to existing portfolios. ETFs and CFDs related to platinum are also available. Regular strategy review is recommended only when there is a rational reason, not based on short-term noise.

High‑dosage tutoring improves academic outcomes and also cultivates belonging and confidence. Teach For America’s Ignite Fellowship reached over 40 communities, trained more than 5,500 virtual tutors and delivered nearly 200,000 hours of customized learning, producing test‑score gains up to 2.5 times the expected rate for middle‑school math and up to three times the average for elementary readers. Research shows that tutoring nearly triples the likelihood participants will apply to a teacher‑training program, with the strongest effects among men, people of color, and non‑education majors. Since the program launched, 550 fellows have joined Teach For America’s teaching corps, and this year alone 280 new teachers entered classrooms after being inspired by their tutoring experience. Effective tutoring requires structured training, ongoing support and strategic use of technology to expand relationships, not replace them; one Los Angeles school saw a 77‑point math score jump after a year of virtual Ignite tutoring. The evidence indicates tutoring can serve as a long‑term teacher‑pipeline strategy and should be integrated into the future of schooling rather than treated only as short‑term remediation.

President returns House Bill No. 7864, an amendment to U.S. immigration law that would exclude all physically capable persons over 16 who cannot read and write English or another language, while allowing limited exceptions for certain elderly relatives, spouses, and minor children of qualified immigrants. The message argues the bill represents a radical departure from the historic open‑door policy that only barred individuals on moral or physical grounds, and contends that a literacy test is an unreliable gauge of desirable citizenship, noting that educated agitators pose greater danger than illiterate workers. It also critiques the family‑reunion provisions as vague, excluding siblings and imposing indefinite support requirements. Sections four and five would ban certain male aliens who have not declared intent to become citizens from public‑works employment and from regularly entering the country for manual labor, making such entry and employment crimes. The President warns that these restrictions would harm cross‑border labor relations with Canada, are illiberal and vague, and concludes the bill is unnecessarily harsh and would cause harm to U.S. citizens.

The passage introduces GeoSQL-Eval, the first end-to-end automated evaluation framework for assessing large language models' performance in generating PostGIS GeoSQL queries. The framework addresses the absence of standardized benchmarks for spatial database query generation tasks. It is built upon four cognitive dimensions (Conceptual Understanding, Structured SQL Generation, Semantic Alignment & Invocation, Execution & Result Accuracy, and Robust Generalization & Reasoning) and five progressive capability levels. GeoSQL-Bench, the accompanying benchmark dataset, contains 14,178 tasks across three categories: Multiple Choice & True/False questions (2,380), Syntax-level SQL Generation questions (7,488), and Table Schema Retrieval questions (4,310). Tasks were constructed using PostGIS 3.5 official documentation and UN-GGIM/ISO 19115 standards, employing a Self-Instruct approach with GPT-4o followed by expert review. The study evaluated 24 models across six categories using the framework, finding that general reasoning-enhanced models performed best, with GPT-5, o4-mini, and DeepSeek-R1-0528 ranking highest. Key challenges identified include function and parameter matching errors (approximately 70% of errors), semantic alignment weaknesses, and significant performance degradation on table schema retrieval tasks. The framework and leaderboard are publicly released.

Informal discussions at Dumbarton Oaks on October 7, 1944, involved the US, Great Britain, and China regarding the League of Nations' dissolution and transition to the United Nations. The US, not being a League member, preferred to await initiative from other governments. In December 1944, the League's Supervisory Committee met in London and appointed a three-person committee to select a Conciliation Committee for handling dissolution-related matters. The US was requested to appoint an expert to consult with the Committee but made no commitment. A further Supervisory Committee meeting was scheduled for January 19, 1945, to discuss general liquidation and preparatory work. It was recommended that the US take no initiative in the League's liquidation, leaving the matter for the United Nations Conference unless initiated by the UK or China. A separate informal meeting on January 31, 1945, involved diplomatic representatives of American republics discussing the Dumbarton Oaks Proposals.

Kyle Busch became the second driver after Kevin Harvick to win three races in the NASCAR Cup regular season, securing a playoff spot unless more than 16 drivers win. He hopes he isn’t peaking early, crediting success to short‑track skills and experience running Kyle Busch Motorsports in racing. After a start at Daytona, he has been strong, but expects a fourth win at Talladega to be difficult due to restrictor‑plate racing’s randomness.

New software patches improve biosecurity screening's ability to detect AI-designed toxic proteins that could slip past security filters. Researchers generated roughly 76,000 blueprints for 72 harmful proteins to test screening weaknesses. While original protein forms were mostly flagged, many AI-adjusted versions evaded detection. Software patches improved detection even for fragmented genes, though about 3% of variants still slipped through. The work was computational only, and actual attempts to produce malicious proteins remain extremely rare.

After Hurricane Katrina devastated New Orleans in 2005, the Lower Ninth Ward remains scarred by abandoned homes and gentrification that has hindered many former residents from returning. The city has responded with evacuation centres, raised homes, solar panels, rain‑garden programmes and raised planting beds to address contaminated soil. Architects Waggonner & Ball have led the Greater New Orleans Urban Water Plan, funded by the Louisiana Office of Community Development, which seeks to manage heavy‑rainfall runoff and ground subsidence by creating “blue‑ways” and “green‑ways”, including the 25‑acre Mirabeau Water Garden in the Gentilly district. Louisiana’s Coastal Master Plan, approved in 2017 by the Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority, outlines $50 billion of projects to rebuild barrier islands and wetlands, redirect Mississippi River sediment, construct levees and flood gates, raise houses and, where needed, purchase property for relocation; a local sales tax helps fund levee work. Research indicates that oil‑ and gas‑extraction induced subsidence is a major driver of land loss, and that about 20–30 percent of U.S. oil infrastructure lies in the Gulf of Mexico. Scientists project U.S. sea‑level rise averaging roughly 1 cm per year by 2050, warning of globally disruptive impacts. Local residents such as Otis Tucker emphasise that all stakeholders must collaborate to adapt to rising waters.

The cup and handle is a bullish continuation chart pattern resembling a tea cup with a handle. It consists of a rounded “U‑shaped” cup that forms after a price rally, followed by a short, slightly downward‑sloping trading range (the handle) on the right side of the cup. The pattern completes when price breaks out above the handle’s resistance, signaling a continuation of the prior uptrend.

Key criteria for the pattern include: occurrence within an existing uptrend, a cup depth of roughly 30–50 % retracement, a handle that does not retrace more than half the cup’s depth, and a breakout with a volume increase. The cup represents a period of consolidation and accumulation, while the handle reflects a brief pull‑back or shake‑out of weaker holders before the next advance.

Psychologically, the pattern reflects shifting investor sentiment from initial pessimism (price decline) to renewed optimism (recovery), with the handle testing conviction before a breakout. Market volatility influences how clearly the pattern forms; low‑to‑moderate volatility yields a more reliable signal, whereas high volatility can distort the cup and handle, increasing false breakouts.

Traders typically set stop‑loss orders just below the handle’s low or the cup’s bottom, wait for the handle to fully develop and for a breakout above resistance, and may confirm entry with other indicators such as moving averages or RSI. Common mistakes include entering before the pattern is confirmed, ignoring volume behavior, mis‑setting profit targets or stop‑loss levels, neglecting broader market conditions, and relying exclusively on the pattern without additional analysis.

Backtesting results show mixed performance. A 2016–2018 test on S&P 500 stocks found the strategy underperformed the index. Thomas Bulkowski’s manual study of 500 stocks over five years reported a 26 % overall failure rate, dropping to about 10 % if traders wait for an upside breakout, and an average gain of 38 %. William O’Neil’s CANSLIM method includes a cup‑and‑handle requirement but also incorporates many other criteria, so profitability cannot be attributed solely to the pattern.

The pattern can appear on various timeframes (daily, weekly, monthly) and across different markets (stocks, forex, commodities). Volume typically declines during cup formation, rises during recovery, and spikes on breakout, confirming strength. While the pattern can provide insight into potential long‑term bullish trends, its predictive reliability varies with market conditions and should be used alongside fundamental and other technical analysis.

The lecture discusses the induced graph removal lemma, which strengthens the standard graph removal lemma by considering induced copies of a graph H rather than regular copies. The induced version allows vertex deletion only, while the standard version allows edge deletion. The challenge in proving the induced version lies in handling irregular vertex pairs during the regularity lemma application, as the previous strategy of removing irregular pairs fails when edges can be both added and deleted.

The solution involves the strong regularity lemma, which produces a pair of vertex partitions (P, Q) where Q refines P and is extremely regular. This lemma uses a sequence of decreasing epsilon parameters to achieve stronger regularity guarantees than the standard lemma. The proof repeatedly applies Szemerédi's regularity lemma to generate progressively finer partitions until energy increments become sufficiently small.

A corollary of the strong regularity lemma provides an equitable partition where subsets Wi within each part Vi are mutually regular with no irregular pairs. This eliminates the problematic irregular pairs from the induced removal lemma proof.

The proof of the induced graph removal lemma proceeds in three steps: partition using the corollary to obtain regular subsets, clean by adding or removing edges between pairs with density deviations, and count using a counting lemma to show that any remaining induced H would imply many original induced copies, contradicting the hypothesis.

The lecture also mentions the infinite removal lemma extending the result to infinitely many patterns and discusses property testing applications, where the removal lemma implies that all hereditary graph properties (closed under vertex deletion) are testable via simple randomized algorithms sampling vertex triples.

Professor Markus discusses a self‑energy correction in higher‑order perturbation theory. The loop integral, after integrating over angular variables, reduces to ∫ q³ / q⁴ dq = ∫ dq/q, which diverges logarithmically at infinite momentum. An infinite result would make cross sections, lifetimes, etc., ill‑defined, stalling early progress of the theory. The problem is mitigated by introducing a momentum cutoff, evaluating the integral up to a scale m and separating the remaining infinite piece. Renormalization absorbs the divergent correction into the bare mass and coupling, yielding finite physical predictions that respect Lorentz invariance. These physical masses and couplings are defined at a chosen scale and run logarithmically with energy for electromagnetic, weak and strong interactions. Adding new particles at higher scales can alter the running and potentially unify the three couplings at a single high scale—an idea for new physics. Experiments are performed at specific scales, so the divergence at arbitrarily high energies does not obstruct comparison with data.

The passage explains two investing approaches: dollar‑cost averaging (DCA) and lump‑sum buy‑and‑hold. DCA invests a fixed amount at regular intervals, buying more shares when prices are low and fewer when high, smoothing volatility, avoiding market timing, and reducing frustration after a purchase. It notes that women more often use DCA and historically obtain better returns. Lump‑sum investing deploys the entire capital at once, aiming to capture market growth early and give money more time to compound; historically it has a higher probability of long‑term success, especially over ten‑year horizons. The article backtests a lump‑sum buy‑and‑hold portfolio of five equally‑weighted, liquid, long‑history ETFs over before‑crisis, at‑bottom‑of‑crisis and after‑crisis periods, presenting equity curves, drawdowns, monthly and annual returns and performance statistics. Results indicate that investing earlier and staying fully invested yields higher profit and that a financial crisis becomes insignificant over a long investment horizon.

NeoWorld is a deep learning framework for interactive world generation from a single image. It uses a hybrid object-centric approach combining lightweight 2.5D Gaussian layers for backgrounds with full 3D reconstruction for foreground objects, progressively unfolding based on user interaction or camera motion. The system integrates panoptic segmentation for instance-level understanding, image-to-3D reconstruction for object completion, and LLM-based user interaction for object manipulation and animation. NeoWorld outperforms prior 2D and 2.5D methods in 3D consistency and user engagement while maintaining computational efficiency, though it has limitations including alignment failures, LLM misinterpretation, reconstruction errors under occlusion, and segmentation issues that can propagate through the pipeline.

The ADS9803 is an eight‑channel, 20‑bit, 2 MSPS ADC with an integrated analog front‑end. Each analog input has an internal clamp protection circuit that allows ±18 V swing and can be current‑limited with an external series resistor, which also forms an antialiasing low‑pass filter. A programmable gain amplifier (PGA) on every channel supports single‑ended and differential inputs with configurable input ranges and selectable low‑pass filter bandwidths. The device provides wide common‑mode voltage rejection up to ±12 V, with mode settings optimized for differential or single‑ended operation. ADC output is 20 bits in straight‑binary or two’s‑complement format; data can be transmitted over a 2‑lane or 4‑lane source‑synchronous interface using single‑ or double‑data‑rate clocks. Built‑in features include a data randomizer, simple and moving‑average modes, digital test patterns (fixed, ramp, alternating), and a speed‑boost mode that samples a single channel pair at up to 8 MSPS. Configuration is performed through a 3‑bank SPI register map with support for daisy‑chain operation of multiple devices. Power is supplied from three rails (AVDD_5V, VDD_1V8, IOVDD) and no specific power‑up sequence is required. The device includes an internal voltage reference with optional external reference, and recommends specific decoupling and layout practices for optimal performance.

Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, caused approximately 10 million illnesses and 1.4 million deaths in 2019, rising to 1.6 million deaths in 2021. The COVID-19 pandemic has reduced TB diagnoses and treatment access. The standard treatment for drug-sensitive TB uses four first-line drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) over six months. Extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) accounts for about 16% of notified cases, with lymph node and pleural TB being most common. This study develops a whole-body physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model to predict drug concentrations at EPTB sites. It is the first PBPK model to include pleural and lymph node compartments and simulate all four first-line drugs. The model was calibrated and validated using plasma and lung tissue concentration data. Results show that rifampicin and isoniazid generally reach effective concentrations at EPTB sites, while ethambutol and pyrazinamide often fail to achieve critical concentrations in certain organs. Limitations include assumptions about a consolidated lymph node compartment and lack of drug-drug interaction modeling. The model can help evaluate and optimize EPTB treatment regimens.

The K‑T collaborative EVT registry merged the South Korean CRCS‑K and the Taiwanese TREAT‑AIS registries, harmonizing 9,941 EVT‑treated patients with roughly 200 common data fields. The Taiwanese cohort was older, had a higher prevalence of vascular risk factors, more severe strokes (higher median NIHSS), and lower 90‑day functional independence (34.7% vs 41.1%); 90‑day mortality was higher in the Korean cohort (14.2% vs 6.2%). Multivariable analysis showed that age was a strong independent predictor of functional recovery and mortality but not of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage; patients ≥80 years had lower favorable outcomes and higher mortality yet still achieved benefit if pre‑stroke independent or treated with bridging thrombolysis. The study’s strengths include its large, multinational, prospective design, while limitations involve differences in data collection, varying inclusion periods, and lack of detailed imaging data. The authors conclude that harmonizing stroke registries can improve care, that advanced age alone should not exclude patients from EVT, and that future collaborative work should refine EVT techniques and address regional variations.

The lecture discusses constructing Probabilistically Checkable Proofs (PCPs) from the GKR protocol. PCPs are proofs where a verifier queries a small number of random locations to check validity, with parameters for completeness, soundness, randomness, and query complexity. For any NP language (e.g., 3SAT), a PCP can be constructed with polylogarithmic randomness and query complexity, completeness 1, and soundness 1/2. The construction uses low-degree extensions of circuit layers and all possible transcripts of sumcheck protocols from GKR, unraveled into a non-interactive proof. The verifier simulates the GKR verifier using the oracle. Soundness relies on the union bound over 2d sumchecks, requiring parameter engineering to keep the proof polynomial in size. The lecture also transitions to discussing computational soundness (arguments) in cryptography.

Portable retinal fundus cameras are emerging as cost‑effective screening tools in low‑ and middle‑income countries (LMICs). This study examined the effect of pharmacological pupil dilation (mydriasis) on image gradability and on the performance of an AI model for diabetic retinopathy (DR) detection. Patients (n = 327, mean age 57.0 years, 45.3 % male) underwent retinal imaging before and after mydriasis with Tropicamide 0.5 % using the Phelcom Eyer portable camera. Two masked ophthalmologists labeled lesions; a third adjudicated disagreements. Images were considered gradable if ≥ 2⁄3 of the retina was visible and the third‑order vessels were assessable. A convolutional neural network (ResNet‑200d) pretrained on ImageNet and trained on the mBRSET dataset (1,291 patients, 5,164 images) was validated on 597 paired images. Mydriasis produced 82.1 % gradable images versus 55.6 % for non‑mydriasis (P < 0.001). In non‑mydriatic images, systemic hypertension, older age, longer diabetes duration, male sex, and Indigenous ethnicity were associated with reduced gradability (P < 0.05). The AI model achieved 82.91 % accuracy, 0.83 F1 and 0.94 AUC in the mydriatic group versus 79.23 % accuracy, 0.79 F1 and 0.93 AUC in the non‑mydriatic group; false‑positive rate was lower with mydriasis (13.9 % vs 17.8 %). No statistically significant difference between groups was observed by chi‑square testing (P = 0.3279). Limitations include the use of a single camera, a learning curve for handheld imaging, and selection bias from focusing on paired images. The findings indicate that mydriasis improves image quality and enhances AI diagnostic performance, potentially reducing unnecessary referrals in resource‑limited settings.

Image registration aligns a moving image M to a fixed image F by finding a coordinate transform φ that minimizes a cost C(F, M∘φ) plus a regularizer R(φ). Modern pipelines combine affine and deformable transforms, using displacement fields of size dN per voxel. Existing methods reliably handle only macroscopic‑scale problems (≈50 M warp parameters) and run out of memory on higher‑resolution images, which can require up to 11 B parameters.

This paper introduces Flash Fused Distributed Primitives (FFDP), a framework that scales registration to arbitrarily large problems on a single GPU and across multiple GPUs. It first identifies three primary memory bottlenecks—grid sampling (deformable interpolation and warp composition), Local Normalized Cross‑Correlation (LNCC), and Mutual Information (MI)—and proposes fused CUDA kernels that replace O(N) high‑bandwidth‑memory (HBM) overhead with O(1) by keeping per‑pixel intermediates in registers or shared memory. These kernels enable fitting problems up to 64× larger on a single A6000 GPU.

To extend beyond a single device, FFDP adds a distributed layer: Grid Parallel shards the fixed image, warp field, and optimizer state across H GPUs while synchronizing boundary data for convolutional losses; the Distributed Ring Sampler interpolates the moving image from sharded shards without an all‑gather, incurring only N/H extra HBM. Loss functions (MSE, LNCC, MI) are computed locally and aggregated with all‑reduce operations, adding only B² + 2B communication overhead for MI.

FFDP accelerates existing registration pipelines by up to 7.48× while cutting HBM usage by ≈59 % for traditional methods, and by 6.14× with ≈24 % memory reduction for deep‑learning pipelines. On a multimodal task aligning a 250 µm in‑vivo MRI to a 100 µm ex‑vivo FLASH brain volume (≈11.8 B parameters), FFDP completes registration in ≈1 minute on 8 NVIDIA A6000 GPUs, outperforming state‑of‑the‑art baselines in accuracy and efficiency.

The passage documents multiple hardware issues and corresponding resolutions for the AMD Geode CS5535 Companion Device. Key issues include SSMI synchronization failures when interrupts occur simultaneously, UDMA bus master failures when enabled before PIO commands, ACPI S3 wake events on GPIO[27:24] not working, RTC CMOS RAM access errors when writing extended then reading legacy ports, block and demand mode DMA blocking LPC I/O, USB controller clock gating causing register read failures, ATAPI packet command failures with specific CD-ROM firmware, AuxOutputFull bit in KEL being incorrectly cleared on Port 60h reads, tACK bits not affecting UDMA timing, ATAC hanging with non-DWORD aligned PRD addresses, LPC aborts on short sync patterns, SMB controller NEGACK bit behavior issues, GLPCI retry counter counting all PCI retries, atomic writes to GPIO High Bank registers clearing non-selected bits after suspend, SMBus hold time being shorter than specified, missing LOWBAT_FLAG after abnormal standby, and Sleep_X not deasserting if delays exceed PM_SED delay. Resolutions involve using the Geode GX processor for SSMI, following proper UDMA procedures, using PWRBTN# for S3 wake, using single transfer mode DMA, disabling USB clock gating, using interrupts for USB keyboard/mouse, using DWORD alignment for ATAC PRD, implementing PLD workarounds for LPC sync, writing twice to SMB_STS for NEGACK, setting GLPCI retry limit to 0, using Read-Modify-Write for GPIO registers post-suspend, and ensuring delay counters are less than PM_SED delay.

Ulysses S. Gandy appealed his second manslaughter conviction to the Supreme Court of Mississippi. On June 26, 1976, Gandy was involved in a two-car collision that killed three people. The collision occurred on a straight stretch of Highway 25 near Starkville, with conflicting testimony about the vehicles' positions and Gandy's intoxication level. Gandy claimed he was in his proper lane while the Toyota crossed into his lane. The jury heard evidence of intoxication from nine witnesses, including officers who detected strong alcohol odors. Medical testimony regarding intoxication was disputed. Gandy's assignments of error included claims that the verdict was against the overwhelming weight of the evidence, improper jury instructions, and the admission of demonstrative sketches. The court affirmed the conviction, finding sufficient evidence that Gandy drove intoxicated into oncoming traffic and that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in its rulings.

The study developed a meta-population model linking Google Community Mobility Reports (GCMR) to SARS-CoV-2 transmission dynamics in Norwegian, Swedish, and German regions. GCMR data in four settings (workplaces, transit stations, retail/recreation, grocery/pharmacy) were modeled additively to transmissibility, while temperature and virus variants had multiplicative effects. Approximately 60% of Swedish and 39% of Norwegian infections were attributed to settings captured by the GCMRs, with transit stations and workplaces contributing most in those countries, while retail/recreation dominated in Germany. A 20°C temperature increase reduced transmissibility by about 40%, and the Delta variant roughly doubled transmissibility compared to wildtype. The model demonstrates GCMR data can inform real-time epidemic assessment but requires complex modeling due to data structure.
