A cross-sectional study was conducted in Denan district, southeastern Ethiopia, to assess the sero-prevalence, knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding visceral leishmaniasis (VL) and sand fly vector abundance. VL is a vector-borne parasitic disease caused by Leishmania donovani and transmitted by sand flies, endemic in 75 countries with the highest burden in Eastern Africa, Southeast Asia, and Brazil. Ethiopia has the third highest VL cases in sub-Saharan Africa. A total of 187 participants from six kebeles were enrolled. The overall sero-prevalence was 9.63%, with significantly higher rates in the 19-36 age group. Risk factors associated with VL infection included houses with damp floors, outdoor sleeping, and sleeping near animal shelters. Regarding knowledge, 53.48% had heard about VL, and only 42% knew sand fly bites transmit the disease. Most respondents (89%) recognized at least one clinical symptom, but only 36% believed VL is preventable and 44% knew it can be fatal if untreated. Entomological surveys collected 823 sand flies representing 12 species, with P. orientalis being the dominant Phlebotomus species (43.9%) and S. clydie the most abundant Sergentomyia species. P. orientalis was found primarily in outdoor habitats (termite mounds and forests) with no indoor specimens collected. The study concluded that VL sero-prevalence is relatively high in this new focus, with poor community knowledge and unfavorable attitudes requiring increased awareness campaigns. P. orientalis likely contributes to VL transmission, necessitating further epidemiological and vector biology studies.

Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) are evaluated for their ability to learn transitive relations by training them on the graph connectivity task. Connectivity is defined as whether a directed path exists between two nodes, and the task is shown equivalent to inferring transitive relations, deductive reasoning, and path‑finding. A grid graph is defined as a graph whose nodes can be embedded in ℝ^k so that a path exists between u and v iff every component of Ψ(v)−Ψ(u) is non‑negative. Disconnected chain graphs consist of multiple linear components and are not easily represented by such a low‑dimensional embedding.

The study addresses three research questions: (1) how well transformers learn connectivity on grid and chain graphs, (2) how model size and graph size scaling affect performance, and (3) how grid dimensionality and number of chains influence learning. Experiments use synthetic directed graphs where each training example is a pair of node tokens labeled “Y” (connected) or “N” (disconnected). Model size is varied by changing the token embedding dimension from 32 to 1024, and graph size by varying the number of nodes from 50 to 800. Grid graphs are generated with dimensions k = 1,…,5, and chain graphs with 1, 5, 10, 15, 20 disconnected components. Performance is measured in terms of training and test loss/accuracy versus training compute (FLOPs).

Key results: Transformers achieve near‑perfect test accuracy on low‑dimensional grid graphs, and test loss decreases as model size increases. For disconnected chain graphs, test loss diverges and scaling model size does not improve accuracy. Scaling graph size keeps performance stable for grid graphs and substantially improves accuracy for chain graphs when the number of nodes per chain grows. Higher grid dimensionality reduces accuracy, but increasing the number of nodes in higher‑dimensional grids helps more than increasing model size. For chain graphs, a small number of chains yields high accuracy; accuracy drops as the number of chains rises, yet scaling graph size (increasing chain length) recovers performance, whereas model scaling does not.

Overall, model scaling benefits grid‑graph connectivity more than chain‑graph connectivity, while data (graph) scaling benefits both but especially chain graphs with many components. Data scaling is more effective than model scaling for learning connectivity in higher‑dimensional grids or in graphs with many disconnected components.
Hawkin's Bazaar, Plymouth gift and gadget shop, will close Feb 4 with sale up to 75% off. It operated for four years after six years at the West End. The Herald requested comment but got no response.

Cincinnati beat No. 14 Iowa State, ending the Cyclones' perfect record. The Bearcats built a 31‑7 lead and held on for an eight‑point win. Cincinnati QB Pryor ran for 111 yards and two TDs; Iowa State QB Rocco Becht passed for 314 yards with two touchdown passes and two rushing scores. The win was Cincinnati's first home victory over a ranked opponent since 2021. Other news includes an Oklahoma WR carted off after hitting his head, a return by former coach Fisher to Florida State, Navy's win behind WR Heidenreich, and Pitt QB Heintschel's four‑TD debut.

Defendant Roy Allen Whisnant was charged with assault with a deadly weapon with intent to kill his brother‑in‑law. He was found indigent and counsel was appointed. After initially pleading guilty to a misdemeanor assault with a deadly weapon, he withdrew the plea after being told it would waive his constitutional right to challenge his arrest. He requested a continuance to obtain witnesses from West Virginia and Florida and a postponement until the following week; both requests were denied. He was tried the next day, convicted, and sentenced to two years. On appeal the court held that the denial of time to prepare and the jurors’ exposure to the withdrawn guilty plea prejudiced his right to a fair trial. The judgment was reversed and a new trial ordered.

MADSEN Cycles produces colored bucket bikes with a rear bucket that can hold up to four children and cargo. The bucket sits on a 20‑inch rear wheel and includes two removable bench seats and four seat belts. Accessories—rain covers, frame‑mounted front racks and a padded middle bucket seat—enhance comfort, security and style, serving for pet transport, diaper changes and drinks. Based in Utah, the company markets these bikes as a family alternative to typical cargo bikes.

Jerome Powell, a Republican former investment banker, becomes Fed chair Monday, succeeding Janet Yellen, the first woman to hold the post, amid 4.1 percent unemployment, low inflation, and four years of growth. Yellen raised the benchmark rate five times, three in 2017, and completed the exit from bond‑buying, leaving a more normalized policy environment. Powell, one of the few non‑economist chairs, faces the challenge of calibrating interest rates as the U.S. economy is late in the cycle while global growth is synchronized and fiscal stimulus is taking effect. January wages posted the largest annual gain in nearly a decade. The first 2018 rate increase is expected in March, and a faster pace could mean four rather than three hikes this year. Policymakers debated inflation outlook and tax‑cut impact.

Supreme Court will hear arguments Oct 7 in Barrett’s case about whether Section 924(j) (causing death through a firearm) creates a separate crime and separate punishment from Section 924(c) (using a firearm in a federal crime of violence or drug‑trafficking). Section 924(c) is a compound crime; Section 924(j) adds a death element. The double‑jeopardy clause bars multiple punishments for the same offense unless each offense requires proof of a fact the other does not. Courts compare statutory elements; if one offense’s elements are a subset of the other, a presumption bars multiple convictions unless Congress clearly intended otherwise. Section 924(c) already contains explicit consecutive‑sentence language, reflecting Congress’s intent for separate punishment for that provision and its predicate. The Court’s 2023 decision held that Section 924(j) does not automatically import Section 924(c)’s mandatory minimums and consecutive‑sentence provisions. The government and Barrett agree that separate sentences for the same conduct are not permitted, but the 2nd Circuit allowed separate convictions and sentences; the Court appointed amicus to defend that judgment. Barrett argues neither statute mentions cumulative punishment; the government largely agrees. The amicus contends Section 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s non‑concurrent‑sentence clause is broad enough to permit separate sentences for 924(j). The Court’s decision will clarify Congress’s intent regarding multiple punishments under Sections 924(c) and 924(j).

Formative assessment in vocational education requires active teacher‑student interaction, immediate feedback, teacher judgment on guidance versus independent practice, and student self‑assessment; it identifies learning gaps, uses descriptive/prescriptive feedback, peer review and multiple attempts, and is more motivating than summative tests because it yields learning rather than merely preparation. Competence‑based education (CBE) shifts assessment from academic written tests to workplace‑oriented performance, defining competence as industry‑standard performance assessed through observed vocational tasks; it emphasizes performance relative to final product, meeting quality standards, observable behaviours, peer‑independent standards, and clear expectations, and improves motivation and engagement. Authenticity in assessment prioritises real‑world relevance over reliability; contextualised skill tests resembling workplace conditions are more authentic but risk reduced reliability, which can be mitigated by clear procedures, rubrics, professional development and inclusion of supervisor feedback during practicums. A comprehensive VET assessment program must combine written tests, technical skill evaluations, workplace practicum assessments, process and product evaluations, and both formative and summative methods; it should cover the full spectrum of competence levels (knows, knows how, shows how, does) and occur before, during and after learning. Overall, vocational assessment must integrate theoretical knowledge and technical skills, use authentic competence‑based methods and clear competency communication to foster deeper learning and student engagement.

The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the district court's decision granting summary judgment to Reisdorf Brothers, Inc. on the plaintiffs' Clean Water Act and Resource Conservation and Recovery Act claims. The appellate court found that the plaintiffs failed to raise a triable issue of fact regarding continuous or intermittent pollutant discharges, as the evidence involved either a single discrete incident or speculation. The court also affirmed the dismissal of state law claims without prejudice and upheld the denial of attorneys' fees to the defendant, finding no abuse of discretion.

Using longitudinal data from the PREVEND cohort (8,569 participants), this study applied a multi‑state model to estimate age‑ and sex‑specific transition rates between KDIGO chronic kidney disease risk stages (low, moderate, high/very high) and their association with new‑onset heart failure (HF). KDIGO stages were defined by estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urinary albumin excretion (UAE). Over a median follow‑up of 12.6 years (373 incident HF cases, 710 deaths before HF), forward transitions (low→moderate, moderate→high/very high) increased exponentially with age and occurred more often in men, while backward transitions (moderate→low) were more frequent in women and younger individuals. Transition rates to HF also rose with age and were lower in women (HR ≈ 0.70). Higher KDIGO stage conferred a greater relative risk of HF that attenuated with older age, but the absolute risk of HF increased with age. Misclassification of risk stages was accounted for; intermediate stage was misclassified as low in 18.4 % of observations and high/very high stage misclassified as intermediate in 15.6 %. Model predictions agreed with non‑parametric estimates. The results indicate rapid CKD progression in middle age and suggest that slowing KDIGO stage progression may substantially reduce incident HF. Limitations include the cohort’s enrichment for albuminuria and predominantly Caucasian composition.

Phil Kessel scored two goals and an assist, and Evgeni Malkin added two goals and two assists as the Pittsburgh Penguins defeated the Washington Capitals 7‑4 on Friday night. Bryan Rust, Carl Hagelin and Patric Hornqvist also scored for Pittsburgh, which earned its fourth straight win and moved within four points of the Capitals in the Metropolitan Division. Sidney Crosby contributed two assists, extending his scoring streak to 11 games, the longest active streak in the NHL. Alex Ovechkin scored twice, pushing his season total to an NHL‑best 32 goals. Braden Holtby stopped 27 shots but was pulled after allowing three goals early in the third period, replaced by Philipp Grubauer. The Penguins went 3‑for‑4 on the power play; the Capitals were 0‑for‑3. Pittsburgh has won seven consecutive home games and posted nine victories in January. Washington hosts Las Vegas on Sunday; Pittsburgh plays at New Jersey on Saturday.

The passage explains how to trade Australian markets. Access methods include US‑listed ETFs (e.g., iShares MSCI‑Australia ETF EWA, Franklin FTSE Australia ETF FLAU, Australian Ethical High Conviction ETF AEAE), American Depository Receipts, direct stock purchase via international brokers such as Interactive Brokers, and stock CFDs. The only currency ETF for the Aussie dollar is Invesco CurrencyShares Australian Dollar Trust (FXA). The primary exchange is the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) in Sydney, which also offers futures; a smaller exchange is the Sydney Stock Exchange (SSX), a subsidiary of AIMS Financial Group licensed in 2013. Australian markets operate Monday‑Friday, opening at 10:00 am AEDT (GMT +11) and closing at 4:00 pm AEDT (11:00 pm–5:00 am GMT). Backtests show that mean‑reversion strategies (e.g., 200‑day moving average, Golden Cross) underperform in the commodity‑heavy Australian market, while seasonal strategies, particularly the Santa Claus effect, have a 92 % win rate, an average gain of 2.4 % per trade, and 1.87 % annual returns versus 7.34 % for buy‑and‑hold. The Australian dollar can be traded against major currencies (AUD/USD, EUR/AUD, etc.). Over 2,000 companies are listed on the ASX, allowing broad diversification into mining and commodities.

The study aimed to develop a valid and reliable instrument measuring prospective teachers’ attitudes toward values education delivered via distance education. Background notes that values education has become a current issue in society, schools, and curriculum, with five main approaches (inculcation, moral development, analysis, clarification, action learning) and various teaching methods (case studies, role‑play, discussion, stories, projects, cooperative learning). Scholars argue that distance education can raise awareness of values and reach diverse populations, especially after the Covid‑19 pandemic accelerated the shift to online learning. However, existing scales examine either values education or distance education separately, prompting the need for a combined scale.

The research used a descriptive survey model and involved 341 prospective teachers enrolled in Gazi University’s Faculty of Education (77.7 % female; 4th‑grade students formed the largest group). Scale development followed DeVellis’s steps: defining the purpose (prospective teachers’ attitudes across cognitive, affective, and behavioral dimensions), generating an initial pool of 43 items from literature review and compositions of 20 teacher candidates, and selecting a five‑point Likert format with both positive and negative statements. An expert panel (computer‑instructional technologies, curriculum, testing‑evaluation) reviewed the items; three items were removed and one edited, leaving 40 items that achieved unanimous expert approval. A pilot test with 30 prospective teachers confirmed the scale was clear and feasible.

Data analysis employed reverse‑coding for negative items, exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with principal components and varimax rotation, and parallel analysis. Kaiser‑Meyer‑Olkin (KMO) was .971 and Bartlett’s test was significant (χ²=11837.828, p=.000). Scree plot and parallel analysis indicated two factors. After removing four items due to low loadings, cross‑loadings, or low item‑total correlation, the final scale comprised 36 items (21 positive, 15 negative). Factor 1, “Necessity and Usefulness,” contained 21 items (variance 35.03 %) with loadings .63–.82; Factor 2, “Feasibility,” contained 15 items (variance 28.26 %) with loadings .64–.83. Total explained variance was 63.29 %.

Reliability coefficients were high: Cronbach’s α .969 (Factor 1) and .961 (Factor 2); split‑half reliability .934 and .930 respectively. Item‑total correlations ranged from .656 to .841; all t‑values for 27 % subgroup comparisons were significant, indicating distinctiveness. The two factors correlated .632 (medium positive). Tukey’s non‑additivity test showed the scale lacks additivity, requiring separate interpretation of each subscale. Minimum and maximum possible scores are 21–105 (Factor 1) and 15–75 (Factor 2); higher scores reflect more positive attitudes.

Limitations include the predominantly female sample, single‑university context, and absence of a comparable external scale for validation. Recommendations suggest confirmatory factor analysis across multiple universities, examination of convergent and discriminant validity, and test‑retest reliability studies.

The Dabhol Power Company board authorized its managing director to issue a termination notice to the Maharashtra State Electricity Board due to payment disputes. MSEB made a protest payment of Rs 134 crore. International lenders supported termination while domestic lenders opposed it. The Maharashtra government opposed termination and planned to appoint a committee for renegotiation. Termination could cost the Centre up to Rs 2,840 crore.

Stephen Paddock’s arsenal included 23 firearms, 12 modified to fire like automatics, and 1,000 tracer rounds purchased at a Phoenix gun show. He set up cameras, booked rooms overlooking the Lollapalooza and Life Is Beautiful festivals, and had 1,600 rounds, fertilizer and Tannerite in his car. Paddock killed 58 people, injured nearly 500, and died as police closed in.

Effective post defense requires team effort with active hands from the player guarding the passer, helpside sag, and strong backside support. Individual techniques include beating the post player to the block, pushing them away from the basket, front or face guarding the passing lane, and influencing the ball toward their weakest side. Teams can also deploy post traps, extend the court with full court presses, and use a 2-3 zone or Diamond & One combination defense to create double and triple teams on talented post players.

Amazon.com, Inc. reported strong net sales growth of 25% year-over-year to $37.96 billion for Q2 2017, driven by a 42% increase in AWS sales to $4.1 billion. However, operating income declined to $0.63 billion from $1.29 billion in Q2 2016, and net income fell to $0.20 billion from $0.86 billion, due to increased investments in technology, content, and fulfillment. Cash flow from operations remained positive at $3.8 billion. The company acquired Souq Group Ltd. and other companies to expand its global e-commerce presence. Amazon also entered an agreement to acquire Whole Foods Market, Inc. for approximately $13.7 billion. Legal contingencies and tax matters are noted, including ongoing IRS disputes regarding transfer pricing and European Union state aid investigations. The company adopted new accounting standards for stock-based compensation and inventory in 2017.

Justice Babatunde Quadri of the Federal High Court, Abuja, admitted EFCC evidence against Chinese national Li Ya Ping on March 30, 2018. The defendant faces charges for allegedly concealing $300,000 while attempting to board a flight to Dubai, contravening the Money Laundering (Prohibition) Act, 2011. EFCC detective Hassan Mohammed Misau testified that Customs arrested the defendant at Nnamdi Azikwe International Airport on March 15, 2018, and handed him over to EFCC the following day.

Aledo Bearcats (No. 22) led Ryan Raiders 2‑0 in a Texas high‑school football game in Denton; Aledo is No. 16 by Massey and No. 28 overall, and Ryan could enter the Top 25 with a win. A safety was awarded. The Sporting News also released high‑school rankings and preseason All‑American teams.

The passage describes sources for U.S. foreign relations with the Soviet Union (1981–1988), including Reagan Presidential Library White House Staff and Office Files (NSC/NSPG meeting files, NSDDs, and staff members' files) and Department of State Executive Secretariat records. It notes that a section provides organizational context on U.S. covert actions and intelligence activities, describing procedures during the Truman presidency. NSC 4–A (December 1947) authorized CIA covert action operations for psychological warfare, and NSC 10/2 (June 18, 1948) superseded it, directing the CIA to conduct covert operations that the U.S. government could disclaim if uncovered.

Children born to obese mothers have double the risk of obesity by age two; paternal obesity also raises risk. Both parents transmit obesity susceptibility via signals in eggs and sperm, including non‑coding RNAs and maternal mitochondrial defects that affect offspring metabolism. Obese men have altered sperm RNAs, and injecting those RNAs into mouse eggs makes offspring fatter; eggs from obese women contain excess fat and defective mitochondria, which are inherited and impair energy metabolism, increasing lifelong obesity and diabetes risk. Interventions—anti‑diabetic drugs, exercise, weight loss—improve egg and sperm quality and can prevent transmission of obesity to offspring. The Council of Presidents of Medical Colleges recommends pre‑conception planning to reduce community obesity.

A cornerback is a defensive position responsible for covering wide receivers in both man and zone coverage. The position name derives from protecting the outside thirds of the field near the boundary. Cornerbacks must be fast and agile, starting each play backpedaling before transitioning to pursue receivers. They face a disadvantage because receivers know their routes while cornerbacks must react. Great cornerbacks, sometimes called 'lockdown corners,' can eliminate a receiver's threat entirely. Notable cornerbacks include Deion Sanders, Charles Woodson, Mel Blount, Champ Bailey, Ty Law, and Darrell Revis. The position is critical because reliable cornerbacks allow defenses to scheme around having a top receiver covered, forcing quarterbacks to hesitate and potentially enabling pass rushers to pressure the quarterback.

Defending goal kicks in soccer involves strategic positioning and aggressive pressing to win the ball or prevent an easy opponent build‑up. Under Law 16 a goal kick is awarded when the ball crosses the defenders’ goal line after last being touched by an attacker; the kick is taken from anywhere in the goal area (six yards from each goal post) and becomes live as soon as it is kicked and moves. Defenders must be outside the penalty area (18 yds from each post) before the kick, but opponents inside the penalty area may stay; if they touch the ball before it is in play the kick is retaken.

Three core defending tactics are: (1) place defenders across the field in a mix of man‑to‑man and zone coverage to mark potential receivers; (2) sprint to the ball first; (3) if the ball is won, transition immediately to attack; if not won, apply a high press in the opponent’s half.

Player responsibilities are detailed: centre striker near the top of the penalty area, wing strikers tightly marking the kicking team’s wing backs, centre midfielder at the centre mark, wide midfielders covering sideline zones, centre backs at the back of the centre circle, and wing backs supporting the wide midfielders.

For youth (generally 10 U and under) a “build‑out line” is used: the kicker places the ball at the outermost corner of the goal area and aims at a designated target; teammates follow a short‑pass/dribble progression while defenders must retreat behind the line before competing. At older youth (11 U and above) a second target farther upfield is added, and the kicker chooses based on defensive coverage; a third midfielder may also be introduced as an option. Adults employ all options, usually with the goalkeeper taking the kick and using short, deep, or lofted balls.

Coaches are reminded that a goal kick is a direct restart, the ball is in play instantly, wind can dramatically affect the ball, and defenders should use their forward momentum to advantage. Regular drilling of positioning, quick reaction, and preparation for every attacking option is essential.

Larry Connors' 3‑day high/low method, from the 2009 book High Probability ETF Trading (with Cesar Alvarez), buys an ETF after it records lower highs and lower lows for three consecutive days. Connors tested only ETFs, emphasizing quantification and dynamic exits. Backtesting through 2008 showed strong results, but a 12‑year follow‑up indicated 13 of 20 ETFs performed worse. A portfolio test with up to five simultaneous positions (20% equity each) across 25 ETFs still produced a profit, with the deepest drawdown occurring in July 2011 during the EU debt crisis. The method remains viable but may benefit from additional variable adjustments.

This study examined how engineering and technical‑management students at a Hungarian university evaluate the skills they need for their future careers under Education 4.0. A cross‑sectional survey was conducted with 147 second‑year undergraduates from the engineering (65.3 %) and the business‑and‑management (34.7 %) faculties. The questionnaire, derived from the literature and from interviews with industry representatives, asked students to select the three most important skills for (1) development during university years, (2) benefits of studying abroad (Erasmus or Stipendium Hungaricum), (3) factors for graduate employability, and (4) perceived contribution of higher education to their knowledge and self‑awareness.

Across both faculties problem‑solving was the most valued skill (66.7 %). Engineering students emphasized knowledge related to their specialization and technical/mathematical knowledge, while technical‑management students gave higher priority to learning decision‑making techniques and analytical thinking (significant differences, p < 0.05). Regarding international experience, 84.6 % of all respondents rated language improvement as the top benefit; engineering students highlighted opportunities for research projects, and business students valued networking and adaptation to international norms.

When assessing career success, the three leading factors were individual talents and skills (53.1 %), professional devotion (51.0 %) and a strong network (49.7 %); no significant faculty difference was found. More than half of the respondents agreed that higher education contributes fully to knowledge of their future job (57.8 %) and to digital‑literacy skills (55.1 %); opinions differed significantly for analytical problem solving, teamwork, and self‑understanding.

A CHAID decision tree confirmed that knowledge related to the future workplace, decision‑making techniques, and a new approach to interpreting learning material are the main factors distinguishing the two student groups. The study concludes that Education 4.0 requires universities to integrate hard and soft skills, adapt curricula to industry‑needed competences, and foster interdisciplinary collaboration.

Slavery is integral to understanding the future of teaching and learning, particularly as digital surveillance becomes ubiquitous in classrooms and workplaces. Scholars suggest that advanced technologies reproduce social inequality and command behavior through extraction, capitalist imperatives, and surveillance as a tool of power. Foucault's theory of panopticism illustrates how surveillance in education shares characteristics with racial surveillance rooted in slavery, with Browne noting that the historical formation of surveillance is not outside that of slavery. This connection is undertheorized despite increasing consequences in academia. The passage introduces "surveillance pedagogy" as a discourse to contextualize the relationship between slavery, pedagogy, and digitalization, building on Givens' concept of "fugitive pedagogy" to highlight how extraction and textualization practices from slavery anticipate modern surveillance capitalism. Historically, pedagogues in Ancient Greece were often enslaved people, a practice that parallels racial chattel slavery in the United States, where surveillance and violence controlled education for the enslaved. The passage traces how slave masters used ledgers and monitoring to extract productivity, foreshadowing modern data-driven pedagogies and surveillance capitalism. Surveillance pedagogy conceptualizes how observation and monitoring in teaching and learning involve extraction, inscription, and datafication, with digitalization enabling unprecedented control over learning. The study concludes that the legacy of slavery flows into the present, reflecting paradoxes in academic, political, and economic systems sustained by divisions like master/slave and teacher/student.

Understanding and predicting ocean currents is important for mapping heat, nutrients, pollutants, and sediments. Drifters are free-floating buoys used as Lagrangian observers to measure ocean velocity, increasingly due to their affordability and ability to sample spatio-temporal flow properties. Existing drifter placement strategies rely on space-filling designs or expert opinions, lacking explicit active learning approaches. This paper proposes BALLAST (Bayesian Active Learning with Lookahead Amendment for Sea-drifter Trajectories), a methodology that uses spatio-temporal vector-output Gaussian process surrogates and an information-theoretic utility function to optimally place drifters by maximizing information gain. BALLAST accounts for Lagrangian observation data by simulating trajectories and introduces active learning to drifter placement. Contributions include introducing active learning to Lagrangian observer placement, developing the BALLAST framework, and creating an efficient GP posterior sampling method using the SPDE approach. Numerical results show benefits of BALLAST for sequential observer deployment in synthetic and high-fidelity ocean current models.

Long‑term visit‑to‑visit blood pressure (BP) variability was examined as an independent risk factor for total cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) burden and its individual MRI features in 1,284 participants from the Kailuan cohort (mean age 56.5 years, 52.7 % male, mean follow‑up 13.1 years). BP variability was calculated for systolic BP (SBP), diastolic BP (DBP) and pulse pressure (PP) using coefficient of variation, standard deviation, variability independent of the mean (VIM) and average real variability; VIM was the primary measure. Brain MRI at the 2020‑2022 survey assessed white matter hyperintensities (WMH), lacunae (LA), cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) and visible perivascular spaces (PVS). cSVD burden was graded 0–4 and categorized as non‑cSVD, mild, moderate or severe.

Logistic regression with three multivariate models (age‑/gender‑adjusted, further adjusted for lifestyle and metabolic factors, and additionally for mean BP) showed:
- High SBP variability was associated with moderate cSVD burden (OR = 1.89) and PVS (OR = 1.62).
- High DBP variability was associated with LA (OR = 1.74).
- High PP variability showed stronger effects on moderate (OR = 1.99) and severe (OR = 2.49) cSVD burden, LA (OR = 1.75) and PVS (OR = 1.77).

Stratified analyses indicated that associations were modified by age and hypertension status. In participants < 60 years, only high PP variability was significantly linked to severe cSVD burden (OR = 3.33), LA (OR = 3.02) and PVS (OR = 1.86). In participants ≥ 60 years, high SBP variability was associated with moderate/severe burden and high DBP variability with LA. The risk effects of SBP and PP variability were significant only among participants with hypertension. No independent associations were found for WMH or CMBs after adjusting for mean BP. Sensitivity analyses (complete data, excluding diabetes, excluding antihypertensive users, using alternative variability indices) confirmed the robustness of the findings.

The study concludes that higher long‑term BP variability—particularly when combined with hypertension—is an independent risk factor for total cSVD burden, lacunae and perivascular spaces, and that PP variability is especially relevant for cSVD risk in younger adults.

Bollinger Bands are a technical indicator developed by John Bollinger in the early 1980s, consisting of a middle band (simple moving average) and upper/lower bands set by standard deviations to incorporate volatility. ChatGPT was prompted to create two Bollinger Bands trading strategies: a classic mean reversion strategy and a squeeze strategy. The squeeze strategy identifies a squeeze when Bollinger Bands are inside Keltner Channels, which use the stock's average true range (ATR) instead of standard deviations. Trading rules involve buying when the lower Bollinger Band is above the Keltner lower band and the upper Bollinger Band is below the Keltner upper band, and selling if conditions aren't met. Backtesting since SPY inception in 1993 showed poor performance with low compounded returns, high drawdown, and erratic results. Adjusting for time in the market improved returns slightly but not dramatically. The strategy is not recommended for live trading despite the backtest being executed correctly.

The case Anna Maria Meola v. Phyllis O. Ziman et al. (Superior Court of New Jersey, 1996) addresses whether an employee's sick time and employer's wages for personal and family illness days are collateral sources under N.J.S.A 2A:15-97, allowing a deduction from a lost wages claim. The plaintiff, injured as a passenger in a car accident, claimed lost wages from the defendant tortfeasor. The defendant argued that the plaintiff's sick pay and wages for personal days should be disclosed and deducted as collateral sources. The court examined the statute's purpose to prevent duplicate benefits and cited Bruwelheide v. Garvey, which held that sick leave is not a collateral source because it is earned compensation and using it reduces future benefits. The court agreed, reasoning that the plaintiff exhausted accumulated sick leave and personal/family illness days due to the defendant's negligence, surrendering benefits in exchange for compensation. Therefore, the court held that such sick pay and compensation are not benefits under the statute and cannot be set off against the plaintiff's lost wages award.

Inclusion is defined as believing that disabled and marginalized students belong in education, not merely inviting them (Carella, 2024). The paper argues that Ontario’s current special education model excludes these students, creating barriers such as limited resources, insufficient teacher training, and lack of systemic planning. Educators face challenges including larger class sizes, reduced funding, and policies that guide but do not equip them to meet diverse learner needs.

The history of special education in Ontario is traced from 1860s institutions labeled with derogatory terms, through 1880s special classes, 1906 day classes, and 1910 official special‑class placements. Civil‑rights movements in the 1960s prompted integration, yet segregation persisted and continues in contemporary placement categories: regular class with indirect support, regular class with resource or withdrawal assistance, partial integration, and full special‑education class.

Racialized students also experience exclusion; multicultural policies introduced in 1971 failed to reverse discrimination, leading to anti‑racist education, but enforcement remains absent. Racialized students are over‑represented in special‑education placements and under‑represented in gifted or autism diagnoses.

Implementation of Individual Education Plans (IEPs) relies on school‑based disability identification, which uses a deficit model and is tied to placement decisions. Although the Ontario Policy on Accessible Education for Students with Disabilities (2018) guarantees equal treatment, it lacks accountability and does not reflect practice; its undue‑hardship criteria restrict accommodations.

The paper concludes that disabled and marginalized students are systematically excluded, and current inclusion claims are not realized. Recommendations include involving students and educators with disabilities in policy development, improving pre‑service and in‑service teacher training, securing adequate funding, and adopting intersectional, non‑ableist approaches to create genuinely inclusive education.

SafeBehavior is a hierarchical jailbreak defense mechanism for Large Language Models (LLMs) that simulates human cognitive processes to detect and mitigate jailbreak attacks. The framework consists of three stages: intention inference (coarse-grained assessment of input queries to quickly filter potential risks), self-introspection (fine-grained verification of model responses against safety guidelines), and self-revision (rewriting uncertain responses to align with safety policies). The approach addresses limitations of existing input-only defense methods, which show reduced effectiveness against sophisticated attacks such as IFSJ, Papillon, and PPPI. The system evaluates defense effectiveness across five types of jailbreak attacks and compares against seven state-of-the-art defense methods.

A study developed and validated a Critical Multicultural Education (CME) learning module for pre-service English language teachers in Turkey. Using a qualitative design with a four-stage development process, the module aimed to introduce CME and encourage critical perspectives in teaching. Findings from interviews with participants indicated personal benefits, such as positive attitudes toward diversity and better understanding of social issues, and professional benefits, including awareness of educational ideologies and guidance on implementing CME. Challenges included limited time and dense content. The module was effective in enhancing pre-service teachers' understanding of diversity, social issues, and critical approaches to education, especially in contexts with limited prior exposure to CME.

Since 1947, higher education in Pakistan was largely neglected, with only 2% enrollment by 2000. In 2002, the government established the Higher Education Commission (HEC) to facilitate access and quality. Reforms increased enrollment to 12.6% by 2021, with a narrowing gender gap. However, growth has been uneven and inequitable. Universities are concentrated in big cities and low-poverty zones, leaving rural and high-poverty areas underserved. Private universities charge high fees, limiting access for low-income groups. Disparities exist by region (e.g., Baluchistan and rural Sindh have lower enrollment), poverty (extreme poverty zones have fewer universities and enrollment), and gender (female enrollment is low in high-poverty areas). Despite government commitments and policies, structural inequalities persist, and reforms have not adequately addressed access for disadvantaged populations.

Digital leader companies foster a growth mindset, use data to create shared context, encourage experimentation and risk‑taking, and invest in long‑term employee development, especially critical‑thinking skills. They share data transparently across teams, discourage hoarding, and rely on detailed metrics to track progress and set ambitious but realistic goals. Structured goals combined with flexible processes align the organization and empower employees to innovate. In contrast, digital laggards prioritize short‑term tasks, limit training to near‑term needs, discourage risk, and keep data on a “need‑to‑know” basis, leading to siloed information and a “culture of genius.” They set aspirational but data‑ungrounded objectives, causing employees to avoid measurement and focus on process compliance. Even digital leaders struggle to balance data use with intuition and may face regulatory constraints. Two case studies illustrate how a regulated pharma firm created a localized experimentation environment, and a retail company implemented real‑time sales reporting. Organizations fall into four patterns—data novice, insight ready, tech enabled, and data reliant—each of which can build on existing strengths to develop a strong data culture.

Blake Geoffrion, winner of the 2010 Hobey Baker Memorial Award for college hockey’s best player, comes from a family of hockey players; his great‑grandfather is Howie Morenz, a fourteen‑year NHL veteran, twelve of those seasons with the Montreal Canadiens, who some consider the best player of all time. Geoffrion’s grandfather is Bernie “Boom‑Boom” Geoffrion, also a Hall‑of‑Famer, and his father Dan played four years in the NHL.  

Howie Morenz was born June 21 1902 in Mitchell, Ontario. He played pond hockey on the Thames River, then five seasons with the Stratford Midgets, leading the team to the 1921 Memorial Cup finals, where he was described as the fastest junior ever seen and earned the nickname “the Stratford Streak.” In 1922 a referee informed Canadiens co‑owner Leo Dandurand of Morenz’s talent; Dandurand travelled to Stratford, and after Morenz finished his apprenticeship at the Canadian National Railway, he signed with Montreal on July 7 1923 – Dandurand’s 34th birthday – and was given sweater number 7.  

Morenz joined the Canadiens in December 1923, quickly becoming a star on a line with Aurel Joliat and Billy Boucher, helping the team win its first NHL regular‑season title in five years and its second Stanley Cup, scoring a hat trick in the first finals game. Over eleven seasons (1923‑1934) he set a league record with 51 points in 1927‑28, scored 40 goals in 44 games in 1929‑30, won the Hart Trophy twice, the Art Ross Trophy twice and added a third Stanley Cup in 1930‑31.  

The Great Depression hurt the Canadiens financially; in 1934 the team, now owned by the Canadian Arena Company, traded Morenz to Chicago, then to New York Rangers. Canadiens coach Cecil Hart returned only after the club re‑acquired Morenz. On January 28 1934, Morenz fell during a game, his left leg breaking in four places; he was hospitalized, suffered a nervous breakdown and died of a heart attack on March 8 1934. His funeral was held at the Montreal Forum, attended by thousands, with teammates serving as pallbearers, and he was buried at Côte‑des‑Neiges Cemetery.

The Dengvaxia scandal remains unresolved after months. The WHO announced that the vaccine should be given only to people previously infected with dengue, requiring a testing system not yet available. WHO defended its guidance for children 9+ and noted a data gap on seronegative recipients; the study prompted Sanofi to warn that Dengvaxia may increase severe dengue risk in seronegative individuals. Sanofi asserted the vaccine’s safety and disease‑reduction potential, denying any deaths. Senators, led by Senate Minority Leader Franklin Drilon, defended former President Benigno Aquino, asserting no intentional felony, reliance on officials, lack of proof linking Dengvaxia to child deaths, and that the vaccine benefited more people. Drilon’s statements contradict WHO’s caution and his prior role in the Corona impeachment trial.

The lecture introduces three methods for solving the Einstein field equations: weak‑field (linearized) gravity, symmetric solutions, and full numerical solution. The focus is on the first method.

The spacetime metric is written as the flat‑space metric η_{αβ} plus a small perturbation h_{αβ} whose components are much smaller than one. This defines “nearly Lorentz coordinates”. In this regime any term of order h² or higher is discarded, so the Einstein tensor becomes a linear differential operator acting on h_{αβ}.

Coordinate transformations in this background are examined. A Lorentz transformation leaves η_{αβ} unchanged and transforms h_{αβ} as an ordinary tensor in flat space, allowing many special‑relativity tools to be borrowed. Raising and lowering indices is done with η_{αβ}.

An infinitesimal coordinate shift x^α → x^α + ξ^α(x) changes the metric. The resulting change in the perturbation is

δh_{μν} = ∂_μ ξ_ν + ∂_ν ξ_μ,

which is called a gauge transformation. It leaves the Riemann curvature invariant, mirroring the gauge freedom of electromagnetic potentials.

To simplify the field equations a trace‑reversed perturbation is introduced,

\bar{h}_{αβ} = h_{αβ} – ½ η_{αβ} h,

where h = η^{μν} h_{μν}. The Einstein tensor, written in terms of \bar{h}_{αβ}, contains only the fully indexed tensor; all terms proportional to the trace disappear.

Gauge freedom can be used to impose the Lorentz gauge condition ∂^μ \bar{h}_{μν}=0, analogous to the Lorenz condition in electrodynamics. With this condition the linearized Einstein equations reduce to a wave equation

□ \bar{h}_{μν} = –16π T_{μν},

identical in mathematical structure to the electromagnetic potential equation.

For a static, non‑relativistic source (a perfect fluid with density ≫ pressure) the time‑ derivatives vanish and the dominant component gives

\partial_i ∂_i φ = 4πρ,

where φ is the Newtonian gravitational potential. Solving yields

\bar{h}_{00} = –4φ_N, \bar{h}_{ij}=0 (i≠j),

and the original metric components become

h_{00}= –2φ_N, h_{ij}= –2φ_N δ_{ij}.

This is the Newtonian limit of General Relativity, which underlies gravitational lensing and post‑Newtonian corrections and accurately describes many binary systems.

A rotating body adds a mass‑current term that modifies the spacetime. The correction behaves like a magnetic field and exerts a force reminiscent of the Lorentz force, giving rise to gravito‑magnetic effects.

The lecture notes that after treating the static case the next step is to solve the full linearized equations with time dependence, leading to a discussion of gravitational radiation. Upcoming homework will explore the rotating‑body case.

BusinessWeek’s 2000 Executive Pay Scoreboard reported that average CEO compensation rose to $13.1 million despite weak returns, with the top‑20 earners averaging $117.6 million; John Reed (Citigroup) took home $293 million, mainly from option exercises, and John Chambers (Cisco) earned $157.3 million.

This qualitative study explores online learning in Mexican higher education, revealing that it has increased access for non-traditional students but is challenged by economic, infrastructural, and digital disparities. Stakeholders perceive online learning as supplementary to in-person education, emphasizing the need for improved internet infrastructure, resources for underserved students, and teacher training to enhance quality and equity.

Renée Rouleau, a Texas esthetician who works with Demi Lovato, helped the author with two skin issues. At age 25 she diagnosed the author’s melasma, linking it to birth‑control use, which prompted the author to stop the pill and avoid heat and aggressive treatments, reducing the discoloration. Years later, after breakouts in a dry desert climate, Rouleau identified acne cosmetica caused by oil‑based foundation and advised using powder foundation, eliminating the problem. The TPS7H500x-SP series are radiation-hardness-assured, fixed-frequency, peak current mode PWM controllers for space-grade DC-DC converters supporting buck, flyback, forward, active-clamp forward, push-pull, and full-bridge topologies with switching frequencies up to 2MHz. Key features include three oscillator modes (internal, external synchronization, and primary-secondary for synchronized dual-controller operation), programmable soft-start via an external capacitor, and primary outputs (OUTA/OUTB) with ~150mA peak current capability requiring external gate drivers. Synchronous rectifier outputs (SRA/SRB) become active when the SS pin exceeds 1V. Dead time and leading edge blank time are programmable using external resistors (8ns minimum to 300kΩ maximum). Duty cycle limits are configurable to 50%, 75%, or 100% depending on DCL pin configuration, with TPS7H5001-SP and TPS7H5004-SP supporting 50% for dual-output operation. Current limiting uses the CS_ILIM pin at a 1.05V threshold, triggering hiccup mode through a cycle-by-cycle limiting period before disabling switching. The FAULT pin provides external fault protection at 0.6V threshold, while thermal shutdown occurs at 175°C with re-initiation at 160°C. Slope compensation is adjustable via the RSC pin to prevent subharmonic oscillation above 50% duty cycle. The controllers operate from a 4V to 14V supply range.

Surgical instrument force transmission mechanism for teleoperated systems (e.g., da Vinci) converts rotational input to translational movement of an actuation member to actuate an end effector. The mechanism includes a drive pulley, a drive cable (single or two separate cables), a driven pulley, and an actuation member (push‑pull rod) connected to the driven pulley via a ball joint. Rotation of the drive pulley winds cable onto the drive pulley and unwinds it from the driven pulley, causing the driven pulley to rotate. The driven pulley's rotation translates the actuation member along its longitudinal axis, actuating the end effector (e.g., jaws of forceps, grippers, or a clip applier) via a pin sliding in cam slots. Mechanical advantage can be set by varying pulley diameters and lever arm length; for example, a nominal 30 lbf cable tension can produce approximately 45 lbf at the actuation rod (mechanical advantage ~1.5). Compared to toothed gear arrangements, the disclosed mechanism offers lower friction, higher force transmission efficiency (exceeding 75 % in some embodiments), greater range of motion, and reduced component deflection under high torque. Cable pre‑tensioning is achieved during assembly by independent rotation of upper and lower sheaves of the drive pulley.

Interprofessional Education (IPE) is defined by the World Health Organization as students from two or more professions learning about, from, and with each other to enable effective collaboration and improve health outcomes. It differs from interdisciplinary studies, which focus on integrating disciplinary knowledge but may lack true collaborative work among students from different fields. IPE emphasizes teamwork, shared knowledge, conflict management, and knowledge integration.  

In 2016, Clarkson College formed an IPE committee under the Vice President of Academic Affairs to develop an IPE curriculum aligned with the Interprofessional Education Collaborative (IPEC) Core Competencies (values/ethics, roles/responsibilities, interprofessional communication, teams/teamwork), the Quadruple Aim (patient experience, population health, cost reduction, provider well‑being), and NCICLE guidance. The resulting model incorporates three key attributes: community involvement, service, and online learning.  

The college’s IPE 301 course is fully online, comprises five modules, and serves undergraduate and graduate on‑campus and distance students. The first four modules provide didactic instruction on IPEC competencies and must be completed in the first semester; the fifth module requires participation in real‑time, face‑to‑face IPE events. Events are categorized as knowledge, community, or service; students must complete at least one in each category. Since Fall 2018, all incoming students are enrolled in the zero‑credit course, which is required for graduation and recorded on transcripts.  

Assessment uses the Interprofessional Collaborative Competencies Attainment Survey (ICCAS) administered as pre‑test, mid‑test, and post‑test, plus student reflection journals. Between Fall 2018 and Summer 2021, 428 students completed all surveys. Quantitative results showed that 88.6 % of students reported “somewhat better” or “much better” collaboration after the first four modules; of those, 93 % reported additional growth after three IPE events, and 56 % of those who saw no early improvement still reported improvement after the events (χ² = 108.2, p < .001). Qualitative analysis of a 20 % random sample of reflection papers indicated that students enjoyed the events, learned about community issues and health topics, and reported positive teamwork, communication, and increased career awareness.  

Success factors include strong leadership support, mandatory faculty IPE training (a parallel five‑module course), and a sustainability plan overseen by an IPE committee organized into four microsystem teams (curriculum, outcome assessment, professional development, clinical application). The Clarkson College model aligns with IPEC competencies, NCICLE best practices, and the Quadruple Aim, and full integration across programs ensures graduates have a collaborative foundation for both academic and professional settings.

The Schwarzschild solution describes a vacuum spacetime with mass but zero stress-energy tensor, featuring a coordinate singularity at r=2GM (the event horizon) and a tidal singularity at r=0. The surface r=2GM causes infinite redshift: light emitted from near it loses all energy, and pulse intervals stretch infinitely as seen by distant observers. This horizon is a one-way membrane—once crossed, no signal can escape. To resolve coordinate issues, the lecture introduces tortoise coordinates, which map the horizon to r-star = -∞, and Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates, where radial null geodesics always travel at 45° and the metric remains non-singular except at r=0. Black holes are classified: Schwarzschild (mass only), Reissner-Nordström (mass and charge), Kerr (mass and spin), and Kerr-Newman (mass, spin, and charge). The No-Hair theorem states that stationary black holes in 3+1 dimensions are completely characterized by mass, spin, and charge; all other structure radiates away via gravitational or electromagnetic waves, leaving a Kerr solution for astrophysical black holes.

The TMS320DM8127 DaVinci Digital Media Processor is a highly integrated, programmable SoC that combines an ARM Cortex‑A8 CPU (with Neon floating‑point extension) and a TI C674x VLIW floating‑point DSP core, together with a high‑definition video and imaging coprocessor (HDVICP2). It includes separate level‑1 and level‑2 caches for the ARM (32 KB instruction, 32 KB data, 256 KB L2) and for the DSP (32 KB L1P, 32 KB L1D, 256 KB L2 with ECC), and a system MMU for address translation. The device provides a rich peripheral set, such as dual‑port Gigabit Ethernet MACs (supporting MII/RMII/GMII/RGMII, IEEE 1588, AVB, and Industrial Ethernet), multiple McASP audio ports, McBSP, two DCAN modules, USB2.0, DDR2/DDR3 memory controllers, GPMC, and GPIO. Development tools include C compilers, a DSP assembly optimizer, and a Windows debugger interface. Boot configuration is performed via GPMC pins and BTMODE[15:0] signals.

The GPU contains 108 streaming multiprocessors (SMs), 40 GB HBM2 memory with 1555 GB/s bandwidth, a 40 MB L2 cache (2.3× the bandwidth of V100) and 192 KB combined L1/shared memory per SM. Multi‑Instance GPU (MIG) capability partitions a single A100 into up to seven isolated GPU instances, each with dedicated compute resources, L2 cache slices and memory bandwidth, providing QoS and fault isolation for multi‑tenant cloud deployments. CUDA 11 adds task‑graph acceleration, asynchronous copy and barrier instructions, L2 cache residency controls, cooperative groups and warp‑wide reductions, reducing launch overhead and improving performance for iterative workloads.

The NVIDIA DGX A100 system integrates eight A100 GPUs connected via third‑generation NVLink through NVSwitch, delivering 5 PFLOPS of AI performance and supporting MIG to create up to 56 discrete accelerators per system. The ADS9803 is an eight‑channel, 20‑bit, 2 MSPS ADC that provides a source‑synchronous data interface. Data are output with a clock on the DCLKOUT pin; the data‑clock frequency is given by Equation 2 and the frame‑clock frequency by Equation 3. The device includes a data‑output randomizer that XORs the conversion result with either a PRBS bit or the LSB of the conversion result, which decorrelates ground‑bounce from the analog input. Two data‑averaging modes are supported: simple averaging (reduces output data rate by two) and moving averaging (no data‑rate change). Test‑pattern modes (fixed pattern, digital‑ramp, alternating pattern) can be enabled for channel groups CH[4:1] and CH[8:5] via registers 0x13–0x1B.

After power‑up or a hardware reset the device requires a free‑running sampling clock and must be initialized with a defined register‑write sequence. A speed‑boost mode is available that drives up to 8 MSPS on a user‑selected analog input pair while the other six channels remain idle. The device can be powered down through a dedicated pin or by writing to the PD_CH field.

All configuration is performed through a 16‑bit SPI interface organized in three register banks. Bank selection is done by writing to address 0x03, and register reads are enabled by setting the SPI_RD_EN bit. Multiple ADS9803 devices can be connected in a daisy‑chain topology; the chain length is set in the DAISY_CHAIN_LEN register, and register writes/reads use N × 24 SCLK cycles per frame for N devices.

A large set of registers (0x00–0xC5, 0x37, 0x3C, 0x44, 0x45, 0x4A, 0x4B, 0x92, 0xC0–0xC5) control functions such as data format, averaging enable, XOR operation, test‑pattern selection, lane mode (4‑lane or 2‑lane), common‑mode range, power‑down, and speed‑boost configuration.

The ADS9803 is powered by three supplies (AVDD_5V, VDD_1V8, IOVDD) with no required power‑up sequence. Board layout recommendations include placing bypass capacitors close to power pins, separating analog and digital signals, and keeping reference decoupling near the REFIO and REFM pins.

In ATE applications the device achieves a total unadjusted error (TUE) of <0.01 % after calibration and offers two bandwidth modes (low‑noise up to 22.7 kHz and wide‑bandwidth up to 700 kHz) to meet fast settling requirements when multiplexing PMU channels. Support resources include TI E2E forums and documentation update notifications.

The passage describes a formalization of constructive nominal sets in Rocq (formerly Coq), following an approach from Agda. It uses Rocq's typeclass system and generalized rewriting to handle setoids, modeling nominal sets as an unbundled typeclass hierarchy. Key formalized concepts include names (infinite atoms with decidable equality), permutations (as lists of swaps), nominal sets with finite support, constructive freshness, name abstraction, and finitely supported functions. They prove the Freshness Theorem and Freshness Condition for Binders (FCB), providing infrastructure toward a nominal framework for proof assistants. The development is available on GitHub.

Netflix, founded in 1997, transformed from a mail‑order DVD rental service to the world’s leading subscription video‑on‑demand (SVOD) provider. By 2019 it had 167 million paid subscribers worldwide, an enterprise value of $157 billion, and 60 % of its members outside the United States and Canada. The company grew by licensing popular content, launching its first original series House of Cards in 2013 (costing $100 million), building an in‑house studio, and investing $15 billion in original content in 2019—out‑spending any TV network or Hollywood studio. Netflix attributes its growth to a distinctive corporate culture expressed in its publicly‑available “Culture Deck.” The culture rests on five values: (1) freedom and responsibility—employees make decisions without committees and are expected to “farm for dissent”; (2) transparency—sensitive financial data and senior‑executive salaries are shared company‑wide; (3) extraordinary candor—employees publicly disclose failed initiatives and give signed feedback to colleagues; (4) keeping only highly effective people—talent density is prioritized, underperformers are let go with four‑to‑nine‑months’ severance, and the average attrition rate is about 12 % per year; and (5) avoiding rules—guidance replaces formal policies, except for strict rules on harassment, insider trading, and data security. Netflix’s strategy focuses exclusively on commercial‑free streaming, offers a large library (≈1,300 TV series and 3,000 movies per country in 2018) with no long‑term contracts, and maintains low churn rates. By 2019 Netflix spent $15 billion on content and $1.5 billion on technology, produced over 2,000 hours of original programming in 2018, and used a “cost‑plus” model that pays the full production cost plus a 30 % premium while retaining global rights. The rise of streaming undercut traditional pay‑TV, prompting incumbents (AT&T, Disney, Comcast) to spend $215 billion on acquisitions and launch competing services such as Disney+, Peacock, and HBO Max. Disney+ signed up 10 million customers on its launch day and reached 50 million within five months. Netflix entered India in 2016, viewing it as the source of its “next 100 million” subscribers. The Indian market was transformed by the “Jio effect”—Reliance Jio’s cheap 4G service that added 100 million subscribers in six months and forced competitors to lower prices. By 2019 India had over 600 million Internet subscribers and 300 million online‑video viewers, with 87 % of video time spent on mobile devices. Netflix initially targeted English‑ and Hindi‑speaking, well‑off urban viewers, but most Indian consumers preferred regional‑language content. To reach a broader audience, Netflix introduced a mobile‑only plan priced at $2.85 per month in July 2019 and announced plans to spend $420 million on local content by the end of 2020 (up from $70 million in 2017). The Indian SVOD landscape is crowded: Disney‑owned Hotstar led with 129 million active users in March 2019, Amazon Prime Video grew to 26 million unique users, ZEE5 reached 26 million visitors, ErosNow reported 16 million paid subscribers, and ALTBalaji reached 13 million. A 2019 survey found that Indian users subscribed to 1.1 paid services on average but used 2.4 services total, spent about 70 minutes per day on online‑video platforms, and only 6 % preferred English‑language content while 30 % favored regional‑language content. Dubbing and original programming in local languages have become key strategies. Netflix faces strategic questions about whether to revise its premium pricing, accept advertising, add live sports or user‑generated content, pursue local partnerships or acquisitions, or decentralize decision‑making for the Indian market.

The DISCARD operation (CMD38) de-allocates blocks partially or completely, with contents treated as 'don't care' by the host. Identification uses ERASE_WR_BLK_START (CMD32), ERASE_WR_BLK_END (CMD33), and CMD38 with argument 00000001h. Host must check DISCARD_SUPPORT bit (b313) in SD_STATUS; if unsupported, card executes ERASE. Out-of-sequence commands trigger ERASE_SEQ_ERROR or ERASE_RESET status bits and reset the sequence. Out-of-range addresses result in OUT_OF_RANGE error. DISCARD is supported for SDHC and SDXC cards only, not via SPI interface, with card indicating progress via DAT0 low and a 250ms busy timeout per command.

The passage documents AMD AGESA procedures: AMD_ENABLE_STACK initializes processor cache as temporary stack before main memory availability; AMD_DISABLE_STACK disables cache-as-RAM when main memory becomes available and flushes cache lines. AmdCreateStruct allocates storage for parameter structures using PreMemHeap, PostMemDram, or ByHost methods. A data eye procedure returns DIMM bitmap results. All procedures use register passing, require a stack, and return status codes indicating success, warnings, or fatal errors.

RADAR is a routing framework for selecting optimal {RLM, reasoning budget} configurations by balancing performance and cost. It formulates routing as multi-objective optimization using Item Response Theory to estimate query difficulty and model ability. RADAR operates in real-time (~7ms latency) as a black-box system, avoiding model fine-tuning or KV-cache recomputation. It employs a two-parameter logistic IRT model with learnable query embeddings and scalar-valued ability parameters, trained on evaluation response matrices. The framework uses linear and Chebyshev scalarization to navigate the performance-cost Pareto frontier according to user-specified tradeoffs. New model configurations can be added via adaptive testing on small query subsets. Experiments across challenging reasoning benchmarks show RADAR matches 90% of OpenAI o4-mini performance on MATH-500 at 1.31% of its cost and demonstrates strong out-of-distribution generalization.

Jill Kearns, an ETS employee injured in 1998, settled a negligence suit for $100,000, with Essex Source Realty paying $87,500 and Anton Kuppeck Landscaping paying $12,500. Researchers at the University of Bonn raised two groups of male African cichlids (Pelvicachromis taeniatus) for two years, exposing one group to water containing alarm substances that signal predator presence. At about one year of age both groups showed similar conspicuous coloration. Females were not affected. The authors suggest that larger body size, spiny fins and larger eyes reduce predation risk, while delaying bright colors trades survival against mating success.

Erase write blocks using CMD32, CMD33, CMD38 in order. CMD38 argument 00000001h or 00000002h may prevent erase if card supports DISCARD/FULE. Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) is a recurring depression pattern linked to seasonal changes. Winter SAD is most common; summer SAD (reverse SAD) accounts for about 10% of cases. Estimates suggest 1–10% of the global population is affected, with higher rates farther from the equator, a female predominance, and onset usually in young adulthood; about 10 million Americans have SAD. Although recognized in scientific literature in the 1980s, the phenomenon has been described since antiquity, and its exact cause is unknown. Reduced sunlight may lower serotonin and raise melatonin, disrupting mood and the internal clock. Common winter symptoms include low energy, fatigue, difficulty waking, cravings for sweets, starches, alcohol, caffeine, nicotine or drugs, weight gain, poor concentration, depressed mood, social withdrawal, decreased libido, and aches. Summer SAD symptoms are poor sleep, loss of appetite, weight loss, and anxiety. Untreated SAD can progress to serious mental health issues such as eating disorders or suicidal thoughts. Treatment options include light therapy (full‑spectrum bright light), medication, psychotherapy, and mind‑body techniques. Prevention strategies involve regular exercise, outdoor time, social activity, 7‑9 hours of sleep, a balanced diet, stress reduction, full‑spectrum lighting, plants, and colorful surroundings. Resources include Norman Rosenthal’s book “Winter Blues,” NIH, Mayo Clinic, and The Royal Institution YouTube channel.

The Arms Index (TRIN) is a market‑sentiment oscillator created by Richard W. Arms in 1967 that compares the ratio of advancing to declining stocks (AD Ratio) with the ratio of advancing to declining volume (AD Volume). A reading of 1.0 indicates market equilibrium; below 1.0 is considered bullish because more volume flows into rising stocks, while above 1.0 is seen as bearish with greater volume in falling stocks. Extreme readings above 3.0 signal an oversold market and possible bullish reversal, and below 0.50 indicate an overbought market and potential bearish reversal. Traders are advised to monitor TRIN changes throughout the day for market extremes, but the indicator should not be used alone; backtesting and combination with other indicators improve its effectiveness. Backtests of a basic TRIN strategy showed 522 trades averaging 0.39% gain—insufficient for trading—whereas adding a second indicator raised average gain to 0.66%, a 77% win rate and a profit factor of 2.4, demonstrating that combining TRIN with additional parameters enhances performance. The AD Volume Line, which measures net buying and selling pressure, can generate bullish or bearish divergences that foreshadow reversals, and market breadth indicates how many stocks contribute to a given index move.

The paper presents the Pilot‑and‑Adaptive Stable Trading (PAST) framework for edge‑assisted UAV networks with spatio‑temporal dynamism (STD‑EUNs). PAST consists of two modules: (i) PilotAO, a futures‑trading stage that establishes pre‑signed pilot trading agreements with overbooking using a many‑to‑many stable matching mechanism, aiming to reduce online negotiation overhead and transaction‑failure risk while ensuring individual rationality, fairness, non‑wastefulness, and weak Pareto optimality; and (ii) AdaptAO, a deep‑reinforcement‑learning‑based stage that dynamically updates the pilot agreements and overbooking rates in real time to cope with UAV mobility, demand fluctuations, and edge‑resource variability. Experiments on a real‑world taxi‑trip dataset show that PAST outperforms benchmark methods in runtime, decision‑making overhead, task‑completion latency, resource utilization, and social welfare, while preserving individual rationality for both UAVs (buyers) and edge servers (sellers).

USDA predicted a record U.S. meat consumption in 2018, but total per‑capita beef has fallen about one‑third since its 1970s peak. Chicken consumption more than doubled over the same period, while pork stayed roughly constant, so beef is no longer the dominant meat. The beef‑to‑chicken shift reduces land use and greenhouse‑gas emissions per gram of protein, though it raises animal‑welfare concerns. Despite recent modest rise, per‑capita beef remains far below its peak, and overall U.S. dietary GHG emissions fell ~10 % from 2005‑2014, mainly due to a 17 % drop in beef consumption. Drivers of the shift include health concerns, more women working, convenience of ready‑to‑cook chicken, and lower relative chicken prices. Beef still accounts for roughly half of the U.S. dietary carbon footprint and is higher than in most other countries. Further reductions in beef consumption are needed to limit global warming to 2 °C, and new plant‑based products could accelerate a transition toward a more sustainable diet.

The lecture covers empirical work on price discrimination, examining whether firms actually price discriminate and what effects this has on consumers. Three empirical papers are discussed in detail.

**Early empirical studies**: Borenstein's analysis of leaded versus unleaded gasoline found price differences too large to be explained by costs, indicating price discrimination. Shepard's study of gas stations found evidence of second-degree discrimination, with wealthier customers paying more for full service. Research on racial and gender discrimination in retail prices produced mixed results—audit studies found significant discrimination against minorities and women in car purchasing, but Goldberg's analysis using expenditure surveys found no racial price differences.

**Morton, Zettelmeyer, and Silva-Risso car pricing study**: Using detailed JD Power data on 671,000 car purchases, this study found smaller discrimination effects than earlier research—Black areas paid 1.5% more, Hispanic areas 1.1% more, women paid 0.2% more, while college-educated and homeowner populations paid less. The researchers argued these patterns reflect discrimination against less sophisticated shoppers with higher search costs, noting that effects largely disappeared for online Autobytel buyers, suggesting online purchasing reduces discrimination.

**Shiller's Netflix paper**: Using ComScore web browsing data, Shiller found demographic targeting would increase profits by only 0.3%, while web browsing variables could increase profits by 13%. Demographics proved largely useless for price discrimination; browsing behavior revealed significantly more consumer information. Welfare effects showed small gains in both consumer surplus and profits from demographic targeting.

**Dubé and Misra's ZipRecruiter study**: Conducting a randomized experiment with prices ranging from $19 to $399, they found ZipRecruiter was undercharging—optimal price was $327 versus the $99 they were charging. Personalized pricing would increase profits by 8.2% but reduce consumer surplus by 25%, reducing social welfare. ZipRecruiter raised prices to $249 but declined to implement personalization. Key findings include substantial heterogeneity in price sensitivity and consumer surplus across firms.

The lecture concludes that empirical evidence suggests price discrimination effects are smaller than theory predicts, demographics are relatively ineffective for discrimination, and online markets may reduce certain forms of discrimination by limiting identifiable buyer characteristics.

The passage describes the need for research‑performing organisations (RPOs) to develop robust policies that support the creation, use, sustainability and recognition of research software, which is increasingly central to modern science. It notes that institutional policies for research software are currently limited and that training, reward and assessment structures have not kept pace with the rapid growth of software‑based research.

To address this gap, the Policies in Research Organisations for Research Software (PRO4RS) Working Group (WG) was established as a joint initiative of the Research Software Alliance (ReSA) and the Research Data Alliance (RDA) for 2023‑2025. The WG, led by eight co‑chairs and involving over 100 participants, aimed to help RPOs worldwide create, share, manage and reuse research software as part of FAIR and open‑science practices. Its main outputs were: (1) a global inventory of publicly available institutional policies that support research software; (2) a report on resources for different stakeholders to enable policy change; (3) a report identifying policy gaps, especially regarding the inclusion of software personnel in research‑assessment reform; and (4) case studies from four research organisations that have implemented such policies.

The PRO4RS WG proposes a layered framework for policy development: a central, optional, research‑software‑specific policy; a middle layer ensuring alignment of other relevant policies (e.g., open‑science, licensing, hiring and promotion); and an outer layer that links to practical guidelines and frameworks. Key recommendations include making the volume of institutional software visible, advocating for the role of software in research, and engaging stakeholders to embed software policy within broader research‑quality initiatives.

The passage also surveys broader international initiatives (e.g., DORA, CoARA, Science Europe, Open‑AIRE) that champion recognition of software as a research output and discusses challenges such as the lack of reliable metrics for software impact. It concludes that while formal research‑software policies are still rare, their development can promote best practices, reproducibility, collaboration and institutional reputation.

The Treasury Department is considering minting a $1 commemorative coin for the 250th anniversary that would display President Donald Trump’s likeness on both sides. Treasurer Brandon Beach and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicized the draft, and a Treasury spokesperson said a final design has not been chosen. A January 2021 law authorizes the minting of $1 coins for the semiquincentennial but bars the inclusion of a living person’s portrait on the reverse, raising questions about the draft’s legality. A long-standing tradition, codified in an 1866 Act, limits reverse portraits to deceased individuals. Treasury declined to comment on the legality. Commemorative coins are legal tender but are not minted for general circulation.

After President Tyler’s 1842 recommendation, Congress funded a diplomatic post to the Sandwich Islands; George Brown was appointed commissioner in March 1843, arrived in Honolulu in October, presented credentials, and sought equal treatment for U.S. citizens. The King promised equal privileges, but a dispute over the denial of jury trial to American John Wiley and the absence of a U.S. treaty created tension. Treaties with France and Great Britain (1844) included jury provisions Brown protested as discriminatory. The King requested Brown’s recall, which the United States approved, and James Ten Eyck became commissioner. The United States recognized Hawaiian independence; France and Britain signed conventions in 1846 modifying the jury clauses. A Danish treaty in October 1846 fully acknowledged independence. Ten Eyck was instructed to model a treaty on Britain’s, but his insistence on the jury clause drew criticism from Buchanan. He resigned in 1848, succeeded by Charles Fames in January 1849.

The NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU, based on the Ampere architecture, is the company's 8th-generation data center GPU designed for AI, HPC, and data analytics applications. Fabricated on TSMC's 7nm process with 54.2 billion transistors, it features 108 Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) with 432 third-generation Tensor Cores. Key improvements over the V100 include: support for TF32, BF16, FP16, FP64, INT8/INT4/Binary data types; 40GB HBM2 memory with 1555 GB/s bandwidth (73% increase); 40MB L2 cache (6.7x larger than V100) with 2.3x read bandwidth; and a new sparsity feature enabling 2x throughput through fine-grained structured sparsity. The Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) capability allows partitioning into up to 7 isolated GPU instances for improved utilization and multi-tenant environments. Third-generation NVLink provides 600 GB/s total bandwidth (doubled from V100), while PCIe Gen 4 offers 31.5 GB/s per direction. CUDA 11 introduces asynchronous copy, asynchronous barriers, L2 cache residency controls, and task graph acceleration for improved programmability and performance. The DGX A100 system integrates eight A100 GPUs with NVSwitch and Mellanox InfiniBand for scalable AI infrastructure.

This passage describes a qualitative case study exploring how an oral history project can benefit elementary preservice teachers' (PSTs') learning and teaching of citizenship. Conducted with 38 PSTs in a South Florida university, the project involved PSTs interviewing community members on citizenship topics such as immigration, military service, civil rights, and poverty. Findings indicate that the project helped PSTs gain a deeper, humanistic understanding of citizenship through firsthand experiences, impacted them personally by fostering empathy, appreciation for diverse perspectives, and civic engagement, and influenced their future teaching by encouraging the incorporation of oral histories and community guest speakers. The study concludes that oral histories can enhance citizenship education, address challenges in teaching controversial topics, and support PSTs in connecting classroom learning to real-world issues.
