The passage describes SD Memory Card lock/unlock mechanisms, command extensions, and performance classifications.  

Lock/unlock operations are controlled by CMD42, which carries a mode field, password length and password data.  CMD42 can set, replace or clear a password (FEP) and can unlock a COP‑locked card; other CMD42 functions are blocked until COP is unlocked.  If the old password does not match, a LOCK_UNLOCK_FAILED error is returned and the password is unchanged.  A “Force Erase” command erases all user data and clears the password, unlocking the card; when FEP is set a matching FEP is required for the force‑erase operation.  The card accepts only a limited set of commands (e.g., CMD0, CMD1, CMD13, CMD42, CMD55, etc.) while locked; all other commands are treated as illegal.  Three lock/unlock types are defined: Type 1 (legacy), Type 2 (Physical Layer v1.10+), and Type 3 (COP, v5.10+); their behavior is detailed in tables that show state transitions, required bit settings and error handling.  

CMD6 (Switch Function) allows the host to query and select up to six function groups: access mode (bus speed), command system, driver strength, power limit, and two reserved groups.  Mode 0 is used to read supported functions and maximum power consumption; Mode 1 is used to change functions.  Function 0 in each group restores the default state; returning to default requires a power cycle, CMD0 or CMD6 with function 0.  

CMD8 (Send Interface Condition) verifies voltage compatibility for cards compliant with version 2.00 or later.  SDSC cards use byte‑addressing and variable block length (CMD16), while SDHC/SDXC cards use fixed 512‑byte block addressing regardless of CMD16.  

The SD bus protects commands and responses with CRC7 and data blocks with CRC16.  Clock control rules require at least eight clock cycles after each transaction before the host may stop the clock, and busy signals are handled as specified.  

Status information is provided via Card Status (R1 response), a 512‑bit SD Status register and a Task Status field for Command‑Queue (CQ) mode.  Speed‑class definitions (Class 2, 4, 6, 10), UHS Speed Grades (U1, U3), Video Speed Classes (V6, V10, V30, V60, V90) and Application Performance Classes (A1, …) each specify minimum write performance, AU size, erase timeout parameters and, for CQ, queue depth.  The host calculates erase timeouts from fields in the SD Status and must respect the maximum busy periods defined for write and erase operations.  In UHS‑II mode several command behaviors differ and data is transferred in bursts with busy indicated after each burst (maximum 1 s).

Over his 21‑year career he has earned $479.5 million in NBA salaries; a two‑year, $97 million extension pushes his total guaranteed career salary to $532 million. In 2022 he earned $126.9 million from on‑ and off‑court activities, including $36.9 million from the Lakers and roughly $90 million from sponsors.

His major endorsement deals include AT&T, Walmart, Intel, Kia, Beats by Dre and a lifetime contract with Nike that includes a dedicated Innovation Center on Nike’s campus. He became a billionaire in 2022, with an estimated $900 million earned from endorsements and business ventures. He makes about $428 K per sponsored Instagram post on his 158 million‑followers account.

James invests across sectors: he holds stakes in Liverpool FC and its parent Fenway Sports Group, is an investor in SpringHill (valued at $725 million), co‑founded the media platform Uninterrupted (which received $16 million from Warner Bros.), owns a New York office building, has invested in Blaze Pizza (25‑times return), Lobos 1707 tequila, Canyon Bicycles, and has interests in Klutch Sports Group (unconfirmed). His assets include a $9 million Miami home (later sold for a profit), a 30,000‑sq‑ft compound in Akron with a recording studio, bowling alley, theater and aquarium, a $23 million Brentwood mansion, and a collection of luxury cars (Porsches, Rolls‑Royce, Ferrari Testarossa, custom Kia, Hummer EV). Despite his wealth, he avoids data roaming, uses free Wi‑Fi and has been called cheap by peers.

He spends heavily on body maintenance with a home gym, ice/hot tubs, hyperbaric chamber, and a team that includes a former Navy SEAL biomechanist, recovery coach and personal chefs. He has tattoos by Bang Bang Tattoos and bought his wife a $300,000 engagement ring.

Family‑wise, he and his wife Savannah have three children—Bronny (now a USC and NBA player), Bryce and Zhuri. James fulfilled his goal of playing alongside Bronny in October 2024, becoming the first father‑son duo in the league.

Philanthropically, he founded the I Promise School in Akron for at‑risk children and pledged roughly $41 million through his Family Foundation to send over 1,000 students to college. He also backs the “More Than a Vote” voting initiative.

In October 2025 James teased a major announcement, sparking a 20‑fold rise in Lakers ticket sales, but the reveal turned out to be a Hennessy ad.

The passage discusses two international documents concerning the Global South: the Baku Declaration from the 2018 NAM Mid-Term Ministerial Meeting and the CHOGM 2018 Communiqué. The Baku Declaration addresses protectionism, the Doha Development Round, South-South Cooperation, and condemns Israeli occupation of Palestinian territories and the Syrian Golan. The CHOGM Communiqué focuses on free trade, challenges faced by small Commonwealth states, refugee and migration issues, and expresses solidarity with Bangladesh regarding the Rohingya crisis. India's participation included Sushma Swaraj at Baku and Modi at CHOGM, where he explored post-Brexit relations with Britain. The author critiques that while both documents contain welcome statements, they fail to address fundamental structural issues affecting the Global South. India is criticized for its position on Rohingya refugees, with questions raised about its commitment to NAM principles of autonomy in policy-making. The author argues the Global South has become a passive stakeholder in global affairs and that meaningful alternatives to the prevailing unequal economic system remain unaddressed by these documents.

Jean Melchior sued Hilite International for infringing three patents related to hydraulic cam phasers used in variable valve timing systems for internal combustion engines. The patents disclose cam phasers that use torque reversals to move hydraulic fluid between chambers without requiring a pump. Following a jury trial, Hilite moved for judgment as a matter of law, which the district court denied. The Federal Circuit reversed, holding that the asserted claims are invalid. The court found that Danckert, a prior art German patent, anticipated claim 22 of the '017 patent because the claimed limitation of "transferring hydraulic fluid between chambers" does not require "direct transfer in a closed line," despite Melchior's expert testimony distinguishing the prior art on this basis. Regarding the remaining claims of the '506 and '254 patents, the court held they would have been obvious over Danckert in view of Shirai. Judge Newman concurred in the judgment of no liability on the grounds that infringement was not established, noting that both parties stipulated no infringement occurs while the pump is operational and no evidence showed the accused devices operated contrary to design during the brief transition between modes.

Digital competence is a mandatory cross‑subject competence in Norwegian schools, yet the use of digital technology in PE is still limited to basic ICT tools. Teacher educators need to move beyond basic ICT to scaffold learning, and limited knowledge exists about how technology can benefit PE and PETE. Flipped learning (FL) is defined as a framework where students first view video content and then engage in active, student‑centred activities in class, replacing passive reception with autonomous learning. Literature reports positive outcomes of FL on motivation, engagement, learning environment, and learning outcomes across teacher education, but research specifically in PE and PETE is scarce. This study aimed to investigate PETE students’ perceptions of an FL framework in Norwegian PETE.

A qualitative approach rooted in constructivist grounded theory was used. Twenty‑two PETE students (average age 24.2 years, equal gender distribution) participated in two FL units—one practical (dance) and one theoretical (motor learning)—over two semesters (2016/2017). Students watched 10–20 minute teacher‑produced videos before class; in‑class time emphasized discussion, problem‑solving, and practice with reduced direct instruction. Semi‑structured interviews were conducted, coded initially by two researchers, then axial coded, yielding five empirical themes.

Theme 1 (Expectations) showed that video preparation generated peer‑pressure to watch, increasing participation. Theme 2 (Simple Input) indicated students viewed videos as more concise and accessible than text, saving time and lowering the preparation threshold. Theme 3 (Deep Learning) revealed that repeated video viewing and in‑class discussions fostered a thorough understanding of concepts and relational knowledge. Theme 4 (Supportive Learning Environment) described how advance video viewing reduced uncertainty, especially for practical dance tasks, and gave students confidence to practice movements before class. Theme 5 (Challenges) reported that students missed immediate teacher interaction during preparation, experienced occasional technical access problems, and perceived FL as more time‑consuming.

Overall, students reported that FL positively affected both motivation and learning, created a richer, more supportive learning environment, and was viewed as a useful tool for future PE teaching. Although some challenges were noted, the perceived advantages outweighed the drawbacks. The findings support FL as a meta‑instructional strategy that can promote deeper learning and increased engagement in PETE contexts.

St. Jude researchers identified kinases Mst1 and Mst2 as hidden regulators of dendritic cell subsets that drive anti‑cancer and anti‑infection T‑cell responses. Using the data‑driven NetBID algorithm and integrated gene‑expression, proteomics and phosphoproteomics data from mouse dendritic cells, they found that Mst1/2 and the Hippo pathway control the functional specialization of dendritic cell subtypes. CD8α+ dendritic cells, which preferentially prime CD8 T cells, were more metabolically active than CD8α− cells, and metabolic manipulation altered their T‑cell priming capacity. Mst1/2 acted via the NF‑κB pathway to produce interleukin‑12, linking metabolic activity and cytokine signaling to selective activation of CD8α+ dendritic cells. The findings suggest strategies for modulating dendritic cell activity in cancer immunotherapy and immune disorders. The study appears online in Nature, with co‑corresponding authors Hongbo Chi and Jiyang Yu, first author Xingrong Du, and funding from NIH and ALSAC.

The Supreme Court of Alabama answered a certified question from the Eleventh Circuit regarding whether an insurance policy provision limiting "insured" to employees acting "within the scope of duties" conflicts with coverage for "violations of constitutional/civil rights," creating ambiguity. The case arose from § 1983 claims by Janice Shrader and Debra Livingston against City of Attalla police officers for sexual abuse. Employers Mutual Casualty Company sought declaratory judgment that its linebacker policy did not cover the officers. The court held no conflict exists, finding the policy language unambiguous and rejecting arguments that it created illusory coverage. The court distinguished the Titan cases as based on different policy provisions and law-of-the-case holdings, concluding insurers may limit liability through scope-of-duties requirements without conflicting with civil rights coverage provisions.

This study investigates the relationship between outdoor temperature and COVID-19 severity in Tomsk, Russia, during the Omicron wave (January–March 2022). It tests the "compromised airway epithelium" hypothesis, proposing that temperature drops further weaken the already impaired respiratory lining of infected individuals, leading to increased symptoms and hospitalizations. The study compared daily temperature fluctuations with COVID-19 hospitalization data using a case-crossover design. Fourteen characteristic temperature drops (over 3°C) were identified, and all were associated with hospitalization surges occurring within 1–2 days. In eight cases, temperature was the primary trigger; in six, it acted as an additional factor alongside other influences. The authors conclude that predictable temperature drops can be used to alert healthcare systems about impending increases in severe COVID-19 cases.

Peter Joseph Saville, a dentist who served the Worthing community for over 40 years at his West Park Lane practice, died on June 27 at age 90. Born May 2, 1928 in Ilford, Essex, he studied dentistry at Guy's Hospital and served in the army dental corps in Cyprus and Egypt in the early 1950s. He married Josephine in 1954 and moved to Worthing, initially joining a practice in Lancing before establishing his own. An avid sportsman, he played cricket, hockey (becoming president of Worthing Hockey Club), founded the squash section at Manor Sports Club in the 1970s, and was a member of Hill Barn and Worthing Golf Clubs and West Worthing Tennis and Squash Club. He was a devoted Catholic who served as a Eucharistic minister, visited the sick and elderly, attended daily mass, and made pilgrimages to Lourdes. He was a member of the Catenian Association for over 50 years and supported various charities. He is survived by his wife Josephine, six children, and eight grandchildren. A funeral mass will be held on July 12 at Saint Mary of the Angels, followed by burial at Durrington Cemetery.

Historical evidence shows U.S. stock markets have generally experienced lower volatility and reasonable returns during wars and geopolitical conflicts, as illustrated by WWII and the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait. Higher defense spending appears to correlate with reduced market volatility. However, wars fought on a country’s own soil, such as post‑WWII Germany or Russia’s current conflict, can devastate markets, leading to closures and large losses. Gold and commodities often rise during conflicts because they are perceived as safe havens and respond to anticipated money printing and supply disruptions. Markets tend to discount war risks early and may advance despite bad news, reflecting their forward‑looking nature.

Breaking chiral degeneracy in a lattice gives rise to chiral phonons that carry angular momentum. Unlike chiral‑induced spin selectivity (CISS), which is limited to conductive materials, chiral phonons can transfer both energy and angular momentum in insulating materials. This study demonstrates chirality‑selective heat transfer in heterostructures composed of ferromagnetic (FM) [Co/Pt] multilayers and chiral material (CM) α‑SiO2, thereby realizing a nanoscale chiral thermal switch. Time‑resolved magneto‑optic Kerr effect measurements reveal a ≈7 % difference in the apparent thermal conductivity (κ_quartz) of α‑SiO2 when the magnetization direction of the [Co/Pt] multilayer is reversed, and a thermal on/off ratio (κ_on/κ_off) of ≈1.07 at room temperature. The ratio increases to ≈1.2 at 50 K because phonon‑phonon scattering is reduced, enhancing the chiral phonon diode effect. First‑principles‑based molecular‑dynamics simulations show that ultrafast demagnetization of the FM layer generates chiral phonons whose angular‑momentum sign follows the magnetization direction; when this sign matches the crystal chirality of α‑SiO2, heat propagates more efficiently across the interface. Non‑chiral amorphous SiO2 exhibits negligible magnetization‑dependent conductivity, confirming that the effect arises from the chiral phonon diode. The results demonstrate that simple FM/CM heterostructuring can provide a chirality‑selective thermal switch and diode, offering a blueprint for nanoscale heat‑management devices.

Successful school‑based mental health programs share common ingredients: strong partnership among school staff, families and the broader community; reliance on existing school personnel (psychologists, counselors, teachers) who serve as the core of the program; and integration of community‑based clinicians who provide services inside schools. Teachers are especially valuable because they interact with students daily and can identify early behavioral changes, making them key referral sources. Minnesota exemplifies this approach: a decades‑long effort led by Mark Sander that adapted the University of Maryland model, secured funding through health‑insurance billing and $20 million in state money, and embedded clinicians in the school culture with protected time for collaboration. Maryland’s early work began in 1989 when school‑based health centers recognized that physical complaints often reflected social‑emotional issues; outreach was hindered by transportation, childcare and stigma, prompting the university to bring mental‑health providers directly into schools. Baltimore schools now advertise widely—classroom presentations, social‑media QR codes, events—making providers visible as school‑community members, which reduces stigma and helps students and families access care. These integrated, locally tailored models, while not identical everywhere, share the principle that delivering mental‑health services where children are ensures better attendance, follow‑up and overall outcomes.

The Economist's "Carrie Bradshaw index" ranks US cities by how affordable they are for single renters by calculating the salary needed to rent a studio without spending more than 30% of gross income. The passage describes a new book by college adviser Jaime Smith designed to help community college students transfer to four-year institutions. The book is clearly written and includes case studies for various student situations. It offers practical tips such as keeping syllabi, taking W over F, prioritizing fit over prestige, checking housing options, and understanding separate admission to institution and major. The reviewer adds that local transfer advisers can reveal nuances like credit limits and transfer scholarships and that many statewide transfer agreements require completing an associate degree, which protects against credit loss and provides a safety net. The reviewer notes the book incorrectly downplays the value of finishing an associate degree, and that while the advice to attend community college after leaving a four-year school can be useful, it is often overlooked. Overall, the reviewer finds the book accessible and practical, with the associate‑degree omission being the only significant error.

Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) reduces heterosexual HIV acquisition by 50–60% and Uganda adopted VMMC in 2007 with a WHO recommendation of 42 days of sexual abstinence after the procedure. This study used cross‑sectional data from the Rakai Community Cohort Study (RCCS) across four survey rounds (June 2013–October 2020) to estimate the prevalence of early sex resumption (ESR) before 42 days and associated risk factors among circumcised men in Rakai, Uganda. Overall ESR prevalence declined from 45.1% in 2013/15 to 21.8% in 2015/16, 21.8% in 2016/18, and 14.9% in 2018/20. Multivariate analysis showed ESR was consistently higher among currently married men than never‑married men across most rounds; men aged 25–34 and 35–44 had higher ESR than 15‑19‑year‑olds in later rounds; having more than one sexual partner was associated with ESR in 2016/18; primary education was linked to higher ESR in 2018/20; fishermen had higher ESR only in 2013/15 and 2016/18; HIV‑positive status was associated with ESR in 2015/16 and 2016/18 but not in other rounds. The authors suggest that strengthened post‑VMMC counseling starting in 2016 may have contributed to the decline and recommend involving female partners and targeting men with lower education or multiple partners to improve compliance with WHO guidelines. Limitations include reliance on self‑reported sexual behavior and possible under‑reporting.

CVS Health’s stock fell about 23% in a 12‑week span from late‑August to early‑November 2016, driven by Walgreens’ 10‑year alliance with Prime Therapeutics (the fourth‑largest PBM) and CVS’s exit from the Tricare pharmacy network. The article contends the market has over‑reacted to 2016 events and CVS remains a leading player in drug stores, specialty pharmacy and long‑term care.

This Phase 1/2 outpatient, crossover, randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled human laboratory study tested the safety and tolerability of 7‑day oral mifepristone (600 mg/day) in non‑abstinent adults with alcohol use disorder (AUD). Participants (n = 32) received mifepristone or placebo followed by a 3‑week washout and the alternate condition. During laboratory sessions, yohimbine (32.4 mg) was administered to induce stress, combined with a cue‑reactivity procedure, a priming alcohol dose and open‑bar self‑administration. The primary outcome (safety) showed no serious adverse events; non‑serious events were few and similar between conditions. Mifepristone did not affect alcohol pharmacokinetics, subjective alcohol effects, or consumption. Secondary outcomes indicated that mifepristone reduced alcohol craving (ACQ, AUQ) and cue‑elicited salivary output at the first alcohol trial, while increasing salivary cortisol. Mediation analysis showed the craving reduction was independent of cortisol increase. Family history density of alcoholism (FHDA) moderated responses: participants with low FHDA showed greater mifepristone‑induced craving reduction, while those with high FHDA exhibited larger cortisol increases. These findings support the safety of mifepristone–alcohol co‑administration and indicate efficacy in reducing stress‑cue‑induced craving, particularly in low‑FHDA AUD individuals.

The lecture discusses moving beyond tree-level diagrams in QED by including loop diagrams that represent quantum fluctuations of the vacuum. Unlike tree-level diagrams with no momentum integration, loop diagrams require integrating over internal momenta, leading to divergences from extrapolating QED to arbitrarily high energy scales where short-distance physics is unknown.

In the late 1940s, Schwinger, Feynman, and Tomonaga developed renormalization techniques to remove these divergences and obtain sensible physical results, which Dyson later simplified and spread through Feynman diagram techniques. This program showed that physical mass and charge differ from bare parameters in the Lagrangian due to interactions.

The three simplest loop diagrams are electron propagator correction, photon propagator correction (maintaining masslessness due to gauge symmetry), and vertex correction (renormalizing charge and generating anomalous magnetic moment). The Dirac equation predicts g=2 for the electron's magnetic moment, but loop corrections make it slightly greater than 2.

Schwinger calculated the first correction as alpha/(2pi) in 1948, which agreed with experiment. Later calculations extended to higher orders in alpha, with the second order involving seven diagrams calculated in 1957, and the third order involving 72 diagrams completed in 1996. The anomalous magnetic moment is one of the most accurately measured quantities in physics.

The study analyzed gene expression in muscle biopsies from patients with granulomatous myositis (GM), a form of inflammatory myopathy defined by non‑caseating granulomas, and compared them with other inflammatory myopathies, disease controls and healthy controls. Using bulk RNA sequencing of 38 GM biopsies from multiple cohorts, they found marked upregulation of IFNγ and IFNγ‑inducible genes, elevated IFNγ receptor expression, intermediate type I interferon signatures, and increased T‑cell (especially CD4+), B‑cell, plasma‑cell and macrophage markers. HLA class I and II expression was higher than in other myopathies. Pro‑inflammatory interleukins (IL1B, CXCL8, IL10, IL26, IL16), their receptors, checkpoint ligands, multiple chemokines (CCL17, CCL22, CCL18, etc.) and their receptors, and TNF‑family molecules (TNF, CD40LG, etc.) were specifically upregulated. TGFβ1 and TGFβ3 were also elevated. Spatial transcriptomics localized these changes to granulomas. Intersecting differentially expressed genes identified 1293 GM‑specific upregulated genes and 256 downregulated genes; the upregulated genes were mainly expressed by macrophages in granulomas and strongly correlated with disease activity markers. CHIT1 was the most overexpressed gene at both RNA and protein levels. Machine‑learning models built on these gene sets achieved near‑perfect classification of GM (SVM AUC 99.6 %, accuracy 98.6 %). The transcriptomic profile mirrors pathways reported in sarcoidosis and suggests potential therapeutic targets such as TNF, IL1 and JAK/STAT inhibition. Limitations include lack of infectious or genetic granulomatous cases and validation only for CHIT1 at the protein level. The study provides a GM‑specific transcriptomic signature that can aid diagnosis and disease monitoring.

The lecture reviews previous material on linear feedback control of the double integrator q¨=u, comparing manual pole placement and optimal minimum‑time control with bounded input. It introduces Pontryagin’s minimum principle as a necessary condition for optimality and explains the use of Lagrange multipliers to convert the constrained problem into an unconstrained one. The lecture then presents dynamic programming as an alternative solution technique, deriving the recursive Bellman equation and showing how the principle of optimality leads to a discrete‑time cost‑to‑go recursion. Taking the continuous‑time limit yields the Hamilton‑Jacobi‑Bellman (HJB) equation, which together with a sufficiency theorem provides sufficient conditions for optimal control. For quadratic cost functions the HJB reduces to a Riccati differential equation whose solution gives a time‑varying linear feedback law u=−K(t)x; in the infinite‑horizon case K becomes constant and the controller is obtained by solving an algebraic Riccati equation (the LQR problem). The lecture applies these results to the double‑integrator example, computing a quadratic value function S and the resulting controller, and notes that while Pontryagin works for bang‑bang policies with non‑smooth value functions, the HJB approach requires smooth value functions.

Femtosecond pulsed-laser irradiation (λ=343 nm, τp=238 fs) was used to form laser-induced periodic surface structures (LIPSS) on Nb thin films (~190 nm thick). LIPSS evolve gradually with increasing pulse energy, achieving periodicity Λ≈260 nm aligned perpendicular to laser polarization, and cause lattice parameter reduction (~1.05%), grain size increase, and film thickness decrease. Critical temperature Tc decreases from 8.93 K to 8.53 K and upper critical field Hc2 decreases isotropically with full LIPSS coverage, correlating with lattice compression. Transport and inductive measurements reveal anisotropic critical current density: higher along LIPSS (Jc∥) than perpendicular (Jc⊥), with anisotropy ratio increasing with temperature and saturating at low fields, collapsing to unity near Hc2. Time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau simulations confirm that thickness undulations (~70–80 nm deep) pin vortices in valleys, enhancing Jc∥ by ~2 times, and explain non-monotonic field dependence via collective-to-individual vortex hopping transitions. Laser patterning enables tailored anisotropic superconducting properties for device applications.

PHIVE is a physics-informed deep learning framework for rapid metabolite quantification in whole-brain MRSI, offering simultaneous uncertainty estimation. It uses a variational autoencoder with a convolutional encoder and physics-informed decoder, trained unsupervised via ELBO minimization. The method processes whole-brain MRSI data in 6 ms, representing a six-order-of-magnitude speedup over LCModel (2 hours), while achieving comparable accuracy across metabolites (tNAA, Glx, tCho, mIns, Tau, GSH) as evidenced by strong correlations (R² 0.27–0.86) and lower CVs for Glx and mIns. PHIVE provides CRLB, epistemic, and aleatoric uncertainty maps, with higher uncertainty in low-SNR regions. It incorporates a conditional baseline approach allowing adjustable baseline stiffness via a K parameter. Training used 12 healthy subjects (8 training, 4 testing) at 7T. Limitations include lack of ground truth, small sample size, no frequency correction preprocessing, lower correlations for tCho and mIns, and interpretability concerns. Future work should address these limitations and validate across diverse datasets.

Maintaining a healthy weight, staying active and strengthening the muscles around the knee (hamstrings, quads, glutes, hip flexors) help prevent knee injury. Keeping supporting muscles flexible improves range of motion and balance, while low‑impact cardio such as cycling or swimming promotes blood flow to ligaments and cartilage, reducing wear‑and‑tear. Early physiotherapy and specific exercises (e.g., quad sets, bridges, wall squats, hamstring and hip flexor stretches) can restore mobility, limit re‑injury and often avoid surgery. Ignoring knee pain and remaining inactive can worsen damage; physiotherapy may also prepare the body for surgery if needed. When knee damage becomes severe, surgery—including total or partial knee replacement—is a common, effective procedure that can last decades, with modern replacements often functioning for 25 years. Post‑operative physiotherapy speeds recovery and protects the new joint. Genetics and age contribute to knee deterioration, but healthy lifestyle habits can limit cumulative wear.

This study investigates behavioral changes in frontotemporal dementia (FTD), comparing behavioral-variant FTD (bvFTD) and semantic dementia (SD). The research addressed two main questions: whether behavioral profiles differ qualitatively between bvFTD and SD, and what specific roles the prefrontal cortex and anterior temporal lobes (ATL) play in social behavior.

The study included 47 FTD patients (26 bvFTD, 21 SD) and 18 healthy controls. Participants completed informant questionnaires (CBI-R, CamQUAIT, AMI-CG), neuropsychological assessments, and structural MRI scans. A transdiagnostic approach was used, treating FTD as a spectrum rather than relying solely on categorical diagnoses.

Key findings include: behavioral changes were common in both bvFTD and SD, but bvFTD patients showed more severe impairments across most domains (apathy, abnormal behaviors, eating habits, everyday skills, self-care). No behavioral "double dissociations" were found—meaning no specific behaviors were more prevalent in SD compared to bvFTD. Instead, differences were quantitative and unidirectional (bvFTD > SD).

Neuropsychological measures of semantic memory and executive function were better at discriminating between bvFTD and SD (AUC = 95.1%) than behavioral measures. Semantic memory was most predictive (AUC = 84.1%), followed by executive function (78.8%) and apathy (78.5%).

Principal component analysis of behavioral data revealed three dimensions: apathy, challenging behaviors, and activities of daily living (ADLs). Apathy was associated with impaired executive function and reduced grey matter in the anterior cingulate cortex in both bvFTD and SD. No association was found between behavioral changes and social-semantic knowledge or ATL volume.

The study supports the controlled social-semantic cognition (CS-SC) framework, proposing that impaired social behavior in FTD results from damage to two interactive components: ATL-based social-semantic knowledge and prefrontal-based social control. However, behavioral questionnaires appeared more sensitive to prefrontal deficits than ATL-related semantic changes.

Regarding the "right temporal variant FTD," the study suggests SD should be viewed as a unitary-yet-graded disorder encompassing both left-dominant and right-dominant variants, as both groups showed bilateral ATL atrophy and overlapping behavioral profiles.

The research highlights the importance of informant reports for assessing behavioral changes, given the discrepancy between patient self-ratings and caregiver ratings of apathy, particularly in bvFTD.

4 Verticals is a passing concept that sends all four receivers vertically to create 1‑on‑1 matchups and exploit open zones, stretching the defense both vertically and horizontally. It works best against man coverage and Cover 3 by targeting seams and voids, but struggles against Cover 4 and soft zone defenses where timing is critical and windows are small. Receivers have specific landmarks: X and Z run go routes, the slot attacks the seam or crosses the field depending on safety alignment, the tight end occupies the boundary two yards outside the hash, and the tailback provides check‑down protection. The quarterback must read the number of safeties, look off deep safeties, and follow a three‑step progression: pre‑snap identification, post‑snap 1‑on‑1/void, then check‑down to the back. Variations include a 3×1 set that isolates the X receiver by forcing a free‑safety decision and an empty formation with a shallow‑crossing back for blitz protection.

Tesla’s energy storage line, marketed under the Tesla Energy brand, includes the 7 kWh and 10 kWh Powerwall for residential use and the 100 kWh Powerpack for commercial/utility applications; production started in the third quarter of 2015. Manufacturing is conducted at facilities in Fremont and Lathrop, California; Tilburg, Netherlands; and the Gigafactory near Reno, Nevada, which will produce lithium‑ion cells and battery packs for vehicles and energy products, with full capacity expected in 2020 (targeting ~500,000 vehicles per year and 50 GWh of battery capacity). The company distributes its vehicles through a global network of 208 company‑owned stores, galleries and service‑plus locations, and operates 584 Supercharger stations and over 1,800 destination charging locations. Tesla sells directly to consumers and offers financing and leasing programs, including resale‑value guarantees. It operates as a single reportable segment. As of January 31 2016, 132,056,338 shares of common stock were outstanding; the aggregate market value of voting stock held by non‑affiliates was $26.3 billion as of June 30 2015. Tesla employed 13,058 full‑time employees as of year‑end 2015. Key risks described include potential delays in ramping production of Model X and Model 3, reliance on single‑source suppliers, consumer adoption of electric vehicles, competition, regulatory and incentive changes, currency fluctuations, and challenges associated with the Gigafactory and international expansion.

During finals season (Dec. 12-20), Lehigh University students struggle to find study spaces as libraries fill up quickly. FML remains open 24 hours during exams, with extended hours at Packard Lab, University Center, Rauch and Williams. Students like Grant Cummings ('19) prefer academic buildings for quiet study environments, while Rachael Grobman ('19) saves seats for friends in FML. This Statistical Analysis Plan outlines methods for analyzing ECG (including QTcF interval thresholds) and immunogenicity (ADA occurrence, including treatment‑induced and treatment‑boosted cases). It details changes to the primary efficacy analysis and secondary efficacy terminology. Appendix A specifies formatting rules for tables, figures, and listings, including handling of missing data and variable derivations. Appendix B describes SAS programming quality control requirements, covering program, log, output, and dataset verification. Appendix C lists the tables, figures, and listings to be generated for the study.

Growing evidence suggests ultra‑processed foods are engineered to be hyper‑palatable and provoke brain responses similar to those caused by addictive substances such as alcohol, nicotine and opioids. Studies show these foods can trigger cravings, loss of control, withdrawal and tolerance, with about 14 % of adults and 12 % of children meeting criteria for food addiction on the Yale Food Addiction Scale. Over half of the calories consumed by Americans come from ultra‑processed products, which the NOVA classification defines as foods largely devoid of whole‑food ingredients and containing numerous additives. Researchers argue that the design of these products undermines personal choice and are calling for policy measures such as warning labels, taxes on unhealthy items, marketing restrictions and bans in schools; Chile’s front‑of‑package labeling has already reduced purchases of sugary, salty and fatty foods. While some companies are reformulating products and foods tailored for GLP‑1 users are emerging, experts emphasize that effective solutions require stronger regulation rather than placing responsibility solely on individuals.

The 2018 Nuclear Posture Review outlines US plans to modernize its nuclear arsenal, including new low-yield weapons and a sea-launched cruise missile, to counter threats from Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran while maintaining deterrence and alliance commitments.

Finance Minister Bill Morneau announced a two‑year agreement giving provinces and territories 75 per cent of tax revenues from legalized marijuana, with Ottawa retaining 25 per cent up to a $100 million annual cap and any excess flowing to provinces. Municipalities will receive a portion of the provincial share, with each province deciding how much to pass on. The federal government projects about $400 million in revenue over the first two years and will review the framework in December 2018. Original 50‑50 split rejected; provinces may add markup above tax rate. Ottawa has committed over $1 billion over five years for policing and border security. Ministers also discussed equalization formula changes, the three‑year CPP review, global economic conditions and a national strategy to share corporate ownership data to combat tax evasion, money laundering and terrorist financing. All 14 jurisdictions at the table agreed to the key principles.

The speaker acknowledges the weight of the oath and outlines the major policies he intends to pursue. He will continue and enforce the reforms aimed at curbing the lawlessness of railroads and large industrial combinations, seeking relief from certain antitrust restrictions for railroads while urging federal supervision of securities issuance. He plans to reorganize the Department of Justice, the Bureau of Corporations and the Interstate Commerce Commission to improve enforcement of interstate commerce and antitrust laws and will propose specific amendments to those laws.  

On the tariff, an extra session of Congress is called for March to revise the Dingley Act, with the goal of securing adequate revenue, establishing protective duties that equal the difference between foreign and domestic production costs, and including a maximum tariff provision for countries with inequitable trade practices; the revision must be enacted promptly to avoid business disruption and no other legislation should be attempted at that session. The current fiscal deficit—receipts falling short of expenditures by about $100 million—requires a tariff that yields sufficient revenue, and if duties are insufficient a graduated inheritance tax is recommended.  

Expenditure policy stresses avoiding both waste and the cutting of essential functions; priorities include scientific agriculture, railway and industrial supervision, conservation of resources, completion of the Panama Canal and adequate national defense. The army must be capable of rapid expansion in emergencies and fortifications are being completed; the navy must be built in advance of need, and defense spending should not be sacrificed for economy. International policy favors peace, arbitration and the Hague Tribunal but maintains military preparedness to protect American interests, especially in the Orient, and to back diplomatic assertions with force.  

Immigration matters include treaty‑based restrictions on Asian immigrants, efforts to reduce friction, and a commitment to enforce treaty obligations for aliens federally rather than leaving enforcement to states. Monetary and banking reform will be guided by a commission studying currency elasticity to prevent panic, and a postal‑savings bank bill will be pushed to encourage small savings without harming existing banks. Foreign trade promotion includes free trade with the Philippines (subject to sugar and tobacco limits), direct steamship lines to South America, and use of the tariff’s maximum/minimum features to remove European market restrictions.  

The Panama Canal, a lock‑type canal, is under construction by a board led by Colonel Goethals with satisfactory progress and expected completion early in the next administration. Dependencies in Porto Rico and the Philippines are progressing; free trade with the Philippines should improve its business conditions while preserving civil liberty and increasing popular control.  

Regarding race relations, the speaker hopes for greater political tolerance in the South, anticipates that electoral qualifications will be brought into line with the Fifteenth Amendment, and stresses industrial education and self‑improvement for African‑Americans; appointments of Negro officials should be made judiciously to avoid increasing race feeling while encouraging progress.  

Labor legislation will continue to be supported, including employer liability laws, safety device requirements, child‑labor rules and arbitration for railroads; the courts’ power to issue injunctions in labor disputes must be upheld, the secondary boycott opposed, and statutory conditions for temporary restraining orders are recommended to prevent abuse. The speaker concludes by asking for the considerate sympathy and aid of citizens and divine assistance in discharging his duties.

ANU and Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris studied alumino-silicate glass, commonly used in phone screens like Gorilla Glass in Samsung Galaxy S8. Researchers found that sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium atoms form clusters or percolation channels at the nanometer scale, contrary to the belief that they are randomly distributed. These microscopic arrangements influence glass flexibility and fracture resistance, potentially allowing manufacturers to develop more shatter-proof screens. ANU plans to partner with industry to apply these findings. Current smartphones like iPhone X and Samsung Note 8 have durability challenges, with drop tests showing vulnerability to damage. Samsung is also developing foldable devices.

South Africa is expected to keep its investment‑grade rating from Moody’s after President Cyril Ramaphosa’s rise, with the rand and business confidence recovering. However, risks remain: missing budget targets, slower growth, and constitutional changes allowing expropriation without compensation. A downgrade to junk would remove South Africa from Citigroup’s World Government Bond Index, potentially triggering outflows of up to 100 billion rand and raising borrowing costs as the country seeks up to $3 billion internationally. S&P and Fitch already rate South Africa’s debt as junk.

The passage describes a study developing AMR-EnsembleNet, a machine learning framework for predicting antimicrobial resistance in E. coli. AMR threatens global health and could cause 10 million deaths annually by 2050, with slow traditional diagnostics contributing to the crisis. The researchers developed a synergistic ensemble combining a lightweight 1D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), which learns local SNP motifs, with an XGBoost model that captures non-local feature interactions. They used the GieSSen dataset comprising 809 E. coli isolates with SNP profiles tested against four antibiotics (Ciprofloxacin, Cefotaxime, Ceftazidime, and Gentamicin). The ensemble achieved robust performance, particularly excelling on imbalanced datasets where it improved recall for resistant cases while maintaining balanced precision. For example, on the highly imbalanced Gentamicin dataset, the ensemble achieved the highest Matthews Correlation Coefficient (0.4030) and Macro F1-score (0.6908) by combining the CNN's high recall with XGBoost's precision. SHAP analysis validated biological relevance by identifying key SNPs in known AMR-associated genes such as gyrB, parC, rpsL, and ampC. The study demonstrates that hybrid approaches combining sequence-aware deep learning with traditional ML can effectively predict antibiotic resistance while providing interpretable genetic insights.

Saskatoon proposes a $1.2‑million plan to remove and replace 1,000 ash trees damaged by tree‑lice (cottony ash psyllids) with other species. Residents can detect the pest by white cotton on leaves and leaf discoloration.

Electrospun polyacrylonitrile (PAN) nanofiber yarns were fabricated using a dual‑syringe electrospinning setup and then densified by liquid‑assisted rolling with water or ethanol, followed by drying and, for a subset, a 110 °C anneal. Tensile testing showed that both liquid treatments raised yarn strength relative to as‑spun controls; water‑rolled yarns attained the highest peak stresses while retaining moderate ductility, ethanol‑rolled yarns were intermediate, and heat‑treated yarns reached the greatest stiffness but fractured at smaller strains. SEM‑based image analysis (Fourier and OrientationJ) revealed that liquid rolling improved fiber alignment (coherency factor) and increased in‑plane packing density. Statistical correlation demonstrated that both alignment and packing density independently predicted peak load (R²≈0.68 and 0.75, respectively), and their combination gave R²≈0.80, indicating synergistic contributions to strength. A stochastic mean‑field constitutive model incorporating Weibull‑distributed recruitment and failure, elastic‑plastic fiber behavior, orientation averaging (ϕ = ⟨cos²θ⟩) and a load‑transfer efficiency factor (ψ) reproduced the observed five‑regime stress–strain response and linked model parameters to the measured microstructural descriptors. Yarns with diameters below ~10 µm approached the mechanical performance of individual PAN nanofibers. The post‑processing routes are simple, scalable and effectively enhance yarn strength by capillary‑driven compaction and improved inter‑fiber adhesion.

Physicists developed a method to self-organize immiscible liquids (oil, water, alcohol) into well-defined layered patterns within confined geometries. Droplets de-mix from the edge inward, forming stripes whose length depends on de-mixing speed, allowing control over emulsion structure. This enables step-wise release of inner droplets and offers potential for developing advanced pharmaceuticals and other products.

In United States v. Verastegui (5th Cir. 2006), the defendant appealed his 120-month sentences for felon in possession of a firearm and unlawful reentry, arguing they were unreasonable because they exceeded the advisory guideline range of 63–78 months and were based on improper departure factors and a guideline calculation error. The district court imposed the higher sentence using an upward departure under U.S.S.G. § 4A1.3 and a variance under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a). The Fifth Circuit affirmed, finding no abuse of discretion and that the challenges were foreclosed by circuit precedent. The defendant’s constitutional challenges to 18 U.S.C. § 922(g) and 8 U.S.C. § 1326(b) were also rejected as foreclosed by precedent.

Nuclear force binds nucleons in nuclei as a residual strong interaction between quarks in different hadrons. Its full theory is challenging due to many particles; a mean‑field approach is used. Experimental evidence comes from nucleon‑nucleon scattering (including spin‑polarized beams), precise binding‑energy and mass measurements, and nuclear‑structure data (energy levels, spins, moments), especially for light nuclei. The force depends on the distance between nucleons, their spin and orbital angular momentum (spin‑orbit and tensor components), and is charge‑independent, i.e., it does not distinguish protons from neutrons. The interaction is short‑range: attractive for separations up to ~2 fm and strongly repulsive below ~0.5 fm. This short‑range nature explains the roughly constant binding energy per nucleon. Charge independence is verified by comparing proton‑proton, neutron‑neutron and neutron‑proton scattering and is applied to mirror nuclei (e.g., helium‑3 and tritium), whose binding energies and excitation spectra are nearly identical after Coulomb effects are removed.

A machine-learned depth estimation model is trained using video data and/or stereoscopic image data to generate depth maps from single color input images. The training process acquires images, extracts depth features and poses using depth and pose models, generates synthetic frames, and calculates loss using an input scale occlusion and motion aware loss function based on photometric reconstruction error between synthetic and input images. The system handles monocular video by projecting temporally adjacent images and stereoscopic pairs by projecting between left and right images. The loss function incorporates upsampled depth features and masks to discount static features. Once trained, the model receives an input image and outputs a depth map. The depth estimation technology is applied within a parallel reality gaming system where players interact with virtual elements mapped to real-world locations.

In July 2015 New Horizons performed the first Pluto flyby, after which its mission was extended to explore Kuiper Belt Objects. The spacecraft’s next target is 2014 MU69, which will be the most distant and primitive object ever visited, orbiting about 1.6 billion km beyond Pluto. Occultation observations in 2017 suggested MU69 could be an extreme prolate spheroid or a close/contact binary. A public naming campaign hosted by the SETI Institute in November 2017 involved ~115,000 participants who submitted ~34,000 names; 37 reached a final ballot. After a five‑day extension, voting closed on Dec 6 2017 and “Ultima Thule” was selected as the working nickname, reflecting a name beyond Thule that symbolizes unprecedented exploration. The name is temporary; a formal IAU designation will be submitted after the flyby, depending on whether MU69 is a single body, a binary, or multiple objects.

Two large exome-sequencing studies of clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) in 454,803 UK Biobank and 173,585 Geisinger participants identified 27 common variant loci (24 novel) and multiple rare variant loci associated with CHIP and its subtypes. CHIP prevalence rises sharply with age and heavy smoking and is linked to increased risks of blood cancers, lung cancer, and all-cause mortality, with genetic risk profiles and clinical associations varying by CHIP gene subtype.

Attacking runs in soccer are off‑the‑ball movements by a teammate into open space in the opponent’s half to receive a pass. About six players on an attacking team should constantly seek to make penetrating runs; they typically involve forwards, strikers, and leading midfielders. Runs are spontaneous decisions during play, distinguished from designed or planned runs. Recognizing or creating open space is the first key; the ball‑carrier must then see the run and deliver a proper pass. Seven components make an effective run: (1) recognizing open space, (2) choosing an appropriate run, (3) breaking away from a defender, (4) getting open, (5) timing the run, (6) receiving an optimal pass, and (7) communicating. Named runs include bending, checking, diagonal, hooking, inside, lateral, onside, outlet, sideline, straight, through (or split), and wide runs. Breaking away exploits the attacker’s brief head start and the defender’s need to change direction; separation is achieved with abrupt direction changes or sprints and maintained by continuing to the open space. Timing must avoid offside and match the expected pass; if the pass is late the runner can turn parallel to the next‑to‑last defender. A good run is only effective if the ball‑carrier delivers a suitable pass, leading the runner or placing it at his feet. Communication may be oral, visual (hand signals), or eye contact, with oral alerts having the drawback of tipping defenders. Coaching progresses from cone demonstrations to stationary players, limited defenders, then full‑sided play, emphasizing rewarding runs with passes, staying involved, and using give‑and‑go and support runs.

The Clock Offense is a basketball strategy designed to attack the Diamond & One defense by positioning the Star player in the middle and using a 1-3-1 zone formation. This offense creates open shots, lay-ups, and offensive putbacks while isolating the Star player against a less prepared defender. Key elements include Corner Pass & Cut, Ball Reversal, Dribble Clear, and High Post Triangle Action, which generate passing lanes and scoring opportunities. The offense relies on continuous movement, player rotation, and exploiting defensive mismatches. Successful implementation requires coordination, timing, and anticipation of defensive adjustments. It also emphasizes offensive rebounding to capitalize on second efforts and maintain pressure on the defense.

The education sector spends billions designing programs but almost nothing creating the stories that help people understand them, causing good ideas to stall. Without a clear narrative, communities interpret reforms through familiar defaults: top‑down control, data as danger, technology as a substitute for teachers. An example shows a school‑board meeting rejecting an AI pilot because its story failed. The authors argue this is a design problem at the start, not a communications fix at the end, and propose a “Frame → Test → Iterate → Scale” process: clarify the core story, map audience mindsets, test values‑based metaphors and explanations, co‑design with teachers, parents and students, and package tools for others. Key recommendations include leading with shared values, using tested metaphors, explaining mechanisms, centering humans, naming and neutralizing risks, and avoiding “silver‑bullet,” crisis‑only or us‑vs‑them framings. Trust is rebuilt by involving communities in authoring narratives, demonstrating transparent safeguards, and delivering early benefits. The authors conclude that narrative prototyping must be funded and placed on the critical path alongside product or policy development so good ideas can be understood, trusted, and adopted.

The Texas Supreme Court has issued a tentative opinion that the American Bar Association should no longer have final authority over law school graduates' eligibility for the Texas bar exam. While the court hasn't decided the matter, conservative figures including Education Secretary Linda McMahon have argued the ABA has too much power and needs competition. The court has no plans to impose additional accreditation burdens but may consider alternative accrediting entities in the future. The court has requested public comments on the proposal by Dec. 1, with changes potentially taking effect in January. The ABA is reviewing the implications and plans to submit comments.

The Las Vegas Aces lead the Phoenix Mercury 3‑0 in the WNBA Finals and can clinch their third championship in Game 4 on Friday (8 p.m. ET, ESPN). In Game 3 the Aces erased a 17‑point deficit to win 90‑88, with A’ja Wilson scoring 34 points and grabbing 14 rebounds. An Akure‑based lawyer and rights activist, Morakinyo Ogele, has given the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) a seven‑day ultimatum to publicly apologise to the Sun Newspaper for invading its premises and to pay N1 billion in compensation.

Police in Guilford and Milford, Connecticut have issued warnings to lock car doors after dozens of vehicles have been targeted each night along the shoreline. Young adults or juveniles working in groups are breaking into cars and sometimes stealing vehicles when keys are left inside. Officers say the thieves drive recklessly when fleeing, posing public safety concerns. Milford police are also investigating break-ins and searching for two suspects who allegedly used stolen credit cards. Residents are advised to lock doors, keep outdoor lights on, and report suspicious activity to 911.

Despite executing well defensively with good gap control and stick positioning, the team was disappointed with the result. US stock indexes fell significantly last week, with the S&P 500 closing at its lowest level since early July, driven by renewed trade war fears after Trump announced 100% tariffs on China. The VIX rose to its highest since June, and crude oil prices declined following an OPEC+ production hike. Analysts suggest a potential correction or consolidation, advising investors to consider defensive positioning due to macro and valuation risks.

Two calculations determine output capacitance: one for allowable voltage deviation (2.5% of Vout) and one for ripple (2% of Vout); the larger is used, requiring at least 1.3 mF, with temperature, aging, and DC bias derating. Space‑grade designs may need extra capacitance for SETs; an example used ≈2.3 mF. An optional secondary filter (inductor plus ceramic cap) can reduce noise; its resonant frequency must be above the crossover frequency but below the switching frequency and bulk‑cap ESR zero, and a damping resistor suppresses peaking. Overcurrent limiting begins at ≈35 A, providing ~45% margin over the 24.25 A peak inductor current; primary current is sensed at CS_ILIM with a 1:100 sense transformer, and equations determine the required sense resistor (RCS).

Japan’s Antarctic hunt caught 333 minke whales, 122 pregnant, 114 not adult. In 2014 ICJ ruled the program a commercial front, prompting Japan to cut its quota from 900 to 333 and claim it studies minke populations.

Congress’s scheduled meeting in Philadelphia was considered for relocation due to a contagious sickness, but was postponed after hopes arose that it could safely convene there; the speaker suggests a legal amendment to authorize postponement. The nation expresses gratitude for internal peace, favorable seasons, agriculture, fisheries, civil and religious liberty, and a firm resolve to defend sovereignty. Two envoys to the French Republic reached Holland and proceeded to Paris; the speaker trusts the negotiation will end equitably. Commerce is vital to the United States’ comfort, growth, and prosperity, and the speaker urges protection of commerce and national defense as essential for peace and justice. The treaty with Spain for withdrawal of its troops and demarcation of the boundary has not been fulfilled; Spanish garrisons remain and the line has not been run, affecting Indian relations. Foreign agents are working to alienate Indian tribes and incite hostilities; counter‑measures are in place, but additional legislation for punishment may be needed. Commissioners under the 5th article of the British treaty examined the St. Croix River, require surveys, and have adjourned to Boston and then Providence. Commissioners under the 6th article on British debts and under the 7th article on captures have heard cases; awards have been paid, and further claims are being arbitrated. A commission under the 21st article of the Spanish treaty has examined Spanish‑related loss claims, with sittings resumed. The United States must provide funds to meet treaty‑based compensation obligations. Captures by French and Spanish cruisers have generated expenses and left seamen destitute; consuls have advanced money and seek reimbursement, prompting a need to revise the consular act, including authority to inspect ship registers. The House is urged to consider the national debt and taxes, emphasizing immediate taxation over loans. The speaker calls for unity and wisdom amid Europe’s turbulent situation.

In July 2001, news reports covered Enron's involvement in multiple energy-related issues. California officials investigated conflict of interest involving state consultants who bought stock in power companies. The London Metal Exchange fined Enron Metals $264,000 for serious rule breaches. A California Senate committee planned to drop a contempt charge against Enron as it agreed to provide information for a market manipulation probe. Terremark Worldwide warned of significant losses and auditors' going-concern doubts. The passage describes defensive strategies to counter the Power Offense, which relies on continuous screening. Key methods include "Show and Recover" to avoid switching and "All Out SOS Disruption" involving wing traps and rotations to disrupt the offense's planned routes.

The team reached the Stanley Cup Finals but did not win, expressing disappointment. Goaltender Bryan and coach Mike were praised for their roles, and the organization noted significant improvement, with plans to return.

Quantum‑correlated phonon pairs are key resources for quantum computation, communication, and metrology. Entangled pairs have been shown with photons and matter qubits, and phonons are promising carriers due to coherent coupling to systems. Recent advances in surface acoustic wave platforms have shown nonclassical phonon states, but optical generation remains difficult due to weak optomechanical coupling and limited high‑order nonlinearity. This work introduces a method using an optomechanical crystal nanobeam cavity where Stokes and anti‑Stokes interactions simultaneously create a degenerate phonon pair via four‑wave mixing, retrieved by a red‑detuned pulse and verified by the Cauchy‑Schwarz inequality.

The TPS7H500x‑SP series are radiation‑hardened, fixed‑frequency, peak‑current‑mode PWM controllers for space‑grade DC‑DC converters. They support switching frequencies up to 2 MHz and can be used in buck, flyback, forward, active‑clamp forward, push‑pull and full‑bridge topologies. The controllers regulate peak current and duty cycle by comparing a sensed switch current with the voltage at the COMP pin; the internal oscillator initiates turn‑on of the primary output which drives external gate drivers.

A design example for a synchronous push‑pull converter using GaN semiconductors is described. Key design parameters include a 500 kHz switching frequency, 5 V output, RT resistor of 205 kΩ, feedback divider resistors RTOP = 10 kΩ and RBOT = 1.4 kΩ, dead‑time of ~25 ns (RPS = RSP = 20.5 kΩ), leading‑edge blank time of ~50 ns (RLEB = 49.9 kΩ), soft‑start capacitor of 33 nF (~7.5 ms soft‑start time), transformer turns ratio of 2.5 and primary inductance of 40 µH, main switching FETs rated at 170 V, synchronous rectifier FETs rated at 80 V with a parallel Schottky diode, an RCD clamp circuit, output inductor of 0.47 µH, minimum output capacitance of 1.3 mF (total 2.3 mF to mitigate single‑event transients), optional LC output filter, over‑current limit set at ~35 A (sense resistor 7.5 Ω), hiccup capacitor of 3.3 nF, Type 2A compensation with RCOMP = 40.2 kΩ, CCOMP = 15 nF, CHF = 47 pF, and slope‑compensation resistor of 102 kΩ.

Power‑supply recommendations specify an input range of 4 V to 14 V with at least 0.1 µF bypass capacitance close to the device. Layout guidelines advise separating analog and power grounds, minimizing high‑di/dt switching loops, routing feedback away from noise sources, using short wide high‑current traces, placing bypass and compensation components near the controller, and for CFP packages connecting the backside metallization to AVSS with multiple vias.

The datasheet includes PCB layout examples for CFP and TSSOP packages, references to evaluation modules and radiation‑test reports, and provides ordering and mechanical packaging information.

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) uses Kikuchi patterns to determine crystal symmetry, phase, and orientation. Direct electron detectors (DEDs) offer higher detection quantum efficiency and modulation transfer function than indirect detectors, but hybrid pixel detectors (HPDs) have larger pixel pitch (>25 µm) limiting angular resolution. This study applies a sub-pixel shift-and-add algorithm to create super-resolution EBSD patterns by combining multiple images with sub-pixel offsets. Using a TruePix detector with 256×256 pixels and 55 µm pitch on a silicon single crystal at 20 keV, experiments compared standard exposure, increased exposure, frame integration, and camera retraction methods. Signal-to-noise ratio analysis showed improvement plateaus at longer exposures, while the super-resolution method increases signal-to-noise from 30 to 70 for 1-second effective exposure. The reconstructed pattern matches camera retraction quality and BWKD simulation, revealing detailed higher order Laue zone rings and fine band structure. The method requires no hardware modifications and can improve pattern analysis for indexing, strain measurements, and addressing pseudosymmetry challenges.

The report provides an overview of newcomer education in California and offers recommendations to improve student outcomes, based on a special data request to the California Department of Education, interviews with staff from 12 districts, and a literature review. “Newcomers” refers to students recently arrived in U.S. schools, with definitions ranging from the first 6 months to four years of enrollment; most have limited English, many are socioeconomically disadvantaged, and a significant but unknown proportion have experienced trauma. Newcomers differ from typical English learners, who generally possess functional English and focus on academic language development.

Key terminology includes Title III Immigrant Students (aged 3–21, not born in a U.S. state, and with fewer than three years of U.S. schooling); Students With Interrupted Formal Education (SIFE), who are at least two years behind grade level; refugees and asylees; undocumented students; and unaccompanied undocumented minors. These groups have distinct legal and educational rights.

Federal court rulings—Lau v. Nichols (1974), Castañeda v. Pickard (1981), and Plyler v. Doe (1982)—guarantee English learner and immigrant minors the right to a free, appropriately tailored public education. While most California districts comply with Lau and Plyler, many may fail the Castañeda three‑prong test for adequate English learner instruction, often due to insufficient resources and expertise.

Data show that during the 2020‑21 school year California had 151,996 Title III Immigrant Students, representing 2.5 % of the K‑12 population. About 67 % of newcomers are socioeconomically disadvantaged, and 58 % attend schools in five urban counties (Los Angeles, Orange, San Diego, Alameda, Santa Clara). Language diversity is high: Spanish is the home language for 43 % of newcomers, followed by English (9 %), Mandarin (6 %), Vietnamese (4 %), and many other languages. Approximately nine in ten newcomers are likely classified as English learners, yet they have dramatically lower English proficiency than the typical English learner. Newcomer enrollment is distributed across the state, with half of districts enrolling fewer than 21 newcomers. SIFE data are unavailable statewide; estimates suggest between 40,000 and 225,000 SIFE may exist in California.

Funding context: California ranks 33rd nationally in per‑pupil expenditure and 43rd in funding effort, resulting in the nation’s highest teacher‑to‑student ratio (22:1). The Local Control Funding Formula (LCFF) provides base grants for all students, supplemental grants (20 % above base) for high‑needs students, and concentration grants (50 % above base) for districts with more than 55 % high‑needs enrollment. Newcomers often qualify as high‑needs but are not double‑counted for both English‑learner and socioeconomic status. State‑funded programs include CalNEW ($5 million annually) for wraparound services and community liaisons, and the Opportunities for Youth (OFY) pilot ($9.7 million) for unaccompanied undocumented minors. Federal funding includes Title III (~$142.7 million total in 2022‑23), with a 3.9 % set‑aside (~$5.6 million) for the Title III Immigrant Student Program, but only 34,041 newcomers (22 % of the total) received these funds because the grant’s growth requirement excluded many districts. Refugee School Impact (RSI) grants support refugee students; California received $2.3 million for 5,643 refugees, $9 million for Afghan students, and additional funds for Ukrainian students.

Effective schooling combines specialized instruction, modified schedules, extended learning time, integrated language and content instruction, translanguaging, collaboration, and oral language development. Curricula for newcomers are insufficient; educators need training, planning time, and resources. Social‑emotional learning, welcoming environments, cultural orientation, and social programs (e.g., sports, leadership councils) foster belonging and success. Robust intake processes, transcript articulation, and partnerships with community organizations address academic, legal, material, and mental‑health needs. Programs such as the Internationals Network for Public Schools demonstrate scalable, evidence‑based models.

Recommendations emphasize collaborative, multisector efforts: establish state leadership capacity and institutionalize collaboration between the California Department of Education and the Department of Social Services; include newcomers and SIFE as distinct groups in state data systems; codify and continue the OFY initiative; adjust LCFF funding for late‑arriving newcomers; involve the Instructional Quality Commission in addressing newcomers in curriculum frameworks; invest in open‑source curricula and instructional resources; support research on language acquisition, pedagogy, and outcomes; and advocate for federal action to include newcomers in national data systems and revise the Title III Immigrant Student Program’s growth requirement. The report argues that modest, targeted investments could yield outsized improvements in practice and outcomes for California’s newcomer students.

Red Same, Red Opposite, and Red Rover are SOS half‑court defensive disruptions that trap the ballhandler near the sideline hash mark while non‑trapping players form a Triangle I. Rotations begin as the ball leaves the passer’s hands, and each scenario concludes with either a pre‑selected “Base Go Red” or “Base Go I” formation determined by the coach. In Red Same, X1 and X3 initiate the trap; in Red Opposite, X1 and X2 trap together. Red Rover designates X4 (Red Rover 4) or X5 (Red Rover 5) to trap with X1. After the ball is passed out, defenders close out, take SNUGGLE denial positions, assume low or high Triangle I spots, and adjust to the ballhandler’s actions such as penetration to the free‑throw line or feeding the low post.

Astronomers detected the exoplanet MOA‑2016‑BLG‑227Lb via gravitational microlensing. The planet has a mass of about 2.8 Jupiter masses (~3× Jupiter) and orbits an M or K dwarf in the Galactic bulge at ~1.67 AU; the host star mass is ~0.29 M☉. The microlensing event was observed on 5 May 2016 with the MOA‑II 1.8 m telescope and later followed up using UKIRT, CFHT, Keck II, VST and Wise telescopes, including the K2 C9 campaign. The detection was made by a team led by Naoki Koshimoto of Osaka University. The planet/host mass ratio is q≈9×10⁻³. Analysis excludes a G‑dwarf host, confirming a super‑Jupiter around a low‑mass star. Further observations with HST, Keck AO, JWST, GMT, TMT and ELT are proposed.

Backtesting evaluates trading strategies by applying them to historical data to assess potential effectiveness, risk, and profitability without risking real capital. It requires high-quality, comprehensive historical data and must account for trading costs, slippage, and transaction expenses. Key metrics include the Sharpe ratio and Maximum Drawdown. Traders should avoid overfitting by using diverse datasets, out-of-sample testing, and sensitivity analysis. Common biases include look-ahead bias and survivorship bias, which can be addressed by including delisted assets and diverse data. Backtesting cannot guarantee future success as market conditions change. Popular tools include MetaTrader and TrendSpider. Best practices involve validating strategies, incorporating market conditions, and balancing backtesting with real-time analysis.

William Skrainka et al. v. Gerard B. Allen, Supreme Court of Missouri, June 24 1879.  

Plaintiffs obtained a judgment of $10,420.21 against the Illinois and St. Louis Bridge Company and, after an execution returned nulla bona, moved for execution against stock‑holder Allen. The company’s authorized capital was $4 million in $100 shares; $3 million had been subscribed, 40 % paid. In 1869‑70 an agreement with Andrew Carnegie gave stockholders the right to buy first‑mortgage bonds and receive a 20 % bonus of stock. Allen received 75 shares credited with 40 % paid but never paid that amount; he later received second‑mortgage bonds worth $20,612 for additional calls on his shares, which he sold for $15,904.59.  

The court affirmed four principles: (1) creditors are preferred over stockholders and members’ personal profits that would diminish the common fund must be held for the corporation until creditors are satisfied; (2) stockholders who subscribed with an understanding that calls would not exceed a certain percentage, and who later receive second‑mortgage bonds to offset excess calls, are liable to creditors for the unpaid stock to the amount realized from the bond sale; (3) a corporation may not increase its liabilities by issuing second‑mortgage bonds to stockholders without valuable consideration; and (4) in a statutory motion for execution against a stockholder, liability is measured by the number of shares owned at the date the motion is filed (after notice), not at the date the execution against the corporation is returned.  

The Circuit Court had held Allen liable for unpaid stock to the amount he realized from the bond sale; the Supreme Court agreed with that part of the ruling. However, the lower court erred by fixing liability based on the shares held at the return of the execution. The Supreme Court reversed the judgment and remanded the case, holding that liability attaches at the date of the motion and notice.

The 3‑3‑5 defense consists of three defensive linemen, three linebackers and five defensive backs. It is a high‑risk, high‑reward scheme relying on fast athletes, usable as a sub‑package or base alignment. Primary strengths are flexibility and versatility: the same pre‑snap shell can disguise Cover 1 or Cover 3, add a fourth rusher from stacked linebackers or overhangs, and adapt to formations. It requires smaller, quicker athletes; coaches often move larger linebackers or backs down to the line. Weaknesses include edge vulnerability, especially to pulling‑guard runs like buck sweep or outside‑zone plays. Offenses attack by throwing into seams, using four verts against Cover 3, and employing trips to reduce box defenders. Common blitzes are the Sam (slanted line with an edge linebacker) and the SAW (two stacked backers with a pinched line). Coverage options include Cover 1 (man with a free safety) and Cover 3 (three deep thirds). Joe Lee Dunn is credited as the inventor; coaches such as Matt Campbell (Iowa State), Tony Gibson (North Carolina State) and Tim Racki (high‑school) have used it, with Racki winning multiple state titles.

The passage describes a patent application for dry electrode films for energy storage devices containing microparticulate non-fibrillizable binders. The electrode films include a dry active material (such as graphite) and a dry binder comprising a fibrillizable binder (typically PTFE) and a microparticulate non-fibrillizable binder with particle sizes of about 0.5-40 μm. The non-fibrillizable binder is typically cellulose or a cellulose derivative such as carboxymethylcellulose (CMC). Jet milling processes reduce non-fibrillizable binder particle sizes (e.g., from ~70 μm to ~10 μm) to achieve more uniform distribution, improved tensile strength, and reduced defects like holes, cracks, and surface pits. The electrode films are self-supporting, free-standing, and solvent-free, suitable for use in lithium ion batteries. Methods of fabrication involve combining dry binders with active materials through high shear and nondestructive mixing processes followed by calendering.
