Markets were briefly rattled by news of inhalation anthrax cases in Washington, D.C., but investors quickly refocused on better‑than‑expected earnings from companies such as American Express, 3M, U.S. Steel and Conoco. Bond yields fell modestly, and the dollar strengthened against the yen while the euro slipped.

Enron Corp. was the day’s biggest decliner, with its shares plunging about 20 % (down $5.40 to $20.65 on the NYSE) after the company disclosed that the Securities and Exchange Commission had requested information on certain related‑party transactions. The SEC inquiry focused on limited partnerships—LJM Cayman LP and LJM2 Co‑Investment LP—that were organized and managed by Enron’s Chief Financial Officer, Andrew Fastow. Enron said it welcomed the request and would cooperate fully; it emphasized that its internal and external auditors, as well as its board, had reviewed and approved the arrangements, which were disclosed in SEC filings.

The inquiry intensified long‑standing concerns about Fastow’s conflicts of interest. The partnerships bought Enron assets, enabling Fastow to earn millions of dollars in management fees and capital gains; The Wall Street Journal reported that Fastow and associates received more than $7 million in fees and about $4 million in profit from a near‑$3 million investment. The deals cost Enron $35 million in the third quarter and forced the company to repurchase 55 million of its own shares to unwind the arrangements, reducing shareholder equity by $1.2 billion. Enron also recorded a $1.01 billion charge in the quarter, resulting in a net loss of $618 million (84 cents per share) versus a profit of $393 million (43 cents per share) excluding the charge.

Enron faced two legal actions filed the same day. A shareholder derivative suit in Texas alleged that the board breached fiduciary duties by allowing Fastow to run the partnerships, causing the company to lose over $35 million. A separate class‑action complaint filed in federal court in Houston accused Enron and several officers of securities fraud, claiming that misrepresentations about the partnerships artificially inflated the stock price during the class period of July 13 to Oct 16 2001. The stock fell more than 20 % in three trading days following disclosure of the losses.

Analysts estimated that dismantling additional affiliated companies could cost Enron up to $3 billion, raising fears of further equity dilution and credit‑rating pressure. Moody’s placed Enron’s debt on watch for a possible downgrade, though its debt remained investment‑grade. The company’s shares touched a low of $19.67, the weakest level since Jan 1998, and were down roughly 75 % for the year.

In economic data, the Conference Board’s index of leading indicators fell 0.5 % in September, the largest drop since early 1996, confirming a deepening economic slowdown. Overseas markets closed higher in London and Frankfurt, while Japan’s Nikkei edged up and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell slightly.

This study simulates the transition from ICE vehicles to BEVs using real-world telematics data from 10,441 users in Asti province, Italy, covering over 10 million trips from October 2023 to September 2024. The researchers tested four BEV models (Fiat 500e, Renault Megane E-Tech, Tesla Model 3, Audi A6 e-tron) with battery capacities ranging from 21.3 to 94.9 kWh, and four charging scenarios: workplace AC charging, low-SoC AC charging, overnight AC charging, and fast DC charging when SoC drops below 25%. Results show current BEV technology suits only part of the population. With the best scenario (Audi A6 e-tron with DC fast charging), 72% of users can complete 100% of trips and 95% are suitable overall, but 5% remain unserved even under optimal conditions. Workplace-only charging performs worst, with the Fiat 500e unsuitable for 93% of users. Overnight charging enables 35% of users to adopt even low-capacity BEVs. The study found that while many users can already transition to BEVs, full electrification cannot yet accommodate all users' mobility needs in the studied population.

IES Holdings, Inc. is a diversified infrastructure services provider operating in 130+ US locations. Its share price has nearly doubled year‑to‑date, outpacing infrastructure and Russell 2000 stocks. While its largest division (residential) faces headwinds, data‑center projects are driving growth in its next two largest divisions. The company's backlog exceeds $2 billion, up roughly 20% year‑over‑year, and it has improved cash flow and record cash balances. Nonetheless, the stock is considered overextended, with a below‑average free‑cash‑flow yield and higher insider selling.

Institute boss Kevin Deery expressed frustration after a third consecutive draw, noting that his side’s last two goals were own goals and they missed several chances, including a long‑range free‑kick that led to Larne’s freak goal. He said decision‑making in both penalty areas is hurting the team, remains optimistic despite being out of luck, and emphasized the side is still in the top six with 13 games left.

The ACC Tournament concluded its two‑year run at Barclays Center with Virginia beating North Carolina 71‑63 in the championship. Brett Yormark hopes to bring the event back. Before the game Virginia coach Tony Bennett quoted Psalm 133, calling the win a healing moment. The top‑ranked Cavaliers, who were picked sixth at the season’s start, shut down UNC to capture the crown. North Carolina also defeated rival Duke in a trilogy game; Duke responded by switching to a zone defense. Duke freshman Marvin Bagley III stood out, reinforcing his status as a possible No. 1 NBA draft pick. Clemson beat Boston College to earn its first NCAA tournament berth in seven years.

On February 6, 2002, multiple congressional committees continued investigating Enron's collapse. Former CEO Jeffrey Skilling was scheduled to testify Thursday, while former Chairman Kenneth Lay had canceled a voluntary appearance and faced subpoenas from multiple committees. Former CFO Andrew Fastow was reportedly in talks with the Justice Department for immunity in exchange for testimony. William Powers, who led Enron's internal investigation, testified that executives used partnerships to hide losses and enrich themselves, and that more than 70 percent of earnings over a 15-month period were false. Arthur Andersen faced criticism for its role in Enron's accounting practices. Labor Secretary Elaine Chao testified about strengthening retirement account protections. Multiple congressional panels were investigating, along with the Justice Department and SEC. Enron filed for bankruptcy December 2, 2001.

The Maui News reported April 17 that County Councilmember and mayor candidate Mike Victorino was the driver in a collision on April 13 at 9:30 p.m. on West Papa Avenue. He struck an 18‑year‑old and a 15‑year‑old, who were injured. Victorino said he was not under the influence or speeding and stopped to wait for police. Police said the pedestrians were not in a crosswalk; the mother of the older teen claimed they were.

Linebackers require toughness, athleticism, and intelligence. They serve as the second line of defense, lining up 3‑5 yards behind the defensive line, and are responsible for aligning the defense, relaying coaches’ calls, and defending both the run and the pass. The position’s name comes from its placement behind the line. Common designations include LB, Sam (strong side), Mike (middle), Will (weak side), and Jack (second middle in a 3‑4 front). Required skills are vision, agility, change of direction, block shedding, explosiveness, tackling, strength, violent hands, and high motor; typical body specs are 5’10”‑6’5”, 215‑255 lbs., lean‑muscular build. Among the best are Ray Lewis (2× Defensive Player of the Year, 2× Super Bowl champion, 13× Pro Bowler, Hall of Fame 2018), Chuck Bednarik (first overall 1949 draft pick, 2× champion, 10× All‑Pro, Hall of Fame 1967), and Lawrence Taylor (2× champion, MVP, 3× Defensive Player of the Year, 132.5 sacks, Hall of Fame 1999). While the value of inside linebackers has decreased as offenses shift to spread attacks, versatile linebackers still create mismatches, allow defenses to pressure or cover, and remain sought after, with 3‑6 selected in first‑round drafts.

The Bank of Canada wants a weaker loonie to aid exporters, while market forces are pushing it higher; on Wednesday the loonie reached about 75.50 U.S. cents, up roughly 2 % from the prior week. Governor Stephen Poloz has signaled the bank dislikes a too‑strong currency. The loonie’s recent volatility reflects mixed signals: oil prices fell below US$45 (down >7 % this month) and the interest‑rate gap is widening (U.S. Fed raised its target to 1.0‑1.25 % while Canada’s rate remains at 0.5 % since July 2015). Strong economic data—3.7 % annualized Q1 growth and recovery from the technical recession—have markets expecting a Bank of Canada rate hike, with CIBC now forecasting one in Q4 rather than 2018.

During a Board of Governors meeting, ASCSU President Josh Silva said students lacked awareness of the new tailgating lot, under‑used it for parking, and outlined rebranding and pre‑game programming plans. Athletics Director Joe Parker reported 37,583 attendees at the first game and 27,038 at the second, noting queuing and concession congestion at the opening that improved in the second. Planning supported transportation. About 50 vehicles were towed from campus lots, half unregistered with CSU; Fort Collins also towed a number. Bicycle and transit usage exceeded forecasts (7,000 vs. 5,000 riders). Post‑event traffic stayed manageable, and the MAX system was heavily used.

The passage describes a study evaluating role-taking and literacy interventions to reduce the influence of demographic and appearance biases (age, gender, ethnicity, attire) on trust and risk-taking in social engineering contexts. An online experiment with Arab participants tested four groups (Persuader, Persuadee, Literacy, Control) using 16 personas in pre/post assessments. Results showed no significant intervention effects on trust or risk-taking; Bayes Factors supported the null hypothesis. Issue of Involvement decreased, indicating reduced engagement. Participant feedback was positive, highlighting increased awareness. The study concludes that while interventions can raise awareness, they may not sufficiently alter deeply ingrained biases, and more immersive or long-term strategies may be needed.

Great Southern Storm has named a 45‑player initial colts squad for the Great Southern Colts Carnival in Kulin next month. Glynn Verbruggen replaces Phil Gilbert as head coach, bringing experience as a former league leading goal scorer and senior coach. The squad includes State‑16 players Heath Spinks and Jacob Blight, and several players who have already featured in State Country colts. North Albany has the highest representation with 12 players, Railways eight, and Albany and Royals seven each. Training is set for 5.30 pm at Railways on June 4 and 11.

District and Sessions Judge Nasir Khan Yousafzai sentenced four convicts in separate murder cases: Shehzado to death with Rs. 200,000 fine under Section 302 PPC; brothers Ajab Khan and Fateh Khan to 25 years imprisonment each with Rs. 200,000 fines; and Dilbar Khan to 25 years imprisonment with Rs. 105,000 fine. Lawyer Samad Khan Mandokhail represented the victims' families.

Allen Iverson, in an interview on ESPN's "First Take," revealed that his lowest point was his divorce from Tawanna Turner in 2013, which he described as self‑inflicted. The divorce, finalized the same year he officially retired from the NBA, prompted a deep self‑reevaluation. Iverson, 50, said he recognized alcohol as a major problem and decided to stop drinking as part of his personal growth. He credited his reconciliation with Turner to persistent effort, joking that he used "a lot of Keith Sweat." His memoir "Misunderstood" chronicles his rapid NBA rise and difficult upbringing. Iverson noted that many current players view him as a role model for allowing them to feel comfortable expressing themselves and expressed optimism about the league's future. The interview was conducted by Stephen A. Smith.

Germany aims to organize Central Europe under its influence to dominate the continent. The U.S. opposes not economic or cultural unification but imperialistic control. Current control rests on an alliance between Berlin, Vienna, Budapest, Sofia, and Constantinople, bound by common interests in subjugating nationalities and debts. The U.S. possesses economic leverage through control of raw materials and markets, and can exploit nationalist discontent in Austria-Hungary to break German control. Policy should involve stirring up nationalist movements while offering Austria-Hungary a path to survival through a league of nations.

Texas public school administrators, parents and education experts worry that a new law replacing the STAAR test with three shorter exams throughout the school year may not reduce student stress and could increase testing time. The law (HB 8) will replace STAAR with beginning, middle and end-of-year tests, ban practice tests, and require faster score releases. Critics say three tests will triple pressure, and accountability ratings will still heavily depend on end-of-year results, creating the same stress with more testing. Education experts note many schools already conduct multiple exams, so the law will "codify what school districts are already doing." The TEA must study how to reduce testing weight on accountability ratings by 2029-30, but findings won't be required to be implemented. Some administrators want relaxed testing protocols and more teacher input in creating the new exams. Schools using programs like MAP exams say those tests cause less anxiety than STAAR, with fewer scheduling restrictions. Supporters say the changes will reduce overall testing time, but critics point to Florida's similar change that didn't reduce total exam minutes. The new testing system launches in 2027-28 school year.

The passage introduces LAPIS, a compiler framework designed to bridge the gap between computational science (CSE) codes written in C++ and machine learning (ML) codes written in Python. Current CSE frameworks like Kokkos prioritize performance and portability but lack productivity, while ML frameworks like PyTorch focus on productivity and portability but require manual interfacing to optimized libraries, limiting architectural support and causing "hardware/software lottery." Interoperability between C++ and Python is cumbersome, requiring significant boilerplate and developer effort.

LAPIS leverages MLIR within the LLVM project to automatically compile Python-based ML code to portable, parallel Kokkos C++ source code, which can be integrated into scientific applications. The framework provides five main contributions: a custom Kokkos dialect for representing Kokkos constructs in MLIR, mapping of Kokkos Kernels linear algebra operations to tensors, lowering passes to the Kokkos dialect for accelerators, a Kokkos-inspired memory reference model, and a Kokkos emitter that generates C++ source code. The Kokkos dialect includes operations for parallel loops (range_parallel, team_parallel, thread_parallel), synchronization (single, team_barrier), and linear algebra calls (gemm, gemv).

LAPIS demonstrates performance portability on AMD MI300A and NVIDIA H100 GPUs and Intel Granite Rapids CPUs, matching hand-optimized implementations for sparse and dense linear algebra operations. It enables coupling between CSE and AI/ML frameworks through automatic lowering from linalg-on-tensors frontends (torch-mlir, MPACT) to portable Kokkos C++ code, addressing the challenges of extensibility, performance, and productivity in scientific computing and machine learning applications.

The paper constructs strong pseudorandom unitaries in the quantum Haar random oracle model (QHROM), where all parties have oracle access to a Haar-random unitary and its inverse. The construction GU(1λ, k) = Xk3 · Uλ · Xk2 · Uλ · Xk1 uses a 3λ-bit key and makes only two queries to the Haar random oracle, requiring O(log1+ε(n)) bits of randomness for security against poly(n) queries. The proof uses the Ma-Huang path-recording framework, replacing Haar unitaries with path-recording isometries that track queries in purification registers. An approximate isometry S merges the databases from separate oracles in the ideal experiment into the combined database of the real experiment. The analysis employs query-by-query techniques with a progress measure, establishing operator norm bounds showing that the real and ideal experiments are statistically indistinguishable. The construction addresses the gap in prior work regarding PRU existence in the full QHROM, following related constructions of pseudorandom states and forward-only PRUs in the inverseless variant.

Chipotle launched its new queso on Sept. 12, selling a small chips‑and‑queso combo for $3.95 and a large for $6.25; customers on Twitter criticized the price and taste, while the company reported 63% of test‑market respondents said it would boost visits and cited higher ingredient costs as justification for the price.

State Bar of Michigan e‑Journal for Wednesday, May 23 2001 includes case summaries covering Bankruptcy, Civil Rights, Constitutional Law, Criminal Law, Employment & Labor Law, Family Law, Insurance, Litigation, Municipal, Negligence & Intentional Tort, and Real Property; a special note highlights one U.S. Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals opinion in Bankruptcy and Constitutional Law. The issue lists upcoming bar events: a Bench/Bar Conference on Social Security Disability and basic and advanced probate‑planning programs for legal assistants. Fields of Practice listings provide contact information for attorneys offering services in areas such as ADR, administrative, adoption, antitrust, construction, criminal, environmental, family, health, immigration, insurance, intellectual‑property, labor, litigation, medical‑malpractice, real‑estate, special‑education, tax, transportation, and workers‑compensation law. Classified advertising offers services including confidential records destruction, expert witnesses (building, economics, geology, legal malpractice), lawsuit financing, legal research, office space for rent, positions available (attorney, paralegal, executive director, associate, senior counsel, in‑house counsel), and typing services. Peggy Mahoney forwarded an Energy Central Deregulation Public Forum email to Enron staff. The email presents a new forum question asking whether policy should be changed to encourage natural‑gas exploration on federal lands and the continental shelf, noting that nearly 95% of planned future power plants will be gas‑fired while supply shortages are expected to push winter prices to record highs, with a response deadline of September 15 2000. It also repeats a previous question about whether power generators are deliberately manipulating the wholesale market in San Diego to obtain higher profits and whether price caps should be imposed to protect ratepayers. The email includes selected responses from a range of industry professionals: some argue that price spikes stem from supply‑demand imbalances, regulatory neglect and market design rather than deliberate manipulation; others claim generators exploit market rules and that caps would deter investment and cause shortages; many suggest long‑term solutions such as removing barriers to new generation, encouraging distributed and peak‑load resources, and allowing market price signals rather than imposing caps.

CEMEX, a Mexican cement producer founded in 1931, grew from a 6,500‑employee, $275 million domestic firm in the early 1980s to a publicly‑traded global leader with about 65,000 employees, operations in over 50 countries and $21.7 billion in annual revenue by 2007. Under CEO Lorenzo Zambrano, the company prepared for international competition after Mexico’s economic opening (NAFTA, GATT) by divesting non‑core assets, building a proprietary communications network (CEMEXNET) and implementing an Executive Information System that enabled real‑time monitoring of operations.

CEMEX’s globalization unfolded in four stages:

* Laying the Groundwork (1982‑1991) – consolidation of the Mexican market (e.g., acquisition of Tolteca, 1989) and early export infrastructure.
* Stepping Out (1992‑1995) – first major foreign acquisition: a majority stake in Spain’s Valenciana and Sanson for $1.8 billion, giving a 28 % market share in one of Europe’s largest cement markets and access to lower‑cost capital; followed by entry into Venezuela, Panama and the Dominican Republic.
* Growing Up (1996‑1999) – acquisitions in Colombia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Egypt, Chile and Costa Rica; NYSE listing (1999); formalization of the post‑merger integration (PMI) process.
* Stepping Up (2000‑2007) – purchase of Texas‑based Southdown (2000), the UK‑based ready‑mix concrete leader RMC for $5.8 billion (2005), and the Australian/U.S. Rinker Group for $15.3 billion (2007), making CEMEX one of the world’s largest building‑materials suppliers.

The cornerstone of CEMEX’s success was its “CEMEX Way” – a systematic PMI approach that standardized business processes, technology and organization worldwide while allowing local operational flexibility. The process involved multinational standardization teams of functional experts who both diffuse best practices and identify superior practices from acquired firms, storing them in a central database for internal benchmarking. Middle‑level managers acted as teachers and advocates, enabling rapid integration (e.g., PMI duration fell from 25 months for the Spanish deals to under five months for Southdown). By some estimates, 70 % of CEMEX’s practices originated from previous acquisitions.

CEMEX also leveraged innovation in operations, marketing (bag‑cement branding in developing markets) and logistics, and used its growing geographic footprint to pool demand and improve capacity utilization. Financially, the company achieved substantial operating‑margin improvements after acquisitions (e.g., Spanish operating margins rose from 7 % to 24 %) but also faced share‑price volatility and elevated debt following large deals, especially during the 2008 global downturn. Despite these challenges, CEMEX’s disciplined integration, continuous learning and strategic acquisition focus allowed it to become a leading global player in the cement, aggregates and ready‑mix concrete industries.

Paul Clement is set to be named Swansea's new manager after Bayern Munich gave permission for him to speak to the club. He will replace Bob Bradley and sign a deal until 2019 with a £30million transfer budget, as Swansea currently sit 19th in the Premier League having conceded 44 goals in 19 games.

In June 1953 East Berlin riots and June 1956 Poznań uprising were suppressed by Soviet troops. The 1956 Hungarian revolt, a nationwide event, became a turning point. After WWII Soviet occupation, Mátyás Rákosi’s Communist government collectivised farms and rapidly industrialised, causing economic failure. Following Stalin’s death, Imre Nagy replaced Rákosi as prime minister in 1953 but was removed in 1955. By early 1956 discontent grew due to indecisive leadership, economic decline, repression after Poznań, and Poland’s liberalization. A 22 October student manifesto sparked a rally that turned violent after an aggressive radio address; revolutionary councils demanded nationalism, neutrality and Soviet withdrawal. Soviet tanks entered Budapest on 24 October; Mikoyan and Suslov visits confirmed Nagy and installed János Kádár. Soviet concessions and the Suez Crisis diverted world attention. On 1 November 250,000 Soviet troops surrounded Budapest; after a brief truce the invasion began at midnight 3/4 November. Despite Hungarian resistance, organized Soviet force prevailed; combat ended by mid‑November and resistance collapsed by month’s end, leaving roughly 25,000 Hungarians and 7,000 Soviets dead.

Judge Jeannette Vargas tossed Drake's defamation suit over Lamar's 'Not Like Us' lyric calling him a 'certified pedophile,' calling it nonactionable opinion in a rap battle. She also dismissed claims against Universal Music Group, and Drake plans to appeal.

A Springfield, Mass., police officer, Conrad Lariviere, wrote “Hahahaha love this” on Facebook in response to the car attack that killed counter‑protester Heather Heyer at a white‑nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Va., and later apologized, calling his comment stupid. Springfield’s police commissioner opened an internal investigation, and the mayor condemned the remarks. Lariviere said he is not a racist.

The DAWN (Donated Antibodies Working against COVID-19) study is a randomized, open-label, phase 2 proof-of-concept multicenter trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of convalescent plasma combined with standard of care versus standard of care alone in hospitalized adult patients with COVID-19. Participants are randomized 2:1. The primary endpoint is the percentage of patients alive without mechanical ventilation at Day 15. Secondary endpoints include clinical status, time to clinical improvement, mortality, safety, and other outcomes. Eligible participants are adults ≥18 with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, hospitalized with oxygen requirement or radiographic infiltrates, and no mechanical ventilation at baseline. Exclusions include certain medical conditions, allergies to plasma, and recent anti-CD20 therapy. Convalescent plasma is administered in 4 doses totaling 800–1000 mL, with at least 1/160 neutralizing antibody titer, within 12 hours of randomization and again 24–36 hours later. The study is conducted according to Declaration of Helsinki and ICH GCP guidelines, with ethics committee approval and informed consent. Six patients withdrew or were screen failures and were replaced; no loss to follow-up after intervention. The hypothesis is that early high-volume high-titer plasma reduces the need for mechanical ventilation.

Williams & Connolly confirmed hackers accessed "a small number" of attorney emails using a zero-day attack but found no evidence of further IT system access or extraction of confidential client data. The firm believes the hackers are affiliated with a nation-state actor responsible for recent attacks on other law firms and companies. Williams & Connolly has blocked the threat actor and reports no current unauthorized traffic on its network.

Video output data comprises three 8‑MSB groups (G/Y/YC, B/CB/C, R/CR). In RGB they are green, blue, red; in YUV444 they are Y, Cb, Cr; in Y/C they are Y, multiplexed Cb/Cr, Cr; in BT.656 G/Y/YC is multiplexed Y/Cb/Cr, B/CB/C unused, R/CR red only for RGB.

Coppin State University, a historically Black university in Maryland, has more than quadrupled out-of-state student enrollment through its Expand Eagle Nation program, which offers in-state tuition to students from states and territories without an HBCU. In 2024, the first year, students from qualifying states doubled to 195, rising to 416 of the incoming class of 1,000 this fall. Overall enrollment increased 26 percent. The institution shifted from recruiting primarily within a 50-mile radius. Officials attribute growth to increased name recognition and the rising popularity of HBCUs following the 2023 Supreme Court ban on affirmative action. Coppin, the least expensive institution in Maryland, also took steps including visiting high schools, advertising in target cities, and forming transfer partnerships with community colleges. The university prepared for growth by coordinating with academic affairs and is constructing new housing. A challenge has been convincing prospective students the offer is genuine. Coppin aims to attract out-of-state students ahead of an anticipated decline in high school graduates.

The TPS7H500x-SP is a radiation-hardness-assured family of fixed-frequency, peak current mode PWM controllers for space-grade DC-DC converter design, supporting topologies including buck, flyback, forward, active-clamp forward, push-pull, and full-bridge. The series operates from 4V to 14V input, supports switching frequencies from 100kHz to 2MHz, and includes features such as programmable UVLO, soft-start, voltage reference (1.23V bandgap), transconductance error amplifier with configurable compensation, programmable dead times, duty cycle limiting, current sensing with hiccup mode protection, slope compensation, and external fault protection. The controllers include internal oscillator mode, external synchronization mode, and primary-secondary mode for multi-device synchronization. OUTA/OUTB primary outputs and SRA/SRB synchronous rectifier outputs are available depending on device variant.

The recent Democratic victories have given the party control of the House, Senate, the presidency and the vice‑presidency, completing a shift that began two years ago. The speaker contends this change means more than partisan success; it reflects the Nation’s wish to re‑interpret its plans and point of view. He acknowledges that the United States is materially and morally great, but notes serious evils: waste of resources, neglect of workers, exploitation of natural wealth, and the debasement of government for private ends. He lists core problems requiring correction: a tariff that isolates the country from world trade, a banking and currency system that concentrates cash and restricts credit, an industrial system that limits labor and depletes resources, an agricultural sector lacking efficiency and credit, and under‑developed water, forest and mining assets. He calls for a restoration that safeguards health, protects equal opportunity, ensures justice, and cleanses government while preserving basic rights and property. Concluding, he frames the moment as a day of dedication, urging all honest, patriotic citizens to support the effort.

Indianapolis Public Schools will hold a public meeting Tuesday to discuss a task force recommendation to close three high schools by 2018‑2019. The district’s enrollment has declined from 109,000 students in 1967 to 30,000, and all seven high schools are under capacity, with Arsenal Tech at 60% and George Washington at 21% (about 400 students). The task force says three schools could accommodate the current high‑school population; four would offer flexibility. Public comments are the first of a series of meetings in April and May, with an administration recommendation due in June and a board vote in September.

Remote sensing change detection (RSCD) identifies surface changes by comparing multi‑temporal images. Traditional methods are sensitive to noise and seasonal or lighting variations, while CNN‑based deep learning improves accuracy but lacks long‑range context modeling. Vision‑Transformer approaches and recent foundation‑model methods (e.g., SAM, CLIP) provide stronger generalization, yet they rely primarily on visual information. This paper proposes LG‑CD, a language‑guided multimodal model that combines SAM2’s visual encoder with CLIP’s text encoder through a text‑fusion attention module and a visual‑semantic fusion decoder. By integrating textual cues, LG‑CD enhances semantic understanding, detection accuracy, and robustness across diverse change patterns.

The White House said it was not defending Roseanne Barr's racist tweet, which led to her sitcom's cancellation on ABC. However, President Trump and Press Secretary Sarah Sanders insisted ABC should apologize for derogatory comments about the administration. Sanders pointed to a double standard, citing examples like ESPN host Jemele Hill calling Trump a white supremacist, Joy Behar likening Christianity to mental illness, and Keith Olbermann attacking Trump as a Nazi. She said Trump was focused on other matters but emphasized he was calling out media bias. Sanders also noted the President's resentment at his portrayal in the media and his long list of perceived slights. The White House said Trump was focused on issues like North Korea and a "right to try" bill for terminally ill patients, but addressed the topic despite earlier saying it was not on his radar.

Head coach Kyle Shanahan said yesterday’s minicamp practice was good, with both offense and defense battling evenly; the offense started strong, the defense responded well in the red zone, and there are areas to improve. He noted his father, who has an office adjacent to his, watches tape and offers ideas, but is not officially on staff and lives in Denver. Shanahan said he hasn’t had time for many phone conversations but appreciates his father’s observations as extra eyes. He described his schedule as fast‑paced since last July and plans to take an extended break in Mexico with his family, avoiding watches and work. He emphasized that play‑action is vital to his offense, allowing him to bind defenses, reduce pressure on the O‑line and QB, and create explosive plays.

The lecture focuses on post‑flop poker strategy, explaining why the preflop aggressor usually receives a check and how a bet should be either a value bet (with strong hands) or a bluff (with very weak hands), while middle‑range hands should be checked to avoid adverse selection. It recommends betting roughly half the pot on the flop, increasing to about 60 % on the turn and 70–100 % on the river, and advises that calling is generally justified only with hands that have enough equity or good implied odds, while raising usually requires two‑pair or better when stacks are deep (40+ big blinds). Position and stack size heavily affect decisions: tighter ranges from early positions demand stronger hands, whereas short stacks allow more aggressive all‑in plays. The class introduces implied odds (future payoff from making a hand), reverse implied odds (risk of being outplayed after hitting a weak pair), set mining (calling a raise to hit a set), and the advanced tactic of leading (betting into the preflop raiser) on boards that favor the caller’s range. It also presents two “bluffing epiphanies”: a bluff’s effectiveness depends on the number of outs against the hands that will call and on what the bluffer’s range can plausibly represent; when a draw misses and the board changes to weaken the opponent’s range, continuing to bluff may be justified, but when the opponent’s range remains strong the bluff should be abandoned.

On July 18, 2001, California faced ongoing energy crisis issues. Southern California Edison, with $3.5 billion in debt, had multiple bailout proposals pending in the legislature before a Friday recess, including plans to buy its transmission lines for $2.4-$2.76 billion or impose $2 monthly rate increases. PG&E sued the state seeking compensation for energy contracts seized by Governor Davis in January, with disputed valuations of $160-347 million. The state was selling surplus power purchased at $138/megawatt-hour for as little as $1/megawatt-hour, with daily power costs dropping from over $100 million in May to under $26 million in July. Consumer inflation rose 0.2% in June with electricity prices surging. Contra Costa County approved $1.7 million for energy conservation upgrades to nine buildings. Consumer groups criticized rescue plans as bailouts that would ultimately cost consumers. The legislature faced an August 15 deadline to approve a rescue plan, and whatever solution was reached for Edison could serve as a model for PG&E's bankruptcy.

Cervical cancer is a malignant tumor of the cervix (neck of the uterus) caused almost always by oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV), especially types 16 and 18. HPV is sexually transmitted; over 100 HPV types exist, about 30 are sexually transmitted, and the high‑risk types are responsible for the disease. The disease develops through a pre‑cancerous (precancerous) stage that is asymptomatic and can be detected by a Pap smear, and if treated at this stage the cancer can be prevented. Invasive cancer progresses from early stage – symptoms include post‑coital bleeding, foul‑smelling vaginal discharge – to late stage with weight loss, anemia, pelvic pain, and spread to other organs. Diagnosis requires a Pap smear for precancerous lesions and a tissue biopsy with histology for confirmation; imaging (X‑ray, CT, MRI, PET) is used for staging. Early‑stage disease can be cured by radical surgery or radiotherapy, with the choice depending on patient factors such as age and sexual activity; radiotherapy may cause vaginal narrowing. Late‑stage disease is managed with radiotherapy, often combined with chemotherapy, and survival is typically limited to months or a few years. In Nigeria cervical cancer is the second most common cancer in women after breast cancer, with about 15 000 new cases and 10 000 deaths annually; in Enugu it accounts for about two‑thirds of female genital cancers. Screening is recommended at least every three years for women of reproductive age, then every five years later. An HPV vaccine covering types 16 and 18 is available, and men can be vaccinated to reduce HPV reservoirs. Pregnancy can occur in early‑stage disease but not in late stage. Some people attribute the disease to witchcraft, but no other myth is noted.

The paper explores the expanding influence of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education. It notes that AI is increasingly present across education because of technological advances and the COVID‑19 pandemic, and that higher‑education institutions are not immune to this trend. According to Li and Yang (2023), AI‑driven higher education differs from traditional models in the pace of technological evolution, data‑based governance, individualized training, and networked research collaboration. A range of AI applications in higher education is identified, including adaptive learning platforms, automated grading, predictive analytics, personalized tutoring, plagiarism detection, language translation, virtual assistants, virtual reality, learning‑management systems, recommendation engines, speech recognition, student‑support chatbots, and text analysis (Zentner, 2022). Advantages highlighted by Churi et al. (2022) include high speed, reliability, ongoing student assessment, efficient administrative management, and support for risky or distance‑learning environments. At the same time, implementation faces challenges such as equitable access, privacy and ethical concerns, teacher training, student autonomy, financial costs, and conservative organizational cultures (Nsoh et al., 2023; Bates et al., 2020). Aldosari (2020) outlines ten fundamental rules for AI in education, emphasizing automation of routine tasks, curriculum redesign, data‑driven student selection, and transformation of teachers’ roles. The authors stress that successful integration requires AI literacy beyond digital literacy, participatory processes involving all stakeholders, development of specific teacher competencies, and critical evaluation of AI tools, while preserving academic freedom. The conclusion calls for collaborative discussion of AI‑related competencies and continued research to guide its responsible use in higher education.

Analysis of campaign contributions by attorneys and staff at the 100 top‑grossing law firms and 50 larger plaintiffs‑side firms shows 92.45% went to Democrats in 2023‑2024, a 12‑1 Democratic‑to‑Republican ratio, up from a 6‑1 ratio in 2017‑2020. During the lecture the professor discussed discrete symmetries (parity P, time reversal T, charge conjugation C) in both complex scalar and Dirac field theories. At the quantum‑mechanical level symmetry transformations are implemented by unitary operators, with the exception of T, which must be anti‑unitary. A short derivation shows that to keep the Schrödinger equation form under t → −t the time‑reversal operator must be anti‑linear, i.e. U_T i = −i U_T, leading to an anti‑unitary definition.  

For a complex scalar field the parity transformation is φ(x)→η_P φ(Px) with η_P² = 1; η_P = +1 corresponds to a scalar, η_P = −1 to a pseudoscalar. Similarly T and C have phases η_T and η_C that satisfy η² = 1. These transformations are generated by unitary operators U_P, U_T, U_C acting on creation/annihilation operators, exchanging particle and antiparticle for charge conjugation.  

The Dirac field requires a matrix D acting on spinor indices: ψ′(x′)=D ψ(x) with x′=Px. D must commute with γ⁰ and anticommute with γᵢ, giving D∝γ⁰ (up to a phase). Charge conjugation is written ψ′=C \barψᵀ, where C satisfies γ_μᵀ = −C γ_μ C⁻¹; such a matrix always exists because the set {−γ_μᵀ} obeys the same Clifford algebra. Time reversal takes ψ′=D_T ψ(Tx) with D_Tᵀ = C⁻¹ γ₅ (up to a phase). All three discrete symmetries are independent of Lorentz boosts.  

The lecture then introduced path‑integral quantisation for fermions. Because fermionic fields obey anticommutation relations, Feynman’s original method fails; the solution, given by Berezin (a former Soviet physicist) in the early 1960s, is to treat fermionic fields as Grassmann numbers—anti‑commuting objects satisfying θ²=0. Functions of a Grassmann variable reduce to f(θ)=f₀+f₁θ; differentiation is defined as a left‑derivative, and integration is required to be linear and to give zero for total derivatives. These conditions uniquely fix ∫dθ f(θ)=f₁, i.e. the integral equals the coefficient of the linear term. Multi‑variable Grassmann integrals follow analogous rules, with a scaling θ′=aθ giving dθ′=(1/a)dθ, opposite to ordinary variables.

U.S. stock index futures were higher Thursday with a strong earnings season underway - 75.4% of S&P 500 companies reporting have beaten expectations, with profits estimated up 10.8%. A system includes a rotating LIDAR sensor that emits light pulses toward an environment and detects reflections, and one or more cameras that detect external light. The cameras together provide a plurality of rows of sensing elements aligned with the LIDAR rotation axis. A controller operates the cameras in a rolling‑shutter manner, obtaining a sequence of image pixel rows each associated with a respective exposure time period. The controller determines timing and order of the camera exposures based on the LIDAR’s pointing direction, rotation rate and arrangement of emitted light beams, so that image pixel rows are captured when the LIDAR’s field‑of‑view overlaps the corresponding rows. Adjacent rows may have partially overlapping exposure periods. The system maps LIDAR data points to the captured image pixels (or vice‑versa) to generate three‑dimensional colored representations of the environment. A method includes rotating the LIDAR sensor about an axis, obtaining the sequence of image pixel rows from the cameras, adjusting exposure start times and time delays according to the LIDAR rotation characteristics, and associating LIDAR data with the image pixels for fused sensor output.

The appellate court affirmed two convictions of Bradford Washington for second‑degree murder and related charges. The court rejected his claims that the trial court improperly allowed a detective’s testimony about police attempts to locate him and gave an improper consciousness‑of‑guilt jury instruction, finding those issues unpreserved and without merit. The defendant’s argument that the prosecutor shifted the prosecution’s theory was also rejected. The judgments on both indictments were affirmed.

Darren Osborne was sentenced to 43 years in prison for driving a van into worshippers outside a mosque in Finsbury Park, north London, killing Makram Ali and injuring nine others. He was found guilty of murder and attempted murder. Osborne shouted "I want to kill all Muslims" after the attack and the judge noted he had targeted people of various ages, abilities, and genders based on appearance. During the trial, the prosecutor said Osborne had been "brainwashed" into Islamophobia after watching a BBC drama. He also planned to kill Mayor Sadiq Khan and Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn at a pro-Palestinian march. Police released CCTV showing he planned the attack in Wales before driving to London. Ali's family expressed satisfaction with the verdict, describing him as a peaceful man. Commander Dean Haydon said Osborne failed in his aim to create division between communities, as the local community came together in response.

The invention relates to electronic smoking devices such as e‑cigarettes that use a battery‑powered heater to vaporize a liquid for inhalation. Conventional devices employ metallic heating wires wrapped around porous wicks; the disclosed device replaces those two components with a single coil‑less atomizer comprising one or more woven fiber tubes. Each tube has a hollow interior and porous fiber walls that transport liquid to the heating section by capillary action. The tube can be made of carbon fibers, nickel‑chromium, ceramic fibers, or composites thereof, and can be formed in U‑, C‑, or L‑shapes. Portions of the tube near the electrical contacts are rendered low‑resistance (≈1 Ω or less) while the mid‑section is high‑resistance (≈3–5 Ω) to define a heating zone that reaches 100–350 °C. The tube ends are immersed in a liquid supply that may be free‑flowing or stored in a porous medium, providing continuous liquid feed to the heating section. The device also includes a housing, power source, control electronics, an airflow sensor or manual switch, an LED indicator, and a mouthpiece. In use, a puff triggers the sensor, the control electronics power the heating element, liquid vaporizes, and the aerosol is inhaled. The heating element can be manufactured by mounting the tube(s) on a board between two leads or contacts, masking a central section, sputtering a conductive material onto the unmasked portions, and removing the mask to leave low‑resistance conductive sections flanking a high‑resistance heating section. Multiple tubes may be arranged parallel or in contact, and may have the same or different diameters; a larger tube may contain the heating section while smaller surrounding tubes act as liquid feed conduits. The design reduces the size of the atomizer, allowing more compact e‑cigarette designs. The disclosed atomizer is wick‑free, as the woven fiber tube serves both heating and wicking functions.

The court entered judgment against Randall Fincke for violating Massachusetts securities law by falsely representing in an October 2002 Business Plan that Access had been advised by patent counsel that its product did not infringe any patents, when no such advice was given. The court found only Joseph Zimmel's October and November 2002 stock purchases totaling $1.5 million were made "by means of" the misstatement, as those sales occurred shortly after the Business Plan was disseminated. The court rejected claims for investments made in April 2003 and thereafter, finding those transactions resulted from separate negotiations and a different document. Fincke's motion for reconsideration was denied. Judgment was entered against Fincke for $1.5 million plus interest to Zimmel under § 410(a)(2), and $281,534.62 plus interest to Access for prior fiduciary duty breaches.

The BIRDS workshop aims to bridge digital library professionals and GLAM institutes with computer science researchers to foster collaboration and develop innovative practical applications. It targets practitioners and researchers from the main conference, especially new members such as students and library representatives, with an expected participation of around 25 attendees. Organizers are Christin Katharina Kreutz and Hermann Kroll.

Coleman v. Coleman (1972) upheld Ohio's one-year durational residency requirement for divorce (R.C. 3105.03), finding it does not violate the constitutional right to travel. The Ohio Supreme Court distinguished this case from Shapiro v. Thompson by stating divorce is a statutory privilege, not a basic need like welfare or voting, and that the state has a compelling interest in regulating the civil status of marriage. The court concluded the requirement is the least restrictive method to verify domicile and prevent non-residents from obtaining divorces in Ohio, thereby serving the state's jurisdictional interests and encouraging reconciliation.

Apple Inc. filed a Form 8-K on August 17, 2022, reporting two key items. Item 5.02 disclosed that Apple's Compensation Committee approved the Apple Inc. Executive Cash Incentive Plan, under which eligible executive team members may receive cash incentive awards based on achievement of performance goals over fiscal year periods. Payouts are determined by the Committee and made in cash, with awards forfeited if participants terminate service before payout unless otherwise determined. Black Monday, the 23 % single‑day crash on Oct 19 1987, preceded the Dec 11 1987 release of Oliver Stone’s Wall Street by less than two months. The film has remained the most influential finance movie, blending a rags‑to‑riches parable, the Hero’s Journey and a fairy‑tale while immersing viewers in the mid‑80s bull‑market era. It follows Bud Fox (Charlie Sheen), a low‑level broker who climbs under Gordon Gekko (Michael Douglas), a character based on real‑world financiers. Douglas, who won the Oscar for Best Actor, gave Gekko a charismatic, non‑criminal persona that became a cultural icon; his lines such as “Greed is good” are still recognized. The film’s authentic 1980s details and cautionary tone explain its lasting impact thirty years later. The author, Comfortably Smug, is a government‑relations professional specializing in financial services and tweets under @ComfortablySmug.

Amazon.com, Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Seattle, Washington, that completed its IPO in May 1997 and trades on NASDAQ under "AMZN." The company organizes its operations into three segments: North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (AWS), guided by principles of customer obsession, invention, operational excellence, and long-term thinking.

Operating income was $4.186 billion and net income was $2.371 billion, with basic earnings per share of $5.01 and diluted earnings per share of $4.90. By segment: North America generated $79.785 billion (59% of total), International generated $43.983 billion (32%), and AWS generated $12.219 billion (9%). North America sales grew 25% year-over-year, International grew 24%, and AWS grew 55%.

Operating cash flow was $16.443 billion, and the company's cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities balances totaled $26.0 billion as of December 31, 2016. The company employed approximately 341,400 full-time and part-time employees. The business experiences seasonality with higher sales volume in the fourth quarter, which historically accounts for approximately 32% of annual revenue.

The board of directors includes Jeffrey P. Bezos (CEO and Chairman), Tom A. Alberg, John Seely Brown, William B. Gordon, Jamie S. Gorelick, Daniel P. Huttenlocher, Judith A. McGrath, Jonathan J. Rubinstein, Thomas O. Ryder, Patricia Q. Stonesifer, and Wendell P. Weeks. Key executives include Andrew R. Jassy (CEO of AWS), Brian T. Olsavsky (CFO), and Jeffrey A. Wilke (CEO Worldwide Consumer).

The company faces risks including intense competition across multiple industries, challenges in managing global expansion, fluctuations in operating results, foreign exchange exposure, inventory management, and regulatory compliance in various jurisdictions.

Justice Anthony Kennedy’s memoir, released Oct. 14, discusses his judicial philosophy, emphasizing humility, integrity, and transparent reasoning, especially in close cases, and acknowledges that justices may not know when they err. He rejects both originalism and pragmatism as insufficient, arguing constitutional meaning can evolve through better perspective. Kennedy describes his 5‑4 rulings in Citizens United, Obergefell, Texas v. Johnson and Bush v. Gore, including the government’s campaign‑finance stance, his view of marriage’s changing nature, and the Court’s protection of free speech. He recounts his break with Justice Scalia over Obergefell and their later reconciliation. He cites his internal conflict over abortion and decision to stay on the Court, his belief that presidents must defer to Supreme Court rulings, and a chilling encounter with Vladimir Putin. Kennedy opposes courtroom cameras, recounts a house ransacking linked to a Manson case, and comments on contemporary music such as the Rolling Stones and Tom Petty.

The Simons Observatory has deployed more than 67,000 superconducting transition‑edge sensor (TES) detectors on four telescopes in Chile’s Atacama Desert. Its 6 m crossed‑Dragone large‑aperture telescope (LAT) carries ≈31 000 detectors that aim to map 40 % of the sky at 6 µK‑arcmin depth, and an upgrade will add ≈32 000 further detectors. Microwave frequency multiplexing with SLAC Microresonator Radio Frequency (SMuRF) warm electronics achieves a multiplexing factor of ≈1 000 per pair of radio‑frequency (RF) transmission lines. For the LAT the SMuRF electronics are mounted directly on the LAT receiver (LATR) inside the receiver cabin, which is kept isothermal with the telescope mirrors; the warm coaxial cables that link the electronics to the cryogenic microwave resonators are therefore exposed to diurnal temperature swings. These temperature variations can induce a systematic phase drift in the RF transmission lines that mimics TES detector signals.

To measure this effect the authors analyse “off‑resonance” (pilot) tones that are not tone‑tracked and pass through the warm cables unchanged. Up to 1 152 off‑resonance tones were recorded across the LATR during a 22.6‑hour observation starting 2 June 2025. Correlating the calculated time‑delay τ of each tone with the cabin temperature reveals a diurnal phase drift of only a few picoseconds. The drift causes a small rotation of the resonator circle in the IQ plane, producing a Q‑shift proportional to the post‑calibration offset Ioffset_res (median ≈ –3.31 × 10⁴ Hz). Converting the Q‑shift to a noise‑equivalent TES current using the measured median d f/dITES ≈ 5.71 × 10⁻² Hz pA⁻¹ shows that the phase‑drift contribution has amplitude spectral densities comparable to the open‑SQUID readout noise and well below the on‑sky detector noise. The authors conclude that the diurnal phase drift is a sub‑dominant source of detector noise and does not limit the LAT’s mapping speed.

Tesla, Inc. designs, develops, manufactures, sells and leases high‑performance fully electric vehicles and energy generation and storage systems. The company operates in two reportable segments: automotive and energy generation and storage. The automotive segment includes electric vehicles (Model S, Model X, Model 3, Model Y, Tesla Semi, Cybertruck, new Tesla Roadster), automotive regulatory credits, and related services such as vehicle servicing, Supercharger network and insurance. The energy generation and storage segment includes solar energy systems (Solar Roof, retrofit solar) and battery energy storage products (Powerwall, Megapack). Tesla sells its products directly to customers via its website and company‑owned stores, and maintains a global network of service centers, Supercharger stations and Destination Chargers. Manufacturing facilities are located in the United States (California, Nevada, Texas, New York), China (Shanghai) and Germany (Berlin). The company also offers vehicle financing, leasing and insurance products. Tesla’s mission is to accelerate the world’s transition to sustainable energy. As of December 31 2022, Tesla employed approximately 127,855 employees worldwide. The company is subject to various regulations and risks including macroeconomic conditions, supply chain challenges, competition, regulatory uncertainties and product launch and manufacturing risks.

Evelyn Montiel’s family has run an ice cream truck on Oakland’s east side for over 20 years. In high school she balanced being an A‑student and class president with working nights at the stand. She wanted to be the first in her family to attend college, attended an East Coast school but dropped out after depression. Students Rising Above (SRA) helped her transfer to USC, where she thrived and completed internships. After graduating during recession she struggled to find work and returned to family business. SRA then secured her an interview at a national investment firm, leading to a broker role at a Silicon Valley startup aiming to democratize investing. Evelyn credits SRA for her success and hopes to share her story.

NVIDIA Corporation, a Delaware corporation headquartered in Santa Clara, California, invented the GPU and now focuses on visual and accelerated computing for AI. The company has two reportable segments: GPU and Tegra Processor, serving Gaming, Professional Visualization, Datacenter, and Automotive markets. GPU brands include GeForce, Quadro, Tesla, and GRID; Tegra brands include DRIVE PX and SHIELD. Sales to ASUSTeK accounted for 12% of fiscal year 2017 revenue. NVIDIA uses a fabless manufacturing strategy, relying on third-party foundries like TSMC and Samsung. R&D expenses were $1.46 billion in FY2017, with 7,282 of 10,299 employees engaged in R&D. Cash and marketable securities increased 35% to $6.80 billion at FY2017 end. The company holds patents expiring March 2017 to November 2035, with numerous pending applications. Executive officers include President and CEO Jen-Hsun Huang, CFO Colette M. Kress, and others. NVIDIA's common stock trades on NASDAQ as NVDA. In November 2016, the quarterly dividend was increased to $0.14 per share, and $261 million in dividends were paid in FY2017. The share repurchase program was authorized up to $2.73 billion as of January 29, 2017. Key risks include competition, dependence on third-party manufacturers, international operations, and rapid technological change.

VentureWire’s September 26 2000 issue reported that Chiaro Networks secured over $100 million in its third round, Bertelsmann and iSyndicate formed a joint European venture, Novalux raised $109 million, online‑jewelry retailer Miadora shut down, Sun Microsystems launched a $50 million Asia‑Pacific venture investment program, and Mayfield Fund appointed a new marketing partner. The edition also listed dozens of funding rounds ranging from $2.8 million to $75 million for companies in sectors such as healthcare ASPs, semiconductor IP, network infrastructure, wireless services, energy marketplaces, digital asset management, interactive TV and online privacy. Several new products were announced (SmartPipes beta, PocketPass.com launch, etc.), and multiple M&A deals were disclosed, including Autodaq’s acquisition of MarketWise and DeepBridge’s acquisition of OnLine Communications. Board appointments and executive changes were noted, and venture‑capital firms announced new funds (Venturelab Partners $100 million second fund, Atle Ventures restructuring) and personnel moves (Edgar Masri joining Matrix Partners).

On Nov 27 2001 Enron was struggling to find sellers in near‑term gas and power markets, with its OTC trading volume estimated at roughly 25 % of a month earlier. Several firms (Aquila, Mirant, Coral Energy, Sempra, Morgan Stanley) were buying from Enron but not selling to it, while Dynegy, Duke Energy, BP, PG&E and Edison continued to trade normally. Moody's kept Enron’s rating at Baa3 and said it would take no action that day; S&P and Fitch had Enron one notch above speculative grade and on review or negative watch.

Dynegy confirmed it was in talks to restructure the proposed merger, which could cut the purchase price by more than 40 % to about $5 billion and lower the exchange ratio from 0.2685 Dynegy shares per Enron share to below 0.15. Enron was also seeking an additional $500 million‑$1 billion cash infusion, and bankers trying to raise $2 billion had been turned down by Prince Alwaleed, the Carlyle Group and Blackstone. Enron’s equity trading unit was being shut down with about 60 employees laid off.

Enron shares rose modestly on the renegotiation news, trading around $4 and down from about $84 a year earlier; the company’s market cap had fallen to roughly $3 billion. Enron’s bonds recovered to roughly 55 cents on the dollar, yielding about 22.5 %. Hedge funds were evaluating trades that combine shorting Enron stock with buying its bonds, noting that a lower exchange ratio makes the trade easier. Three employee lawsuits over lost 401(k) savings seeking $850 million have been filed, and more than a dozen shareholder suits have been initiated. Analysts noted that Enron’s core trading business is deteriorating and that the deal’s success depends on stabilizing that business and securing the needed financing.

The Pauli–Fierz Hamiltonian describes electron–photon interactions in optical cavities; molecular electronic structures differ from free‑space. Standard quantum chemistry fails. The non‑local coupling demands a suitable basis; sinc basis is orthonormal, converges to complete basis limit. Direct implementation scales as O(N^4) for two‑electron integrals, but off‑diagonal decay permits sparse approximations.

The DAWN-Plasma trial was a randomized, open-label, multicenter, phase 2 proof-of-concept study comparing convalescent plasma plus standard of care (SOC) versus SOC alone in 489 hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Patients received four units (800–1000 mL) of high-titer plasma. The primary endpoint—proportion alive without mechanical ventilation at Day 15—was not different between groups (83.7% plasma vs. 84.1% control; odds ratio 0.99, p=0.976). No significant differences were observed for any secondary endpoints, including mortality, ventilation, or clinical status at Day 15 or Day 30. Adverse events, serious adverse events, and transfusion-related side effects were similar between groups. The study concluded that early administration of high-titer convalescent plasma did not improve outcomes in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.

In this nationally representative study of 32,498 US adults from NHANES 2009-2020, four empirical dietary patterns were identified: American (least healthy), Prudent, Legume, and Fruit/Whole Grain/Dairy. The American pattern was most common overall (33.7%) and more prevalent among those with cardiovascular disease (CVD), higher social determinants of health (SDOH) scores, or SNAP participation. Higher SDOH scores and SNAP participation were associated with less healthy dietary patterns (more American, less Prudent and Fruit/Whole Grain/Dairy) but more Legume pattern consumption. Associations between SDOH score and dietary patterns varied by race/ethnicity, with no significant association between increasing SDOH and American pattern among Hispanic individuals. Findings support the need for interventions targeting diet quality in at-risk populations, particularly those with CVD or socioeconomic vulnerability.

A player with stable personality, skill, size, and strength has performed well in playoffs by scoring big goals while remaining composed.
