North Tyneside cabinet voted unanimously to approve the North of Tyne devolution deal, which includes an elected mayor and is expected to bring £600 million over 30 years and up to 10,000 jobs. Mayor Norma Redfearn said the door remains open for councils south of the River Tyne to join later, though joining at this stage is not possible. The deal was announced in November 2017, more than a year after a previous all‑seven‑council deal was abandoned. A referendum on that earlier deal in Durham cost £200,000 before the council withdrew. The new combined authority is planned for summer 2018, with the first mayoral election in May 2019. Newcastle leader Nick Forbes rejected claims the authority would be “under‑powered,” stating the deal offers higher per‑head investment than comparable deals and includes health, disability and housing components. A vote on splitting the existing North East Combined Authority was postponed to mid‑April. Northumberland County Council also considered the devolution proposal.

Blackwell architecture introduces power savings of up to 50% for small‑language‑model inference by reducing active periods, using power/voltage gating and faster entry to deep sleep states. DLSS 4, powered by fifth‑generation Tensor Cores and a cloud‑based AI supercomputer, offers Multi Frame Generation (MFG) that can produce up to three additional frames per traditionally rendered frame, with a new AI model that is 40 % faster and uses 30 % less VRAM. Blackwell’s enhanced Flip Metering moves frame‑pacing logic to the display engine, doubling pixel‑processing capability for smoother output.

DLSS 4 adopts transformer‑based neural networks for Super Resolution (SR), Ray Reconstruction (RR) and Deep Learning Anti‑Aliasing (DLAA), providing greater temporal stability, reduced ghosting, better lighting detail and improved image quality across all RTX GPUs. The transition from CNN to transformer architecture enables models to ingest twice the parameters and better capture long‑range patterns, resulting in a significant image‑quality leap.

Neural shaders represent the next evolution of GPU shaders, moving from fixed‑function pipelines through programmable vertex, pixel, geometry, compute, mesh and ray‑tracing stages to AI‑augmented rendering. Blackwell integrates AI directly into the traditional rendering pipeline, supported by the new Cooperative Vectors API for DX12 and Vulkan, which enables Tensor‑Core access from any shader type. This unlocks techniques such as RTX Neural Materials, RTX Neural Texture Compression (NTC) – achieving over three‑times memory reduction – Stochastic Texture Filtering, Neural Radiance Cache, RTX Skin (real‑time subsurface scattering) and RTX Neural Faces (real‑time generative AI face rendering).

The Blackwell GPU family includes three chips: GB202 (flagship, 92.2 B transistors, 12 GPCs, 192 SMs, 24 576 CUDA cores, 192 RT cores, 768 Tensor cores) powering the GeForce RTX 5090; GB203 (high‑end, 45.6 B transistors, 7 GPCs, 84 SMs, 10 752 CUDA cores, 84 RT cores, 336 Tensor cores) powering the RTX 5080 and RTX 5070 Ti; and GB205 (performance, 31 B transistors, 5 GPCs, 50 SMs, 6 400 CUDA cores, 50 RT cores, 200 Tensor cores) powering the RTX 5070. All GPUs incorporate Blackwell’s fourth‑generation RT cores, fifth‑generation Tensor cores, DLSS 4 and the new AI gaming features.

Plymouth Studio School is to close at the end of the summer term 2018, three years after opening, because it operates at roughly 50 % capacity (155 of 300 students) and is not financially viable, according to MP Johnny Mercer. The closure, pending government approval, follows an imminent Ofsted report expected to heavily criticise the school. Mercer, who attended the official opening with then schools minister Nick Gibb, says he is deeply disappointed and will focus on helping affected students find new places by September 2018. A local‑authority consultation is under way; the region has a surplus of secondary‑school places, allowing placement of the 155 students. The school, built on the Plymouth Marjon University campus to train future sports professionals, will be the 19th studio school to close nationwide. A recent Ofsted inspection rated it inadequate, noting insufficient timely progress despite some management improvements.

Assembly Republican Leader Chad Mayes voted to extend California’s cap‑and‑trade program, saying he would do it again but regrets missing the signing ceremony on Treasure Island. The vote split the party; conservative critics called it a betrayal, with RNC member Shawn Steel labeling the post‑vote photo “repugnant.” County chairs, local committees and donor groups have demanded Mayes step down, and the state party board is set to vote on his removal Friday. Obernolte has challenged Mayes for caucus leadership; after a meeting Mayes said he will stay. Other Republicans who backed the legislation faced protests, including an office sit‑in at Marc Steinorth’s district and angry town‑hall comments toward Devon Mathis. The dispute has stalled a fundraising agreement and intensified the historic tension between relevance and orthodoxy for California Republicans. Assemblywoman Melissa Melendez, who left her deputy leader post over the vote, was moved to a cramped “doghouse” office.

The 2017 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons for its work to achieve a treaty-based prohibition of nuclear weapons. ICAN, a coalition of NGOs in 100 countries, was the driving force behind the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, adopted July 7 with support from 122 nations. The treaty prohibits development, production, possession and other nuclear activities. The five UN Security Council permanent members, which possess nuclear arsenals, did not participate in the treaty negotiations.

Dead time ~25 ns with 20.5 kΩ resistors; leading edge blank time ~50 ns with 49.9 kΩ resistor; soft‑start capacitor 33 nF giving ~7.5 ms; transformer turns ratio 2.5 and primary inductance 40 µH; main switching GaN FETs rated 170 V; synchronous rectifier GaN FETs rated 80 V with optional Schottky diode; RCD clamp values calculated from overshoot target; output inductor 0.47 µH; output capacitance ≥1.3 mF (7 × 330 µF polymer tantalum, total 2.3 mF for SET mitigation); overcurrent limiting begins at ~35 A with 7.5 Ω sense resistor; hiccup capacitor 3.3 nF; Type‑2A compensation with RCOMP 40.2 kΩ, CCOMP 15 nF, CHF 47 pF; slope compensation resistor 102 kΩ; controller operates from 4 – 14 V with 0.1 µF bypass; layout guidelines include separating analog and power grounds, minimizing switch‑node copper, routing feedback away from noise sources, using short wide high‑current traces and placing bypass and compensation components close to the controller.

The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Shimon Sakaguchi, Mary Brunkow, and Fred Ramsdell for discovering regulatory T cells (T‑regs). T‑regs calm the immune system after infection or wound healing and prevent it from attacking the body; their failure can cause autoimmune disease or harmful inflammation and is needed to protect a fetus during pregnancy. Sakaguchi first identified T‑regs in 1995; Brunkow and Ramsdell traced a mutation that causes fatal autoimmune disease in male mouse pups to the forkhead transcription factor FOXP3, showing the same defect in humans in 2001. The prize, worth 11 million Swedish krona (over $1.1 million), was announced on 6 October by the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute.

The defendant moved to dismiss a bigamy indictment, arguing his second marriage was void because it was performed by a Justice of the Peace when he was 19, violating subdivision 5 of section 11 of the Domestic Relations Law. The court reviewed the statute, which requires marriages to be solemnized by authorized individuals and restricts justices of the peace from performing marriages where either party is under 21. It examined conflicting case law, including Caplan v. Caplan and De Martino v. De Martino (holding subdivision 5 invalidates such marriages) and Andrews v. Andrews and Graves v. Graves (reaching the opposite conclusion). Following the reasoning in Caplan and De Martino, the court granted the motion to dismiss the indictment.

Santa Claus rally backtests across US, European and emerging equity markets show statistically higher returns during the last week of December and first days of January. For the S&P 500, a simple strategy holding from the last trading day before Christmas to the first trading day after produced 0.7% per trade (66 % win, profit factor 2, max drawdown 9 %); extending the holding period increased the gain to 1.6 % per trade (72 % win, profit factor 4, max drawdown 11.7 %). Entering one week later (after Dec 20) yielded 1 % per trade (67 % win, profit factor 4.5, max drawdown 5.9 %).

In Europe, the DAX‑tracking ETF (EWG) posted 2.1 % per trade (81 % win, profit factor 13) and the Euro Stoxx 50 ETF (FEZ) posted 1.5 % per trade (81 % win, profit factor 9). Both indices showed stronger performance than random weeks (average random weekly gains ≈0.12 % for DAX and ≈0.18 % for Euro Stoxx) but recent returns have fallen below historical averages.

Emerging‑market proxy (Fidelity Emerging Markets Fund FEMKX) gave 2.7 % per trade (73 % win, profit factor 6, max drawdown 7 %). The NIFTY 50 index, backtested from 2008, returned 1.2 % per trade (71 % win, profit factor 6, max drawdown 7 %). All markets exhibited higher win ratios and profit factors during the holiday period.

US market holidays: Christmas Day is not a trading day; the day before or after is a trading day unless it falls on a weekend, in which case the holiday is observed on the preceding Friday (if Christmas is Saturday) or the following Monday (if it is Sunday). The bond market closes at 2 PM on the day before Christmas.

The rally typically begins on the third Friday of December and is also referred to as the turn‑of‑the‑year or Christmas effect. The analysis concludes that the Santa Claus rally is a real seasonal pattern in multiple markets, though recent performance has weakened and future results are not guaranteed.

The University of Maine cancelled its AFLOAT summit, citing shifting federal priorities; the Trump administration suspended a $12.5 million grant, but the university launched an experimental floating turbine and plans private meetings to commercialize its technology, while Maine’s state energy plan includes offshore wind as a renewable goal.

The passage describes the TMS320DM814x DaVinci Digital Media Processor’s architecture. It details the ARM Cortex‑A8 subsystem, which integrates a Cortex‑A8 processor with a Harvard architecture, an NEON 64‑/128‑bit SIMD engine, an enhanced VFPv3 floating‑point coprocessor, separate L1 instruction and data caches, a 128‑bit interconnect, an embedded trace module (ETM) connected to a 32 KB embedded trace buffer (ETB), an interrupt controller (AINTC) that prioritizes peripheral requests and generates IRQ/FIQ, a PLL controller (PLL_ARM), and an arbiter linking to a 64‑bit L3 interconnect port and a 128‑bit DMM port for direct DDR memory access.  

The DSP subsystem contains a C674x CPU with eight functional units (.M, .L, .D, .S), two 32‑register files, L1 program/cache (up to 32 KB) and a 256 KB unified L2 RAM/cache, little‑endian operation, support for 8‑/16‑/32‑/40‑/64‑bit data types, complex and 32‑×‑32‑bit multiply instructions, parallel add/subtract, SPLOOP buffering, compact 16‑bit instructions, exception handling, and user/supervisor privilege modes. A free‑running time‑stamp counter aids RTOS robustness.  

The system MMU remaps C674x MDMA accesses and optionally EDMA TC0/TC1 accesses to protect ARM memory regions. A Media Controller manages the HDVPSS and ISS modules, while the HDVICP2 accelerator supports hardware encoding/decoding of MPEG1/2/4, H.264, VC‑1, RV9/10, AVS‑1.0, and VP6.2/VP7. A face‑detection module supports QVGA inputs, uses 51.25 KB of DDR, and provides size, position, angle, and confidence data.  

A Spinlock module provides 128 hardware semaphores for efficient single‑read lock operations. A Mailbox module enables communication among the ARM, DSP, and Media Controller with four‑message FIFO queues and interrupt signalling.  

Device memory organization includes L3 and L4 peripheral maps, with TILER extended addressing for rotated/mirrored DDR views. The document also provides extensive terminal‑function tables describing pin multiplexing, pull‑up/pull‑down configuration, supply voltages, and functional details for boot configuration, DDR controllers, Ethernet (EMAC), GPIO, GPMC, HDMI, I2C, McASP, PCIe, timers, UARTs, USB, video input/output, and power supplies.

Amazon.com, Inc. filed its Form 10‑Q for the quarter ended June 30 2019. Net sales for Q2 2019 were $63.4 billion, up 20% year‑over‑year; net income was $2.6 billion. Operating cash flow was $9.1 billion for the quarter and $11.0 billion for the six‑month period. Total net sales for the six months were $123.1 billion, up 18% year‑over‑year, with net income of $6.2 billion.

Segment results: North America generated net sales of $38.7 billion and operating income of $1.6 billion; International generated net sales of $16.4 billion and an operating loss of $601 million; AWS generated net sales of $8.4 billion and operating income of $2.1 billion.

Balance sheet at June 30 2019: total assets $191.4 billion; cash and cash equivalents $22.6 billion; marketable securities $18.8 billion; inventories $18.6 billion; property and equipment, net $64.7 billion; goodwill $14.7 billion. Liabilities included accounts payable $36.1 billion, accrued expenses $26.1 billion, unearned revenue $7.5 billion, long‑term lease liabilities $35.1 billion, and long‑term debt $23.3 billion. Stockholders’ equity was $53.1 billion.

Cash used in investing activities was $7.5 billion in Q2 2019 and $15.7 billion for the six months, primarily for purchases of property and equipment and marketable securities. Cash used in financing activities was $2.2 billion in Q2 2019 and $4.5 billion for the six months, reflecting repayments of finance leases and debt.

The company adopted the FASB lease standard (ASC 842) and the film cost standard in 2019, resulting in recognition of operating lease assets and liabilities of approximately $21 billion and $342 million of additional capitalized film costs. Amazon has $24.3 billion of senior notes outstanding and a $7 billion commercial paper program with no borrowings. Stock‑based compensation expense was $1.97 billion for Q2 2019 and $3.2 billion for the six months. As of July 17 2019, 494.7 million common shares were outstanding. Tax contingencies of approximately $3.7 billion were recorded, and the company is involved in various legal proceedings.

Volkswagen’s U.S. unit asked a judge to postpone upcoming trials, citing inflammatory remarks by lawyer Michael Melkersen in a Netflix documentary. Melkersen referenced VW’s diesel‑fume monkey tests and compared the company to Hitler and the Holocaust, which VW argues could prejudice jurors. The first trial, involving a North Carolina plaintiff, is scheduled for Feb. 26. VW faces lawsuits from owners who opted out of a 2016 settlement that has cost the company more than $25 billion. Daimler and BMW also sponsored the monkey tests, which VW says were approved by an independent review board.

President James Madison returned a bill for internal improvements, stating that it exceeds Congress's constitutional authority. He argues the bill's proposed power is not enumerated, cannot be derived from the commerce clause, and cannot be justified by the “common defense and general welfare” clause without nullifying the Constitution's specific enumeration of powers and undermining state authority. He also notes that state consent cannot confer powers not granted by the Constitution and that limiting the clause to spending would still grant broad powers. While acknowledging the benefits of roads and canals, he withholds his signature because the Constitution does not expressly grant such authority and because extending congressional power would endanger the defined division of powers. He expressed hope that the objectives may be achieved through constitutional amendment.

NATO’s 2017 annual report shows upward trend lines, Secretary‑General Jens Stoltenberg said. The alliance deployed four multinational battle groups to the Baltic states and Poland, increased forward presence in the Black Sea, boosted hybrid‑war resilience, joined the coalition to defeat ISIS, and welcomed Montenegro as its 29th member. Burden‑sharing rose: three consecutive years of higher defense spending added $46 billion; NATO troops grew from under 18 000 in 2014 to over 23 000 in 2017. Russia remains a focus: the poisoning of former spy Sergei Skripal with a nerve agent traced to Russia was first use on alliance territory, clear breach of international norms. Stoltenberg cited Russia’s 2008 attack on Georgia, illegal annexation of Crimea, support to Ukrainian separatists, attempts to subvert elections, and integrated conventional‑nuclear doctrine as destabilising. NATO will maintain strong conventional forces and a nuclear deterrent, increase its Resolute Support mission in Afghanistan to about 16 000 troops, support Afghan‑led peace and call on the Taliban to negotiate. NATO trains Iraqi forces, launched a training mission in Iraq and supports Jordan and Tunisia.

Scalping is a short‑term trading style that seeks small profits from tiny price changes in stocks, forex, futures and other instruments, typically lasting seconds to minutes. The article argues that scalping is ineffective because traders face: (1) competition from sophisticated, better‑equipped market participants (banks, hedge funds, HFT firms) with lower latency and superior technology; (2) high transaction costs (commissions, spreads, slippage) that consume any theoretical profit; (3) difficulty of backtesting short‑term strategies, as noise and randomness cause backtest results to overstate real‑world performance; (4) need for extensive automation, which introduces operational risk and still cannot guarantee profitability; and (5) increased stress from rapid decision‑making. A real‑world example describes a trader who invested heavily in infrastructure and co‑location, yet lost money after being out‑paced by faster competitors. The author recommends focusing on longer‑time‑frame strategies where profit potential is larger, backtesting is more reliable, and costs are a smaller proportion of returns, or alternatively using long‑term diversified investing. Overall, the article concludes that most scalpers lose money and that scalping is generally a waste of time.

SUMMARY: Using density functional theory (DFT) with the CASTEP code, the structural, electronic, mechanical, thermal and optical properties of three novel out‑of‑plane ordered MAX (o‑MAX) phases Mo₂A₂AlC₃ (A = Zr, Nb, Ta) were investigated. The compounds crystallize in a hexagonal P6₃/mmc structure with two formula units per cell. Lattice parameters, internal coordinates and formation energies (–0.506, –0.349, –0.386 eV/atom) indicate chemical stability, with Mo₂Zr₂AlC₃ the most stable. Phonon dispersion calculations show no negative frequencies, confirming dynamic stability, and elastic‑constant analysis satisfies Born mechanical‑stability criteria. Electronic‑band and density‑of‑states calculations reveal metallic character, dominant Mo‑4d contributions and mixed ionic‑covalent‑metallic bonding; charge‑density maps confirm strong covalent Mo‑C bonds and metallic Mo‑Al interactions.

Mechanical analysis gives bulk moduli 205–230 GPa, shear moduli 138–145 GPa and Young’s moduli 342–361 GPa; the phases are anisotropic and brittle (G/B > 0.571, negative Cauchy pressure, Poisson’s ratio ≈0.22–0.24). Vickers hardness values (~6 GPa) fall within the typical MAX‑phase range; Mo₂Nb₂AlC₃ shows the highest hardness and crack‑resistance, while Mo₂Zr₂AlC₃ exhibits the best damage tolerance. Fracture toughness (2.59–2.78 MPa·m¹ᐟ²) and machinability indices (B/C₄₄ ≈ 1.3–1.9) are comparable to those of established thermal‑barrier‑coating materials.

Thermodynamic properties include Debye temperatures 525–634 K, minimum lattice thermal conductivities 0.74–0.90 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹, melting temperatures 2064–2237 K, thermal‑expansion coefficients 9.9–11.5 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ and Grüneisen parameters ≈1.37–1.44. Optical spectra show high infrared reflectivity (≈98 %), moderate visible/UV reflectivity (≈42–55 %) and anisotropic dielectric response.

Overall, the computed data indicate that Mo₂A₂AlC₃ phases are dynamically, chemically and mechanically stable, possess suitable thermal‑barrier‑coating attributes (low Kmin, high Tm, appropriate TEC and hardness) and may serve as heat‑shielding layers for high‑temperature and optoelectronic applications.

Becton, Dickinson and Company (BDX) has a long record of dividend growth, having increased its dividend each year since 1962. Since 2004, 12 of 13 years showed double‑digit growth, averaging 16.3% annually; 2012 recorded a 9.8% increase. The company projects a 2017 dividend of about $2.98 per share, a 10% rise over 2016, and expects GAAP EPS to exceed dividend payments. Its 2017 GAAP diluted EPS guidance is $7.90–$8.00, representing an 78% increase over 2016 and a 135% increase over 2015, with Q1 2017 EPS at $2.58, up 143% year‑over‑year due to a litigation reserve reversal. BDX’s 2015 $12.2 billion CareFusion acquisition has boosted margins and profitability. The dividend payout ratio fell from 59% in FY 2016 to an estimated 37% in FY 2017, leaving room for continued growth. Net profit recovered as merger costs declined; FY 2017 is on track for near‑record profit, potentially surpassing the FY 2010 record of $1.317 billion, helped by a $336 million one‑time gain in Q1. Key risks include manufacturing disruptions, higher interest rates and advanced competing products. BDX’s dividend is considered safe, with about 10% annual increases and strong product innovation and acquisition activity.

The paper discusses the ethical and practical integration of generative AI in education by drawing on philosophical perspectives. It introduces Anders’ concept of the Promethean discrepancy and the influence of technology on the human condition, and Foucault’s regimes of truth to analyze AI’s power dynamics. It argues that, despite AI’s potential inaccuracies and biases, Freire’s concepts of humanization and conscientization provide guidance for employing AI in ways that promote critical consciousness. To address educational objectives, the paper links Bloom’s taxonomy of learning with Arendt’s hierarchy of labor, work, and action, proposing that AI use should aim beyond consumptive labor toward humanizing action. The authors present a spectrum‑based framework for assessing AI‑assisted student work, emphasizing ethical, purpose‑driven use that fosters agency and civic engagement. They illustrate the framework with examples of community‑based political action and Socratic AI‑mediated research, adaptable across online, blended, and in‑person modalities. The paper concludes that AI must be employed to support humanizing ends and that educators need ongoing creativity to align pedagogy with evolving AI capabilities.

This patent application describes methods for a Wireless Transmit/ceive Unit (WTRU) to manage processing limitations in low-latency cellular systems using short Transmission Time Intervals (TTIs). The WTRU determines its Processing Capability (PC), reports it to the network (eNodeB/gNB), and limits the applied Timing Advance (TA) based on PC and TTI length to ensure sufficient processing time. The WTRU monitors the headroom between its processing value and PC; if thresholds are crossed, it may suspend or drop uplink transmissions to avoid exceeding limits. The passage also outlines the system architecture including WTRU components, Radio Access Networks (RAN) supporting LTE and NR, and Core Networks (CN) with entities such as AMF, UPF, and SMF, covering concepts like HARQ timelines, Time Alignment Timers (TAT), and processing constraints.

The government is accelerating emissions standards, requiring Bharat IV rollout and leapfrogging to Bharat VI within four years, faster than Europe’s decade-long shift. The disclosure describes a device and method for implementing fundamental computational primitives using a matrix multiplication accelerator (MMA). The device includes a processor (e.g., a DSP) with L1 and L2 caches, two programmable streaming engines (SE0, SE1), source A and source B buffers, and the MMA. The MMA contains a 1×32 multiplier (A) buffer, two 32×32 multiplicand (B) buffers, two 32×32 result (C) buffers, configurable format components for input and output data, a row‑offset component for non‑sequential data placement, and a nonlinearity component that implements a ReLU. The MMA executes a combined Load‑Store‑Execute (LSE) instruction each cycle, allowing simultaneous loading of a vector into the A buffer, loading or storing rows of the B/C buffers, and performing matrix multiplication between the A vector and a selected B matrix. Ping‑pong operation of the B and C buffers enables background loading while foreground computation proceeds.

The streaming engines fetch data from the L2 cache using multi‑dimensional nested‑loop addressing, delivering formatted vectors to the source buffers for the MMA. Input formatting options include zero‑padding, even/odd vector generation, value copying, known matrix creation, and linked operations; output formatting supports seam removal, stride removal, transpose, and zero‑padding.

Control software configures the streaming engines and MMA, then executes a sequence of LSE instructions to realize each primitive. Supported fundamental primitives include: batch small and large matrix‑matrix multiplication, matrix‑matrix pointwise multiplication, matrix‑matrix addition, small vector‑matrix multiplication, vector summation, affine transformation, two‑dimensional convolution (CNN), matrix row and column permutation, small and large one‑dimensional FFTs, discrete cosine transforms, one‑dimensional convolution/filtering, correlation, matrix assignment, and matrix transpose. Implementation details for each primitive include specific configurations of the streaming engines, row‑offset values, and MMA operations, as well as handling of strides, seams, and zero‑padding.

The NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU Architecture In‑Depth paper presents a comprehensive technical overview of the A100 GPU, the 8th‑generation data‑center accelerator built on the NVIDIA Ampere architecture (GA100). It details the third‑generation Tensor Cores that support TF32, FP64, BF16, INT8, INT4 and binary formats, and introduces a fine‑grained structured sparsity feature that doubles Tensor Core throughput. The GPU includes 40 GB of HBM2 memory providing 1555 GB/s bandwidth and a 40 MB L2 cache (≈7× larger than V100) with residency controls and compute data‑compression that can boost effective memory bandwidth up to 4×. A new Multi‑Instance GPU (MIG) capability allows a single A100 to be securely partitioned into up to seven isolated GPU instances, improving utilization for cloud service providers while maintaining QoS and fault isolation. The document covers the third‑generation NVLink (12 links, 600 GB/s total), PCIe Gen 4 with SR‑IOV, enhanced error/fault detection and containment, asynchronous copy and barrier operations, and hardware‑accelerated task‑graph acceleration. Software support includes CUDA 11, GPU‑accelerated libraries, NVIDIA GPU Cloud containers, Kubernetes on NVIDIA GPUs, and Magnum IO SDK with Mellanox InfiniBand/Ethernet interconnects. Performance sections provide speedup data for deep‑learning training and inference (e.g., BERT‑Large) and for HPC applications, along with tables of specifications, memory bandwidth, cache sizes, and decode rates. Numerous figures illustrate SM architecture, memory hierarchy, MIG partitioning, NVLink topology, and system configurations such as the DGX A100.

Earlier, two UN camps in Douentza were hit, killing a Malian soldier and a UN peacekeeper and lightly wounding another. The Treasury Department recommended rolling back several Obama‑era Wall Street regulations, including eliminating a requirement that publicly traded firms disclose the pay gap between chief executives and workers. The report, the second in a series ordered by President Trump, calls for easing IPO rules, allowing companies to test investor interest before filing publicly, raising the crowdfunding limit from $1 million to $5 million, and streamlining regulation of derivatives markets. It notes that the number of publicly listed companies has declined 50 percent over the past two decades, arguing that a streamlined regulatory system will spur economic growth. Republicans and business groups support the recommendations, while consumer advocates warn that further deregulation could increase the risk of future industry bailouts.

Douglas Haig, an ammunition dealer, was charged with manufacturing armor‑piercing bullets after unfired rounds in Stephen Paddock’s Las Vegas hotel suite bore his fingerprints. He sold Paddock 720 rounds at a gun show and at his Mesa home, lacking a license. Haig said he had no indication of Paddock’s intent and was shocked after the Oct. 1 attack that killed 58 people. After his name was released in court documents, he held a news conference, closed his business, received threats, but does not plan legal action.

Large Language Models are increasingly used as synthetic agents in social science, raising questions about their statistical limitations and future role. While LLMs can emulate human respondents via pattern matching learned from massive text corpora, they are not Bayesian inference engines; their “probabilistic” outputs derive from static weights and sampling, not from posterior belief updating. Empirical studies demonstrate that LLMs violate the martingale property, producing order‑dependent predictions and “introspective hallucination” rather than coherent probabilistic forecasts. Despite these issues, LLMs have shown predictive success on in‑domain tasks, yet fine‑tuning and alignment methods improve conversational performance at the cost of statistical coherence. The passage recommends treating LLMs as high‑capacity predictors under explicit conditioning, measuring algorithmic fidelity and subgroup accuracy, flagging unnaturally low variance, augmenting human data rather than replacing it, avoiding self‑conditioning and order sensitivity, and conducting routine stress‑testing with transparent failure reporting. It concludes that a single universal synthetic agent is unlikely; the responsible path forward is developing domain‑specific models and using LLMs for near‑term prediction and ethically difficult research while clearly acknowledging their limitations.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has updated its password advice, moving away from complex rules. New guidelines recommend simple, long, memorable passphrases using only lowercase letters and common words, and advise against mandatory expiration and forced use of special characters. NIST says longer passwords are cryptographically stronger, and that users often make minimal changes when forced to change passwords, which hackers exploit. Password managers are optional, and the security community has welcomed the change.

Early childhood education (ECE) is critical for brain development, with 85 % of cumulative brain growth occurring before age six and a documented 7–13 % return on investment through health, education and socio‑economic outcomes. UNESCO and SDG 4 stress universal access to quality ECE. In India, rural primary schools face heterogeneous competency levels, partly because children lack exposure to foundational programs. The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme launched in 1975 delivers health, nutrition and informal pre‑school education through about 1.34 million Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) serving 84 million children. Despite a 2013 ECCE policy, quality remains inconsistent; national studies (e.g., Kaul et al., 2017; ASER Centre, 2020) highlight inadequate infrastructure, limited teacher preparation and weak community involvement.

This study evaluates ECE quality in Mewat, a minority‑concentrated, low‑literacy district in Haryana where 88.6 % of the population lives rurally (male literacy 70 %, female 37 %). A mixed‑methods approach surveyed 71 AWCs across 25 villages in the Nuh block, using checklists for physical infrastructure, observations of learning environments, structured interviews with all 71 Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) and semi‑structured phone interviews with 36 workers.

Results show poor infrastructure safety: 57.75 % have boundary walls, 54.93 % a main gate, only 32.39 % a safe building and 19.72 % leveled floors. The physical learning environment is deficient—49.30 % have seating space but zero desks, chairs, durries or mats; 36.62 % have ventilation, 4.23 % have lights/fans; 38.03 % have outdoor play areas and 1.41 % have play equipment. Health and hygiene are critical: only 11.27 % have safe surroundings, 4.23 % have functional toilets, clean drinking water or a safe kitchen. Learning resources such as stationery, books, flashcards, puzzles and indoor equipment are absent in all centres.

AWW qualifications are low—43.66 % have only an 8th‑grade education (below the required matriculation), 30.99 % passed 10th grade, 18.31 % 12th grade and 7.04 % only 5th grade. Knowledge assessments reveal that none of the workers are familiar with the five developmental domains or curriculum content, 50 % are unaware of school‑readiness concepts, and 97.18 % lack awareness of their strengths or development needs. Pedagogical practices are mainly rote: 63 % rely on repetition and memorisation, 37 % use activity‑based methods. Interviews confirm a shortage of basic resources and limited parental involvement; most workers receive infrequent training and do not maintain child‑records or parent‑meeting logs.

The discussion notes that these findings align with broader rural ECE challenges (infrastructure deficits, unqualified staff, socio‑economic barriers, language‑cultural mismatches and weak monitoring) and aligns with the National Education Policy 2020, which advocates play‑based, holistic ECE, capacity‑building for educators, parental engagement and robust evaluation. State‑level implementation varies.

The study concludes that rural Indian ECE suffers from inadequate infrastructure, scarce learning materials, insufficiently trained AWWs, socioeconomic constraints, language barriers, low parental participation and weak monitoring. Addressing these issues requires a multi‑faceted strategy: establishing standardized physical infrastructure and learning resources, enhancing AWW training in child development and curriculum delivery, fostering parental and community awareness, and implementing effective monitoring and evaluation systems to ensure equitable, quality pre‑school education.

This document describes known hardware issues and deviations from specifications in the AMD Geode CS5535 Companion Device Silicon Revision A3. Issues include: PIT count mode and latch command deviations; debug port system hang; PIC incorrect operation during auto-end-of-interrupt; DMA rotating mode not functioning correctly; thermal alarm recovery mechanism missing in Standby domain; PMC Sleep_Clock control side effects; GLIU error MSR address flag failure; UART register inaccessibility during DMA cycles; software DMA memory write failure from LPC; system hang on I/O addresses 10000h or higher; USB over-voltage protection non-compliance; illegal LBAR I/O base settings; PIC failure when clock turns off with interrupt still high; PRD table alignment issues for ATAC and ACC; UDMA write CRC corruption after device termination; and ATAC SSMI blocking failure during DMA. Most issues have no operational impact or are resolved through specific programming workarounds such as avoiding certain command sequences, not using specific modes, or ensuring proper register settings and alignments.

The passage discusses challenges in evaluating advanced AI systems, especially large language models, in unseen tasks. Concerns include data contamination from large pre‑training data, static benchmarks mismatching evolving models, and the complexity of internal mechanisms. Proposed future benchmarking should dynamically generate evaluation samples, support varied difficulty levels, and provide multi‑faceted analysis of capabilities. Additional challenges involve cultural sensitivity and adherence to safety principles. DyVal is presented as an early dynamic evaluation framework that uses directed acyclic graphs to generate controllable, diverse samples with low duplication.

Dana White's Contender Series continues to award contracts; MMA pound‑for‑pound and divisional rankings have been updated after Alex Pereira's 80‑second TKO and Merab Dvalishvili's win; Conor McGregor is suspended 18 months for missed tests; a White House UFC event is slated for June 14; the PFL saw Khabib Nurmagomedov capture a vacant belt; Arman Tsarukyan‑Dan Hooker will headline UFC's debut in Qatar; Dustin Poirier wants a boxing match with Nate Diaz; UFC 320 and UFC 305 results show Du Plessis retaining his title while Pereira reclaims the light‑heavyweight crown; upcoming UFC 308 features a Topuria‑Holloway bout and a return by Khamzat Chimaev. Case No. 12,391 was a probate proceeding where Toll sought to set aside a sale of property at 820 Detroit Street in Denver, and Case No. 12,392 was an action to enjoin foreclosure of a trust deed on the same property. The property originally belonged to McKenzie, who borrowed funds from Casey using a trust deed. After McKenzie’s death, Casey discovered an unrecorded deed and arranged for a new deed to be recorded in Mrs. McKenzie’s name, eliminating the interests of McKenzie’s minor daughters. Mrs. McKenzie then sold the property to Toll, who later learned of the minors’ claim. To resolve this, Mrs. McKenzie and Casey entered into a contract (A) to probate the will, institute guardianship proceedings, and perfect Toll’s title at their expense. Probate and guardianship sales were conducted, but Toll challenged them, alleging fraud and breach of contract. The court found constructive fraud but no intent to harm the minors and held that the contract’s spirit was fulfilled. The judgments were affirmed with modifications: Toll pays his own costs in both cases; Mrs. McKenzie pays costs in case No. 12,391; Casey pays costs in case No. 12,392; and Toll must pay Casey the balance due on the encumbrance, minus Casey’s obligations under contract A, after which Casey will release the trust deed.

Micro E‑mini Nasdaq 100 futures are electronically traded on CME Globex, representing one‑tenth of the standard E‑mini contract and tracking the Nasdaq 100 Index (the 100 largest non‑financial Nasdaq‑listed companies). One contract unit equals the index value multiplied by $2; the minimum price fluctuation is 0.25 index points ($0.50 per contract) for outright trading and 0.05 index points ($0.10) for calendar spreads. Contracts are listed quarterly (March, June, September, December) for five consecutive quarters and are cash‑settled on the third Friday of the contract month at 9:30 am ET, using the special opening quotes of the index. Trading runs Sunday 6:00 pm ET through Friday 5:00 pm ET, with a daily maintenance break from 5:00 pm to 6:00 pm; ClearPort hours are Sunday 6:00 pm – Friday 6:45 pm ET with no reporting between 6:45 pm and 7:00 pm. The contract has no block‑trade eligibility. Price drivers include movements of heavily weighted component stocks, macroeconomic data, interest‑rate policy, overall economic conditions, and sociopolitical events. Historical data show an all‑time high of 16,676.50 (November 2021) and an all‑time low of 6,628.75 (March 2020). Because futures are leveraged, a 1% adverse index move with 10× leverage produces a 10% loss on capital; losses are calculated on the index value rather than the margin deposited. Strategies typically combine technical and fundamental analysis with risk‑management and position‑sizing rules; a published backtested system uses three buy and one sell variables, and it was first released around 2017. To trade, open an account with a futures broker, fund it above the required margin, and execute trades on the CME platform; some brokers also offer CFDs that trade continuously without expiry. ETFs tracking the Nasdaq 100 are available.

Mashal Khan was born in 1992. He was described as an exceptional student who loved learning. He studied at Abdul Wali Khan University in Pakistan. Four days before his death, he spoke to Khyber News about problems including an absent vice chancellor preventing graduations and excessive college fees. On April 13, a fight broke out on campus. Mashal was chased by students and shot. His father, Muhammad Iqbal Khan, received the news within an hour. Police arrested several young men. Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is a common household disinfectant with oxidizing properties. An Instagram post shows @wiredbrainmedia using hydrogen peroxide‑baking soda to clean a stovetop. Leveraged ETFs are exchange‑traded funds that use debt and derivatives to amplify the daily return of an underlying index, targeting ratios such as 2:1, 3:1 or inverse exposure. They magnify both gains and losses, making losses far larger than with traditional ETFs and exposing investors to higher risk and costs. Because daily rebalancing and volatility decay erode value over time, leveraged ETFs are unsuitable for long‑term holding and are most effective for short‑term strategies—typically day‑trading or swing‑trading that capture intra‑day momentum without being affected by daily rebalancing.

Taxation follows standard stock‑trading rules: profits held less than one year are taxed at short‑term capital‑gain rates (ordinary income), while gains held longer are taxed at the lower long‑term rate. Performance is measured with ratios such as the Sharpe ratio, Jensen’s alpha, and appraisal (Treynor‑Black) ratio; the Treynor ratio may not fully capture leveraged risk.

Risk management techniques include setting stop‑loss orders, diversifying across directional and inverse ETFs, and monitoring market conditions with volatility indexes to rebalance as needed. Liquidity, underlying index behavior, and fundamental drivers are key selection criteria.

Backtesting examples show that a short‑term strategy on an unleveraged ETF (QQQ) yielded an average 1.25% per trade and 7.6% annual return with an 18% max drawdown, while the 2× leveraged version (QLD) achieved 2.25% per trade and 13.6% annual return—close to QQQ’s buy‑and‑hold—but experienced drawdowns exceeding 55% during the 2008‑2009 crisis. Most traders cannot tolerate drawdowns larger than 25%, emphasizing that leverage can be lethal and should be used with a clear, disciplined short‑term plan.

TLV322x features an open‑drain output that can be pulled up to an external voltage up to 5.5 V independent of the supply. TI recommends pull‑up currents of 100 µA–1 mA; lower resistor values improve rise‑time at the cost of higher VOL and dissipation. Large pull‑up resistors cause exponential rise‑time. Output shorts to a voltage source may cause thermal runaway; a series current‑limiting resistor is advised. Unused open‑drain outputs may be left floating or tied to V–.

The device has internal ESD protection on inputs and outputs, limiting input voltage to 0.2 V beyond the rails. For low‑impedance sources, add a series resistor to limit transient currents to ≤10 mA.

An internal power‑on‑reset (POR) holds the output low for up to 32 µs after VPOR reaches 1.65 V, after which the output follows the differential input.

A comparator compares VIN with a reference; output is low when VIN < VREF and high when VIN > VREF. Propagation delay exists and can differ for rising and falling transitions. Smaller overdrive voltage (< 100 mV) increases propagation delay; maximum overdrive gives fastest response. Rise and fall times are measured between the 20 % and 80 % points of the output.

External hysteresis can be added via positive feedback to prevent chatter. Inverting hysteresis uses a three‑resistor network; equations give high‑to‑low and low‑to‑high trip voltages and total hysteresis. Non‑inverting hysteresis uses a two‑resistor network with a reference; equations give the two trip points and hysteresis.

Typical application: low‑side current sensing using an amplifier and the comparator; an alert is generated when the amplifier output exceeds 1.1 V. Critical design practices include low‑ESR bypass capacitors on the supply pins, short lead lengths, a series output resistor (< 100 Ω) to damp ringing, and avoiding parallel input‑output traces. Keep bypass capacitors close to the device and use a solid ground plane.

TI provides E2E support forums, documentation update notifications, and references to application notes for comparator hysteresis circuits.

Clinical trial phases 1–3 of the BNT162b1 and BNT162b2 vaccines showed that injection‑site reactions (redness, swelling, pain) within 7 days were mild or moderate, with pain being the most common; systemic events (fever, tiredness, headache, chills, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle or joint pain) were also mild or moderate, with tiredness and headache most common. In Phase 1 all tested doses were well tolerated except the 100‑µg BNT162b1 dose, which was stopped after the first injection because of reactions. BNT162b2 at 30 µg was selected for the Phase 2/3 expansion. In Phase 2/3 only a small proportion of participants (≈0.1 % in both vaccine and placebo groups) discontinued due to medical problems, and most adverse events were mild or moderate; no single medical problem affected more than 1 % of participants aged ≥12 years besides injection‑site or systemic events. Serious medical problems were rare (≤4 % in any group); researchers did not consider them related to the study vaccine, except for a few temporary events observed in participants 16 years and older. Deaths occurred in all groups (85 in the initial vaccine group, 62 in the placebo‑crossover group, 23 in the placebo‑only group) and were not attributed to the vaccine. Results after booster doses were similar to those after the primary series.

Erby et al. v. Columbus Paraprofessional Institute; Technology Education Corp. (TEC) (1991) – 74 Ohio App.3d 462. The Franklin County Common Pleas awarded three plaintiffs $5,225 each against TEC for breach of contract concerning an educational services agreement. Plaintiffs originally contracted with Paraprofessional Institutes of Ohio (PIO). Before classes began, PIO sold its assets to Educational Leadership Corp. (ELC), which conducted the training; after plaintiffs graduated, ELC sold the school to TEC. Ohio law provides successors are generally non‑liable unless they expressly or impliedly assume liability or the transaction is a de‑facto merger, mere continuation, or fraudulent. Trial court found implied assumption because TEC knew of the suit and expressly assumed “all rights, title and interest.” Appellate court held that asset purchase agreement excluded prior liability and contract disclaimed liability, defeating express or implied assumption. Continuation theory requires common identity of stockholders and directors, which was absent. Even if successor liability existed, plaintiffs must prove their claim, unsupported by record. Appellate court sustained TEC’s assignments, reversed judgment, and remanded.

The patent describes endpoint security techniques to prevent ransomware encryption by using virtual honeypot files and directories created by a lightweight agent. The agent employs a mini filter driver to intercept file system operations, inject fake entries at the beginning and end of directory enumerations, and redirect access to pre-created honeypot files. Unauthorized activity such as opening, writing, renaming, deleting, or enumerating honeypot files triggers policy‑based responses including process termination, alerts, or logging. The system supports configurable protected directories, process whitelists, user interfaces for policy settings, and can be deployed across Windows, macOS, iOS, and Linux platforms.

The Chande Momentum Oscillator (CMO) is a technical momentum indicator created by Tushar Chande and introduced in his 1994 book “The New Technical Trader.” It measures momentum by comparing the sum of higher daily closes to the sum of lower daily closes over a chosen period, typically 20 periods, and is calculated as  

CMO = 100 × (SHₒ – SLₒ) / (SHₒ + SLₒ)  

where SHₒ is the sum of higher closes and SLₒ the sum of lower closes. The resulting value oscillates between –100 and +100. Positive readings indicate upward momentum, negative readings downward momentum; values above +50 signal overbought conditions and below –50 signal oversold conditions, although these thresholds are trend‑dependent. Divergence between CMO swings and price movements (e.g., a lower price low paired with a higher CMO low) can warn of potential reversals. Traders often add a 9‑period moving average of the CMO as a signal line, generating bullish crossovers when the CMO crosses above the signal line and bearish crossovers when it falls below.

The CMO differs from other momentum tools: unlike the RSI (which uses a ratio of gains to losses) it uses the difference between sums of higher and lower closes, and unlike the stochastic (which compares the close to the price range) it focuses on close‑only data.

In backtesting a 9‑day CMO strategy on the SPY ETF, a simple system with a maximum 5‑day holding period achieved a higher risk‑adjusted return than a buy‑and‑hold approach, with lower drawdown despite modest absolute returns. Extending the holding period reduced performance.

The CMO works best when combined with trend‑following tools (e.g., moving averages or trendlines) to identify the main direction, then used to spot pullback ends for entry. It can be applied on various timeframes – intraday frames for day traders, daily or 4‑hour frames for swing traders – but the optimal period setting must be determined by backtesting each market and strategy. The indicator is less effective in choppy, non‑trending volatile markets, where price spikes can keep the CMO flat or extended for long periods.

Key limitations include its inability to directly identify the primary trend (it only reflects short‑term swings) and the need for complementary indicators to avoid false signals. To implement, users locate the CMO in their trading platform’s indicator list, adjust the period, and may install a custom version if unavailable. Overall, the CMO can enhance trading results by signaling when momentum exhausts counter‑trend moves, allowing traders to position for the next impulse wave in the prevailing trend direction.

The global corrugated packaging market is forecast to expand at a 4 % CAGR from 2014 to 2020, reaching $173.6 million in 2020, driven by e‑commerce growth, rising disposable income, and demand for lightweight, low‑cost, sustainable packaging. Key trends include high demand for electrical goods, slower demand for paper products, and a shift toward lightweight boards that may erode growth in some segments. Growth is supported by end‑user industries such as food, medicine, consumer durables, rubber and petroleum, while low durability and slower uptake in certain industries restrain the market. Corrugated packaging is segmented by application (liner board, container board, sheets, boxes) and flute types (A–F). This bibliometric study examined 2,295 peer‑reviewed articles from the Web of Science to map the intellectual structure and emerging trends in primary science education. Using bibliographic coupling and co‑word analysis in VOSviewer, it identified five thematic clusters: technology‑enhanced instruction (AR/VR/ICT), equity and teacher competence, cognitive and metacognitive scaffolds, dialogic and integrative pedagogies, and computational thinking in STEM. Co‑word analysis revealed four additional clusters focused on argumentation and scientific literacy, teacher beliefs and professional development, achievement and conceptual change, and technology integration. The study notes gaps in culturally responsive computational thinking and teacher identity, proposes the DIG‑EDU‑QUEST framework, and recommends inclusive digital integration, culturally responsive teaching, and interdisciplinary frameworks for future research and policy.

Leeuwenhoek observed intestinal bacteria in the 1680s, but microbes were long regarded as harmless. Over the past two decades, the microbiota has been recognized as essential for digestion, metabolism, immune function, and inflammation; disruptions are linked to asthma, obesity, colitis and colon cancer. Recent studies reveal daily (circadian) rhythmicity in the gut microbiota, explaining how late‑night eating or artificial light after sunset may affect health. A Weizmann Institute study in mice showed that gut microbes release metabolites that alter liver gene expression in a time‑dependent manner. Administering antibiotics or shifting feeding times changed liver physiology, and the liver’s detox response to acetaminophen varied with the time of day—least toxic at dawn, most at dusk. The authors conclude that the microbiota regulates the liver’s daily detox capacity, implying that medication timing could affect efficacy and side effects. Advances in DNA sequencing and analysis enabled these findings, which suggest that antibiotics and shift work may increase obesity and metabolic‑syndrome risk through microbiome pathways.

Multi-organ research integrating AI with imaging genetics creates endophenotypes for precision medicine. Three key advances drive the field: large-scale multi‑omics datasets such as UK Biobank and FinnGen; open‑science GWAS resources (FinnGen, PGC, GWAS Catalog, OpenGWAS, GWAS ATLAS, brain imaging portals BIG40, BIG‑KP, BRIDGEPORT, MEDICINE); and advanced statistical methods using GWAS summary statistics and linkage disequilibrium information (LDSC, Mendelian randomization). The authors derived 2024 multi‑organ AI endophenotypes (2003 structural covariance networks, 9 neuroimaging endophenotypes, 12 biological age gaps across nine organ systems). They publicly released GWAS summary statistics for these and for 525 disease endpoints (521 FinnGen and 4 PGC neurological disorders) to enable systematic genetic architecture analyses.

Center for Diagnostic Imaging Miami provides imaging services such as X‑ray, PET, PET/CT, CTA, MRI, ultrasound, open MRI, 3D mammography and nuclear medicine. Its board‑certified physicians, radiologists and technicians perform a Total Body Scan that includes CT of head, neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis, cardiac calcium scoring and a consultation within 24‑48 hours, screening for cancers, diabetes, heart disease, brain tumors, vascular and structural abnormalities, thyroid disease and other conditions. The center also offers thallium stress testing, bone scans, thyroid imaging and preventive cancer screenings for breast, ovarian and prostate cancer.

UHS‑II contacts (Table 3‑3) include SD bus pins 7‑8 used for RCLK; unused lines (CLK, CMD, DAT[3‑2]) must not float and are driven low or pulled up, DAT[2] may serve as interrupt for UHS‑II SDIO cards. ROM cards are read‑only; they ignore write‑type commands (CMD24‑33, CMD38) and optionally support CMD42 and security commands; full‑size ROM cards have no WP switch.

UHS‑I cards operate in DS (≤25 MHz, 3.3 V), HS (≤50 MHz, 3.3 V), SDR104 (≤208 MHz, 1.8 V) and DDR50 (≤50 MHz, 1.8 V) modes. UHS‑I is applicable only to SDHC/SDXC. Host‑card performance combinations (Table 3‑5) show max 104 MB/s requires host SDR104 + card UHS104; otherwise performance is limited to 50 MB/s. Bus speed mode is selected by CMD6 function group 1; driver strength by CMD6 function group 3; power limit by CMD6 function group 4. Voltage‑switch sequence (CMD11) follows ACMD41 with S18R/S18A negotiation; after switch to 1.8 V the card stays in SDR12 default. CMD19 tuning (mandatory for SDR‑VD hosts, optional for SDR‑FD) adjusts sampling points; only 4‑bit bus mode is supported.

UHS‑II cards support SD bus modes (DS, HS, SDR104, DDR50) and UHS‑II interface modes: FD156 (full‑duplex, ≤156 MB/s), HD312 (half‑duplex 2‑lane, ≤312 MB/s, optional), FD312 (full‑duplex, ≤312 MB/s) and FD624 (full‑duplex, ≤624 MB/s). Host and card combos are defined (Table 3‑8). Initialization follows a five‑step sequence: PHY init (PLL sync), device init, enumeration (4‑bit Device ID), configuration, SD‑TRAN init (emulated SD commands). The card disables UHS‑II interface before ACMD41 completes. If D1 lane does not assert STB.L within 200 µs the host falls back to legacy SD bus init. UHS‑II can operate up to 2.88 W (embedded) or 1.80 W (removable); minimum host power is 0.72 W from PHY init. UHS‑III is an enhanced UHS‑II supporting FD624 (max 624 MB/s) and additional Range D; UHS‑III cards support Range A‑D while UHS‑II cards support Range A‑B.

Application Performance Class defines minimum random (500 IOPS write, 1500 IOPS read) and sequential (10 MB/s) performance; higher class requires Command Queue and Cache (2000 IOPS write, 4000 IOPS read). Cache improves write speed but data may be lost on power‑off; Self‑Maintenance allows background management; Command Queue (CQ) supports task re‑ordering (voluntary or sequential) and works with 4‑KB I/O. Low‑Voltage Interface enables 1.8 V init; Table 3‑11 lists LV bus speed options.

Communication is master‑controlled: broadcast commands reach all cards, addressed commands target a specific card. Two operation modes exist: Card Identification (reset, voltage validation, RCA assignment) and Data Transfer (after RCA published). State diagrams and command tables (4‑23 to 4‑33) define transitions.

Card init uses CMD0 (software reset), CMD8 (verify voltage), ACMD41 (HCS, S18R, CCS, S18A). Host repeats ACMD41 until busy bit clears (≤1 s). CMD11 switches to 1.8 V signaling; CMD19 tunes sampling for SDR‑VD hosts. Bus width is set by ACMD6 (only when unlocked); CMD6 function groups select access mode, command system, driver strength and power limit.

Data read/write use block transfers (max 512 B), 1‑ or 4‑bit CRC, busy on DAT0, optional pre‑erase (ACMD23). Erase sequence is CMD32/CMD33/CMD38; DISCARD (CMD38 arg 1h) and FULE (CMD38 arg 2h) are optional for SDHC/SDXC and involve the same start/end commands. Write protect methods: mechanical switch, internal card protection, password lock. Password protection (CMD42) stores PWD/PWD_LEN; optional FEP enables Card Ownership Protection (COP). COP cards require CMD42[1Fh] unlock after power‑on or reset when FEP is set; FEP disables Force Erase and Reset PWD. Force Erase erases all memory and clears PWD (disabled if FEP set); FEP Force Erase requires correct FEP. Locked cards accept only a defined command set (CMD0, CMD1, CMD2, ACMD41, CMD7, CMD8, CMD13, CMD16, CMD17, CMD18, CMD24‑27, CMD30‑33, CMD38, CMD42, CMD55, CMD60‑63); all others are illegal. ACMD6 is rejected when locked; CMD56 (GEN_CMD) is not defined in this version.

CMD6 Switch Function selects access mode, command system, driver strength and power limit; it is mandatory for cards Version 1.10 and higher and valid only in Transfer state.

The recent employers’ liability law is deemed insufficient; the full burden of inevitable industrial accidents should fall on employers, who can add the cost to production. Federal and state laws need strengthening, especially for navy‑yard and arsenal employees. A presidential commission recommended that governments provide compulsory investigation of labor disputes, and a bill to that effect has been introduced. From 1881‑1900 strikes affected 117,509 establishments and 6.1 million workers, lockouts involved about 10,000 establishments, and total losses exceeded $450 million. The author urges a federal conciliation and arbitration commission to hear disputes, clarify misunderstandings, and shape public opinion, while cautioning gradual implementation because its decisions would not be legally binding.

The Massachusetts Court Probation Department filed a motion seeking clarification on Michelle Carter's stay of sentence. Carter was convicted of involuntary manslaughter for the 2014 suicide of her boyfriend Conrad Roy III, sentenced to 2.5 years with 15 months to serve. The court granted her appeal stay but ordered probation monitoring, which the department argues creates a split sentence requiring clarification on procedure and violations. A hearing is scheduled for August 21.

Quest Diagnostics consolidated its 20 regional customer service centers into two (Lenexa, Kansas and Tampa, Florida) in 2013, creating the National Customer Service (NCS) organization. The consolidation aimed to reduce costs and improve performance, but NCS faced high labor costs, severe employee turnover (60% of reps left within a year, costing $7,000–$10,000 per departure), long phone wait times, and low first‑call resolution. Customers and sales staff reported losing business because calls went unanswered or representatives could not answer questions.

In 2015, CEO Steve Rusckowski and Executive Vice President Jim Davis hired MaryAnn Camacho as Executive Director of NCS to address these problems. Before her arrival, a review identified four critical issues: the need for step‑based pay, career‑path development, supervisor training, and better workforce planning. After joining, Camacho spent her first weeks observing the call center floor, interviewing staff, and listening to calls to understand the full scope of operational challenges.

The case describes Quest’s background, its diagnostic testing business, competition (primarily LabCorp), and the broader context of its turnaround strategy. It details NCS staffing, training (six weeks of classroom instruction plus nesting), compensation ($13/hour starting pay, 2.5% raise after first year), performance metrics (speed to answer, calls per hour), and the stress of handling complex, life‑affecting inquiries. Supervisors dealt with high absenteeism (12.4%) and frequent escalations, often working long hours.

The summary highlights that NCS struggled with structural problems after consolidation, prompting leadership to focus on pay, career development, supervisor skills, and workforce planning to improve service, reduce turnover, and achieve operational excellence.

After the reciprocity treaty, the Hawaiian King sent a commissioner to Japan; the U.S. minister at Honolulu opposed it, fearing trade diversion and British competition. President Johnson noted Hawaii’s weak institutions and said a reciprocity treaty would guarantee goodwill until the islands sought U.S. admission. In 1868 an annexation party formed in Honolulu, but Secretary Seward deferred due to Reconstruction. The United States also protested the import of coolies, and the Senate called the traffic abhorrent, though British influence kept it alive. In February 1871 Minister Henry A. Pierce recommended annexation; President Grant confidentially asked the Senate for its views, noting the islands’ likely political destiny.

A Clemson University food scientist tested double-dipping and found it transfers significant bacteria to communal dips. Double-dipped water contained 1,000 times more bacteria than single-dipped. Single-dipped dips showed no bacteria, while double-dipped salsa had five times more bacteria than chocolate and cheese dips due to salsa's thinner consistency. After two hours, salsa's bacteria levels equalized with other dips due to acidity. Double-dipping can spread diseases including flu, herpes, and legionnaires' disease.
Kapil Sibal forgave Arvind Kejriwal after Kejriwal and Manish Sisodia admitted baseless allegations and apologized, saying everything is forgotten and they will move ahead.

The Money Flow Index (MFI) is a momentum indicator that combines price and volume data to measure money flow into and out of a security over a specified period. The study is a bibliometric content analysis of modern physics education research in Turkey from 2000 to 2023. A purposive sample of 273 studies (theses, articles, conference papers) was retrieved from multiple databases (mainly Tübitak Ulakbim 41.8 % and YOK 27.5 %). Most were journal articles (69.2 %) and written in Turkish (68.9 %); publication peaked between 2010 and 2019 and declined in the last five years. The most frequently investigated topics were the atom, photoelectric effect, theory of relativity, nuclear energy and the Compton effect. Study objectives centered on the effectiveness of instructional methods and techniques, determining the current state, and examining cognitive/affective characteristics, with many also addressing curriculum and textbook issues. Quantitative designs (especially quasi‑experimental and descriptive surveys) were preferred, while qualitative case studies and mixed‑method approaches were also used; some studies did not report their design. Non‑probability purposive sampling dominated, with education‑faculty undergraduates as the most common sample group and sample sizes typically between 31 and 100 participants. Intervention durations varied widely and were often unreported; short‑term (0‑4 weeks) interventions were most common. Data were collected mainly through interviews, tests, scales and questionnaires; observation and documents were less frequent. Analysis relied heavily on frequency/percentage and t‑tests for quantitative data and content analysis for qualitative data. Validity was supported chiefly by expert review and detailed process description; reliability was most often addressed via inter‑coder consistency and direct participant quotations, though reporting of these measures was often insufficient. Results generally showed positive outcomes (e.g., increased achievement, concretisation of knowledge) alongside negative outcomes (persistent misconceptions, negative emotions). Textbooks were criticized for lack of clarity and developmental appropriateness, and curricula were seen as inadequately reflecting modern‑physics philosophy. Most discussions were supported by literature but explanations were weak or absent, and some studies omitted a discussion section. Recommendations emphasized enlarging sample sizes, diversifying methodological approaches, employing simulations and interactive experiments, incorporating modern‑physics philosophy into curricula and textbooks, and conducting longer interventions with broader subject coverage.

Altermagnetism (AM) is a magnetic phase that breaks time‑reversal symmetry while preserving the combination of T with certain non‑symmorphic crystal symmetries, yielding zero net dipole moment. This symmetry pattern splits spin‑degenerate bands even without spin‑orbit coupling (SOC) and produces nodal structures labelled d‑wave, g‑wave, etc. Group‑theoretic analysis combined with density functional theory (DFT) shows that typical collinear altermagnets such as MnF₂ (d‑wave) and CrSb (g‑wave) host higher‑order atomic magnetic multipoles (octupoles, dotriacontapoles/32‑poles) in real space. The spin density around each magnetic ion can be expanded in tesseral harmonics; allowed multipoles are constrained by magnetic site symmetry, and their in‑phase (IP) or out‑of‑phase (OP) arrangement across symmetry‑related atoms determines macroscopic contributions. In MnF₂ the lowest‑order IP multipole is the d‑wave octupole dxymz, while in CrSb it is a g‑wave 32‑pole gyz(y²–3x²)mz. Both materials exhibit non‑collinear spin density (NSD) that is symmetry‑allowed but vanishes without SOC; finite SOC generates non‑collinear octupoles and 32‑poles linearly in the SOC strength λSOC, whereas collinear multipoles are only weakly perturbed quadratically. In the perovskite KMnF₃ a structural transition (fluorine‑octahedron rotation ≈6° about c) breaks anti‑translation symmetry and induces AM; the resulting IP 32‑pole gxy(x²–y²)mz scales linearly with the rotation angle. These higher‑order multipoles couple to tensor observables such as piezomagnetism and second‑order magnetoelectric effects, linking microscopic multipole order to macroscopic response. The study demonstrates that NSD, higher‑order multipoles and SOC are essential for describing altermagnetic materials.

The study used CiteSpace to conduct a visual analysis of literature on the relationship between open education and vocational education from 2012 to 2023. Chinese literature was retrieved from the CNKI database (515 valid documents) and international literature from the Web of Science database (319 documents). Keyword frequency analysis, timeline mapping, and citation‑burst detection were applied to identify research hotspots and trends. In China, high‑frequency keywords included open education, vocational education, higher vocational education, open university, distance education, and integrated development, with integrated development becoming the dominant theme after 2016. Internationally, adult education, online learning, vocational training, lifelong learning, and blended learning were prominent, and after 2018 research increasingly focused on online learning for adult vocational learners. Citation‑burst analysis revealed that in China the strongest bursts after 2018 concerned integration, integrated development, and coordinated development, whereas internationally bursts emphasized online learning, blended learning, technology, and personality traits. The findings indicate a divergence: Chinese research emphasizes integrating open and vocational education, while international research focuses on enhancing adult vocational skills and online learning. 1-3-1 zone is a versatile defensive alignment that overplays passing lanes, forcing offenses to throw over the defense or make vulnerable cross-court passes. The zone requires active, arms-out defenders moving as a unit, with recommended player roles: strong rebounder on left wing, quick baseline defender, tall top defender against small guards. Defensive shifts change based on ball location (middle, wings, corners), involving specific positioning for each defender. Adjustments include weakside skip pass closeouts and role exchanges for dribble penetration denial. A "Three in a Line" variation keeps a big player near the basket, with wings covering corners. The alignment facilitates trapping using corner zones with out-of-bounds lines, employing hard or soft traps while avoiding fouling. Traps involve tracing the ball with both hands and anticipating passes out. The zone can extend to half-court or full-court press.

The passage describes container‑based distributed‑system patterns at both single‑node and multi‑node levels.  

Single‑node patterns include:  
* **Ambassador** – a client‑side proxy that routes requests to sharded storage, brokers service connections, or splits traffic for experiments. The application sees a single local endpoint while the ambassador handles sharding, discovery, or traffic splitting.  
* **Adapter** – a container that transforms heterogeneous interfaces (monitoring, logging, health‑checks) into a uniform format, allowing reuse of off‑the‑shelf components without modifying them.  

Multi‑node patterns cover:  
* **Replicated load‑balanced services** – stateless servers behind a load balancer, optionally using session tracking (IP‑hashing or cookies) for consistent user routing, adding caching tiers (e.g., Varnish) for performance and SSL termination via nginx for secure traffic.  
* **Sharded services** – data or requests are distributed across independent shards using a sharding function; consistent hashing minimizes resharding impact. Shards can be replicated for reliability and can be dynamically rebalanced (“hot sharding”).  
* **Scatter/gather** – a root node fans out a request to all leaf nodes, each processes a portion of the work, and results are merged. Leaves can be homogeneous or sharded; the pattern provides parallelism but suffers from straggler latency and overhead that grows with leaf count.  
* **Event‑driven / Functions‑as‑a‑Service (FaaS)** – functions are stateless, auto‑scaled, and triggered by events. Benefits include rapid code‑to‑service, automatic scaling, and modularity. Challenges include debugging complexity, lack of background‑processing support, latency from loading large data into memory, and cost trade‑offs between per‑request and continuous‑run pricing.  

The passage also illustrates these patterns with concrete Kubernetes examples: deploying sharded Redis or Memcache with twemproxy ambassadors, using Varnish caches and nginx SSL termination, implementing request‑splitting experiments with nginx, and using adapters for Prometheus monitoring and fluentd logging. It emphasizes that choosing the right pattern depends on team structure, deployment environment, and whether code is written or consumed as off‑the‑shelf software.

This cross-sectional study evaluated the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) in 46 adult patients with urinary tract infections (UTIs). Options trading in TSLA involves derivatives that give the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell a specified number of shares at a predetermined price by a certain date. It offers leverage, hedging, and speculative opportunities but also carries the risk of large losses and complexity. Common strategies include long calls, long puts, covered calls, and spreads, chosen based on risk tolerance, investment goals, and market outlook. Potential returns depend on the difference between the strike price and the underlying asset’s price at expiration. Risks include leverage amplification and possible total loss. Best practices involve using quantified analysis and backtesting, employing risk management such as stop‑loss orders, and avoiding overtrading. Fees vary by broker and include commissions, platform, regulatory, and margin charges. Liquidity depends on expiration length, trading volume, and premium levels. Tax implications depend on the trader’s country of residence, generally subject to capital gains tax. Market sentiment can inform trades, but decisions should be based on backtested, quantified analysis.

Recent research shows that time spent outdoors, not near‑work or screen exposure, is the key environmental factor influencing the development of myopia in children. Myopia, or nearsightedness, is a condition where distant objects appear blurry because the eye grows too long; it typically begins in early elementary years and requires corrective lenses. A worldwide increase in myopia has been linked to genetic and environmental factors. Long‑term studies of 4,979 children (CLEERE Study) found that near‑work, computer use and television viewing were not major contributors to the need for glasses. Children with two myopic parents have about a 60 % chance of needing glasses if they spend little time outside; about 14 hours per week outdoors lowers that risk to roughly 20 %, similar to children with no myopic parents. Once a child already wears glasses, additional outdoor time does not alter prescription changes. Theories for the protective effect include brighter outdoor light stimulating retinal dopamine release, which slows abnormal eye growth. Parents are advised to ensure children use sunscreen and sunglasses to avoid UV‑related skin and eye damage.

The paper investigates how early‑stage startups develop Internet‑of‑Things (IoT) systems. Using a multiple‑case exploratory study, eight startups from aquaculture, surveillance, robotics, logistics, medical, and smart‑home domains were selected. Data were collected via semi‑structured interviews (12 interviews total) and analyzed thematically with the SEMAT Essence framework, focusing on four alphas: Team, System, Work, and Way of Working.

Team compositions in the cases include internal software and hardware engineers plus external competence (consultants, component providers, manufacturers). Six of eight startups relied on external help for MVP development.

Systems represent the startups’ value propositions across the three IoT layers (perception, network, application) and can start from either the application or perception layer.

Work is captured by Minimum Viable Products (MVPs) which the study classifies into three types: (1) looks‑like MVPs that simulate the product’s user experience but use manual processes; (2) functional works‑like MVPs that demonstrate real hardware and software integration; and (3) quality works‑like MVPs that emphasize non‑functional attributes such as performance, scalability, and security. All startups began with type‑1 MVPs and progressed toward type‑3 as product development matured.

Common ways of working identified are in‑house design combined with outsourced implementation and manufacturing, rapid prototyping (3D printing, CAD tools), reuse of ready‑made components (Arduino, Raspberry Pi, commercial sensors), and iterative development adapted to hardware constraints. Agile practices are applied but sprint durations are longer and frequent releases less feasible due to physical‑unit production costs.

The findings reveal that IoT startup MVP development mirrors software startup practices (iterative, opportunistic, use of work‑arounds) while requiring methodological adjustments for hardware‑related complexity, vendor dependencies, and integration of heterogeneous layers. Future work is suggested to expand the comparative analysis between software and hardware startups and to investigate larger samples.

Link-cut trees are data structures for maintaining dynamic forests of rooted trees, supporting operations including make-tree, link, cut, find-root, and path aggregation in logarithmic time per operation. The structure uses preferred path decomposition to partition a tree into paths stored as balanced binary search trees (auxiliary trees), connected by path parent pointers. The access operation, which makes a root-to-node path preferred and moves the node to the root of the overall structure, underlies all other operations and involves splaying within auxiliary trees. Heavy-light decomposition, which classifies edges as heavy or light based on subtree sizes, is used to analyze the total number of preferred child changes and bound the amortized cost. The implementation using splay trees achieves O(log n) amortized performance per operation through the access lemma and telescoping sums. Alternative worst-case O(log n) implementations use weight-balanced trees with an explicit heavy-light decomposition rather than preferred paths.
