The Commodity Channel Index (CCI) is a momentum oscillator that measures the current price of a security relative to its average price over a set period, identifying overbought and oversold conditions. Originally created for commodities, it now applies to stocks, ETFs, and bonds. CCI fluctuates around zero; readings below‑100 may signal a new downtrend and above +100 an overbought state. Thresholds are not fixed, so traders examine a security’s historical CCI values to locate reversal points. The calculation uses typical price (high+low+close)/3, a simple moving average, and mean deviation, with the constant 0.015. Optimal use is as an overbought/oversold indicator with a short lookback (5‑9 days) on daily charts. The indicator can reveal bullish or bearish divergences, warning of possible trend changes. Advantages include quantifiable extreme‑condition detection; disadvantages are lagging, limited applicability to stocks/bonds, and poor trend identification. CCI was invented by Donald R. Lambert in 1980 and was originally published in Commodities (now Futures) magazine. Backtesting on SPY with a 9‑day lookback and a buy threshold of ‑90 produced a profit factor of about 1.8, average gain per trade 0.55%, and maximum drawdown 23%, but the result may be curve‑fitted and other indicators are considered superior. Similar oscillators include RSI, ROC, Stochastics, and MACD.

HPCaaS enables enterprises to offer HPC‑based services and insights, with 81 % of surveyed firms already using HPC planning to launch such business models. It reduces upfront investment, allowing gradual customer acquisition; 49 % view HPCaaS as complete outsourcing and 42 % as a way to avoid building their own infrastructure, though skilled IT and analysis staff are still needed. Respondents value rapid access to cutting‑edge hardware and methods (52 % cite this as a core benefit) and see new data‑processing techniques as a source of competitive advantage and digital products. IDC concludes that HPC is becoming essential for modern simulations, modeling and data analytics, and that enterprises must integrate data across the product life‑cycle and adopt a single source of truth. The report recommends that firms: set up virtual product development, create a holistic data strategy, select an appropriate HPC operating model, ensure scalability, security and energy efficiency, and leverage external expertise. The President transmits a treaty signed on 1 December with Nicaragua for an interoceanic canal across Nicaraguan territory. The canal is required to link the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the United States, which are currently separated by the length of the continents and are dependent on rail. The treaty asserts that the United States seeks no territorial acquisition or political control beyond present borders; the waterway is a joint domestic project – Nicaragua provides the route, the United States provides funding – and it will be open to all nations on equal terms while reserving coastal trade privileges for the two parties. The agreement allows construction of a railway and telegraph as accessories. The proposed route follows Lake Nicaragua (about 90 miles long, 40 miles wide, fresh water, deep enough for the largest vessels) and the San Juan River. It requires six locks on the Pacific side and five on the Atlantic, with a total canal excavation of roughly 43½ to 53½ miles and lake‑river navigation of about 119 miles. The canal would cut sailing‑vessel travel times by up to 75 days between New York and San Francisco and substantially reduce distances to Asian ports. Economically, it would give U.S. manufacturers access to Asian markets, bring South‑American Pacific nations into close commercial contact with the Gulf States, and generate a large domestic coasting trade. The treaty provides a $4 million loan to Nicaragua for internal improvements supporting canal business, and the United States expects the canal to be immediately profitable due to shorter voyages and lower tolls. The President urges ratification and the appropriation of funds to begin work promptly, noting that the U.S. Army Engineer Corps can build the canal efficiently.

Inflation is a gradual reduction in purchasing power due to general price increases. Major causes include monetary expansion, demand-pull inflation, cost-push inflation, and built-in inflation. Short-term backtests show inflation is bad for stocks, as it reduces consumer spending, increases volatility, and raises interest rates. Value stocks tend to outperform during high inflation while growth stocks underperform. High inflation can reduce corporate profits, decrease money available for investment, and potentially cause market decline or crash. Recommended investments during inflation include diversified index funds, stocks, bonds, commodities, gold, real estate, and Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS).

Bibliotherapy, using books therapeutically, is applied in educational and clinical settings; developmental bibliotherapy aids growth without pathology, while therapeutic bibliotherapy targets mental‑health issues. This systematic review followed PRISMA‑P and the PICO principle, searching ERIC, Elsevier, ResearchGate, and Google Scholar (2006‑2021). Thirty‑five peer‑reviewed articles (quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods) were included.

Five themes emerged:

1. Perceptions and practices – Practitioners reported benefits but noted low awareness and limited formal training; challenges included time, resources, and reader reluctance.

2. Socio‑emotional outcomes – Significant reductions in aggression and social anxiety, and improvements in social skills, cooperation, and emotional awareness were reported; affective bibliotherapy was more effective than cognitive bibliotherapy for some outcomes.

3. Academic outcomes – Bibliotherapy improved reading comprehension, vocabulary, articulation, English language, and mathematics performance.

4. Self‑esteem, resilience, and hope – Significant gains in self‑esteem, hope, and resilience (including vulnerable children) were found.

5. Stress, trauma, anxiety, depression – Reductions in anxiety, stress, and depressive symptoms were observed; bibliotherapy facilitated discussion of past trauma but did not directly treat trauma effects.

Overall findings support bibliotherapy as a beneficial intervention in educational contexts, though limitations such as small samples, varied methodologies, and cultural differences were noted. The review highlights a need for a unified framework and improved practitioner training.

The paper proposes Virtual‑Node‑based Heterogeneous Graph Convolutional Network (VN‑HGCN), a model that learns node embeddings in heterogeneous graphs without predefined meta‑paths. It introduces hierarchical virtual nodes (type‑level nodes for each node type and one central node) that connect all original nodes, shortening any node pair’s distance to a path of length 4 and enabling long‑range information flow with only four layers, thereby mitigating over‑smoothing. The framework consists of three steps: (1) adding virtual nodes, (2) linear transformation of node embeddings into a shared feature space, and (3) aggregation via node‑level normalized adjacency and an attention‑based type‑level mechanism that weights intra‑ and inter‑type contributions. The total number of parameters grows linearly with the numbers of node types, nodes and attention dimensions, and the overall time complexity of an N‑layer model is O(N|A|(|V|+|E|)). Experiments on three real‑world heterogeneous graphs (ACM, DBLP, IMDB) for node classification show that VN‑HGCN consistently outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines (HAN, MAGNN, HGT, HetSANN, SimpleHGN, ie‑HGCN, ie‑HGCNvn) in both Micro‑F1 and Macro‑F1 across most training ratios. Parameter sensitivity analysis on IMDB demonstrates that performance is stable for different hidden dimensions, peaks at four layers, and is robust to varying numbers of type‑level virtual nodes. The virtual‑node strategy can be integrated into other heterogeneous graph models, enhancing their long‑range message passing. The authors conclude that VN‑HGCN effectively addresses over‑smoothing, captures long‑range dependencies, and provides a simple, scalable framework for heterogeneous graph representation learning.

Post‑operative hyperglycemia is common after cardiac surgery (60‑80 % of diabetic and >50 % of non‑diabetic patients) and is linked to infections, kidney injury, arrhythmias, longer stay and higher mortality. Current insulin‑titration protocols are static and often fail to individualize treatment, leading to frequent hypo‑ and hyperglycemic episodes and only 15 % of patients achieving recommended glucose levels (70‑180 mg/dL) on the first post‑operative day.

The authors developed GLUCOSE (Glucose Level Understanding and Control Optimized for Safety and Efficacy), a distributional offline reinforcement‑learning (RL) algorithm that recommends hourly regular‑insulin doses for the first 24 h after cardiac surgery. The model uses Conservative Q‑Learning combined with Implicit Quantile Networks to capture the full distribution of outcomes rather than just the expected return, improving safety under uncertainty. State inputs include demographics, comorbidities, laboratory values, vital signs, SOFA scores, vasopressor/inotrope doses, mechanical ventilation, and the prior four‑hour glucose history (≈70 features). Actions are continuous insulin doses rounded to the nearest unit and capped at 10 units/h. Rewards maximize time in the 70‑180 mg/dL range, with stronger penalties for glucose outside this window.

GLUCOSE was trained on the single‑center MIMIC‑IV database (6 148 patients) and externally validated on the multicenter eICU‑CRD (649 patients). Off‑policy evaluation showed GLUCOSE achieved higher estimated performance returns (0.0 [‑0.07, 0.06] internal; –0.63 [‑0.74, –0.52] external) than clinicians (–1.29 [‑1.37, –1.20] internal; –1.02 [‑1.16, –0.89] external). Time‑in‑range was highest when clinician‑administered doses matched GLUCOSE’s recommendations; discrepancies reduced TIR.

Three‑phase human evaluations compared GLUCOSE to endocrinologists, senior and junior intensivists, and nurse practitioners. GLUCOSE’s mean absolute error (MAE) in hourly insulin dosing was significantly lower than treating clinicians (0.9 vs 1.97 units internal, p < 0.001; 1.90 vs 2.24 units external, p = 0.003) and comparable to senior intensivists. Blinded expert panel ratings for safety, effectiveness, and acceptability were at or above the level of senior cardiac intensivists in both datasets.

Feature‑importance analysis (SHAP) identified current glucose, recent glucose trends, weight, and ventilation parameters as the most influential variables, aligning with clinical intuition. Evaluation of patients excluded due to ambiguous medication records (3 001 insulin‑only; 1 804 insulin + vasopressor/inotrope) showed similar action distributions, supporting model generalizability.

Limitations include the retrospective design, restriction to the first post‑operative day, lack of dietary data, and reliance on accurately documented medication dosing. Prospective studies are needed to confirm clinical impact.

Overall, GLUCOSE provides personalized, dynamic insulin titration using distributional RL, demonstrates robust performance across diverse ICU settings, and achieves dosing accuracy comparable or superior to experienced clinicians.

SimulRAG is a simulator-based RAG framework for long-form scientific QA that integrates scientific simulators as retrieval tools to improve answer factuality and informativeness. It features a generalized simulator retrieval interface that transforms between textual and numerical modalities, enabling seamless querying of simulators. The framework employs a claim-level generation method that decomposes answers into atomic claims for verification and updates, guided by uncertainty estimation scores and simulator boundary assessment (UE+SBA) to efficiently select claims for verification. A benchmark covering climate modeling and epidemiology domains was constructed, with ground truth verified by simulations and human annotators. Experiments demonstrate that SimulRAG outperforms traditional RAG baselines by 30.4% in informativeness and 16.3% in factuality, while UE+SBA consistently improves efficiency and quality in claim-level generation across various verification budgets. The framework assumes question-simulator relevance and suggests future work on automatic relevance detection to enhance applicability.

He urged expanding credit facilities for agriculture, coordinating rail, water, and motor transport, and addressing freight rates to aid farmers. The President called for an impartial labor tribunal with power to enforce decisions, modifications to the Railroad Labor Board, and measures to prevent paralyzing strikes. He supported a new tariff with flexible duties, registration of aliens, federal cooperation in immigrant education, a constitutional amendment to regulate child labor, and an amendment limiting tax‑exempt securities. He also mentioned pending studies on reclamation, timber, and fuel, and a proposed superpower survey for the eastern industrial region. Domestically, he stressed enforcement of Prohibition, a conference with state governors on its administration, and protection against revolutionary influences. Internationally, the President highlighted the U.S. role in peace through the Washington treaties, the four‑power Pacific pact, and cooperation with Central American nations, while affirming respect for national sovereignty and moral influence in world affairs.

TaintDroid is a system for tracking sensitive data exfiltration on Android by propagating taint labels from information sources (e.g., GPS, contacts) to sinks (network). It uses 32-bit bitvectors to tag data, with taint flowing through Dalvik VM opcodes via union operations. Special handling exists for arrays, native methods, IPC, files, and Java state, with taint stored adjacent to variables for cache efficiency. Overhead is moderate (~3-5% memory, 3-29% CPU). Limitations include inability to detect implicit flows and reliance on manual analysis for native methods. Alternatives like static checking (e.g., Jif) and legacy system tracking (e.g., TightLip) are discussed.

The "Chase" Box & One offense is a secondary offense designed to counter the Box & One defense by isolating the star player and freeing them from pass denial. The 52‑week high is the highest daily closing price of a stock over the preceding 52 weeks and serves as a resistance level; the 52‑week low is the lowest closing price and serves as a support level. The high is used to calculate the “percentage off the 52‑week high,” a metric for stock selection, and is viewed as an indicator of bullish sentiment. Because the metric relies on closing prices, intraday breaches that do not close above or below the levels are not counted. Traders may buy when price exceeds the 52‑week high or sell when it falls below the low, expecting a breakout to generate continued momentum. Academic research reports a “52‑week high effect,” showing stocks near their 52‑week high outperform those far away. Backtests on S&P 500 proxies (e.g., SPY) using simple moving‑average‑crossover rules opposite to a death cross did not yield profitable strategies, and performance resembled a buy‑and‑hold index approach. The 52‑week high and low can be found on financial platforms such as Bloomberg, Wall Street Journal, or Yahoo Finance.

The NHS Patient Charter (part of the NHS Constitution) defines patients' legal rights, the NHS's extra pledges beyond the law, and patients' responsibilities. It guarantees free care at point of use with exceptions (prescriptions, dentistry, eye care). It promises treatment based on need, equal access irrespective of personal characteristics, and waiting‑time standards with alternatives if not met. It also includes the right to safe, qualified care in clean environments, nutritious food, and continuous safety monitoring. Patients have rights to NICE‑recommended medicines, fair local funding decisions, and routine vaccinations, as well as to give or refuse consent, receive clear risk/benefit information, and keep personal data private. The charter grants choice of GP, access to comparative information, involvement in treatment decisions, and a duty of candour if errors occur. It provides a complaints pathway that can be escalated to the Ombudsman, allows judicial review, and may lead to compensation. In return, patients are expected to maintain their own health, treat staff and other patients respectfully, follow treatment plans, and participate in vaccination and screening programmes. The charter aims to empower patients, guide staff, and remind society that the NHS is a partnership built on trust and shared responsibility.

The lecture discusses biomimicking examples where natural structures are replicated in engineering: wood pyrolized into carbon templates infiltrated with silicon carbide; Jennifer Lewis's Harvard group's 3D-printed fiber-reinforced honeycombs; foamed metals for orthopedic implants mimicking trabecular bone; and tissue engineering scaffolds inspired by extracellular matrix. It also covers plant and animal structures with solid outer shells and foam cores—such as grass stems, porcupine quills, hedgehog spines, and toucan beaks—which help prevent buckling and wrinkling. Technical plant stems made from fiber-reinforced composites have been developed to mimic natural structures like horsetails. The lecture also addresses test preparation covering thermal conductivity of foams, trabecular bone, sandwich panels, and energy absorption, followed by Q&A about problem set questions involving stress-strain graphs and energy absorption calculations.

The company was reviewing operations globally, including its Japan subsidiary and assets such as Wessex Water and Dabhol Power in India, with several financial institutions expressing interest in purchasing Wessex Water. Long COVID, defined by the CDC as new, returning, or ongoing health problems occurring ≥4 weeks after SARS‑CoV‑2 infection, has affected an estimated 200 million people worldwide with a global prevalence of 43 % among infected individuals. Vaccines demonstrate high effectiveness against infection (≈89 %) and severe outcomes such as hospitalization (≈97 %), ICU admission (≈97 %), and death (≈99 %), yet some people remain susceptible to infection and long COVID; >3,500 deaths have been linked to long COVID. Long COVID can follow both mild and severe acute disease, and risk factors include female sex, socioeconomic deprivation, obesity, and various comorbidities. Healthcare workers (HCWs) are especially vulnerable due to frequent occupational exposure. The present study aimed to analyze epidemiological data and risk factors for long COVID among HCWs in Brazil.  
Methods: This case‑control study enrolled HCWs (≥18 years) at Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein (HIAE) from March 1 2020 to July 15 2022. Inclusion required a laboratory‑confirmed COVID‑19 infection by RT‑PCR (tested only symptomatic HCWs). Cases were defined as developing long COVID—signs and symptoms persisting >4 weeks that could not be explained by another diagnosis—while controls recovered within four weeks. Participants were followed for 180 days via the Employee Health Clinic. Vaccines administered included Oxford‑AstraZeneca (ChAdOx1), CoronaVac, Pfizer/BioNTech, and Janssen. Symptoms considered for long COVID spanned general (e.g., fever, fatigue), respiratory and cardiac (e.g., dyspnea, cough, chest pain), neurological (e.g., headache, concentration difficulty, loss of smell/taste, anxiety), digestive, and musculoskeletal categories. RT‑PCR confirmation used nasopharyngeal swab specimens with kits such as XGEN MASTER COVID‑19 and cobas® assays.

HeartLands Conservancy, a nonprofit, is leading the effort in partnership with Madison County and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, gathering input through open houses held in Edwardsville on Jan. 17 and in Glen Carbon on Jan. 19. Project manager Janet Buchanan (biology and environmental policy background) states that the information collected will be used to secure funding for projects targeting flooding, insufficient storm‑water infrastructure, water‑quality problems (littering, dumping, petroleum leaks, algae), recreation issues, and subsidence from past mining. The resulting watershed plans will guide infrastructure and land‑management improvements affecting agricultural and residential areas. Feedback can be submitted via HeartLands Conservancy.

Coaches must train players to adapt to diverse field conditions, which are rarely ideal. Field surfaces range from artificial turf—faster, hotter, requiring lighter passes and careful hydration—to natural grass, where ball speed and footing depend on grass type, height, moisture, and hardness; crowns and slopes can hide the ball and affect its trajectory. Anomalies such as hard or soft dirt, grass clumps, uneven ground, rocks, exposed sprinkler heads, worn seams, and dual‑use baseball markings can alter bounce, grip, and safety. Field dimensions vary widely (50‑100 yd × 100‑130 yd), and tactics must adjust: longer/wider fields demand extra fitness and weight on passes; shorter/narrower fields require earlier, softer service and tighter passing. Weather impacts safety and play: severe storms and lightning require immediate evacuation, cold necessitates layered clothing, heat/humidity can cause hyperthermia, rain creates skipping balls and wet footing, snow can render fields unplayable unless packed and lined, and wind alters flight and requires playing with or against it. Referees and assistants are part of the environment; players must play to the whistle and adapt to varying interpretations. Perimeter hazards (ad boards, drainage ditches, tracks, unauthorized spectators, thrown objects) and lighting (sun, shadows, floodlights, glare) affect visibility and safety. Equipment must be secure (goals anchored, nets intact) and balls must be uniform, correctly sized, and free of defects; extra or waterlogged balls are dangerous. Missing or multiple field markings can be supplemented with cones or paint. Coaching should incorporate condition‑based drills, pre‑game inspections, proper clothing, hydration, and knowledge of local rules to maximize safety and performance.

Retail sales rose to 10.9 % in March after a 9.5 % gain in January‑February. State‑owned‑enterprise fixed‑asset investment (FAI) grew 13.6 % in the first three months of 2017 and 13 % year‑over‑year in March; private FAI increased 7.7 % year‑to‑date and 8.6 % year‑over‑year. This preprint reports a comparison of REM sleep microstructure among isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), Parkinson’s disease with RBD (PD+RBD), and matched controls using video‑polysomnography. In each group (n = 20), phasic REM sleep proportion, sawtooth wave (STW) characteristics, and NREM/REM transition duration were quantified. iRBD patients showed a higher phasic REM sleep ratio than controls and PD+RBD patients, while PD+RBD patients exhibited lower STW density and shorter STW duration compared with controls and iRBD. Spectral analysis of STW segments revealed a shift toward higher frequencies in both patient groups, with a reduced predominance of low‑frequency peaks in PD+RBD. NREM/REM transitions were progressively longer from controls (shortest) to iRBD (intermediate) to PD+RBD (longest). The sequence of microstructure events at transitions differed: controls predominantly showed atonia‑first patterns, whereas patient groups more often showed STW‑first patterns. The findings indicate that REM sleep anomalies in RBD extend beyond loss of muscle atonia and include altered phasic REM proportion, STW generation, and transition timing, potentially reflecting brainstem, subcortical, and cortical involvement.

Cheryl Tickles v. PNC Bank was decided by the Supreme Court of Delaware. Tickles, a PNC employee, was injured on February 17, 1994, in the parking lot of Building 103 at PNC's Bellevue Complex. She had arrived early for overtime work and stopped to use an employee-only ATM in Building 103 before proceeding to Building 400, where her job was located. While returning to her neighbor's car, she slipped on ice and injured her back and left arm.

Tickles filed for workers' compensation benefits. The Industrial Accident Board denied her claim, concluding the injury was not compensable because she had not yet begun her workday and was engaged in a personal errand. The Superior Court affirmed, also finding the injury did not arise out of or in the course of employment.

On appeal, the Supreme Court applied Delaware's "going and coming" rule and its employer premises exception. The court held that the parking lot was part of PNC's premises, and once an employee reaches the employer's parking lot, injuries are compensable. The court also found that using the ATM was a preparatory act incident to employment, as it was reasonably necessary and occurred on the employer's premises within a reasonable time before her scheduled start.

The Supreme Court reversed the Superior Court's judgment and remanded the case to the Board for further proceedings consistent with the opinion, concluding Tickles was entitled to workers' compensation benefits.

Turing GPU architecture introduces a unified L1 cache and shared memory design that can be reconfigured between 64 KB L1 / 32 KB shared and 32 KB L1 / 64 KB shared, doubling L1 hit bandwidth per TPC versus Pascal and increasing L2 cache to 6 MB on TU102. The new SM delivers a 50 % performance improvement per CUDA core.  

Tensor Cores in Turing add INT8 and INT4 precision modes for inference while retaining FP16 support. A TU102 SM contains eight Tensor Cores, each performing up to 64 FP16 FMA ops per clock, yielding 512 FP16 multiply‑accumulate ops per clock per SM (1024 total FP ops) and 2048 integer ops per clock in INT8 mode. Turing Tensor Cores accelerate deep‑learning inference and matrix‑matrix operations for training; they power NGX Neural Services features such as Deep Learning Super Sampling (DLSS), AI In‑Painting, AI Super Rez, and AI Slow‑Mo. NGX runs on Turing GPUs via TensorRT and the NVIDIA driver, with models downloaded by GeForce Experience.  

The Tesla T4, the first Turing‑based inferencing GPU, integrates 2,560 CUDA cores and 320 Tensor Cores, delivering up to 130 TOPS (INT8) and 260 TOPS (INT4) and up to 40× higher inference performance and >50× higher energy efficiency than CPU‑based servers. It includes 16 GB GDDR6 memory with 320 GB/s bandwidth.  

Turing’s memory subsystem is the first to use GDDR6, achieving 14 Gbps signaling and a 20 % power‑efficiency gain over Pascal’s GDDR5X, with 50 % higher effective bandwidth through combined raw bandwidth increases and lossless compression. The GPU supports HBM2 and GDDR5X in earlier generations.  

Enhanced video engine adds HEVC 4:4:4 (8/10/12‑bit) and VP9 (10/12‑bit) decode, plus NVENC for H.265 8K‑encode at 30 fps with up to 25 % bit‑rate savings versus prior generations. The display pipeline supports DisplayPort 1.4a with DSC 1.2 for 8K @ 60 Hz, native HDR tone mapping (BT.2100), and USB‑C/VirtualLink for single‑cable VR headsets.  

NVLink (second‑generation) provides 25 GB/s per direction per x8 link; TU102 has two links (50 GB/s each direction) and TU104 one link, replacing MIO‑based SLI bridges.  

Ray tracing hardware (RT Cores) is integrated in each SM, accelerating BVH traversal and ray‑triangle intersection, delivering >10 Giga Rays/s and roughly 10× the ray‑tracing performance of Pascal’s software emulation. Turing enables hybrid rendering that combines rasterization with ray‑traced shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections, using denoising to reduce required ray counts. Real‑time ray‑traced reflections, contact‑hardening shadows, and ambient occlusion are demonstrated in games such as Battlefield V and Shadow of the Tomb Raider.  

New shading technologies include: Mesh Shading (Task and Mesh shader stages) for efficient handling of hundreds of thousands of objects, LOD selection, and dynamic cutaways; Variable Rate Shading (VRS) offering per‑16×16‑pixel region shading rate control for content‑adaptive, motion‑adaptive, and foveated rendering; Texture Space Shading (TSS) decoupling visibility from appearance sampling, enabling temporal stability and reuse of shaded texels; Multi‑View Rendering (MVR) expanding Pascal’s Simultaneous Multi‑Projection to four views per pass (up to 32 at API level) for stereo VR, cascaded shadow maps, and single‑pass instancing.  

Turing includes bindless Constant Buffer and Unordered Access views (DX12 Tier 3) and supports co‑location of multiple resource types in a single heap (Tier 2). VR enhancements comprise VirtualLink, MVR, VRS‑based foveated rendering, and VRWorks Audio accelerated by RT Cores.

In Maclam v. City of Marquette, the plaintiff sued for personal injuries sustained when he tripped over poultry crates obstructing a city sidewalk. The city moved for a directed verdict based on a charter provision (subd. 16, §1, chap. 7, Act No. 409, Local Acts 1895) exempting the city from liability for damages from sidewalk obstructions. The Michigan Supreme Court upheld the charter provision, holding that it was not repealed by a later act (Act No. 423, Local Acts 1899) since both could stand without conflict, and it did not constitute unconstitutional class legislation. The court affirmed judgment for the defendant city.

The passage lists twelve reasons to avoid forex trading. The primary reason is high leverage, which allows brokers to offer up to 50:1, so a small 2% move can wipe out a deposit. Traders with limited capital are forced into forex, and leverage makes survival during the learning curve almost impossible. Forex markets are zero‑sum: unlike stocks, there is no long‑term inflation or productivity tailwind. Currency moves are erratic, making predictions difficult; the best predictor is the forward rate, and risk‑management tools are often ineffective. The market operates 24 hours, encouraging overtrading, and is less regulated, creating counterparty risk and exposing traders to scams and fraud. Many forex strategies lack backtesting, and profitable backtests rarely survive the incubation period, especially for systematic traders. Overall, the article argues that forex trading is extremely challenging, largely unsuitable for retail traders, and recommends focusing on stock markets instead.

Lake Havasu City recorded Arizona's highest temperature of 128°F on June 29, 1994, the second highest in the United States after Death Valley, California (134°F in 1913). The heat results from lack of monsoon clouds, very dry air, rocky terrain that retains heat, creating a heat‑island effect, an isolated location, and minimal agricultural irrigation. Other hot Arizona locations along the Colorado River include Bullhead City, which reached 126°F and recorded 17 days of at least 123°F, but Lake Havasu City's record remains the state's highest.

This lecture introduces a class on the evolution of proofs in computer science from the mid-1980s to today, focusing on proof systems rather than cryptography per se. Traditional proofs are line-by-line verifications, but starting in the mid-1980s, the concept changed with zero-knowledge proofs (Goldwasser, Micali, Rackoff, 1985), leading to interactive proofs (IP). IP involves a polynomial-time randomized verifier and an all-powerful prover, with power derived from interaction and randomness; completeness and soundness parameters (e.g., 2/3 and 1/3) can be amplified through repetition. The non-interactive randomized version (MA) is believed more powerful than NP, as shown by an example verifying matrix multiplication using randomization (related to the Schwartz-Zippel lemma). The lecture then details the sum-check protocol, an interactive proof for verifying sums of multivariate polynomials of degree d in each variable over a set H. The protocol proceeds in m rounds, with the prover sending univariate polynomials and the verifier checking low degree and consistency, reducing the problem dimension by one each round. Soundness relies on the field size being much larger than m·d, ensuring the probability of accepting a false statement is small. This protocol is foundational for many proof systems (e.g., PCP, MIP, IP = PSPACE) and is used via low-degree extensions to embed problems into polynomials. Cryptography later enables succinct proofs and non-interactive proofs via the Fiat-Shamir paradigm, leading to SNARGs.

Korus is a night-time seizure management system designed to prevent sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) by autonomously repositioning patients after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure (GTCS). SUDEP, often occurring after nocturnal GTCS in the prone position, is a leading cause of death in young epilepsy patients. The prone position increases SUDEP risk by over 60-fold due to apnea and autonomic instability. The Korus mattress contains inflatable cells that expand up to 14 inches, a pressure sensor array with 1,152 nodes, and a machine-learning algorithm (Random Forest Classifier) to detect body position. Testing on 18 normative control subjects achieved 100% repositioning success from prone within an average of 21.75 seconds and 96.8% accuracy in prone detection. Long-term recording showed correct position detection 97.3% of the time, with false alarms at 2.3 events/hour. The system addresses a critical gap: current seizure detection devices cannot intervene within the ~3-minute window after a seizure before SUDEP occurs. Future development aims to integrate seizure detection, improve sensing and computing, and achieve an expected SUDEP risk reduction of over 50%, comparable to SIDS prevention from "back to sleep" campaigns.

The invention concerns a landing device for a rotorcraft that does not have an image‑capturing function. The device comprises a landing portion, a position‑recognition portion using multiple infrared cameras mounted on the landing portion, and a remote‑control portion that guides the rotorcraft to land on the basis of the recognition result. The landing portion can be accommodated in a cylindrical body with an opening/closing mechanism that is closed when not in use, protecting components from UV, rain, snow and debris. Movable plates attached to the edges of the landing portion take a first (vertical) posture when the mechanism is closed and a second (outward‑upward) posture when open, forming a funnel‑like shape that receives a suspended package and later pushes the package toward the center of the landing portion. An ascending/descending mechanism can lower the package into the user’s residential space and rise again to receive another load. The position‑recognition portion may include a distance‑measuring sensor and the remote‑control portion can verify the drone’s ID before enabling landing. The system uses a management system, an in‑warehouse control device, an in‑house control device and databases for routes, drones and weather data; drones navigate autonomously by GPS to a threshold distance from the destination and then are remotely controlled to land. The device can be installed above a residential area, and modifications describe a simplified direct‑to‑user version, integration with ventilation or smoke‑exhaust systems, weather‑observation equipment, portable emergency landing devices, battery and black‑box management, and countermeasures for unauthorized or terrorist drones.

Section 7.3.3 describes the PGA848 output‑stage difference amplifier, which uses a 6.67 kΩ feedback resistor. External access to the inverting (DA_IN–) and noninverting (DA_IN+) inputs allows designers to add capacitors for noise filtering or custom gain adjustment. The internal resistor network achieves 0.01 % accuracy, providing ≥80 dB CMRR, but mismatched leakage currents can degrade CMRR and the resistors have ±15 % absolute tolerance.

The device operates in a single functional mode (Section 7.4) when the input‑stage supply exceeds ±4.5 V (9 V total) and the output‑stage supply exceeds ±2.25 V (4.5 V total).

Section 8.1 introduces the PGA848 as a monolithic, high‑voltage, high‑bandwidth, precision programmable‑gain instrumentation amplifier with a single‑ended output. It combines a current‑feedback input stage with an internally matched gain‑resistor network and a four‑resistor differential output stage. Eight binary gain settings from 0.5 V/V to 100 V/V are selected via pins A0, A1, A2. Target applications include factory automation, analog input modules, data acquisition, test and measurement, and semiconductor testing.

The linear input range extends to within 3 V of either supply (Section 8.1.1), with CMRR maintained throughout; common‑mode limits depend on input voltage, differential voltage, gain, and reference level.

Section 8.2.1 shows a typical circuit driving a 16‑bit, 1 MSPS SAR ADC (ADS8860). The input stage is powered from ±15 V and the output stage from a unipolar 5.3 V supply shared with the ADC. A low‑noise 5 V reference (REF6250) is divided to set the PGA848 REF pin at 2.5 V, centered at ADC midscale. The OPA192 buffer drives the REF pin with dual feedback (RF = 2 kΩ, CF = 2 nF, RISO = 20 Ω), yielding ≈86° phase margin. Three filters are employed: an input EMI/RFI filter, a CFB filter (75 pF) across the 6.67 kΩ resistors giving a nominal –3 dB bandwidth of 318 kHz (≈277 kHz at the resistor‑tolerance high end), and a charge‑reservoir RC filter (RFIL, CDIFF) at the ADC inputs using C0G capacitors. The overall front‑end achieves –0.1 dB flatness to 41 kHz.

Layout guidance (Section 8.4) emphasizes symmetrical input paths, low‑ESR bypass capacitors (0.1 µF) near supply pins, separation of sensitive traces from noisy ones, and minimization of leakage and parasitic capacitance on DA_IN pins. Thermal paths should be minimized and the device kept away from high‑power sources.

Section 9 describes TINA‑TI™ simulation software (free, SPICE‑based) and lists related documentation, support forums, and trademark information. A caution warns that supply voltages above ±20 V (40 V total) will permanently damage the device, and ESD handling precautions are required.

Launched in 2013, ESA’s Gaia space observatory is cataloging over a billion objects to create a detailed 3D map of the Milky Way. Using Gaia’s first data release together with the RAdial Velocity Experiment (RAVE) survey, a University of Toronto team led by Jason Hunt measured the orbital speeds of more than 200 000 stars relative to the Sun. The analysis revealed a dip in relative velocities corresponding to zero angular momentum, allowing the researchers to determine the Sun’s orbital speed around the Galactic centre as 240 km/s. Combining this with proper‑motion data for Sagittarius A* gave a refined distance estimate of 7.6–8.2 kpc (≈24 800–26 700 light‑years), narrowing earlier estimates that ranged from 7.2 to 8.8 kpc. The work builds on earlier radial‑velocity studies by Prof. Ray Calberg and Prof. Kimmo Innanen and is based on only Gaia’s initial release. The team expects that Gaia’s final data release in 2017 will improve the Sun’s velocity precision to about 1 km/s and further tighten the distance measurement.

Lawyers for Venezuelan citizens in the U.S. asked the Supreme Court on Monday to preserve a federal judge’s order that temporarily bars the Trump administration from terminating their Temporary Protected Status (TPS). Congress created TPS in 1990 to let the Homeland Security secretary grant protected status to nationals who cannot safely return home because of natural disaster, armed conflict or other extraordinary conditions. In 2021, then‑DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for TPS; two years later he redesignated the country and extended the program through October 2026. After taking office, new DHS Secretary Kristi Noem rescinded both the 2023 designation and the 2025 extension. The National TPS Alliance and several Venezuelan TPS holders sued, arguing the termination violated the administrative‑procedure law and the Constitution because it was allegedly motivated by racial animus (citing Noem’s reference to TPS holders as “dirtbags”). U.S. District Judge Edward Chen issued a March 31 order halting the termination, calling Noem’s conduct unprecedented and based on negative stereotypes. The 9th Circuit declined to stay Chen’s order, and Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the Supreme Court to intervene; on May 19 the Court granted a stay, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson the sole dissenter. On September 5 Chen issued a final judgment that Noem’s actions were unlawful; lower courts denied the government’s request to stay that ruling. Sauer returned to the Supreme Court on September 19, asserting the lower courts defied the Court’s stay. In their Monday filing, challengers argued the earlier stay did not prevent final adjudication and that Chen’s judgment rests on a different statutory basis and a more developed record.

The firm also bought a 2005‑built 2 500 TEU secondhand ship (CMA CGM L’Etoile) and continues to explore newbuilding and second‑hand opportunities. Management notes that larger vessels have driven recent demand gains, with smaller sizes likely to follow. The author states he is buying CMRE stock.

Myanmar's inclusive education for children with visual impairment follows a "limited inclusive education in phase" model, where students attend special schools for primary education (Phase 1) and regular schools for secondary education (Phase 2). The system leverages resources from both school types, with special schools providing Braille instruction, life skills training, supplementary study time, and psychological support, while regular schools offer opportunities for social and communication skill development. Key limitations include insufficient communication and coordination between special and regular school teachers, regular teachers' reliance on special school expertise, and limited social integration between students with and without disabilities. About half of surveyed parents, particularly in rural areas, were unaware of educational opportunities for children with disabilities. The study suggests Myanmar's model could serve as a reference for other countries but requires addressing identified challenges and considering broader needs of children with disabilities.

The ADS9803 is an eight-channel, 20‑bit, 2 MSPS data acquisition device featuring simultaneous sampling of multiple devices via the SMPL_SYNC signal, an internal low‑drift voltage reference with optional external reference support, and a flexible data interface supporting 2‑lane or 4‑lane modes with single‑data‑rate (SDR) or double‑data‑rate (DDR) operation. It includes a data‑output randomizer that XORs the conversion result with a PRBS bit or the LSB to minimize ground‑bounce interference, and offers two data‑averaging modes (simple averaging reduces output data rate by half; moving average preserves data rate). Test‑pattern generation supports fixed, digital‑ramp, and alternating patterns for channels 1‑4 and 5‑8. Power‑down is可控通过 RESET pin or register write, and an initialization sequence programs default registers after power‑up or reset. A speed‑boost mode allows up to 8 MSPS sampling on a user‑selected channel pair while the remaining channels are idle. The device uses a three‑bank SPI register structure with bank selection via address 0x03, and supports daisy‑chain configuration for multiple ADCs where register writes and reads are broadcast through the chain. The ADS9803 targets ATE applications, achieving <0.01 % total unadjusted error after calibration, with configurable bandwidth modes (low‑noise up to 22.7 kHz and wide‑bandwidth up to 700 kHz) for fast settling when multiplexing PMU channels. Power is supplied via three separate rails (AVDD_5V, VDD_1V8, IOVDD) with no required power‑up sequence, and PCB layout recommends separating analog and digital traces, placing decoupling capacitors close to power pins, and using a solid ground plane. The device includes development tools, technical support resources, and ESD handling precautions.

The study was conducted to improve the measurement of COVID‑19 mortality in India by using a representative sample of deaths and WHO‑standard verbal autopsy (VA) surveys to determine cause of death.  India’s official COVID death counts (~530,000) are thought to understate the true burden; excess‑death estimates range from 4 to 6 million.  The research obtained a representative sample of all deaths reported in the Consumer Pyramids Household Survey (CPHS) between 2018 and 2021, a panel covering roughly 237 k households and representing the urban and rural population of all Indian states except the northeast.  CPHS tracks living and deceased household members every four months.  For every reported death, CMIE attempted a VA interview with the next‑of‑kin using the 2016 WHO VA instrument, supplemented with questions for COVID‑19 symptoms; two physicians independently assigned ICD‑10 codes, and a third adjudicated disagreements.  Deaths with ICD‑10 codes U07 or U08 were classified as potential SARS‑CoV‑2 deaths; excess SARS‑CoV‑2 deaths were estimated by subtracting the average annual U07/U08 death rates in 2018‑2019 from those in 2020‑2021.

The CPHS recorded 30,447 deaths reported between 2018‑2021; VA surveys were completed for 22,178 (72.8 % response rate).  After excluding 1,719 deaths that occurred before 2018, the final VA sample contained 20,453 decedents.  Statistical adjustments included: (1) imputed CPHS sampling weights for decedents; (2) an “under‑inclusivity” adjustment to account for the average 52.7 % of deaths reported within four months, rising to 98.3 % after 31 months; and (3) propensity‑score weights to correct for non‑random VA non‑response (e.g., urban, smaller, higher‑caste households were more likely to respond).  Composite weights were used for all death counts and death‑rate calculations.

Key results:
- The all‑cause annual death rate in 2020‑2021 was 81.19 % higher than the 2018‑2019 average.
- SARS‑CoV‑2 (U07/U08) accounted for 17.93 % of all deaths during the pandemic and 33.15 % of excess deaths; cardiovascular disease accounted for 23.15 % of excess deaths; respiratory‑disease deaths fell by the equivalent of 1.52 % of excess deaths.
- SARS‑CoV‑2 death rates peaked at annualized rates of 0.8 % (May 2020), 0.9 % (June 2020) and 1.1 % (May 2021), coinciding with the end of the national lockdown and the second wave.
- Death rates increased with age, with the highest rates among those >80 years, but the bulk of deaths occurred in the 61‑80 age group. Urban residents had higher SARS‑CoV‑2 death rates, yet total deaths were larger in rural areas because of the larger population.
- State‑level excess SARS‑CoV‑2 death rates ranged from 0.07 % in Bihar and Jharkhand to 2.13 % in Goa.
- Income quartile was not significantly associated with SARS‑CoV‑2 death rates.
- Non‑COVID deaths (cardiovascular, “other”) also spiked during the lockdown and the second wave, but their relative increase was smaller than that for SARS‑CoV‑2.

The study notes several limitations: U07/U08 codes include non‑SARS‑CoV‑2 deaths (e.g., vaping‑related disorders), which may inflate pre‑pandemic counts; adjustments for delayed reporting and non‑response may be imperfect; the VA modification for COVID‑19 has not been fully validated; and the analysis cannot capture deaths reported more than 32 months after occurrence.  Despite these caveats, the results demonstrate that verbal autopsy surveys can provide detailed, population‑representative cause‑of‑death data in lower‑income settings and that COVID‑19 was the dominant driver of excess mortality in India during 2020‑2021.

NVIDIA’s GA10x Ampere architecture delivers up to 2× performance gains in programmable shading, ray tracing, and AI compared with the prior Turing generation. The second‑generation RT Core doubles ray‑triangle intersection performance and adds an Interpolate Triangle Position unit that accelerates ray‑traced motion blur up to 8× over Turing, while the third‑generation Tensor Core introduces structured sparsity for up to 2× higher matrix‑throughput, enabling DLSS enhancements that support 8K gaming at high frame rates. The architecture introduces GDDR6X memory with PAM4 signaling, achieving up to 936 GB/s bandwidth (a >52 % increase over previous GPUs) and new RTX IO technology that offloads asset loading and lossless decompression from the CPU to the GPU via Microsoft DirectStorage, reducing CPU utilization dramatically and cutting load times. GA10x also supports hardware‑accelerated AV1 video decoding (first GPU to do so), seventh‑generation NVENC encoding, and display interfaces (HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4a) that enable 8K 60 Hz and 4K 120 Hz output. For data‑center workloads, the A40 and RTX A6000 GPUs combine second‑generation RT Cores, third‑generation Tensor Cores with sparsity, PCIe Gen4, up to 48 GB of GDDR6 memory, and NVLink support, providing up to 2× FP32, 2× ray‑tracing, and 5×‑10× AI throughput compared with Turing‑based predecessors.

The 3-4 defense consists of 3 down linemen, 4 linebackers, and 4 defensive backs, using outside linebackers to create favorable matchups. Since 2005, coaches from this defensive tree—Bill Belichick, Nick Saban, and Kirby Smart—have won 9 college national championships and 7 Super Bowls, totaling 16 major titles. Its strengths include versatile pressure packages and two-safety alignments that can shift between coverages. Weaknesses emerge against modern spread offenses, where a 5-man box becomes vulnerable to blockers and speed receivers. Common variations include the Weakside Edge Blitz and Crossfire Blitz, along with Cover 4 and Cover 2 Man coverages. The system traces to Bill Parcells and Bill Belichick, whose coaching tree includes Saban and Smart, both achieving extensive success at the college level.

The lecture covers full factorial experimental design and ANOVA. Professor discusses quiz grading (average 78-79), advises students to review solutions rather than contest individual points, and notes students over-complicated problem 2 using detailed tests when simpler confidence intervals sufficed. The lecture then shifts to design of experiments, explaining that 2^k full factorial designs use corner points to fit regression models with main effects and interactions. The contrast approach estimates effects by averaging high versus low settings; extending to three factors includes three-way interactions, with interaction columns generated by multiplying factor columns. Dividing contrasts by 2^(k-1) gives estimates, and regression provides equivalent coefficient estimates. ANOVA tests significance by comparing sum of squared deviations to noise estimates via F-tests. Checking model adequacy involves examining residuals for trends and testing for curvature using center points or additional data points, distinguishing between model error and replication variance. Blocking and confounding manage nuisance factors: randomizing converts systematic effects to noise, while block designs can be arranged so nuisance factors confounded with higher-order interactions rather than main effects, preserving ability to detect important factors. Fractional factorial designs subset corner points by accepting confounding with higher-order terms.

The Neofoot study assessed newborn foot length as a diagnostic tool to identify low birth weight (LBW) and preterm birth (PTB) in a resource-limited setting in Papua New Guinea. A prospective diagnostic accuracy study enrolled 342 newborns, using birth weight <2.50 kg and gestational age <37 weeks as reference standards. Foot length was measured within 72 hours of birth. The optimal cut-off for both LBW and PTB was <7.7 cm, with sensitivities of 84.7% and 88.0% respectively, and specificities of 69.6% and 61.8%. Agreement between researcher and volunteer measurements showed a mean difference of 0.07 cm with limits of agreement from -0.55 to +0.70 cm. Foot length measurement proved simple, feasible, and accurate for identifying at-risk newborns in community and facility settings, with potential for implementation by trained health workers and volunteers.

Iran’s parliament gave initial approval to a bill boosting spending on its missile program and Revolutionary Guards, allocating over $260 million each to the ballistic‑missile program and the Quds Force. Lawmakers, overwhelmingly chanting “Death to America,” backed the measure, which must pass a second vote before clerical approval.

The MSPM0G3519, MSPM0G3518, MSPM0G1519, and MSPM0G1518 microcontrollers are low-power Arm Cortex-M0+ based devices. They support five operating modes (RUN, SLEEP, STOP, STANDBY, SHUTDOWN) managed across two power domains (PD1 for CPU/high-speed logic, PD0 for low-power peripherals). Key analog features include 12-bit ADCs (4Msps) and a 12-bit DAC. Integrated digital peripherals encompass UART, I2C, SPI, and CAN-FD interfaces; a 12-channel DMA controller; general-purpose and advanced timer blocks; an RTC; and watchdog timers. Security features include an AES-128/256 accelerator, TRNG, and CRC. Memory consists of dual-bank Flash (up to 512KB with ECC) and SRAM (up to 128KB) with write-execute protection. Debug and programming support are provided via a Serial Wire Debug interface and a password-protected Boot Strap Loader.

Blackwell introduces fast clock gating that shuts entire clock trees, saving dynamic power, and adds a separate voltage rail for GPU cores and memory, enabling per‑workload voltage control, reduced leakage, and frame‑level power gating for battery gaming.

A Berliner Testament appoints spouses mutual sole heirs and their children final heirs after both die, offering financial security but creating a binding testament that cannot be unilaterally altered. Changes in circumstances such as divorce or new relationships can cause complications. Clauses to relax binding effect and tax allowances should be considered, and legal advice is advisable.

Delta expects its premium‑cabin revenue to surpass coach revenue in 2025. In the most recent quarter, premium ticket sales rose 9% year‑over‑year to nearly $5.8 billion, while main‑cabin ticket revenue fell 4% to just over $6 billion. CEO Ed Bastian said there is no sign of a slowdown in premium‑travel demand. At an investor day, Delta noted that main‑cabin tickets represented 43% of its 2024 revenue, down from 60% in 2010, with premium seats and its loyalty program together accounting for about 60% of total revenue.

The U.S. opioid overdose epidemic has caused over 450,000 deaths in the past eight years, with the highest single‑year toll in 2022 (more than 80,000 deaths). Effective responses require targeted interventions informed by spatiotemporal forecasts of fatal overdoses. The current epidemic evolved through four waves (prescription opioids, heroin, fentanyl, and combined stimulant‑fence doses), and overdose patterns vary across regions. Prior research has mostly identified past hotspots rather than predicting future spikes, and most public‑health agencies lack resources for person‑level predictive modeling.

This study aims to forecast opioid‑related fatal overdoses at the census‑tract level on an annual basis to help agencies plan geographically and temporally targeted interventions. Two datasets are used: Cook County, Illinois (overdose deaths from August 2014‑May 2023, 1,328 tracts) and Massachusetts (deaths from 2001‑2019, 1,620 tracts). Covariates include historical overdose counts, tract latitude/longitude, calendar year, and Social Vulnerability Index features.

Models evaluated include simple baselines (all‑zeros, last‑year, historical average with a tuned look‑back window, and weighted historical average) and more complex approaches (Poisson GLM, Gradient Boosted Trees, Gaussian Process, Bayesian Spatio‑Temporal model, Negative‑binomial regression with spatially‑lagged features, and a neural‑network method CASTNet). Performance is assessed with standard error‑based metrics (RMSE, MAE) and a new intervention‑focused metric called “Best Possible Reach” (% BPR), which measures the proportion of actual overdose deaths occurring in the K = 100 tracts a model recommends for intervention.

Training periods were 2010‑2018 for Massachusetts and 2015‑2019 for Cook County; validation used 2019 (MA) and 2020 (Cook), and testing covered 2020‑2021 and 2021‑2022, respectively. Resampling was used to quantify uncertainty.

Key results: The % BPR metric often ranks models differently from RMSE/MAE, leading to different intervention recommendations (e.g., in Massachusetts, a Bayesian Spatio‑Temporal model identifies 18 more deaths per year in the top 100 tracts than the Gaussian Process). Simple historical‑average baselines performed competitively with complex models in both regions—sometimes within uncertainty bounds of the best performers. The study releases open‑source code and a cleaned Cook County dataset.

Limitations include reliance on only two geographic areas, a single budget size (K = 100), and a limited set of covariates. Conclusions emphasize that simple baselines should be included in future overdose‑forecasting studies and that intervention‑aware metrics like % BPR more closely align with public‑health decision‑making, potentially improving the number of preventable overdose events.

The Relative Strength Index (RSI) is a momentum oscillator, calculated from average gains and losses over a set period (commonly 14 days) and displayed on a 0‑100 scale. Readings below 30 signal an oversold condition, while readings above 70 indicate an overbought condition. Traders use these levels to anticipate price reversals and to build mean‑reversion strategies that profit when prices revert to their average.

A Contract for Difference (CFD) is a financial agreement that settles the difference between an asset’s current value and its value when the contract is opened. CFDs enable speculation on the price movements of stocks, commodities, currencies and indices without owning the underlying asset; profit or loss depends on whether the price move is correctly anticipated. CFD trading is a zero‑sum game and typically involves leverage, which magnifies both gains and risk.

In CFD markets, traders often apply shorter time frames and more extreme thresholds for the RSI (e.g., 15 for oversold and 85 for overbought) to increase sensitivity for day‑trading strategies. Time‑frame choice influences performance: shorter intervals produce faster, more erratic signals, while longer intervals smooth the readings.

Backtesting is essential to evaluate a strategy’s viability; historical tests on assets such as SPY have shown that a basic RSI threshold approach can yield about 0.86 % per trade but with large drawdowns. A two‑day RSI strategy combined with a “QS” exit reduced average profit to 0.67 % per trade while producing fewer and smoother drawdowns. An RSI‑momentum trend‑following approach, using a 100‑day look‑back and a 14‑day RSI, can capture longer‑term trends but generates fewer signals.

The RSI works best when combined with other indicators (e.g., volume or relative performance) and when multiple time frames are used to confirm direction. Divergences between price and RSI can provide additional buy or sell cues, although they are harder to quantify.

Effective risk management is critical in leveraged CFD trading: attention should be given to commissions, slippage, taxes and the use of stop‑loss orders, though stop‑losses can sometimes degrade performance. Systematic backtesting on the specific assets and market conditions intended for CFD trading is required before live implementation.

Science is pursuing mind‑hacking methods ranging from established stimulants to neurotechnologies. Caffeine and nicotine have long been used to block sleep‑promoting adenosine and mimic the attention‑enhancing neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Current projects include Tim Tully’s effort to develop a memorization pill, funded by billionaire Ken Dart, sequencing genomes of individuals with exceptional memory and engineering fruit flies with photographic memories via CREB activators. Researchers are also attempting to identify the hundreds of genes underlying intelligence for possible genetic enhancement. Others are building deep‑brain stimulation devices that monitor brain activity and automatically deliver electrical pulses to restore normal function during panic attacks, depressive or psychotic episodes. These advances raise both therapeutic hopes and dystopian concerns.

Chapter describes host environment responsibilities for accessing AGESA™ software interface. Host must establish a valid stack before any call, use bridge procedures that locate binary image entry points and invoke the AMD dispatcher. Entry point identifiers are in AMD.H; an example bridge file is AmdBridge32.asm. Call‑out functions are routed through a host‑implemented router that translates function numbers to execution addresses; the router must match defined interface parameters. Stack‑related macros AMD_ENABLE_UEFI_STACK, AMD_ENABLE_STACK, and AMD_DISABLE_STACK create and tear down a pre‑memory stack using cache‑as‑Ram, preserving EBX and using register‑based passing.  

UEFI boot consists of SEC, PEI, DXE, and RTP phases; code is built with different tool sets (MASM 6.15 for 16‑bit SEC, ml/CL for 32‑bit, ml/CL for 64‑bit). Two build models are supported: binary modules (indirect) and source integration; configuration is customized via <plat>Options.c. Build control files for PEI and DXE phases (e.g., AgesaPei0Libs.inf) and environment variables AGESA_ROOT, AGESA_OptsDir are required.  

PEI phase includes two PEIMs: AmdProcessorInitPeim publishes AMD_PEI_INIT_RESET_PPI, AMD_PEI_INIT_EARLY_PPI and depends on AMD_MEM_INIT_PPI; AmdMemoryInitPeim publishes AMD_MEM_INIT_PPI and AMD_MEMORY_INFO_HOB after memory initialization. DXE driver calls AmdInitLate to generate DMI, PState, CRAT, CDIT, WHEA, ACPI IVRS tables and publishes AgesaDxeProtocol. Host must implement required call‑outs AgesaAllocateBuffer and AgesaDeallocateBuffer; optional call‑outs are described elsewhere.  

Entry procedures include AmdInitReset, AmdInitEarly, AmdInitPost, AmdInitEnv, AmdInitLate, AmdInitRtb, AmdInitResume, AmdInitWr. Service functions provide CPU identification, APIC/PCI base addresses, cache size, data eye results, MMIO mapping, and event logging. All procedures require a stack established by the host; MTRRs must not be modified during Cache‑As‑Ram period.

Peter Fassbender, a former Langley City mayor serving one term as Liberal MLA, is considering running for mayor again, with a decision expected by early August. Two incumbent councillors have already declared for the mayoralty. Fassbender previously served on the Langley School Board, was elected to city council in 2002, and served as mayor from 2005 to 2011 before winning the Surrey-Fleetwood MLA seat in 2013.

The Supreme Court will hear the case of a Texas man, Hunter, who pleaded guilty to wire fraud in 2024, waived his right to appeal, and was sentenced to 51 months, supervised release, and $235,000 restitution after appealing a medication condition. Thuro et al. v. Meredith et al., 1924, affirmed a judgment for real‑estate brokers seeking commission. The defendants employed plaintiffs to find a buyer for property; plaintiffs introduced Della B. Thuro and Mrs. Charles Tallman, who signed a purchase contract. George W. Thuro was absent and did not authorize Della to sign on his behalf. The Tallmans took possession, made payments, and later abandoned the contract, after which the Thuros repossessed the property. The court held that a principal cannot defeat a broker’s commission by refusing to be bound by or to sign the contract with the purchaser produced, and that the brokers fulfilled their duty by procuring at least Mrs. Tallman as a purchaser. Alleged variances, refused instructions, and motions to strike were deemed immaterial or harmless errors. Judgment affirmed.

Yankees rookie Cam Schlittler pitched eight scoreless innings with 12 strikeouts and five hits in Game 3 of the AL Wild Card series. Yankees scout Matt Hyde, who first saw Schlittler at Northeastern University, praised the performance as "unbelievable" and "surreal," especially against Boston. Montecito Union School District settled a sexual abuse lawsuit for $7.5 million with two brothers who claimed a former principal molested them in the 1970s. The settlement represents about 40% of the district's 2025-26 budget, and the district has no insurance coverage for that period. This study compares statistical parametric mapping (SPM) and a convolutional neural network (CNN) for detecting outliers in multi‑center plantar pressure data. The dataset comprised 1,031 recordings (798 valid, 233 outliers) categorized into four outlier types (General Acquisition Error, Double Foot Capture, Inverted Orientation, Incorrect Side Annotation), augmented to 2,798 samples. SPM used affine registration to a reference template, pixelwise non‑parametric testing, and cluster‑based permutation correction. The CNN employed three convolutional blocks with side‑embedding and generated SHAP explanations. Both approaches were evaluated with nested stratified 5‑fold cross‑validation and a semantic differential survey involving 16 domain experts. The ML model achieved higher performance (MCC = 0.96 ± 0.01, F1 = 0.99 ± 0.00) than SPM (MCC = 0.78 ± 0.02, F1 = 0.93 ± 0.01). Participants rated both explanations positively across clarity, correctness, usefulness, relevance, understandability, trustworthiness, and completeness; SPM was perceived as simpler and ML as more complex, but differences were not statistically significant. Experts rated similarity between approaches as high and preferred the ML approach (43.5 %) over SPM (34.8 %). The results indicate that both SPM and CNN can detect technical errors in plantar pressure data, with ML offering higher accuracy and SPM providing simpler explanations, emphasizing the importance of human‑centered evaluation of explainability.

The passage argues that the common 20 % drop definition of a bear market and similar percentage thresholds for corrections, dips and crashes lack a rational basis or supporting data and are not useful for managing risk or allocating capital. It cites the 2015 and 2011 corrections where the S&P 500 and Russell 2000 fell different amounts, showing that the labels provide no actionable guidance. The author proposes alternative definitions: a secular bull market is a 10‑20‑year period of rising corporate revenues and earnings driven by broad economic shifts, with decreasing volatility and increasing price‑to‑earnings multiples; a secular bear market is the opposite, characterized by higher volatility, frequent rallies and retreats, and shrinking willingness to pay for earnings. He emphasizes that most long‑term gains stem from multiple expansion rather than earnings growth, illustrated by the 1982‑2000 bull market, and advises investors to focus on underlying economic and psychological drivers rather than arbitrary percentages.

The passage describes defensive tactics against the High Post Split Offense, which combines a high‑post split followed by down screens. The defense proceeds in two phases. Phase 1 defends the high‑post split by having guard defenders sag one stride in front of the post, wings assume help positions with hands pointing toward opponent and ball, and the post defender drops off an arm’s length away then steps up to jam the high post toward the weak‑hand corner; this prevents hand‑offs and cuts between the guards. Phase 2 defends the down screens by sending defenders out to “Show” shooters wide and then recover to three‑quarter pass‑denial positions; most NBA teams favor Show & Recover over switching to avoid giving the big screener a mismatch. An aggressive SOS version of the defense adds early ball‑handler pressure, snuggle denial on entry passes, switches on splits and screens, and employs double‑team traps on wing passes, with continuous rotation and “pack‑in” principles as the ball moves.

Deutsche Bank plans to sell its 8.8% stake in Dubai-based private equity firm Abraaj, which is under investor scrutiny over alleged misuse of funds in a $1bn healthcare fund. The sale, non‑core, has gained urgency as Deutsche restructures, cutting 7,000 jobs and closing its Dubai equities research team. Valuation of Deutsche’s holding is hampered by Abraaj’s undisclosed debt; one estimate values its investment‑management unit at up to $500m. Abraaj, managing $13.6bn, has cut about 15% of staff, suspended new investments and is reviewing its corporate structure. It is considering selling part or all of its investment‑business unit and its stake in Pakistani utility K‑Electric to ease cash‑flow pressures. Its CFO and COO have resigned.

The passage reports a study that investigated Turkish teachers' perspectives on integrating the metaverse into education. The metaverse is described as a virtual universe that allows users to be present via avatars, combining gaming, social media and digital communities, and is classified into four types: augmented reality, lifelogging, mirror world, and virtual‑reality. After moving from science‑fiction to platforms such as Second Life (2003), Roblox (2006), Pokemon Go (2015) and Fortnite (2016), it has attracted millions of users and major technology investments. In education it offers immersive collaboration, first‑person simulations of scientific investigations, virtual tours of historical periods, personalized learning, and risk‑free practice for hazardous tasks. However, limitations include difficulty for teachers to monitor students, higher mental effort for augmented reality, limited learning gains from virtual‑reality compared with traditional media, and requirements for reliable platforms, network connectivity, devices and teacher training.

A survey was conducted with 333 Turkish teachers; most taught at private (N=171) or public (N=146) schools, with primary‑school, English, and ICT teachers the largest groups. The questionnaire contained 28 Likert‑type and open‑ended items. Findings show an average knowledge score of 5.25/9, with 78.1 % reporting prior metaverse experience, mainly via virtual‑reality or 3‑D worlds. Teachers follow metaverse research (4.80/9) and hold a positive attitude toward its educational use (6.23/9). They see many advantages: attracting student interest (76.3 %), realistic practice environments (74 %), learning‑by‑doing (67.8 %), exposure to new technologies (67.8 %), elimination of educational boundaries (59.2 %), and development of digital competence (57.7 %). At the same time they express concerns: technical problems (76.9 %), psychological issues such as addiction (69.5 %), inequality of opportunity (67.8 %), data security (57.1 %), teacher readiness (55.9 %), difficulty of content preparation (54.1 %), physical side‑effects (52.7 %) and cost (47.3 %). Despite these concerns, teachers report a willingness to use metaverse in lessons (6.37/9), perceive their own lessons as moderately suitable (6.05/9) and show high readiness to attend training (8.08/9). They regard subjects such as Information Technology (72.1 %), Physics (71.2 %), Biology (68.8 %), Chemistry (68.5 %) and Mathematics (63.4 %) as most appropriate for metaverse delivery, and think the technology is especially useful for concretizing abstract concepts, conducting experiments, enabling collaborative learning and creating realistic environments.

Overall system readiness is perceived as low: teachers estimate that schools, colleagues, parents and other stakeholders are almost never ready, while students are relatively more ready (4.59 %). Most teachers expect that the education system will need a few years to integrate the metaverse, with 37.2 % predicting effective use within 3‑5 years, 23.7 % within 1‑2 years, and 22.8 % within 5‑10 years.

The discussion highlights that the metaverse can reduce cognitive load, lower costs and enable safe instruction, but health concerns, infrastructure demands and pedagogical challenges remain. It recommends small‑scale pilots, collaborative content development, robust infrastructure, teacher training and continuous user feedback. The conclusion affirms the metaverse’s transformative potential for creating immersive, interactive and safe learning environments, provided prerequisites such as reliable connectivity, devices, and teacher preparation are met, and further research and investment are needed.

The "Box & One - Chase" Offense targets the middle vulnerability of the Box & One defense using post flashes, back cuts, and high/low feeds.
