NEC established the NEC Satellite Operation Center, operational in April, operating the ASNARO‑2 radar satellite launched January. It uses GroundNEXTAR and a secure data center, supporting multi‑satellite control, visualization and image distribution. NEC will market ASNARO‑2 images with JEOSS from September. Hiroyuki Nagano said NEC will provide comprehensive space solutions.

The TPS7H500x‑SP family are radiation‑hardened, fixed‑frequency, peak‑current‑mode PWM controllers that use a transconductance error amplifier (OTA). They support two frequency‑compensation schemes: Type 2A adds a capacitor CHF in parallel with RCOMP and CCOMP for high‑frequency noise attenuation, while Type 2B omits CHF. Compensation is selected by choosing a crossover frequency, calculating RCOMP from the OTA transconductance (1800 µA/V) and reference voltage (0.613 V), then calculating CCOMP to place the compensation zero at the power‑stage dominant pole, and optionally adding CHF to create a high‑frequency pole for the ESR zero. The power‑stage transconductance gmPS depends on transformer turns ratios, current‑sense resistor and other parameters, and can be simplified for buck topologies.  

The device includes a thermal shutdown that stops switching at a typical junction temperature of 175 °C and restarts below 160 °C. Operation is peak‑current‑mode: the internal oscillator initiates turn‑on of the primary output, the sensed current is compared to a divided COMP voltage, and the switch is turned off when the sensed current reaches that level.  

These controllers are intended for space‑grade DC‑DC converters using GaN semiconductors, support switching up to 2 MHz and can be used in buck, flyback, forward, active‑clamp forward, push‑pull and full‑bridge topologies.  

An example synchronous push‑pull design at 500 kHz illustrates component selection: RT = 205 kΩ, output = 5 V with feedback resistors RTOP = 10 kΩ and RBOT = 1.4 kΩ, dead‑time ≈ 25 ns (RPS,RSP = 20.5 kΩ), leading‑edge blank time ≈ 50 ns (RLEB = 49.9 kΩ), soft‑start capacitor 33 nF (≈ 7.5 ms), transformer turns ratio 2.5, primary inductance 40 µH, primary FETs rated 170 V, synchronous rectifier FETs rated 80 V, RCD clamp design, output inductor 0.47 µH, output capacitance 2.3 mF (seven 330 µF polymer tantalum caps), optional output filter and damping resistor, cycle‑by‑cycle current limit ≈ 35 A (RCS = 7.5 Ω), hiccup capacitor 3.3 nF, compensation network RCOMP = 40.2 kΩ, CCOMP = 15 nF, CHF = 47 pF, slope‑compensation resistor 102 kΩ.  

Layout guidance includes: routing the feedback trace away from power magnetics, minimizing switch‑node copper area, separating analog (AVSS) and power grounds, making high‑current traces short and wide, placing bypass capacitors close to the controller, keeping compensation components near the COMP pin, and keeping high‑dv/dt traces away from sensitive pins such as VSENSE, COMP, CS_ILIM, etc. An RC filter on CS_ILIM and a capacitor on HICC (≥ 3.3 nF) are recommended. The controller operates from a 4 V to 14 V supply with at least 0.1 µF of ceramic bypass capacitance. ESD precautions should be observed when handling the device.

Commands in the ring buffer are distributed to multiple execution units for parallelization. To achieve precise halting, the halting command must be the last entry; for precise error halting only one command may be queued. Interrupt status bits are cleared by writing PM_RBCtl[CLEAR_INTS] when the buffer is empty or paused; PM_RBTail may advance while paused.

System Physical Addresses (SPAs) encode encryption information when SMEE or SME‑MK is enabled; setting the C‑bit indicates encrypted memory and firmware selects the appropriate key. SPAs must be well‑formed and in correct ranges; reserved fields are set to zero.

The firmware provides page‑migration commands:

• PM_GET_CAPABILITIES returns firmware capabilities and version; only PM_LIST_ADDR, PM_SUB_COMMAND and interrupt flags are used.

• PM_PAGE_MOVE_IO moves 1‑128 pages in SNP or non‑SNP systems; in SNP it operates only on hypervisor‑owned pages. Software must prevent CPU access, make pages non‑present, issue ATS invalidations for unsecured ATS devices, and update host page tables after completion. 2 MB pages must be fragmented into 4 KB pages. Firmware validates addresses, obtains exclusive RMP access, checks page size, performs IOMMU/CPU TLB invalidations, copies the data, updates the host PTE and releases RMPs.

• PM_PAGE_MOVE_GUEST moves SNP‑guest pages and is faster than the SNP PAGE_MOVE command. Source pages must be Guest‑Valid or Guest‑Invalid and destination pages Pre‑Migration; 2 MB pages must be 2 MB aligned and composed of contiguous 4 KB pages. DMA to the pages is not supported. The command requires RMP_ENFORCE and follows similar validation, exclusive‑access, TLB and copy steps.

• PM_END marks the end of a migration command sequence and may generate an interrupt on completion.

Errors are reported in command status fields, migration list entries or the PM_STATUS register. Format or content errors reject the command; list errors may cause partial success. Hardware failures are reported via status and the Machine Check Architecture; a timeout forces MCA logging and appropriate recovery. Memory may become unrecoverable, but the system will attempt to save state before halting.

The McEachern Indians (SN NEXT No. 1) visited the Harrison Hoyas in Georgia on Friday night, both 5‑0 after a bye. McEachern sought to reinforce its top bubble ranking, while Harrison aimed to upset and raise its profile. The game began at 8 p.m. EST in Kennesaw.

Astronomers using the Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR) and the RAD@home citizen science platform discovered the most distant and most powerful odd radio circle (ORC), designated RAD J131346.9+500320, at redshift ~0.94. Its double‑ringed structure, only the second known, challenges theories that ORCs arise from merging black holes; the study proposes they are linked to superwind outflows from spiral host radio galaxies. The discovery also includes two other unusual radio galaxies in massive clusters: RAD J122622.6+640622, a 3‑million‑light‑year galaxy with a bent jet forming a 100,000‑light‑year ring, and RAD J142004.0+621715, a 1.4‑million‑light‑year source with a ring at a jet end. All three objects suggest interactions between relativistic magnetized jets and surrounding hot plasma shape these rare rings. Citizen scientists played a key role, highlighting human pattern recognition. Upcoming telescopes such as the Square Kilometre Array and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are expected to find more ORCs.

Peter Marks, former top FDA vaccine regulator ousted by RFK Jr., has joined Eli Lilly to lead molecule discovery and infectious diseases. He confirmed his new role at Lilly Research Laboratories, with his first day being Monday. The appointment drew criticism for the revolving door between the agency and industry.

State of Louisiana sued the Banking Department of Citizens’ Bank for a license tax on a separate banking department. The president of Citizens’ Bank excepted, claiming no authority to represent a separate corporation and that no such corporation existed. The court ruled that a department of a corporation may be sued only in the corporation’s corporate name if its charter authorizes the suit; otherwise the suit must be against the corporation itself. It found that Act 246 of 1853 and the 1853 compact did not create a separate corporation with authority to sue and be sued and that the citation was directed to the “Banking Department,” not to the Citizens’ Bank of Louisiana, violating the rule that corporations must be sued by their corporate name. The lower court’s judgment for the defendant was reversed; the suit was dismissed as a nonsuit, leaving other issues undecided. Monroe, J., dissented.

- Enron’s pipelines and power plants are generating steady income during its Chapter 11 filing; UBS Warburg launched a trading unit with about 625 former Enron traders, paying no upfront cost but giving Enron a 33 % profit share. Enron has agreed to sell Portland General Electric, sold its wind‑power business to General Electric and its Indian oil‑and‑gas assets to BG Group for $350 million, and is trying to unload its broadband unit. The company plans a new name, consolidation of its reduced workforce (now under 3,000) and has proposed retention bonuses and severance packages to the creditors committee.

- The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission disclosed 25 contacts between its commissioners or senior staff and Enron officials between August 2000 and June 2001. New FERC chairman Pat Wood said Enron exerted “no undue influence” on agency decisions; he ordered ethics training for staff after criticism from senators, including Barbara Boxer, who alleged regulators were wined and dined by Enron.

- Dutch utility Nuon may take over Azurix’s Buenos Aires province water‑service concession when it ends on March 2; Azurix is seeking $150‑200 million in compensation for the early termination.

- BG Group plans to more than double its India investment to $1.3 billion over three‑to‑five years, targeting upstream oil‑and‑gas and LNG. It recently bought Enron’s Indian upstream assets for $350 million, is developing an LNG import terminal at Pipavav, Gujarat, and holds majority stakes in Gujarat Gas Company Ltd. and a 50 % joint‑venture in Mahanagar Gas Ltd. A dispute with state‑owned Oil & Natural Gas Corp. over operatorship of the offshore fields remains unresolved; BG CEO Frank Chapman will raise the issue with India’s petroleum minister.

- Enron Japan’s creditors may receive little or no repayment; a meeting on March 27 will determine distribution. The company’s 70‑80 employees are owed one month’s salary (≈60‑70 million yen), and its assets consist mainly of office equipment and a modest bank deposit; a ¥2 billion trading system cannot be sold because it is tied to the U.S. platform.

- Enron obtained $1.2 billion in U.S. government‑backed loans for overseas power projects: the Overseas Private Investment Corp. is owed $453 million and the Export‑Import Bank $512 million. Four OPIC‑backed projects are paying on time, while a $160 million OPIC‑funded Dabhol plant in India sits idle and a $200 million insurance claim is pending. Two OPIC applications for Brazil projects were abandoned after the bankruptcy filing.

- The Senate is set to take up broad energy legislation that splits over ANWR drilling, vehicle fuel‑economy standards (proposals to raise fleet average to 35 mpg), ethanol‑fuel mandates, $16 billion in tax breaks, and the regulation of power‑company holding companies. The House has passed a more production‑oriented version; the Senate Democratic bill emphasizes conservation. At least two weeks of debate and many amendments are expected.

- California Governor Gray Davis is considering delaying the ban on the gasoline additive MTBE until 2005 because a consultant’s report warned of a potential 5‑10 % gasoline supply shortfall and price spikes; the state would need about 580 million gallons of ethanol per year to replace MTBE, requiring new storage and pipeline infrastructure.

Real-time auction advertising requires budget pacing to align spending with campaign goals. Pacing systems adjust a multiplier λ to modify bids, monitor spend, and correct deviations in near real time. Existing controllers rely on empirical tuning, lacking stability guarantees. This work proposes a Bucketized Hysteresis Controller (BHC) that combines hysteresis control with proportional feedback. BHC discretizes the error between desired and observed spend rates into K non‑overlapping bands, each assigned a gain; large errors receive larger step sizes for rapid convergence, small errors receive smaller steps for stability. The controller updates λ multiplicatively using the selected band’s gain and the sign of the error. A baseline variable‑step controller adjusts a scale α based on a fluctuation factor measuring recent oscillation, and BHC extends it with quantized multi‑step hysteresis. Contributions include implementation of BHC, an analytical framework for parameter selection, and real‑world experiments showing significant improvements over the legacy system. The approach bridges control theory with advertising platforms to achieve more accurate pacing for small‑budget campaigns while remaining applicable across use cases.

In Windows 10, mouse pointer size and color can be changed via Settings → Ease of Access → Mouse, offering small, medium, or large size and white, black, or inverting color. For additional pointer shapes, use Control Panel → Mouse → Pointers tab, which provides a wide selection of styles. In Safari on iOS, to close all open tabs press and hold the Tabs icon (bottom right) or the Done button in the tab view; iOS then offers the option “Close xx Tabs”, which instantly closes every open tab. Restarting Safari does not clear tabs, as the app restores the previous tab set.

NASA’s Dawn spacecraft released the closest images ever taken of Ceres, showing the Occator Crater and its bright sodium‑carbonate deposits (faculae). The images were captured from 24–39 km altitude on June 14 and 21–34 km on June 22, during Dawn’s second extended mission that brought it within 22 mi (35 km) of the surface. The largest deposit, Cerealia Facula, and the Vinalia Faculae are the biggest carbonates known outside Earth; their origin—whether shallow or deep brines—is still unknown. Dawn, launched in 2007, previously orbited Vesta and has been studying Ceres since March 2015. The spacecraft is running low on fuel and will remain in its final orbit, not crashing into Ceres, with mission operations expected to end in the second half of 2018.

ISDA Press Report (May 16, 2001) covers multiple derivatives industry news: witnesses urge the IRS to adopt a broader risk standard for hedging regulations; Bank for International Settlements data shows OTC derivatives growth slowed in the second half of 2000; Federal Home Loan Bank of New York achieved FAS 133 compliance using Principia Partners software; a former CFTC head says single‑stock futures have higher costs than stock options; CME and CBOE announced a joint venture to list single‑stock futures; FASB issued an implementation guideline offering end‑users a partial reprieve from reporting option time‑value volatility; the FSA’s stance on the Basel Committee’s capital charge for credit derivatives is examined; UK Treasury proposed legislation allowing building societies to use credit derivatives; a surge in credit‑linked note issuance caused a widening negative basis between default swaps and bonds, creating arbitrage opportunities; Lightrade is expanding its US pooling‑point network for bandwidth trading; ISDA published a restructuring supplement to its 1999 Credit Derivatives Definitions limiting deliverable securities maturity.

Canadian Pacific Railway is reducing delivery times for imported goods from Vancouver to the U.S. industrial heartland by up to 48 hours compared to Canadian National Railway, using changes in Vancouver and North Dakota to create a seamless operation through Chicago to Detroit. Shorter transit times lower shipper costs and enable faster container reuse. Hapag-Lloyd emphasizes efficient market access, while CN claims its service is faster due to avoiding Chicago congestion. CP's faster service may pressure CN, with CP noting that CN would likely improve speed if in a competitive position.

Euro zone stocks rose to a more than one‑year high on the first trading day of 2017 after a purchasing‑managers’ index showed factory activity expanding at its fastest pace in over five years. Most Asian markets remained closed for the New Year holiday, leaving trade thin and prompting analysts to warn of possible volatility. The euro slipped 0.3 percent below $1.05 after briefly touching $1.07, while the dollar index gained 0.4 percent as investors anticipated further Federal Reserve rate rises and fiscal stimulus under Donald Trump’s administration. Italy’s FTSE MIB led European indexes, up 1.3 percent and hitting its highest since early 2016, while German and French indices also reached multi‑month peaks. Lower‑rated euro‑zone government bond yields fell to multi‑week lows. An ISIS‑claimed gun attack in Istanbul that killed 39 people had limited market impact, though the Turkish lira fell to near a record low. China’s manufacturing sector grew for a fifth month in December, but the pace slowed more than expected, and the yuan posted its biggest annual loss in over two decades. Bitcoin began the year above $1,000 for the first time since late 2013.

Horns offense mirrors the MidScreen offense by using high‑post screens. An on‑ball defender caught on the screen yields an easy layup, so the defender should steer the ballhandler toward the weaker screener. To stop the action, teams use a Show & Recover scheme: X1 pushes the ballhandler to the sideline, X5 steps out and bumps the ballhandler wide, X1 goes over the pick, X2 denies the shooter, X3 and X4 cover the roll. After the screen, X1 recovers, X4 closes out, and defenders assume pass‑denial positions. An all‑out “SOS” disruption forces an early trap of the point guard before any screen, creating a free‑lance situation. Rotations follow the near‑player concept, resulting in high/low helpside positions and additional traps if the ballhandler drives baseline or passes to the post.

Roger Poole, chairman of Petworth and Bognor Angling Club, reports the start of the coarse‑fishing season on Britain’s rivers. He advises anglers to re‑evaluate baits, tactics and swim choices as conditions differ from March to June. The club seeks young members and highlights legal close season allowing fish to spawn and regain strength; natural river foods such as insects and worms abundant. National Fishing Month, led by Jeremy Wade and Nick Hancock, runs July 27‑September 2 with over 250 events, backed by Environment Agency; children under 16 receive a free licence. Early‑season observations show tench active in pond mornings, chub dominating river margins, and soft cheese effective for chub. Float‑trotting with maggot catches dace, roach and occasional perch on the Rother; margins on the Arun produce chub, while mid‑water feeder or ledger tactics target bream, chub and barbel.

NEC Display Solutions will provide five‑year warranties on four P‑series digital signage models (P404, P484, P554, P703); P404, P484, P554 covered from first shipment, P703 covered for purchases on or after Aug 1 2017. Other manufacturers charge for extensions.

The Internal Bar Strength (IBS) indicator measures the relative position of a bar’s close between its high and low using the formula (Close – Low)/(High – Low). It is a mean‑reversion tool: buy when IBS is low, sell when it is high. Backtests on U.S. stock indices show that IBS has performed well over decades: a simple IBS strategy on SPY (1993‑present) produced a 15.3% CAGR, was invested only 36 % of the time, had a 74 % win rate and a profit factor of 2.73, with only three losing years (1994, 2002, 2018). On Nasdaq (QQQ) the results were even stronger (0.56 % per trade, 16.6 % compounded). IBS works best in volatile bear markets because large up days cluster there, and adding filters—such as requiring VIX above its 100‑day moving average or restricting positions when SPY is more than 5 % above its 200‑day MA—improves profit factor. Combining IBS with a second indicator further boosts performance on both SPY and QQQ. The indicator does not perform well on commodity‑heavy stocks, gold, or markets with high commodity exposure (e.g., Norway, Australia). Execution requires entering at or just before the close; a delay to the next open reduces average gain from 0.41 % to 0.31 % per trade. The article offers purchasable code and membership for the strategies.

High cholesterol is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of death in the U.S., accounting for about 17 % of healthcare spending. Conventional medicine focuses on acute care and lowering cholesterol numbers, not on underlying causes, so patients often require lifelong statin use. Hyperlipidemia is described as a metabolic condition linked to liver, kidney, and spleen function, with multiple underlying causes that differ among individuals. A newly developed functional‑food therapeutic lifestyle change program aims to address these underlying causes through individualized, natural interventions, and a book titled “Naturally Balanced your Cholesterol Level: Functional Food Therapeutic Lifestyle Change Intervention Program” identifies 14 common types of high cholesterol with corresponding treatment solutions. The program emphasizes a system‑oriented, patient‑practitioner partnership for 21st‑century healthcare. Contact Maxwell Chan at SkyBlue Cross for more information.

After moving to Tarrytown in 1950, the author watched barges build the original Tappan Zee Bridge, intended to last 50 years. The replacement, the Governor Mario M. Cuomo Bridge, opened in 2017 with a 3.1‑mi crossing, a 2,230‑ft main span for ship traffic, and a design expected to last 100 years. Its eight chamfered towers, tilted five degrees, support 12 cable pairs per side holding over 74 million lb of roadway. Project Director Jamey Barbas, one of three female engineering majors, led the effort and outreach. Construction used “I Lift NY,” a 1,900‑ton floating crane, and three river‑based concrete plants, eliminating 20,000 truck trips. About 7,000 workers contributed nine million work hours, and an educational program reached 50,000 students.

Kelsey Hall, a University of Alabama student, posted a photo of herself in a Christmas tree costume on Twitter, promising to wear it for the rest of the semester if she received 1,000 retweets. High School Sports Talk airs Saturday 10 AM EST to Noon on ESPN Radio 94.1, with Matthew Hatfield and Ed Young. Hatfield covered Nike Elite Youth Basketball League’s session at Boo Williams Sportsplex, featuring six guests; replays on Dropbox.

Alpha Theory's Analytics Department identifies investor biases through deviations between actual and optimal position sizes. Common biases include failing to reduce exposure after large price gains despite diminished probability-weighted returns, gradually building positions instead of sizing optimally at initiation, lacking disciplined price target coverage, and over-diversifying portfolios. Research shows concentrated portfolios outperform diversified ones by 2.2% alpha, and optimal sizing could improve returns by 5.1%. Re-underwriting positions at critical levels is recommended to mitigate biases.

The lecture discusses the history and development of experimental design in engineering, comparing simple one-at-a-time methods with factorial designs. It highlights R.A. Fisher's contributions to factorial experimentation at Rothamsted and the evolution of robust design methods like Taguchi's. The professor presents research showing that adaptive one-factor-at-a-time experiments can outperform fractional factorial designs under certain conditions, such as moderate interactions and moderate experimental error. The lecture also covers trade-offs in experimental design, the importance of adaptation, ensemble methods, and strategies for applying robust design across many factors in complex systems. Practical considerations for engineers, including sequential experimentation and dealing with uncertainty, are discussed. The latter part addresses questions about problem sets and exam preparation.

GPU segment generated $940 million in revenue (up 5%), driven by gaming and Tesla products. Tegra Processor segment revenue was $145 million (up 4%), supported by automotive and SHIELD sales. The company announced plans to wind-down Icera modem operations with estimated restructuring charges of $100-$125 million. NVIDIA is engaged in patent litigation with Qualcomm and Samsung. Capital returns included $53 million in share repurchases (2.4 million shares) and $46 million in dividends. The Board authorized an additional $1.62 billion for share repurchases, bringing the total authorized to $2 billion. Cash and marketable securities totaled $4.79 billion. The team is emphasizing winning tonight to bring the series back to New Jersey, seeking more shots and rebounds on the opposing goalie, Quick, while blocking his vision. Zach Parise's performance and the opponent's defense are highlighted as key factors, with the defense’s gap control and neutral‑zone play allowing Quick to see many shots. Markets shifted decisively to risk-off last week, breaking down from all-time highs with a confirmed bearish engulfing pattern and negative internals. Economic data was mixed: GDP beat expectations (3% vs 2.5%) but was clouded by tariff distortions, while the jobs report disappointed (73k added vs 100k expected) with significant prior-month downward revisions. 2‑1‑2 zone is a compact variation of the 2‑3 zone that protects the middle instead of the baseline and corners. An athletic middle defender places bigs on blocks for rebounding, but the zone is vulnerable to shooting, used against poor shooters or high‑post offenses. Middle player guards the high post when the ball is out front and fronts the low post when the ball is on the wing or corner; defenders keep a foot in paint. Shifts depend on ball location: quickest outside defenders move together to cover sideline‑to‑sideline, while baseline players maintain weakside rebounding positions. Adjustments and variations exist.

These changes aim to reduce friction while maintaining security. The features are inferred from APK teardown evidence and are not yet live for all users.

Options trading in Amazon (AMZN) offers multiple strategies: buying call or put options, writing covered or naked calls/puts, and spread trading. Each strategy has distinct risk‑reward profiles; naked positions expose investors to unlimited loss. Options are leveraged instruments, so a small stock move can greatly affect option value, and most options expire worthless. Key risks include expiration, liquidity, and margin calls that can require additional capital.

Traders can place market, limit, or stop orders. The strike price determines whether an option is in‑the‑money, influencing potential profit. Profit arises from price moves aligned with the position; delta measures the option’s sensitivity to stock price changes.

To start trading, investors need a margin account, sufficient capital (typically at least a $2,000 deposit), and a solid understanding of options. Fees vary by broker, usually a flat commission plus exchange/clearing/platform fees. Higher volatility raises option premiums, increasing costs.

Tax treatment depends on hold period: short‑term capital gains for quick sales, long‑term for positions held to expiration. Brokers require a minimum margin, which may be higher for naked or spread strategies.

Analysis is best performed through quantified methods using statistical data to identify trends and entry/exit points. Order execution speed is generally sub‑second, with algorithmic trading available.

Expiration dates are typically the third Friday of the month, with weekly and monthly options also offered. Risk can be limited using spread trading, which simultaneously buys and sells options with different strikes or expirations. When selecting a platform, consider fees, execution speed, and available research tools.

The paper investigates ground states of classical bilinear-biquadratic Heisenberg models on a partially anisotropic triangular lattice composed of isosceles triangles. The model involves four interaction parameters (K, L, A, B) representing linear and biquadratic exchange couplings between spins. The analysis reduces to examining one triangular plaquette, where spin configurations are described by angles α, β, and γ forming a tetrahedron parameter space. Ground states are determined by minimizing the energy function across the tetrahedron's vertices, edges, faces, and interior points. The study presents comprehensive phase diagrams for both Heisenberg and XY models at various parameter values, showing regions of ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, coplanar, and noncoplanar spin configurations with continuous and discontinuous phase transitions.

Offensive guards are a critical but often overlooked position on the offensive line in football. They are responsible for blocking in both the run and pass games, using a combination of intelligence, tenacity, and quickness. Guards line up between the tackles and center, typically with a sturdy, compact build, around 6'3"-6'5" and 300-320 pounds. They must possess functional strength, footwork, agility, speed, and solid blocking technique. In pass protection, guards often face strong defensive tackles and blitzing linebackers, needing to maintain positioning to give the quarterback time to throw. In the run game, they contribute to double teams, establish interior push, and pull to block for second and third-level defenders. Their role includes communicating with other offensive linemen to handle stunts, twists, and blitzes. While the origin of the term "guard" is unclear, the position is essential for setting the tone against massive interior defensive tackles and executing various offensive schemes. Notable guards include Larry Allen and John Hannah, both considered among the best at the position.

According to a KPMG survey of 130 U.S. C-suite leaders at organizations with $1B+ revenue, AI agent deployment quadrupled from 11% to 42% in six months. Employee resistance dropped from 47% to 21%, with over half the workforce now accepting or embracing AI agents. Spears describes AI as a "toddler" requiring human oversight in most enterprise uses. The shift from "fear factor" to "cognitive fatigue" reflects workers viewing AI as an enabler rather than replacement. 78% of leaders say traditional KPIs miss AI's value, though 97% track productivity, 94% profitability, and 91% quality improvements. 56% of leaders expect to reshape entry-level recruiting within the year, as entry-level roles become less menial and more critically oriented.

Phase 1 (Early Push) targets a quick 2‑4‑second advance into the offensive area to create out‑numbered situations—break‑aways (1‑on‑0/2‑on‑0), 2‑on‑1, 3‑on‑1, 3‑on‑2 and 3‑on‑3. The primary goals are lay‑ups and steals; players are taught to pass the ball ahead, finish hard, stay in bounds, avoid charging, and use the backboard. A missed‑layup rule enforces automatic 10 push‑ups for the shooter and any involved passer, emphasizing finishing habits.

Phase 2 (Early Flow) begins when the initial push fails to produce a good shot. The team immediately moves into predefined early‑offense flow actions or half‑court sets, preventing the defense from resetting. These flow actions rely on on‑ball and off‑ball screens, isolations, and “go‑to” player options and can serve as the team’s primary half‑court offense if early pushes are unavailable.

Phase 3 (Continuity) follows by flowing directly into continuous play patterns—Flex, Passing‑Game, Mid‑Screen, Side‑Screen and Inside‑Triangle. Each continuity uses continuous screening (pick‑the‑picker, down screens, on‑ball screens) to generate open shots, maintain court balance, deliver the ball to the desired handler as the shot clock winds down, and create rebounding position and second‑effort opportunities.

The passage presents a theoretical framework linking STEM education and architectural design education, reports an ethnographic study of first‑year architecture students, and derives six analogical conclusions for STEM pedagogy.

STEM education, rooted in the 1990s USA, aims to develop 21st‑century skills and has evolved into STEAM with the addition of art. Project‑based learning (PBL), grounded in constructivist theory, aligns with STEM by emphasizing real‑life problems, iterative design and learner‑centred instruction. Design is described as a non‑linear, feedback‑driven decision‑making process that involves creativity stages (preparation‑incubation‑enlightenment‑testing). Architectural education historically began with the 1671 French Academy and was refined by Bauhaus; it centers on a studio (design‑studio) where students confront open‑ended design problems, receive regular instructor critique, and develop spatial thinking, problem‑solving and graphic communication skills through “learning by doing.” Technical drawing and visual communication are identified as essential for presenting design ideas.

The study’s purpose was to identify prominent elements of first‑year architectural design education and, by analogical inference, inform STEM education. An ethnographic method was chosen; a researcher with a science‑education background observed a first‑semester Architectural Design course at BUU Faculty of Architecture for four weeks (01‑12‑2022 to 22‑12‑2022). Thirty students worked in groups on five city‑center plots, presenting sketches, models and storyboards twice weekly; an external architect participated in juries. Unstructured observation notes and post‑semester interviews with eight volunteer students were recorded; data were validated by course instructors and triangulated with the literature.

Content analysis of observation notes and interview transcripts yielded four themes: (1) confronting open‑ended problems and fostering student motivation; (2) deep thinking about problem situations, emphasizing in‑depth research, strong arguments and field investigation; (3) gaining experience in presentation techniques, including portfolio preparation and graphic communication; (4) meeting the culture of criticism, where instructors critique spatial errors, question design adequacy and stress professional knowledge and skills. Student interviews highlighted difficulties in model making, time management, hand drawing, presentation, and the invention process.

The discussion applies analogical reasoning to draw six recommendations for STEM education:
1. Students at all levels should be allowed to solve open‑ended problems independently, with emphasis on trial‑and‑error learning.
2. Project courses should be high‑stakes graduation qualifications to boost motivation at undergraduate and high‑school levels; lower‑grade activities should focus on problem situations.
3. STEM problems should have authentic real‑life context, emphasizing sustainability and value rather than artificial or teacher‑derived topics.
4. Even without producing a final product, K‑4 and K‑8 students should have hands‑on contact with materials and tools related to their problem.
5. Technical drawing and graphic‑communication courses should be introduced into high‑school curricula, including non‑technical schools.
6. Undergraduate STEM instruction should adopt a paradigm shift toward reflective practice (technical rationality + reflection‑in‑action) and implement jury‑based assessment, mirroring the architectural studio’s criticism culture.
The application for a writ of error coram nobis was denied; appellant did not establish ineffective assistance of appellate counsel.

The lecture examines the soundness of the Fiat‑Shamir transform in the random‑oracle model. It first shows that the transform is not sound when applied to a protocol with non‑negligible soundness: a cheating prover can make repeated queries to the random oracle, guessing the verifier’s challenge bits and “re‑running” the protocol until it succeeds, breaking soundness. The lecture then demonstrates that even if the original protocol has negligible soundness (obtained by sequential repetition of a constant‑soundness protocol), the same attack still works in the random‑oracle model because the prover can adaptively query the oracle for each round.

To formalize, the lecturer states a theorem: for a public‑coin, constant‑round protocol with negligible soundness, the Fiat‑Shamir transform is sound in the random‑oracle model. The proof sketches a reduction: if a poly‑time cheating prover P* succeeds with non‑negligible probability ε, then at most q = poly queries are asked. By guessing the index of the query that determines the verifier’s challenge in each round and simulating the oracle, an interactive prover can succeed with probability at least ε / q^c (c constant), which is non‑negligible, contradicting the negligible soundness of the original protocol. The argument extends to any constant number of rounds; for log‑rounds the soundness becomes quasi‑polynomially small.

The lecture then discusses extensions: protocols with “round‑by‑round soundness” (e.g., GKR) remain sound under Fiat‑Shamir even with many rounds. It notes that the transform is sound for the four‑round Kilian‑Micali protocol, providing a concrete constant‑round example.

Finally, the lecture addresses zero‑knowledge. It explains that repeating the Hamiltonian‑cycle zero‑knowledge proof in parallel breaks zero‑knowledge, because the Fiat‑Shamir version is sound for that protocol. If a simulator could reproduce the verifier’s view for all inputs, it would break the soundness of Fiat‑Shamir, which is impossible under the assumed hash family. Hence, for this specific protocol, parallel repetition is not zero‑knowledge, and more generally any interactive proof that is sound under Fiat‑Shamir cannot be zero‑knowledge. The lecturer concludes that the random‑oracle model serves only as a sanity check and does not guarantee a standard‑model security proof. The lecture also briefly mentions historical notes (RSA, NSA) and the practical rarity of cryptographic breaks due to implementation flaws rather than theory.

Artificial Intelligence is transforming higher education globally by reshaping teaching, research, and administrative practices. Institutions worldwide are integrating AI technologies, with China and the United States leading implementation. A 2024 survey shows 86% of students use AI tools for academic purposes, with nearly 25% using them daily.

AI applications in higher education include intelligent tutoring systems like Carnegie Learning's Cognitive Tutor, predictive analytics for identifying at-risk students, and adaptive learning platforms such as DreamBox Learning. Case studies demonstrate AI's effectiveness: Squirrel AI in China has provided personalized instruction to millions of students in rural areas, while Arizona State University improved retention rates by 20% through predictive analytics.

Institutions are responding through faculty training programs, curricular innovation including AI courses across disciplines, and policy initiatives aligned with frameworks like UNESCO's Beijing Consensus. However, significant challenges persist: faculty resistance, concerns about algorithmic bias and data privacy, and infrastructure limitations particularly in developing regions.

The paper examines three AI tools: ChatGPT for text creation and writing support, Bard for real-time research and data analysis, and Gemini for emotional intelligence applications in counseling and psychology. AI's impact spans disciplines from performing arts to sciences, enabling personalized learning, virtual simulations, and adaptive platforms.

Key recommendations include developing robust policy frameworks for ethical AI integration, prioritizing faculty training and digital literacy, fostering interdisciplinary research, ensuring equitable access to AI technologies, and promoting collaborative models where AI complements rather than replaces human educators. Future trends point toward emotional recognition systems, virtual and augmented reality applications, and AI-enabled language translation for global collaboration. Successful integration requires balancing innovation with ethical stewardship while addressing challenges of equity, privacy, and academic integrity.

The Supreme Court of North Dakota reversed a district court order suppressing evidence against Denise Hahne for driving under the influence. The district court had suppressed evidence because it found there was no safe or legal way for Hahne to avoid the temporary sobriety checkpoint. The Supreme Court held that law enforcement checkpoints need not, as a matter of law, provide motorists with a way to avoid them; avoidability is only one factor in evaluating the intrusion on personal liberty. The case was remanded for proceedings consistent with this opinion to determine whether the checkpoint was constitutionally reasonable.

Alan A. Brister sued the United States in the Court of Federal Claims for a tax refund. He sought to recover monies withheld by the IRS from refunds for tax years 1989–1992 after the IRS adjusted his 1985 and 1986 tax returns by disallowing withholding credits. The adjustments were made in 1993, more than three years after the returns were filed, and the government claimed the time limitation was waived under 26 U.S.C. § 6501(c)(1) because the returns were false or fraudulent with intent to evade tax. Brister argued the adjustments were untimely. The court found that Brister, as accountant for Solar Roofing, Inc., arranged with the company to overwithhold federal income tax to repay loans, and filed tax returns for 1985 and 1986 claiming refunds based on overwithheld amounts that were never paid to the Treasury. The court determined the returns were knowingly false and filed with intent to deceive the government, satisfying the fraud exception to the assessment limitations period. Consequently, the IRS' 1993 adjustment was timely, and Brister was not entitled to a refund. Judgment was entered for the defendant.

The 13/48 trading strategy uses the 13-period exponential moving average (EMA) crossing above or below the 48-period EMA to identify bullish or bearish trading opportunities. It's a momentum-based strategy that works better in trending markets than sideways ones. Backtesting on the S&P 500 from 1960 shows the strategy was invested 66% of the time, capturing 5.1% annually versus 7.2% for buy and hold, with a slightly better risk-adjusted return at 7.8%. The strategy is not a guaranteed way to riches and is prone to whipsaws as a lagging indicator.

The study examined the impact of distance education on equality and inequality of opportunity in education through a qualitative case‑study approach. Semi‑structured interviews were conducted with 21 faculty members (12 females, 9 males) and 26 students (16 males, 10 females) who had experienced a semester of distance education. Content analysis yielded the following themes. Faculty members reported that distance education can promote equality by allowing learners to work at their own pace and by providing easy, time‑ and location‑free access to information. Conversely, they cited challenges such as students’ difficulty in accessing technology, unreliable internet connections, neglect of learners’ competencies, inadequate learning environments, and widening performance differences among students. Students described benefits including freedom from time constraints, free‑of‑charge instruction, and access to diverse resources, while also noting that financial limitations and internet problems create inequality. To reduce inequality, participants suggested determining learners’ characteristics, ensuring technology access, improving digital literacy, resolving internet‑infrastructure issues, allocating state budgets for technology, and providing teacher‑led consultancy services.

The lecture defines entanglement as a state of two subsystems that cannot be written as a product of separate wave functions. It distinguishes true entanglement as a resource from cases where subsystems cannot be physically separated. The simplest entangled state discussed is the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) or Bell state, such as (|01⟩+|10⟩)/√2, which cannot be factorized. The lecture contrasts entangled photons with helium's spin-singlet ground state, noting that photons can be separated, enabling entanglement as a resource. It explains that entangled states have two key properties: non-local correlations and fragility against decoherence. The lecture then introduces entanglement purification as a method to convert weakly entangled states into maximally entangled Bell states by performing controlled-NOT operations and measurements on pairs of copies, with the success probability proportional to the initial entanglement measure. It defines entanglement for a pure state as the von Neumann entropy of the reduced density matrix after tracing out one subsystem, which equals one for the four Bell states. The lecture discusses creating entangled atoms via photo-dissociation of mercury molecules and via the "poor man's entangler" method using light emission and measurement. It describes the Hong-Ou-Mandel interference effect at a beam splitter, where identical photons bunch together, enabling probabilistic atom entanglement. The lecture concludes by outlining the use of circular polarizers and detection of coincidences to identify the required input states for atom entanglement.

In May 2007 Victor Reinoso, Deputy Mayor for Education, had twelve hours to recommend a chancellor for Washington, DC Public Schools (DCPS), a system of 150 schools, 55,000 students—82 % African‑American—and roughly 4,000 teachers. DCPS was ranked among the nation’s worst urban districts despite spending $13,000 per student; it spent the highest share of its budget on administration and the lowest on instruction, and half its schools failed federal standards. The district had cycled through six superintendents or acting superintendents since 1998. A legislative decree passed by the DC Council in April 2007 gave Mayor Adrian Fenty control of the school system, effective June 12, 2007.

Reinoso, an MBA from MIT Sloan and a former DC school‑board member, viewed the takeover as a turnaround opportunity. During the transition (November 2006‑January 2007) he built a flat “internal‑consulting” team, hired the Parthenon Group to benchmark DCPS against other mayoral‑control districts, and drafted the DC Public Education Reform Act of 2007. The Parthenon report showed DCPS last in 4th‑ and 8th‑grade reading and math achievement, a 13 % enrollment decline since 2000, and an average superintendent tenure of 2.4 years versus 4.6 years in the 50 largest U.S. cities. It also identified six “pain points”: lack of accountability, weak teaching focus, operational inefficiencies, failure to serve special‑education students, facilities disrepair, and poor community engagement.

The legislation made DCPS a mayor‑run agency, removed non‑core functions such as facilities management, created a separate state education board, and required results within five years. Reinoso began an under‑the‑radar chancellor search in March 2007, seeking an entrepreneurial leader who would reject incremental reform and align adult incentives with student achievement. He considered traditional educators like Rudy Crew (former Miami‑Dade superintendent with a record of aggressive turnarounds) and non‑traditional candidates such as Michelle Rhee (founder of The New Teacher Project, known for challenging union staffing rules). He also weighed keeping incumbent superintendent Clifford Janey, whose long‑range plan was comprehensive but whose slow, consensus‑driven style limited implementation.

In early May, a plagiarism incident—Reinoso copied sections of a Charlotte‑Mecklenburg plan into a strategic document for the council—caused a temporary congressional hold on the takeover and drew criticism, though Reinoso called it a “sloppy mistake” rather than plagiarism. Hours before his recommendation was due, Reinoso focused on selecting a leader capable of “rocking the boat, but not capsizing it.”

This paper develops quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) methods for uncertainty quantification in computational oncology, specifically for estimating expectations of quantity of interests from semi-linear parabolic reaction-diffusion PDE models of tumor growth. The authors model uncertain diffusion and proliferation coefficients as random fields and employ QMC methods to address high-dimensional integrals arising from truncated series expansions. They establish well-posedness results and prove rigorous error estimates for uniform random fields. A novel parametric regularity bound is developed for the nonlinear term u(1-u), which is not monotone and requires a proof exploiting the property that solutions remain bounded if initial conditions lie in [0,1]. This work extends QMC theory to nonlinear PDEs, with numerical validation on complex domains modeling brain gliomas.

Mesh is a short‑to‑intermediate passing concept that creates natural picks and confusion for defenses. It is effective against man coverage, allowing playmakers to stay on the move, and against zone coverage, enabling receivers to settle into voids. The concept works best when two of the offense’s best athletes, such as a running back and a slot receiver, run crossing routes that provide pick opportunities. Against base zone defenses (Cover 2, 3, and 4), drag‑route runners settle their routes while corner routes can attack near safeties; however, a zone blitz or simulated pressure can force early releases and limit the concept’s effectiveness.

Coaching points detail route landmarks for each position: tight ends and X receivers run shallow drags at 3‑5 yards, staying in motion; the Z receiver runs a steep vertical cut to about 10 yards; backs check pass protection and release to arrow or flare routes. The quarterback’s post‑snap progression is flare → shallow drag → deep drag → full‑back arrow route, and he must anticipate blitzes to get the ball out quickly.

Two primary variations are described. The “mesh rail” uses a running back on a rail route and the Z receiver on a sit‑route over the ball, making the back the primary target; the X receiver can run a speed‑out as a pre‑snap decision. The “sit route” variation adds a stationary target at 8‑10 yards over the football, giving the QB an easy completion in zone while setting picks for other drag runners. Mesh can also be employed in a single‑wing offense as a variation of the smash concept.

Overall, mesh provides a stable, adaptable short‑to‑intermediate passing tool that works against most coverages and can be customized with tags and variations for any offensive system.

Mattress fabrics segment posted quarterly sales of $48.8M (flat) and full‑year sales of $190.8M, a record, with operating income of $7.2M for the quarter and $29.4M for the year, up 11% year‑over‑year. This document specifies the SEV-ES and SEV-SNP Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) protocol for encrypted VM communication. It defines protocol versions (v1, v2, revisions) and hypervisor feature advertisement via a bitmap. The GHCB is a 4KB shared memory area used for VMGEXIT-based interactions. It describes Non-Automatic Exit (NAE) events including MSR protection, IOIO protection, #NPF/MMIO faults, page state changes, AP creation/destruction, AP reset hold, doorbell pages for restricted injection, timer support, APIC ID lists, VMPL level transitions, Secure AVIC backing pages, termination requests, and unsupported events. The document covers SMP booting challenges, NMI handling via #HV doorbells, debug register support, and EFI configuration tables for secrets and CPUID pages. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported.

The invention concerns sealing high‑pressure fluid passages in flow control devices such as plug valves and fluid ends used in oil and gas production. Prior designs mount seals on closure components, causing the valve body bore or fluid‑end body to erode from corrosive/abrasive fluids and leading to leakage that requires cumbersome weld repairs. The disclosed technology transfers erosion from the body to the closure by forming recesses (e.g., endless grooves) in the body that intersect the bore, mounting seals in those recesses, and sizing the seals to extend beyond the bore to seal against surfaces of the closure (inserts, plugs, valve seats, stuffing box sleeves). The body thus becomes the sacrificial element, while the closure—replaceable or resurfaced more easily—bears the wear. The sealing arrangement can use axial, radial, or crush seals and may incorporate wear‑resistant coatings on the closure or disposable wear members. The invention applies to plug valves with conical or cylindrical inserts and to fluid‑end assemblies having a manifold body with intersecting conduits, a plunger, and valve seats.

CTPNet is a framework for multivariate long-term time series forecasting that models three complementary dependencies: inter-channel, intra-subsequence, and inter-subsequence. The method uses Channel-wise Representation Learning with a temporal query-based Multi-Head Attention to capture interactions across variables. Downsampling based on periodicity decomposes sequences into subsequences, which are encoded into a D-dimensional hidden space. Trend-wise Representation Learning uses an efficient attention mechanism within each subsequence to capture local temporal structures. Periodic-wise Representation Learning captures dependencies across subsequences. The authors claim CTPNet achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmark datasets including ETTH1, ETTH2, ETTM1, ETTM2, ECL, SOLAR, TRAFFIC, and WEATHER, outperforming methods like TQNet, TWINS, LEDDAM, iTransformer, PatchTST, Cross, and FED.

AI is rapidly advancing, and generative AI (e.g., LLMs) can create content, provide feedback, and simulate human‑like interactions, raising both opportunities and concerns for higher‑education assessment. Traditional formats (MCQs, SAQs, essays) are criticized for limited authenticity and difficulty in capturing broad student skills; authentic assessments aim to mirror professional tasks. Generative AI challenges academic integrity because tools such as ChatGPT can produce high‑grade essays that often evade plagiarism detectors, while AI‑detection software suffers from false positives, bias against non‑native speakers, and rapid obsolescence. Studies show ChatGPT performs comparably to junior professionals on MCQs and exams, making lower‑order MCQs particularly vulnerable; redesigning questions to test higher‑order cognition and moving to in‑person, invigilated formats can mitigate some risks. Institutions may adopt three strategies: avoid AI, outrun AI with complex tasks, or embrace AI by integrating it into assessment design. AI can support immediate, personalized feedback, rubric generation, practice question creation, and peer‑review simulation, but it also risks over‑dependence and superficial responses. Two broad assessment approaches are proposed: mitigation (clinical assessments, fieldwork, vivas, OSCEs) and integration (AI‑generated case studies, Socratic debates, critique of AI output). A case study at a UK university redesigning an immunology essay allowed students to use ChatGPT for draft outlines, followed by peer evaluation and individual writing; surveys showed about 58 % had used AI, primarily ChatGPT, with low confidence but interest in using it for planning, drafting, and revision. Students recognized AI’s capabilities (academic support, summarising, text generation) and limitations (accuracy, outdated information, lack of critical thinking). Approximately 26 % considered AI use plagiarism, 37 % were unsure, and 37 % disagreed. Advantages of the approach included a useful starting outline and engagement with AI capabilities; disadvantages included uniform, generic output and superficial detail. The study concluded that integrating AI into assessment can meet learning outcomes, but requires training educators and students in AI literacy, ethical use, and critical evaluation. Institutions should adopt holistic assessment redesigns that embed AI while preserving academic integrity, focusing on higher‑order cognitive skills and providing equitable professional development for teachers.

Ray Jones, Jr. was indicted for the first‑degree murder of his 2½‑month‑old son in violation of La. R.S. 14:30. A jury found him guilty and recommended life imprisonment without probation, parole, or suspension; the trial judge imposed that sentence. On appeal Jones raised two assignments of error.

Assignment 1 challenged the admission of three incriminating statements. The first was made to psychiatrist Dr. Diana Bienvenue on the morning of Jan 19, 1979, after Jones had been given Haldol; Dr. Bienvenue found him calm, rational and lucid, and Jones described choking the mother and hitting and throwing the infant. The second statement was made to a nurse and a security guard in the hospital on Jan 24, 1979, while Jones was rational; he said he “snuffed out the life of the only thing he ever loved, and that was his son.” The third statement was made at the police station after Jones had been advised of his Miranda rights and had requested an attorney; Detective Lindsey told Jones “God takes care of little babies” and Jones then confessed to choking the mother, hitting the baby and discarding the body. The trial judge ruled the statements voluntary, not products of custodial interrogation, and therefore admissible. The Supreme Court agreed, finding the statements voluntary and, if any error existed, harmless because the same admissions were proven by other overwhelming evidence. The court also held that no Miranda warnings were required for the first two statements because they were unsolicited and not police‑initiated interrogation.

NBA commissioner Adam Silver said Monday there is no contemplation of moving the 2026 All‑Star Game from Intuit Dome in Los Angeles while the league investigates whether the Clippers violated salary‑cap rules involving a $28 million endorsement contract between Kawhi Leonard and Aspiration Fund Adviser LLC, a sustainability services company that filed for bankruptcy this year. Scotland’s Abusive Behaviour and Sexual Harm Act creates an offence April 1 for disclosing or threatening to disclose intimate images, punishable by five years’ imprisonment. The offence applies to images showing nude, in underwear, sexual act, targeting sharing. Justice Secretary Michael Matheson says law warns, acknowledges distress, legislation cannot end abuse.

The present description relates to controlling a mobile agricultural machine using active ground terrain mapping. A pose detection sensor (e.g., a GNSS receiver) mounted on the machine generates position and orientation signals at multiple points along its route. Based on these signals and the machine’s dimensions, a point cloud of points estimated to lie on the ground surface under the machine is identified. Elevation values are computed for each point, and a best‑fit plane can be calculated to predict ground elevation ahead of the machine. Each point receives a weight that decreases with its distance from the sensor, providing a confidence value for its elevation estimate. The elevation and weight values are aggregated over fixed map cells, creating georeferenced elevation map layers (average elevation, confidence, sample count, variance). The map data are used by a control signal generator to adjust movable subsystems—such as a sprayer boom height actuator or a harvester header height actuator—to follow the terrain and improve crop‑volume calculations. Operators can configure point‑cloud resolution, width, length, offset, and map cell size. The system supports on‑the‑fly predictive control, merging new measurements with prior maps, and can be implemented in a remote server architecture.

Micro‑credentials are certifications that recognize knowledge and skills from short learning experiences, especially in technology‑enabled contexts. Various agencies define them differently, and the widening gap between traditional higher education and required digital skills drives their uptake. The study investigates, in Mauritius, education and industry leaders’ familiarity with micro‑credentials, the feasibility of integrating them into higher‑education credit systems, and their perceived value for recognising skills. A qualitative methodology was used, conducting semi‑structured interviews with 10 educational leaders (six public, four private) and four industry leaders from ICT and finance sectors. Results indicate that education leaders view micro‑credentials as credit‑bearing short courses or competence‑based units, while industry leaders describe them as personalized qualifications or badges. Both groups agree that formal assessment is needed for credibility. Respondents favor a hybrid model that combines existing credit systems with micro‑credential pathways, allowing flexible, demand‑driven learning. They also regard micro‑credentials as a disruptive innovation requiring incremental implementation, regulatory review, and alignment with the National Qualifications Framework (NQF) to ensure employer recognition. The authors conclude that, despite lack of a national framework, stakeholders see importance of integrating micro‑credentials into a unified system that contributes to university credits and enhances employability.

Matthew Shashy, 29, was sentenced to four years of probation for firing a shotgun three times toward Maxwell Air Force Base’s Day Street entrance on Jan 3 2017. He was convicted of impeding and interfering with Air Force personnel. Police found firearms; investigated by Montgomery police and FBI.

Brookfield Infrastructure Partners (BIP) presented at Brookfield’s recent investor day, offering additional perspective for investors. BIP, the most successful listed partnership managed by Brookfield Asset Management, has delivered 20% annualized returns since its 2008 inception and grew adjusted AFFO from $352 M to $926 M between 2012 and the present, driven by strategic investments and a favorable environment. BIP currently offers a 4% distribution yield and a 5.84% AFFO yield, retaining 1.84% for growth while raising additional capital through unit sales. The partnership aims to increase distributions 6‑9% annually, though the author notes this target may be aggressive given low inflation in developed markets. Same‑store EBITDA growth has averaged 5% on a constant‑currency basis, and reinvested cash flows could add 2‑3% growth by rotating mature assets into higher‑yielding ones. Historically, BIP traded at higher yields; the recent lower yield reflects price appreciation and benefits current unitholders by allowing new capital to be invested above the current AFFO rate. Growth via unit issuance is dependent on unit price, so a price decline would hinder distribution growth. While past performance has been strong, current valuations suggest future returns may be lower, yet BIP still offers a safe 4% yield, an expected 6% distribution growth, and a total return around 10%. The author holds a long position in Brookfield Asset Management.

A Phase 2 Stanford trial enrolled 48 children (4–15 years) with multiple food allergies. Participants received omalizumab or placebo for 16 weeks while daily oral immunotherapy (OIT) began at week 8 and continued to week 36. At week 36, 30 of 36 (83 %) omalizumab‑treated children could ingest at least 2 g of two or more allergenic foods, versus 4 of 12 (33 %) placebo. Omalizumab reduced adverse events and enabled faster desensitization; larger studies are needed to confirm findings.

Archaeologists searched a gap at City Hall for a rifle dropped by Irish Citizen Army rebel Willie Halpin during 1916 Easter Rising. No rifle was found, but they uncovered roof fragments with a bullet hole, bottles and pottery. Consultant Franc Myles said weapon was likely removed soon after Rising by Black and Tans. In 1874 a ledger tracking creditworthiness of shoppers marked the start of Equifax's model. Credit bureaus serve lenders, making consumers the product. Now massive, they collect nearly all financial data without consumer consent and face decades of regulatory challenges.

It lists hand signals such as arm up then down to start a set piece, opposite‑arm up to show openness, arm sweeps to indicate runs around defenders, pointing to direct runs or passes, both arms down palms toward teammate for a pass to feet, hands circling to request substitution, head nods to reposition a teammate on a free kick, finger counts to specify wall size, palms forward to order a push‑forward, palms together overhead to stop an anchor player, waist‑high palms to calm play, index‑finger pointing to eyes to remind teammates to watch the field, point to opponent or space for through balls, point to where to deliver the ball, point to intended receiver, chest or head taps for throw‑in direction, forehead tap to signal a head throw, two hands thrust out to move defenders upfield, specific signals for corner, throw‑in and free‑kick types, and a wave or arm motion for a goalkeeper punt. Physical Layer Simplified Specification for SD Memory Cards covers initialization, bus speed modes, and command protocols. After power-up, cards operate at 3.3V signaling; UHS-I switches to 1.8V via CMD11 after ACMD41 negotiation. UHS-II adds faster modes (FD624 up to 624MB/s) with a different initialization sequence involving PHY and device initialization. CMD6 selects bus speed, driver strength, and power limit; CMD42 handles lock/unlock and password protection. Card types include SDSC, SDHC, SDXC, with UHS-I supporting SDR12/25/50, DDR50, SDR104 modes, and UHS-II supporting FD156, HD312, FD312, FD624 modes. Write protection, erase operations (erase, discard, FULE), and ACMD55 for application-specific commands are also defined.

The Blackwell GPU architecture introduces the AI Management Processor (AMP), a RISC‑V based programmable context scheduler that offloads GPU scheduling from the CPU, reducing latency and improving performance for AI and graphics workloads. Blackwell adds hardware support for 4:2:2 chroma‑sampled video encoding and decoding in H.264 and HEVC via the ninth‑generation NVENC (5 % BD‑BR PSNR gain) and sixth‑generation NVDEC (2× faster H.264 decoding). DisplayPort 2.1b UHBR20 provides up to 80 Gbps, enabling 8K @ 165 Hz and 4K @ 480 Hz with DSC. Power management enhancements include advanced clock, power, and rail gating; accelerated frequency switching that reacts 1000× faster than prior generations; separate voltage rails for GPU cores and memory; and low‑latency sleep that enters 10× faster than Ada, delivering up to 50 % power savings for small‑language‑model inference. DLSS 4 brings Multi Frame Generation that can produce up to three additional frames per traditionally rendered frame (40 % faster AI model, 30 % less VRAM) and enhanced flip‑metering on the display engine. A new transformer‑based neural network architecture improves Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and DLAA with better temporal stability, detail in motion, and reduced artifacts. Blackwell introduces neural shaders via the Cooperative Vectors API for DX12/Vulkan, enabling neural texture compression (up to 7× VRAM savings), RTX Neural Materials, Neural Radiance Cache (real‑time indirect lighting inference), RTX Skin (real‑time subsurface scattering), and RTX Neural Faces (real‑time generative AI face rendering). The architecture is implemented in three GPUs: GB202 (flagship) with 92.2 B transistors, 12 GPC, 192 SMs, 24,576 CUDA cores, 192 RT cores, 768 Tensor cores, powering the GeForce RTX 5090; GB203 (high‑end) with 45.6 B transistors, 7 GPC, 84 SMs, 10,752 CUDA cores, 84 RT cores, 336 Tensor cores, powering the RTX 5080 and RTX 5070 Ti; and GB205 (performance) with 31 B transistors, 5 GPC, 50 SMs, 6,400 CUDA cores, 50 RT cores, 200 Tensor cores, powering the RTX 5070. All GPUs include the architectural features described above, with memory subsystems comprising L1 cache, register file, and L2 cache sized according to each chip.

Mud Bay, a 45-store pet chain in the Pacific Northwest, launched a "Good Jobs Vision" in 2014 to create better jobs while maintaining business success. They introduced an ESOP in 2015. Employee turnover dropped from 48% to 31%, and sales grew 70% over the period. However, net profit margins declined due to higher labor costs and lower prices. The company faced internal debate about reducing store hours from 9pm to 8pm to improve employee work-life balance and reduce labor costs, with COO Tracy Yamane proposing the change and co-CEO Lars Wulff opposing it until sales impact analysis could be reviewed.

South African North‑West University offers a Bachelor of Education (B.Ed.) in distance mode with Physical Education (PE) as a major within Life Orientation. Using Moore’s Theory of Transactional Distance as a theoretical lens, this qualitative study examined the effectiveness of PE teacher training delivered at a distance. Data were collected through open‑ended questionnaires from 17 third‑year distance students and semi‑structured interviews with four PE lecturers; purposeful sampling was applied and ethical clearance obtained. Five themes emerged: (1) lecturer–student interaction, reported as timely and supportive via e‑mail and WhatsApp, though lacking physical contact; (2) lecturers’ competence, passion and enthusiasm, which enhanced students’ confidence and subject knowledge; (3) obstacles including insufficient foundational PE knowledge, limited technology skills and internet access, and administrative delays in assignment processing; (4) practical training experiences, where video demonstrations were valued for skill development but delayed feedback on submissions was problematic; and (5) the program’s positive impact on participants’ perception of PE, shifting views from considering it a waste of time to recognizing its holistic value. Recommendations include increasing face‑to‑face contact, improving technology training, expanding video/media use, enhancing LMS interaction functions, and strengthening administrative systems to support effective PE teacher training in distance education.

Document management is important for all businesses, not just large ones. Poor management causes lost time, money, and customers, and can expose sensitive documents. A Xerox survey found 40% of business processes remain document‑driven; improved workflow is the main benefit, with growth and productivity cited as key reasons for change. Tracking printing costs is the first step—97% of surveyed businesses know their print costs, and 81% plan better document management. Solutions include cloud scanning with ConnectKey‑enabled devices to Google Drive, Dropbox, Box, OneDrive and Office 365; the CapturePoint Transformer App automates workflow; the Mobile Link App enables scanning from mobile devices. Setting PIN‑protected printing, restricting colour use, and receiving low‑toner alerts help reduce waste and improve security.

Passports are issued only to U.S. citizens by the Secretary of State and diplomatic/consular officers under Presidential rules, to law-abiding applicants who establish citizenship, U.S. domicile, and intention to return. Issuance is not obligatory, and rejection does not deny citizenship. Expatriated persons and those permanently domiciled abroad cannot receive passports. Expatriation is quitting one's country with abandonment of allegiance to become a permanent resident elsewhere, determined case by case; mere residence abroad does not constitute expatriation if intent to return remains. Adults who settle abroad are presumed to have adopted the national character of their new domicile. Passport applications are influenced by connections to the U.S., reasons for residence, and whether applicants represent American enterprises. Americans in countries with extraterritorial jurisdiction may receive continued passport protection if their pursuits are legitimate, with special provisions for those in American communities abroad.

The 200‑day moving average (200 DMA) is a technical indicator that calculates the average closing price of an asset over the past 200 trading days. It smooths short‑term price fluctuations and classifies the long‑term trend: price above the 200 DMA signals an uptrend, price below signals a downtrend.

The 200 DMA is most often used as a simple, trend‑following tool. Its main advantages are simplicity, ability to ride trends, and defensive exit before bear markets. Without a recession or prolonged price decline, the strategy tends to underperform buy‑and‑hold because of frequent whipsaws, commissions, slippage and lost opportunities. The indicator is not a “silver bullet” and carries both pros and cons.

Backtests on the S&P 500 from 1960 show that a basic 200 DMA crossover system captured most of the index’s gains while substantially reducing maximum drawdowns; however, its compound annual growth rate (≈8.5 %) fell short of buy‑and‑hold (≈12.8 %) when no major recession occurred. The strategy’s win rate is low (about 28 % of trades) and it can experience up to nine consecutive losers, requiring disciplined execution.

Paul Tudor Jones cites the 200 DMA as a defensive metric that keeps investors out of collapsing markets, noting that it helped exit the S&P 500 near the end of 2007 and re‑enter in mid‑2009. Jeremy Siegel’s variant—buying when the close is at least 1 % above the 200‑day SMA and selling when at least 1 % below—improved risk‑adjusted returns slightly compared with the plain 200 DMA rule.

In practice, the choice between a simple moving average (SMA) and an exponential moving average (EMA) is minor; the SMA is used for its simplicity. Daily bars are the most common timeframe, but weekly bars can also be employed. The 200 DMA can be added as a trend filter to other strategies, lowering drawdowns and improving win rates despite reducing total return and number of trades.

Historically, the S&P 500 has spent roughly 70 % of the time above the 200 DMA since 1960 (85 % since 2010), reflecting a long‑term upward bias in equity markets. Volatility tends to be higher when prices are below the average, and the 200 DMA is often used in crossover systems (e.g., 50‑day vs. 200‑day) or as a market‑timing rule. No single timeframe is universally best; backtesting determines effectiveness for each asset or market.

The NVIDIA A100 GPU improves memory hierarchy performance with a 5‑site HBM2 subsystem delivering 1555 GB/s bandwidth (1.7× V100), a 40 MB L2 cache (≈7× V100) with 2.3× read bandwidth, and L2 cache residency controls that let applications mark data as persistent or streaming. Compute Data Compression provides up to 4× DRAM and L2 bandwidth savings. A100 introduces Multi‑Instance GPU (MIG) which partitions the chip into up to seven isolated GPU Instances, each with dedicated SMs, L2 slices, memory controllers and DRAM bandwidth, guaranteeing QoS and fault isolation for multi‑tenant, single‑tenant multi‑user and VM scenarios. The third‑generation NVLink increases links to 12 per GPU (600 GB/s total) and PCIe Gen 4 doubles per‑direction bandwidth; SR‑IOV enables sharing of a single PCIe‑connected GPU. Error detection and containment are enhanced for large clusters and MIG. New hardware accelerators include a 5‑core NVJPG decoder, an optical‑flow accelerator, improved FP16/FP32 atomics (11×/2.7× over V100), and five NVDEC units. CUDA 11 adds task‑graph execution to cut kernel‑launch overhead, asynchronous copy from global to shared memory, asynchronous barriers for fine‑grained synchronization, L2 cache set‑aside for persistent data, and cooperative‑group reductions. The DGX A100 system integrates eight A100 GPUs via NVSwitch providing 4.8 TB/s bidirectional bandwidth, delivers 5 PFLOPS in a 6U form factor, and supports MIG to create up to 56 isolated accelerators. A100 also implements fine‑grained structured 2:4 sparsity that yields near‑native accuracy with increased throughput.

The lecture discusses hinged dissections, noting the lack of software tools for animating them and highlighting Greg Frederickson's pioneering work and books. Project ideas include developing animation software, implementing slender adorn chain folding, designing new dissections, and building physical models like furniture. A universal hinged dissection for polyominoes, polyhexes, and polyiamonds exists, proven via induction using spanning trees on grids, with pieces formed from half-squares and hinges on every edge. Extensions to 3D require matching both volume and Dehn invariant (edge lengths tensor dihedral angles); Sidler proved these are sufficient in 3D and 4D, but higher dimensions are open. Practical analogs include salt-triggered folding and DNA origami. Robots inspired by hinged dissections can change shape while remaining connected, contrasting with modular reconfigurable robots.

New Caledonian crows and kea parrots learn to use objects as tools through playful exploration, similar to human infants. NAE events are exit events in SEV-ES guests that trigger #VC exceptions. Upon a #VC, the guest inspects the error code, copies register state to the GHCB, and invokes VMGEXIT to generate an AE event. The hypervisor responds via VMGEXIT, allowing the guest to resume and copy results back to its internal state. The guest must reset the VALID_BITMAP field before each NAE event, setting bits for SW_EXITCODE, SW_EXITINFO1, and SW_EXITINFO2. The hypervisor returns results by setting corresponding bits. Supported NAE events include Page State Change, SNP Guest Request, SNP Extended Guest Request, SNP AP Creation, #HV Doorbell Page, #HV Send IPI, #HV Timer, APIC ID List, SNP Run VMPL, SNP TIO Guest Request, Secure AVIC, and Termination Request. Each event has specific input/output requirements in the GHCB. For example, the Page State Change NAE allows guests to request page state changes using a structure in the GHCB Shared Buffer, supporting operations like making pages private or shared and PSMASH/UNSMASH hints. The SNP Guest Request NAE enables communication with SEV-SNP firmware using request and response pages. The hypervisor must translate GPAs to SPAs, assign response pages to firmware using RMPUPDATE, and handle errors via SW_EXITINFO fields. The #HV doorbell page allows the hypervisor to notify guests of events when the Restricted Injection feature is enabled, using a PendingEvent field and an EOI assist (NoEoiRequired). Guests must atomically exchange PendingEvent to acknowledge interrupts and may clear NoEoiRequired to perform an EOI without exiting the VM. Specific sections cover guest identification of SEV-ES support, SMP booting challenges, AP Reset Hold mechanism, and limitations like SMM, nested virtualization, and vCPU hotplug support only via AP Creation NAE. The document specifies error handling, termination requests, unsupported NAE handling, debug register virtualization, and NMI injection protocols requiring guest "NMI Complete" messaging.
