Address obfuscation techniques for memory devices prevent malicious actors from reverse-engineering wear-leveling patterns that could compromise device security or longevity. A selection component chooses mapping functions that convert logical addresses to physical addresses unpredictably, varying across devices, dice, arrays, or over time. Each physical address bit is determined by selectable logic operations including invert, XOR, XNOR, pass-through, and address swap, enabling a vast number of possible configurations. Mapping functions may be selected based on random numbers, unique identifiers, schedules, or trigger events. This obfuscation obscures the relationship between logical and physical addresses, complementing wear-leveling by making attacks such as row hammer more difficult to execute.

SanDisk Sansa Fuze player manual includes safety warnings to avoid headphone use while driving, high‑volume listening, and moisture exposure; cleaning instructions advise using a soft lint‑free cloth, not allowing unsupervised child use, and not disassembling or forcing connectors. The device is a portable MP3/AV player with a 1.9‑inch color screen, FM tuner, built‑in microphone, and microSD/SDHC expansion slot; it supports MP3, WAV, WMA, secure WMA, Audible and audiobook formats, and video in MPEG‑4 SP QCIF+ 20 fps via optional Sansa Media Converter software. A rechargeable battery provides up to 24 hours of audio or 5 hours of video playback and is not user‑replaceable. Basic operation involves sliding the power switch to turn on/off or reset, using the Hold/Lock switch to disable controls, and navigating with the thumbwheel; the player connects to a computer via USB for charging, file transfer (drag‑and‑drop or Windows Media Player), firmware updates (available from www.sandisk.com/support/sansa), and formatting. Media files are transferred to Music, Photos, Videos or Recordings folders; the Sansa Media Converter converts photos and videos before transfer. Playback options include repeat, shuffle, equalizer (MusicEQ), bookmarks for video, slideshow settings for photos, and FM preset programming (up to 30 stations) with auto‑scan and voice recording. Content can be deleted directly or via computer; system settings allow customization of wallpaper color, display art, backlight timer, power‑saver timer, language, date/time, brightness, USB mode (Auto Detect/MTP/MSC), reset to factory defaults, and info display. Troubleshooting tips cover supported bit rates (MP3 32‑320 kbps, WMA 32‑256 kbps), missing ID3 tags, microSDHC compatibility, power reset, and firmware updates. The product carries a one‑year limited SanDisk warranty (repair, replacement or refund), excludes liability for lost data, and is not for high‑risk uses. The accompanying software license grants a limited, non‑exclusive right to use the software, prohibits modification, reverse engineering, and sublicensing, and includes an “AS IS” disclaimer and limitation of liability.
The 12,000‑year‑old camel engravings at Jebel Misma reveal early human presence in a formerly lush Nefud landscape and are color‑highlighted with a woman figure for scale.

Current education discourse emphasizes teaching skills such as critical thinking, collaboration and metacognition while de‑emphasizing the acquisition of substantive knowledge. The passage argues that skills cannot operate without a knowledge base; examples include readers unable to understand a cricket sentence and the need for advanced mathematics to comprehend string theory. It notes that knowledge is often equated with memorization, a label that has become pejorative, yet experts in many fields must retain large amounts of information, and without stored knowledge learning is impaired. Research from cognitive and educational psychology, sociology and curriculum studies is cited to show that knowledge acquisition underpins complex thought and reading. The passage documents recent trends that reflect a retreat from knowledge: grade inflation (average GPA rose from 2.68 in 1990 to 3.00 in 2009 and 3.11 in 2019 while ACT/SAT scores fell), a decline in state graduation testing requirements (now only six states require such tests), and stagnant or falling NAEP scores. A notable counter‑movement is the adoption of high‑quality instructional materials (HQIM); fifteen states have joined a Council of Chief State School Officers effort to shift to curricula that meet the “building knowledge” standard, yet many EdReports‑approved English language arts curricula still do not build sequential knowledge. AI tools could assist knowledge acquisition but also risk diluting rigorous content. In 2021 Nigeria reported an estimated 68 million malaria cases and 194 000 deaths, representing nearly 27 % of global cases. Insecticide‑treated nets (ITNs) are a WHO‑recommended, cost‑effective vector‑control measure that has contributed to more than 50 % of malaria case reductions and a 27 % drop in child mortality over the past two decades. This study performed a secondary analysis of the 2021 Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey (NMIS), which covered 13 727 households and 14 476 women aged 15‑49, to assess associations between socio‑demographic factors and ITN ownership and use among children under five and pregnant women.

Household ownership of at least one ITN was 56 %; only 25 % of households owned enough nets to cover all members. Ownership was higher in rural (57.5 %) than urban (52.8 %) areas, highest in the North West (75.8 %) and North East (72.0 %) zones, and among lower‑wealth quintiles (68 % and 64 % in the second and lowest quintiles versus 44 % in the highest).

Among all surveyed children under five, 41.4 % slept under an ITN the night before the survey. Usage was significantly associated with younger age, rural residence, North West or North East zone, and lower household wealth; sex of the child showed no significant association.

Approximately 49.6 % of pregnant women slept under an ITN. Usage was higher in the North East and North West, among lower‑wealth quintiles, and among women with no or primary education compared with those with higher education.

These findings indicate that ITN utilization among children under five and pregnant women remains well below the Nigeria National Malaria Strategic Plan’s 80 % target. Targeted interventions to address regional disparities, socioeconomic factors, and awareness are needed to achieve universal and equitable ITN coverage.

This systematic review examines AI applications in higher education assessment, grading, and feedback, guided by the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework. Its objectives are to evaluate AI’s effectiveness in automating and standardizing assessment, assess the accuracy and fairness of AI‑driven grading compared with traditional methods, and describe AI‑driven personalized feedback benefits. Using five academic databases, the review selected 20 peer‑reviewed studies published between 2010 and 2023, applying inclusion criteria focused on AI in higher‑education assessment contexts. Findings show that AI can process large‑scale assessments, reduce manual grading workloads, and enhance consistency and efficiency. AI‑driven systems also provide real‑time, personalized feedback that improves student engagement and self‑regulated learning. However, challenges persist, including algorithmic bias, data‑privacy concerns, and limitations in evaluating complex or subjective responses. Ethical considerations and stakeholder acceptance are identified as critical for responsible AI integration. The review concludes that while AI has transformative potential for assessment, grading, and feedback, mitigating bias, ensuring transparency, and aligning AI with pedagogical goals are essential to achieve equitable and effective educational outcomes.

The Deepwater Horizon rig, owned by Transocean and leased by BP, exploded on April 20 2010 in the Gulf of Mexico, killing 11 crew members and injuring 17. The rig burned for 36 hours and sank, releasing an estimated five million barrels of oil—the largest marine spill in U.S. waters.  

BP, the operator of the Macondo prospect, had previously experienced serious safety incidents (2005 Texas City refinery explosion, 2006 Prudhoe Bay pipeline leak) that highlighted process‑safety deficiencies. In the mid‑2000s the company underwent cost‑cutting and organizational restructuring under CEO Tony Hayward, reducing layers of management and pushing decision‑making to site‑level “asset managers,” which created incentives to prioritize speed and cost over safety.

Closing the Macondo well involved three contested decisions:  
1. Casing design – BP chose a single‑string “long‑string” casing rather than a liner‑tieback, providing fewer barriers to gas flow, saving time and $7–10 million.  
2. Number of centralizers – Halliburton’s OptiCem model recommended ≥21 centralizers to prevent cement channeling and severe gas flow; BP used only six, citing time constraints, despite warnings from its own engineers.  
3. Cement bond log and mud circulation – BP performed only a partial mud circulation (30 minutes instead of the recommended 6–12 hours) and cancelled the cement bond‑log test, which could have detected cement failure.

These choices increased the risk of a blowout and, after a loss of 3 000 barrels of drilling mud, the well erupted.

The disaster caused extensive environmental damage: oil contaminated wetlands and 25 wildlife refuges across five Gulf states, harming birds, fish, and reptiles. Economic losses included $560 million for the rig, $374 million for lost oil, a drop in BP’s stock price, and an estimated 250 000 jobs lost in the Gulf region. A federal moratorium on deep‑water drilling was imposed, halting production and reducing Gulf‑coast employment by 8 000–12 000 jobs.

BP established a $20 billion Gulf Coast Claims Facility (GCCF) to compensate victims; by early 2011 it had paid over $3.6 billion on 500 000 claims. Investigations by the U.S. Coast Guard, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, and congressional committees were ongoing, focusing on whether BP’s cost‑driven decisions and BP’s organizational culture contributed to the blowout.

The MACD and RSI strategy combines two momentum indicators to analyze and trade markets. MACD (Moving Average Convergence/Divergence) is an oscillator derived from a 12‑period EMA minus a 26‑period EMA, with a 9‑period EMA signal line and often a histogram; it identifies trends but does not directly indicate overbought/oversold levels. RSI (Relative Strength Index), created by J. Welles Wilder, is a single line oscillating between 0 and 100; readings above 70 signal overbought conditions and below 30 signal oversold conditions. Both gauges measure market momentum.

Traders may use MACD to determine overall trend direction and RSI to spot price swings. One approach is to buy when MACD crosses above its signal line and RSI rises after leaving the oversold region, selling when the reverse occurs. Others combine both as confirming oscillators, or employ a slower MACD with a faster RSI and a mean‑reversion filter to trade in the MACD‑defined direction.

Backtesting a strategy requiring all three conditions (MACD, RSI, and a mean‑reversion filter) on SMH (2001‑present) yielded 235 trades, an average gain of 0.88 % per trade (including 0.03 % commission/slippage), and a 73 % win rate; the method performed best for semiconductor stocks. Some analysts argue that because both indicators measure momentum, using them together may be redundant, and accuracy depends on the specific rules, parameters, and markets tested. Consequently, the effectiveness of a MACD‑RSI combination hinges on clear entry/exit rules and thorough backtesting rather than on which indicator is inherently more accurate.

The flexbone is a run‑heavy offensive system derived from the wishbone that emphasizes option plays and misdirection. It positions two “A‑backs” closer to the line than in the original wishbone, creating a pass threat while maintaining a triple‑option run game.  

Key personnel: the quarterback must be a decisive runner with enough passing skill to threaten defenses on play‑action; the fullback (B‑back) is a powerful, athletic interior runner and blocker; A‑backs are quick, agile athletes who block, run and catch; wide receivers must be strong blockers and occasional deep threats; the offensive line needs athletic cut‑ and combo‑blockers who understand rules for each defensive front.  

Strengths: the scheme’s rarity forces defenses to spend limited practice time learning its basics, and it excels at ball control, long possessions, and creating assignment confusion. Its option‑based run game physically wears opponents down and exploits poor tacklers.  

Weaknesses: the limited pass volume makes comebacks and two‑minute drills difficult, and the offense requires extensive practice to master timing. It also struggles in bad weather because precise mesh reads and pitches are easily disrupted.  

Common formations include the Double‑Slot (balanced pre‑snap look with motion), Trips (moving an A‑back to the opposite side), and Receivers‑Over (outside receiver shifted to the line, ineligible to catch).  

Signature runs are the Triple Option (dive/keep/pitch), Midline Option (attacking the middle with a read on the 3‑technique tackle), and Rocket Toss (quick outside run with a pitch to a motion A‑back).  

Passing concepts include the Play‑Action Wheel Route (mimics run action then targets post/wheel routes), Toss Boot (fake toss then bootleg with flat and crossing options), and Four Verticals (four deep routes with adjustments based on coverage).  

The flexbone is traditionally used by the service academies (Navy, Army, Air Force) and by coach Paul Johnson at Georgia Southern, Navy and Georgia Tech, culminating in Georgia Tech’s 2009 ACC title. Lower‑division programs such as 2023 Division II champion Harding University and many high‑school teams continue to employ the offense.

The paper investigates how an Australian university addresses the gap in primary pre‑service teachers’ (PSTs) arts education competencies by developing an “Arts Specialism” within its primary teacher‑education programme. Using a qualitative methodology grounded in Stephen J. Ball’s education‑policy sociology, the study examines three contexts: influence, policy‑text production and policy practice.  

The context of influence reviews literature showing that neoliberal reforms from the 1970s onward shifted education toward market‑driven models, resulting in reduced curriculum time for arts education. Global initiatives (e.g., UNESCO’s Lisbon Road Map, Seoul Agenda, Abu Dhabi Framework) and national policies recognise the benefits of the arts, yet pre‑service teachers consistently receive insufficient training and limited exposure to arts pedagogy.  

In the context of policy‑text production, critical discourse analysis (CDA) is applied to the Arts Specialism text and related documents from AITSL, ACDE and NAAE. Policy formulation relied on government reports (e.g., Action Now: Classroom Ready Teachers) that required primary PSTs to obtain at least one subject specialisation; subsequent guidance allowed arts specialisations. NAAE advocated for an arts specialisation, influencing ACDE and AITSL. Curriculum design produced standards emphasising “expert content knowledge, pedagogical knowledge and highly effective classroom teaching,” leading to the creation of four courses following a compulsory foundation arts course. Professional arts organisations (e.g., Australian Dance Council, Art Education Australia) supported the development.  

The context of policy practice describes implementation of the four courses, each 120 hours (total 600 hours), covering five arts subjects (dance, drama, media arts, music, visual arts) through experiential “making and responding” activities. Courses were structured as 12‑week blocks, with flexibility for weekly or fortnightly delivery. COVID‑19 forced a shift to online delivery for Course 2, prompting robust external learning tasks. School‑based projects and a partnership with a children’s arts festival provided real‑world teaching experiences.  

Findings indicate that the Arts Specialism mitigates insufficient preparation and limited curriculum time; PST feedback reports transformative learning, increased confidence and stronger arts‑teaching competencies. CDA reveals that the text’s use of modality (“will”) and inclusive language (e.g., Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander arts) shapes its authority and alignment with policy.  

Discussion highlights alignment with government requirements and national arts curriculum, fostering interdisciplinary connections and culturally responsive pedagogy. Challenges include persistent time constraints, staffing and changes in industrial‑relations law affecting casual staff support. Partnerships with First Nations artists and community organisations enhance inclusive content.  

Conclusion notes that the Arts Specialism offers a pioneering model for integrating arts education into primary teacher preparation. While challenges such as limited curriculum time remain, opportunities exist for broader institutional implementation, enhanced policy support, industry collaboration and longitudinal research tracking graduate professional journeys and school‑based arts curriculum outcomes.

Section 4.4 specifies that NMI injection must intercept #DB but not IRET, using the guest’s “NMI Complete” message to determine when another NMI may be sent. Debug‑register virtualization for SEV‑ES guests is enabled by the DebugVirtualization bit in the VMSA; if unavailable the hypervisor must intercept reads/writes of DR7, cache its value, and on writes perform normal VMGExit processing. System Management Mode and nested virtualization are not supported.

SEV‑SNP guests run with the SNP RestrictInjection feature, limiting host injection to a single #HV doorbell. The doorbell page contains a 16‑bit PendingEvent field (bits for NoFurtherSignal, virtual #MC, NMI, and an 8‑bit interrupt vector) plus a NoEoiRequired byte; bytes 3‑63 are reserved. The page must be host‑owned and accessed with C=0.

The host delivers an interrupt by writing the vector into PendingEvent.Vector, schedules a #HV only if NoFurtherSignal is clear, and may overwrite a pending vector with a higher‑priority one without sending another #HV. When no further EOI is needed the host sets NoEoiRequired; when multiple interrupts are pending it clears it. The host tracks the last presented vector and performs an internal EOI when NoEoiRequired transitions to zero.

The guest acknowledges an interrupt by atomically exchanging PendingEvent.Vector with zero, then processes the vector. For EOI the guest atomically exchanges NoEoiRequired with zero; if already zero it issues a VMGEXIT write to the X2APIC EOI MSR. Non‑maskable events are dispatched even when IF=0, requiring an atomic clear of the event bits and NoFurtherSignal. Non‑cooperative host or guest behavior can cause denial of service but does not corrupt state. The doorbell page is configured via VMGEXIT with SET/QUERY/GET actions.

Last‑shot situations require more than a simple play design; teams must be prepared, keep poise and put the ball in the best player's hands. Preparation includes reading the defense, using soft or pressure tactics, drilling non‑shooters to crash the offensive boards, keeping the play simple, practicing various scenarios with the game clock and improving physical conditioning. Holding for the last shot of a period can swing the score by up to 12 points (+6 to –6), or even 14 points if the shooter is fouled. The basic timing rule is to automatically hold when less than 30 seconds remain and the margin is eight points or less, then execute within the 10‑8‑3‑5‑0‑2 second sequence. Fundamental skills needed are crisp skip, baseball or semi‑hook passes, half‑court shooting and quick tipping. Teams should also practice intentionally missing free throws and know the rules. Key strategies include saving at least two timeouts, communicating the situation, inbounding to half‑court with 1–3 seconds, using quick‑break after opponent scores, shooting in line with the basket, having the bench stand and count down, reminding the timer, practicing plays from both sides, and designating a skilled inbounds passer. Guidelines give specific out‑of‑bounds and quick‑break options for endline, sideline and baseline situations with time windows of 1‑3, 3‑6 and 6‑12 seconds.

The passage describes the SD Memory Card Physical Layer Simplified Specification (Version 6.00). It details block‑oriented write data transfer, where the host appends 1‑ or 4‑bit CRC to each block and the card checks CRC before programming; write commands are rejected on BLOCK_LEN_ERROR or ADDRESS_ERROR. Block length is set by CMD16 and must be 512 bytes for block writes regardless of the WRITE_BL_LEN value, and partial‑block access is restricted unless WRITE_BL_PARTIAL is allowed; misaligned addresses cause ADDRESS_ERROR and abort the operation. Write protection includes a mechanical switch, internal card protection and password‑based lock (CMD42). Pre‑erased setting via ACMD23 speeds multiple‑block writes; the host can interleave writes to several cards and may deselect a busy card with CMD7 without interrupting the operation. Erase, Discard and Full User‑Area Logical Erase (FULE) are performed with the command sequence CMD32, CMD33, CMD38, with specific timeouts (250 ms for Discard, 1 s for FULE). Lock/unlock operations use CMD42 and optional Card Ownership Protection (COP), which introduces Force Erase Password (FEP) registers and a state machine that blocks CMD42 functions until a COP‑Unlock (CMD42[1F]) is issued. The specification also covers application‑specific commands (APP_CMD via CMD55), the switch function command (CMD6) for selecting access mode, driver strength, power limit and command system, high‑speed mode, the Send Interface Condition command (CMD8), bus timing including clock control and required post‑transaction clocks, CRC7 for commands/responses and CRC16 for data blocks, command format (48‑bit code words with start and end bits, 6‑bit index, 32‑bit argument, 7‑bit CRC), command classes (mandatory classes 0, 2, 4, 5, 8 and optional others), timeout conditions for read (100 ms), write (250 ms, up to 500 ms for SDXC) and erase operations, and busy indication via the DAT0 line held low while programming.

October 2025 offers a supermoon on the 6th, when the full moon coincides with perigee, appearing up to 14 % larger and about 30 % brighter than a typical full moon. International Observe the Moon Night occurs on October 4. The Draconid meteor shower peaks around October 8, derived from debris of comet 21P Giacobini‑Zinner, delivering up to 10 meteors per hour from near the constellation Draco; bright moonlight may limit visibility. The Orionid meteor shower peaks on October 21, producing about 20 meteors per hour as Earth passes through Halley’s Comet debris; the new moon that night provides a dark sky, ideal for viewing. Best viewing for Orionids is between before midnight and about 2 a.m., looking southeast in the Northern Hemisphere and northeast in the Southern Hemisphere. The full duration of the Orionids spans September 26 to November 22.

Professor James Swan discusses several topics in a linear algebra lecture. He notes a correction to a homework typo and mentions two remaining lectures on linear algebra before moving to other subjects. The lecture focuses on eigenvalue decomposition, which will be followed by singular value decomposition on Monday.

Swan emphasizes the importance of reordering rows or columns during Gaussian elimination to minimize numerical error and fill‑in; permutation matrices, which are unitary (P Pᵀ = I), perform these swaps and serve as a form of preconditioning.

He illustrates diffusion using a Plinko board model: a chip spreads probability evenly to neighboring cells, modeled by a sparse matrix with half‑diagonals. Multiplying by this matrix repeatedly yields a uniform distribution; some distributions remain unchanged, revealing eigenvectors with eigenvalue 1.

Eigenvectors are vectors that are stretched but retain direction under multiplication by a matrix; eigenvalues are the stretch factors. They are obtained by solving det(A – λI) = 0, whose roots form the characteristic polynomial. For diagonal or triangular matrices, eigenvalues equal the diagonal entries. The determinant of a matrix equals the product of its eigenvalues, and its trace equals the sum; complex eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs.

Algebraic multiplicity refers to root multiplicity of the characteristic polynomial, while geometric multiplicity is the dimension of the null space of (A – λI), i.e., the number of linearly independent eigenvectors. If geometric equals algebraic multiplicity for all eigenvalues, a matrix has a complete set of eigenvectors and can be diagonalized as A = W Λ W⁻¹, where W’s columns are eigenvectors and Λ’s diagonal entries are eigenvalues. For symmetric matrices, eigenvectors are orthogonal, yielding W⁻¹ = Wᵀ.

Eigendecomposition simplifies solving linear systems (x = W Λ⁻¹ Wᵀ b) and decouples linear ordinary differential equations (ẏ = Λ y). When a complete set of eigenvectors is absent, other forms such as Jordan normal form or Schur decomposition are used; the upcoming lecture will cover singular value decomposition.

Exponential moving average (EMA) is a moving‑average indicator that gives greater weight to recent price data, making it more responsive than a simple moving average (SMA). The EMA is calculated as EMA = (K × (C – P)) + P, where C is the current price, P the previous period’s EMA, and K the smoothing constant = 2/(n + 1) for n‑day period.

The article backtests four EMA strategies on the S&P 500 (SPY). Short‑term mean‑reversion strategies work best with short EMAs: using a 5‑day EMA to buy when the close falls below and sell when it rises above yields a CAGR of 7.41% with a maximum drawdown of 30.54%, outperforming buy‑and‑hold. Long‑term trend‑following strategies work best with long EMAs: buying when the close crosses above a 200‑day EMA and selling below yields a CAGR of 7.84% with a drawdown of 26%, roughly half that of buy‑and‑hold.

Timed‑exit strategies (Strategies 3 & 4) show that exiting after N days improves profitability; the best result is buying when the close drops below a 50‑day EMA and selling after 200 days, producing 10.17% per trade. The EMA helps identify trend direction, support/resistance, and can be combined with other indicators such as RSI or MACD, but it still lags price and may generate false signals if the period is shortened.

The authors conclude that EMA strategies are most effective with either a low or a high number of days: mean‑reversion favors short periods, while trend‑following favors long periods. No single EMA period is universally best; backtesting is required to determine the optimal period for a given asset class.

A systematic literature review of 17 leading Information Systems journals (2000‑2017) used the terms “Digital business strategy,” “Digital transformation,” and “Business digitalization.” The initial search returned 292 papers; after title/abstract/keyword screening 54 were kept, and after full‑text examination 28 were retained for analysis. Following Wolifswinkel’s coding guidelines (open, axial, and selective coding), the review identified 12 underlying dimensions of digital transformation (e.g., use of technology, value creation, structural changes, digital leadership, agile operations, digital artefacts, external collaboration), 6 dimensions of digital business strategy (e.g., IT infrastructure, cross‑functional integration, new dynamic capabilities), and 10 dimensions of organizational capabilities (e.g., digital leadership, agile & scalable operations, dynamic capabilities, plug‑and‑play capabilities). Overlap analysis showed a shared “external collaboration of ecosystem of digital platforms” across all three concepts; additional overlaps were found between digital transformation and the other two concepts (use of technology, structural changes; digital leadership, agile operations, digitally enabled CSU, digital artefacts; dynamic capabilities). The resulting framework posits that digital business strategy is a blueprint that, when successfully deployed via the identified organizational capabilities, yields digital transformation. The review also notes publication growth from 2009 onward, a focus on automotive, banking, telecom, healthcare, oil & gas, and manufacturing sectors, and a predominance of studies from the US and Europe, with limited coverage of Asia, the Middle East, Latin America, and Africa. The findings provide CEOs, CIOs, and IS researchers with a structured view of the inter‑relationships among organizational capabilities, digital transformation, and digital business strategy.

The editors of the Foreign Relations series have access to retired Department of State records, including central files, decentralized office files, Executive Secretariat files, and overseas diplomatic post files. Central and decentralized files for 1981–1989 will be transferred to the National Archives after declassification and processing. Research for the series involves special access to restricted documents at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and other agencies; all printed material has been declassified, though some is extracted from still-classified documents. Presidential papers at the Reagan Library include foreign-affairs documentation from various federal agencies. Some research was conducted via the Remote Archives Capture project, which coordinated declassification across Presidential libraries, but scanning methods sometimes prevented editors from confirming attachment inclusion, noted as “Not found attached.” Editorial methodology presents documents chronologically by Washington DC time, preserving original text with silent corrections for obvious typographical errors, bracketed insertions for corrections or omissions, and footnotes identifying original brackets and ellipses. Undeclassified material and withheld documents are noted with extent and nature indicated.

This paper addresses the multi-period resource allocation problem under stochastic demands. The authors analyze a static approach where allocation decisions are made at the beginning of the horizon, which fails to adapt to observed demands. They propose a sequential adaptive policy based on shrinking horizon optimization that updates the distribution of future demands based on observed history. The policy is evaluated using synthetic jointly log-normal data. Results demonstrate that the sequential approach outperforms the static solution when demands are correlated, while both methods perform equivalently when demands are independent. Aggregate results over 100 trials for different time horizons (T=20, 50, 100, 200) show the sequential allocation consistently achieves higher revenue than the static allocation, with revenue closest to an oracle upper bound.

Research across ~150 firms shows a strong link between a company’s technology intensity and business performance, with digital leaders outperforming laggards in revenue and enterprise‑value growth. Four cultural themes distinguish firms with strong data cultures: (1) a growth mindset that embraces risk, continuous learning and data‑driven evolution; (2) using data to create shared context and transparency across the organization; (3) empowering teams to examine data and set realistic, measurable goals; and (4) aligning the organization with common targets that allow creative, autonomous pursuit of objectives.  

Digital leaders actively encourage experimentation, long‑term development, and transparent data sharing, while laggards focus on short‑term optimization, restrict data access, and rely on authority rather than metrics. Leaders employ detailed, data‑driven metrics to track progress and grant teams flexibility; laggards set aspirational but unrealistic goals, avoid measurement, and emphasize procedural compliance. Effective goal alignment, achieved through a combined top‑down and bottom‑up process, creates shared purpose and reduces siloed decision‑making.  

Organizations fit one of four patterns: data novice (culture and systems not yet aligned), insight ready (culture supports risk but capability limited), tech enabled (technology present but culture lacks experimentation), and data reliant (high maturity but over‑reliance on data). Success in digital transformation requires embedding these cultural beliefs and behaviors throughout the organization.

The article examines how anti‑critical race theory (CRT) legislation in Idaho, Utah, and Arizona affects the inclusion of Native content in teacher education at predominantly white institutions. Using Tribal Critical Race Theory (TribalCrit) and the concept of colonial unknowing, the authors analyze data from multiple IRB‑approved projects—including stories, interviews, and observations—to address the question: What are the impacts of a CRT ban on Native content instruction? The analysis identifies three primary impacts: (1) the continued silencing of Native perspectives and content in curricula; (2) the perpetuation of invisibilizing Native peoples in public education through policies and everyday practices; and (3) a refusal by some educators and students to learn culturally sustaining pedagogies, evidenced by resistance to critical race–focused coursework. Contextual background describes state‑level legislation (e.g., Idaho HB 377, Utah S.R. 901/H.R. 901, and Arizona HB 2898), noting that such laws have a chilling effect on educators and embolden white supremacist ideologies. Demographic data indicate that the teacher workforce in these states is overwhelmingly white, with less than 1 % American Indian teachers, and that teachers rarely enter the profession with knowledge of Native peoples or tribal sovereignty. The authors situate teacher education within a broader history of U.S. policies aimed at assimilation and highlight the role of “colonial unknowing” in rendering Native knowledge illegitimate. Findings draw on ethnographic narratives, including a Utah teacher’s experience of administrators canceling culturally responsive training after HB 377, a detailed account of Arizona’s unenforced Native history laws, and student resistance to diversity courses in Idaho and Arizona. The article concludes that critical democratic education must recognize and support tribal nationhood and sovereignty to enable all students to become informed democratic citizens.

In this lecture, the professor discusses walking robots, emphasizing that their key differences from robotic arms are the need to handle limit cycles (periodic motions) and impacts (hybrid dynamics combining continuous and discrete time). A limit cycle is a stable closed orbit where trajectories converge to the orbit itself rather than a point, requiring analysis tools beyond standard Lyapunov theory. The Van der Pol oscillator is presented as a simple example with state-dependent nonlinear damping, showing how trajectories from various initial conditions converge to a stable limit cycle.

To analyze limit cycle stability, the professor introduces Poincaré sections and maps: defining a surface in state space that the orbit crosses periodically, allowing continuous-time limit cycle stability to be converted into discrete-time fixed-point stability on the map. The stability of the fixed point on the map depends on the magnitude of the map's gradient at that point being less than one. Unimodal maps with local stability can imply global stability under certain conditions.

Historically, the study of walking began with Eadweard Muybridge’s motion photography of animal gaits in the late 1800s, followed by McMahon’s ballistic walker model at Harvard, which suggested walking could be approximated as vaulting over a stiff stance leg with passive swing. Tad McGeer later demonstrated passive dynamic walking—machines with no motor or controller walking down slopes using ballistic principles, sparking significant research.

The rimless wheel is introduced as a fundamental model for walking dynamics: a massless-legged pendulum on a slope, with inelastic ground impacts causing energy loss. Its dynamics are energy-conserving between impacts, and the Poincaré map can be derived analytically, revealing two stable fixed points: a rolling limit cycle and a standing state. The homoclinic orbit marks the energy threshold distinguishing rolling from standing, and the map’s basins of attraction are fully characterized.

The compass gait model extends this by adding a hip torque and modeling swing leg dynamics as an Acrobot, showing stable limit cycles on slopes but with limited basins of attraction. Knees introduce an additional impact at the kneecap, improving gait appearance but requiring the leg to be straight during stance. The dynamics of these walking models are dominated by ground collision energy loss, with efficiency gains achievable through push-off before impact.

The lecture concludes by noting that applying optimization methods to walking requires careful handling of hybrid dynamics and impacts, and that future topics will include the state of the art in walking control and methods for computing gradients in these systems.

A 12-month (250-day) moving average trend-following system for gold achieved significant outperformance compared to buy-and-hold, turning $100,000 invested in 1971 into $10 million versus $4 million for passive holding over 26 trades. The system instructs going long when gold is above the moving average and holding cash when below, helping avoid major drawdowns like those in 1980 and 2012. Gold differs from stocks by lacking inherent utility or cash flows and requires storage costs. The USD and gold became formally independent after 1971. Gold moves in extended periods of inactivity followed by significant moves, creating favorable conditions for trend-following. The optimal moving average range is approximately 200-250 days. Practical gold investment options are limited to ETFs like GLD or futures contracts.

This study evaluated the Disk Potentiation Test (DPT) for detecting KPC and MBL carbapenemases in 147 gram-negative clinical isolates from Evercare Hospital, Dhaka (January-June 2020). All isolates showed 100% resistance to Imipenem. KPC was detected in 26.53% (39/147) of isolates, predominantly in ICU patients, with Acinetobacter baumannii being the most common producer. MBL was detected in 44.89% (66/147) of isolates, also most prevalent in ICU. Both enzymes were present in 24.49% (36/147) of isolates. The >60 age group exhibited the highest resistance. The findings underscore the urgent need for antimicrobial stewardship and infection control measures to manage carbapenem-resistant infections.

MSPM0G3519, MSPM0G3518, MSPM0G1519, MSPM0G1518 are 80MHz ARM Cortex-M0+ microcontrollers with up to 512KB flash and 128KB SRAM. They support five operating modes (RUN, SLEEP, STOP, STANDBY, SHUTDOWN) and two power domains (PD1 for high-performance peripherals, PD0 for low-speed peripherals). The clock module provides multiple sources including internal oscillators, external crystals, and a system PLL. Peripherals include a 12-bit ADC (up to 4Msps), 12-bit buffered DAC, three comparators with blanking sources, UART, I2C, SPI, CAN-FD, general-purpose and advanced timers, RTC with calendar and alarms, and watchdog timers. Security features include AES-128/256 encryption/decryption, CRC-16/32, and secure key storage for up to four keys. Additional features include DMA with 12 channels, an event fabric for peripheral interconnection, GPIO with up to 93 pins, IOMUX for pin configuration, and a temperature sensor connected to the ADC. The devices operate over recommended supply voltage and temperature ranges, with detailed electrical characteristics provided for ADC, DAC, comparators, and other peripherals.

Trial court ordered Kenneth to pay $4,800/year rehabilitative alimony for two years, $7,800/year child support, half of mortgage, taxes, insurance and maintenance ($4,230/year), provide a car, cover the children’s medical and dental expenses, and maintain life insurance. AMD supplies pre‑memory service procedures for x86‑64 platforms. AMD_ENABLE_STACK is a stackless assembler routine that creates a per‑core pre‑memory stack, maps it to global address space, sets MTRRs, creates a UEFI_SEC_PEI_HAND_OFF structure and returns AGESA_SUCCESS/WARNING/FATAL. AMD_DISABLE_STACK runs once after main memory is available, disables CAR mode, flushes all cache lines, and returns AGESA_SUCCESS. AmdCreateStruct allocates storage for a parameter block using PreMemHeap, PostMemDram or ByHost methods, calls the structure initializer and returns AGESA_SUCCESS/ERROR/FATAL. Data‑eye retrieval returns a 31‑element bitmap for a specified DIMM, requires coherent HT links and a stack, and must be called before memory structures are created. A routine to obtain the APIC address of a core applies only to x86‑64 APUs and also requires HT links and a stack. A cache‑size query returns the number of bytes available for execution caching during the pre‑memory phase on the current core; it applies only to x86‑64 APUs. AARCH64 APUs equipped with a Platform Security Processor do not use these stack procedures; the PSP initializes DRAM.

Curriculum literacy is defined as the ability to understand, evaluate, and apply educational programs, encompassing skills such as using teaching materials, adapting curricula to students’ needs, and integrating digital technologies. The passage emphasizes its critical role for teachers, administrators, and students in 21st‑century education, noting that well‑structured educational programs support lifelong learning and informed decision‑making. It outlines how digital transformation has expanded the concept, requiring educators to go beyond traditional curriculum mastery and to incorporate technology effectively.

A literature review highlights diverse definitions and core components (understanding content, evaluating methods, analyzing outcomes, and assessing materials). Program literacy contributes to innovative, egalitarian teaching, enhances teachers’ professional development, and can reduce educational inequities. However, the passage reports that teachers worldwide—including in Turkey—often have insufficient curriculum literacy due to inadequate training, time constraints, bureaucratic obstacles, and frequent curriculum changes.

The study’s purpose is to investigate curriculum literacy’s role, importance, and hindering factors; to discuss components and strategies; and to include teachers, administrators, and other stakeholders. Five research questions address demographic information, keyword distribution, yearly study counts, subject focus, and common themes.

Methodologically, the research employs thematic content analysis of Scopus‑indexed articles in English and Turkish, applying inclusion/exclusion criteria (peer‑reviewed, accessible, original studies on curriculum literacy). From an initial set of 35 articles, 29 were analyzed after excluding unrelated works.

Findings show a steady increase in publications: limited work before 2000, 10 studies (2000‑2010), 11 (2010‑2015), 26 (2015‑2020), and 89 (2020‑2025). Keyword trends evolved from basic concepts and social‑studies education (2010‑2015), to activity theory and cultural contexts (2015‑2020), and to dyslexia diagnosis, empowerment, and AI‑related themes (2020‑2025). Most studies belong to social sciences, followed by psychology, arts/humanities, and a few other disciplines. Geographically, Australia and the United States lead in publication volume, with Turkey ranking third; other countries show limited output.

Analysis of themes indicates that curriculum literacy positively—yet weakly—correlates with teachers’ digital technology usage. Improved curriculum literacy enhances pedagogical skills, student outcomes, and inclusive education, especially for low‑income learners. Teachers face challenges aligning digital tools with curricula and need further support to develop content and pedagogical strategies.

The discussion notes that unlike prior research, this study foregrounds digital transformation and AI integration, employs qualitative thematic analysis, and provides a global perspective, revealing gaps in interdisciplinary and geographic coverage. The conclusion stresses curriculum literacy as essential for effective teaching and student success, advocating for stronger teacher training in digital platforms, interdisciplinary approaches, and equitable, inclusive program design. Suggestions include targeted teacher preparation, fostering student participation, and encouraging innovative teaching methods to advance curriculum literacy across education systems.

Vietnamese higher education (HE) is undergoing rapid digitalization, driven mainly by national policies. The country has 237 universities, mostly public, overseen by the Ministry of Education and Training (MOET) and other agencies. Curriculum, enrollment and operations follow MOET standards. Before the COVID‑19 pandemic, digitalization was uneven; a few universities had adopted learning management systems (LMS) and digital data platforms, while most lacked infrastructure, funding and digital skills. Vietnam’s digital evolution index ranked low compared with regional peers, and workforce digital skills were weak.

Policy frameworks guide the transition. The 2020 National Digital Transformation Program sets targets for distance‑learning platforms, digital content, data warehouses and individualized instruction. A follow‑up project for 2022‑2025 aims to make online teaching and learning a daily activity for half of students and teachers, to have over 50 % of HEIs offering online degree programs, and to digitalise institutional management. MOET has relaxed regulations to allow up to 30 % online teaching in regular bachelor programmes and 20 % in joint master/PhD programmes.

COVID‑19 accelerated adoption. Most HEIs now operate LMS for teaching, administration and student services. MOET has integrated a national higher‑education management information system and a national e‑learning warehouse containing thousands of e‑lectures, theses and question banks. Blended learning and paperless procedures have become common, and private providers have built additional data platforms.

To sustain progress, recommendations include: clearer MOET guidance and evaluation frameworks; increased government funding and infrastructure, especially in provinces; partnerships with private and international organisations; training for leaders on digital literacy; and comprehensive lecturer training in intellectual property, pedagogy, digital skills, personalised learning models and digital mentorship. Students should receive digital‑skill instruction and full online administrative services. Continued coordinated effort across institutions is expected to keep Vietnam’s HE digitalization moving forward.

Nasdaq 100 E-mini futures are electronically traded derivative contracts that track the Nasdaq 100 index, which is composed of the 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq exchange, primarily in the technology sector. One contract is worth $20 multiplied by the index value. They debuted on June 21, 1999, and are one-fifth the size of the full Nasdaq futures contract. They trade on the CME Globex platform and are cash-settled on the third Friday of quarterly contract months (March, June, September, December). The contract’s all-time high is 16,676.50 (Nov 2021) and low is 797.50 (Oct 2002). Price factors include Fed rate decisions, individual component prices, economic news, and the US Dollar Index. As a leveraged product, significant price movements can result in losses that far exceed the initial margin, making strict risk management essential. Successful trading requires a strategy combining technical and fundamental analysis.

The team feels confident in the series, with Jannik and LapPy delivering a strong third period. Coach Manny has encouraged the speaker to relax and stick to their natural north-south style of play.

A 29-year-old man named Jonathan Rinderknecht was charged with starting the fire that destroyed LA's Pacific Palisades, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,000 homes. He was arrested in Florida and faces charges including malicious destruction by fire. Officials say he lit a fire on New Year's Day that initially was extinguished but smoldered underground before reigniting during high winds. He fled the scene but returned to watch and record the fire. He made several 911 calls reporting the fire, which officials say indicated an attempt to create evidence of a more innocent explanation. Investigators found a "barbecue-style" lighter in his car and determined the fire was intentionally lit by a lighter, excluding other causes. The blaze erupted on Jan. 7. A second fire broke out the same day with unknown cause. An outside review found delayed evacuation warnings due to weaknesses in emergency alert systems.

Pets at Home in Burton has partnered with the National Autistic Society to hold the UK's first autism hour on Sunday, Oct 8, opening an hour early with dimmed lights, reduced music and till bells to give autistic people a break from sensory overload; 64% avoid shops.

A bear trap is a bullish pattern in which a price temporarily breaks a support level in an uptrend, luring traders into short positions, then reverses sharply upward. It exploits retail‑trader fear of missing out (FOMO) and the automatic execution of stop‑loss orders. Market manipulators (liquidity providers) create the trap by placing large sell orders that trigger stop‑losses, after which they buy back at a lower price. Characteristics that may signal a bear trap include a sudden break below a key support or moving average, and divergence between price and technical indicators such as the RSI or MACD; positive earnings or acquisition news can also trigger a reversal. To avoid being caught, traders should base decisions on fundamentals and multiple indicators rather than price alone, back‑test and stick to a disciplined strategy, be wary of crowd‑following, and use stop‑losses cautiously because they can amplify the trap. A practical example showed that on Apple a bearish breakout was a trap, whereas MACD divergence would have warned against shorting. A trend‑reversal strategy that buys on breakdowns and sells on strength achieved on QQQ 181 trades with 1.7 % average gain, 13 % CAGR, 80 % win rate, and 20 % max drawdown (10 % capital invested). The leveraged version on QLD produced similar returns with a slightly higher drawdown.

Samsung's Chromebook Pro, launching in April, and Chromebook Plus, shipping next week, are 2‑in‑1 devices with built‑in digital pens, designed to run Android apps from Google Play. Unveiled at CES 2017, both have 12.3‑inch Quad HD Gorilla Glass displays, 360° hinges, 4 GB RAM, 32 GB storage, up to eight hours of battery, two USB‑C ports and 4K streaming. The Plus uses a 2 GHz hexa‑core ARM processor and starts at $449.99; the Pro has a 2.2 GHz Intel Core m3 processor and starts at $549. Early reviews range from “lot of potential” (Engadget) to “nearly perfect budget laptop” (Gizmodo). Analysts note Chromebooks have outsold Macs (IDC, early 2016) and could threaten Windows. New Chromebooks also include enhanced ChromeVox assistive technology for visually impaired users.

NVIDIA Turing GPUs improve memory bandwidth via lossless compression, delivering ~50% higher effective bandwidth than Pascal. They include a new display engine supporting DisplayPort 1.4a with DSC for 8K @ 60 Hz, native HDR processing and tone‑mapping, an enhanced NVENC for HEVC/H.264 with bit‑rate savings, and an updated NVDEC for HEVC 4:4:4 and VP9 HDR. Turing adds hardware‑based USB‑Type‑C and VirtualLink for single‑connector VR headsets and introduces second‑generation NVLink for higher‑bandwidth SLI (2× 25 GB/s per link). The architecture implements dedicated RT Cores per SM that accelerate BVH traversal and ray‑triangle tests, enabling real‑time ray tracing while using denoising to keep ray counts low. Hybrid rendering combines rasterization and ray tracing, using RT Cores for reflections, shadows and ambient occlusion; BVH structures are built or refitted each frame and RT Cores free the SM for other work. Turing also introduces Tensor Cores for AI‑accelerated NGX features: DLSS (standard and 2× modes) trained on 64× supersampled images for high‑quality upscaling, InPainting for intelligent content removal, AI Slow‑Mo for interpolated frames and AI Super Rez for sharp upscaling. New shader stages (Task and Mesh Shaders) enable Mesh Shading to eliminate CPU draw‑call bottlenecks and support level‑of‑detail control and dynamic cutaways. Variable Rate Shading (VRS) allows per‑16×16‑pixel shading‑rate control for Content‑Adaptive, Motion‑Adaptive and Foveated Rendering, and can increase shading for MSAA. Texture Space Shading decouples shading from screen‑space, reusing texels for stability and LOD‑based rate control. Multi‑View Rendering extends Pascal’s SMP to up to four views per pass for efficient stereo and wide‑FOV VR rendering. Turing resource handling supports bindless Constant Buffer and Unordered Access Views (DX12 Tier 3). The TU102, TU104 and TU106 chips provide 13.6 B, 13.6 B and 10.8 B transistors respectively, with 48/36 RT Cores, 3072/2304 CUDA cores and 368/288 Tensor Cores; TU104 includes one x8 NVLink link, TU106 lacks NVLink/SLI. RTX‑OPS is a workload‑based metric combining FP32, INT32, RT‑core and Tensor‑core utilization (e.g., RTX 2080 Ti reaches ~78 RTX‑OPS). Overall, Turing’s combination of hardware‑accelerated ray tracing, AI inference, advanced shading control, and modern display/VR interfaces enables hybrid rendering, real‑time ray tracing and AI‑enhanced graphics for games and professional applications.

UC1825B‑SP supports push‑pull, forward, half‑bridge and full‑bridge power‑conversion topologies. Use a low‑EMI ferrite‑type closed‑core inductor (toroid or encased E‑core) or a low‑EMI open‑core placed away from low‑power traces with its poles perpendicular to the PCB. Route the feedback trace far from the inductor and noisy power traces, on the opposite PCB side with a ground plane separating them, and keep it as short and thick as possible. Place input filter and feed‑forward capacitors close to the VIN pin and IC respectively, using surface‑mount parts to reduce lead inductance. Locate compensation components near the IC, surface‑mount, and away from the inductor. Keep high‑current power traces short, direct, and at least 15 mil per amp; group the inductor, output capacitors and output diode together and connect their grounds to a common ground plane. For multilayer boards, separate power and signal planes with one via per 200 mA of current. Arrange components so the two switching current loops curl in the same direction to limit magnetic field reversal and radiated EMI. Designate a dedicated power‑ground section for high di/dt currents (connected to PGND), bypass VCC to power ground and VREF to signal ground with low‑ESR/ESL ceramic 1‑µF capacitors.

MSPM0C1105/6 are ultra-low-power 32-bit MCUs based on Arm Cortex-M0+ (up to 32MHz) with up to 64KB flash and 8KB SRAM. They integrate a 12-bit 1.6Msps ADC, comparator with 8-bit DAC, multiple timers (one advanced 16-bit with deadband, four general purpose 16-bit), three UARTs, one SPI, two I2Cs, and a 3-channel DMA. They support five power modes (RUN, SLEEP, STOP, STANDBY, SHUTDOWN) and operate from 1.62V to 3.6V over -40°C to 125°C. Pin functions are configured via PINCM registers and IOMUX.

The passage consists of a chronological list of documents concerning American preparation for the post‑World‑War I peace conference, spanning August 1917 to November 1918, with dates, locations and file references. It also includes a memorandum from Third Assistant Secretary of State Breckinridge Long proposing the creation of a secret bureau to study and prepare likely peace‑conference issues. The bureau would be overseen by a board of designated members, supported by expert advisors covering regions such as Russia, the Balkans, Turkey‑Persia, Japan, Germany‑Austria, and England‑France‑Belgium. Long recommends the bureau be organized immediately and quietly, housed at the War College or a comparable hidden location, supplied with relevant literature, and report directly to the Secretary of State. Jonathan Toews, Kimmo Timonen and Trevor van Riemsdyk said the series is tightly contested with no overtime games yet, and both teams are regarded as equally deserving and confident about playing at home. All four forward lines are contributing offensively and defensively, and both sides trust their players to gain an edge regardless of matchups. Gary McLaren, executive director of Henrico County Economic Development Authority, said Facebook’s planned $750 million data center in White Oak Technology Park is a good deal for the county. The park was built for a former Infineon semiconductor plant; its legacy provides 10 million gallons per day of excess water capacity, 13 million gallons of sewer capacity, multiple fiber‑optic trunk lines and dual‑feed power from Dominion. The Western Association of Schools and Colleges Senior College and University Commission has removed all references to diversity, equity and inclusion from its accreditation standards. The commission began considering the change last December following President Trump's re-election and temporarily held DEI standards during a review period. After a public comment period, the commission accepted revised 2023 standards. Two examples show changes: Standard 1 now emphasizes "institutional excellence" instead of DEI commitments, and Standard 3 removed DEI language from resource allocation language. The changes follow pressure from Trump's directives to end DEI requirements, and other accrediting agencies have similarly suspended or are considering dropping DEI standards.

The lecturer reviews the formal definition of convergence (a sequence xₙ converges to x iff |xₙ–x|→0) and the squeeze theorem for sequences. He states the binomial theorem  

\[
(x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk x^{n-k}y^k,
\]

and uses it to prove three special limits:  

1. \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1{n^p}=0\) for any fixed p>0;  

2. \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}p^{1/n}=1\) for any fixed p>0 (proved by the inequality \((1+x)^n\ge1+nx\) for x≥–1);  

3. \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{1/n}=1\) (proved by applying the binomial theorem to \((1+x_n)^n=n\) with \(x_n=n^{1/n}-1\)).  

He then turns to bounded sequences and subsequences. For a bounded sequence \(x_n\) define  

\[
a_n=\sup\{x_k:k\ge n\},\qquad b_n=\inf\{x_k:k\ge n\}.
\]

The sequences \(a_n\) and \(b_n\) are monotone (decreasing and increasing, respectively) and bounded, so their limits exist; they are called \(\limsup x_n\) and \(\liminf x_n\), with \(\liminf x_n\le\limsup x_n\).  

Examples: for \(x_n=(-1)^n\) we obtain \(\limsup=1\) and \(\liminf=-1\); for \(x_n=1/n\) we get \(\limsup=0\) and \(\liminf=0\).  

The lecture proves that any bounded sequence possesses a subsequence converging to its \(\limsup\) and another converging to its \(\liminf\); consequently every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence (Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem).  

Finally, it is shown that a bounded sequence converges if and only if its \(\limsup\) and \(\liminf\) coincide, and in that case the common value equals the limit of the sequence.

Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) is a major public‑health burden. Intravenous alteplase improves outcomes but has moderate fibrin specificity, a short half‑life (4–5 min) and requires a one‑hour infusion. Newer thrombolytics (rhPro‑UK, ancrod, desmoteplase) failed to show benefit and had higher hemorrhage risk. Tenecteplase (TNK‑tPA) is a third‑generation variant of alteplase with ≈10‑fold higher fibrin specificity, 80‑fold greater resistance to PAI‑1, a plasma half‑life of 20–24 min and can be given as a 5–10 s IV bolus.

This retrospective study compared tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg) with alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg) in AIS patients treated within 4.5 h of symptom onset at a single Chinese hospital. Demographics, risk factors, baseline NIHSS/mRS, time metrics (onset‑to‑treatment, door‑to‑needle [DNT], door‑to‑puncture [DPT]), 24‑h NIHSS improvement, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH), any intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) and hospital stay were recorded and analyzed with univariate tests and binary logistic regression.

264 patients were included (120 tenecteplase, 144 alteplase). Baseline characteristics were similar except hyperlipidemia and atrial fibrillation were more common in the tenecteplase group. Median onset‑to‑treatment time (133 vs 163.7 min), DNT (36.5 vs 50 min) and DPT (117 vs 193 min) were significantly shorter with tenecteplase. The proportion meeting DNT ≤45 min (65.8% vs 40.4%) and DPT ≤120 min (59.1% vs 13.8%) was higher for tenecteplase; tenecteplase was an independent predictor of both targets. 24‑h NIHSS improvement occurred in 64.2% vs 50% (p = 0.024) and tenecteplase independently predicted improvement. sICH (3.3% vs 4.9%) and any ICH (13.3% vs 15.3%) were not significantly different. Hospital stay was shorter (6 vs 8 days, p < 0.001). Higher baseline NIHSS and atrial fibrillation were independent risk factors for ICH.

The authors conclude tenecteplase offers comparable safety to alteplase, greater early neurological improvement, faster workflow and shorter hospitalization, supporting its use in AIS intravenous thrombolysis, although larger multicenter studies are needed.

U.S. officials regard the Sandwich Islands as a strategic Pacific outpost and will not accept their transfer to another maritime power. Concern over Hawaii’s unstable government and desire for annexation by wealthy island interests prompt requests for detailed data on population, trade, resources and debt, with instructions to gather information, avoid discouraging pro‑annexation sentiment, and discreetly probe Hawaiian authorities on possible terms. In February 1874 King Lunalilo died without a named successor; the legislative assembly elected David Kalakaua, prompting riots by supporters of Queen Emma. Foreign naval forces intervened: U.S. ships Tuscarora and Portsmouth landed troops at the American minister’s request, while British sailors from H.B.M.S. Tenidos arrived unbidden and occupied the barracks for eight days before withdrawing on the 20th. Later that year Kalakaua visited the United States on the USS Benicia, received friendly treatment, and sought reciprocity negotiations, a move opposed by British and French commissioners.

The study investigates digitalization in education via semi‑structured interviews with 20 private‑sector education experts. Data were analysed with content analysis. Participants were mainly from national companies, most with >15 years experience and firms employing >300 staff. Challenges identified include technological problems, insufficient financial resources, content unsuited to digitization, participants’ fear of change, lack of non‑verbal cues, simultaneous work‑training demands and resistance to new methods. Adaptation measures reported include online and hybrid training, digital learning platforms, LMS usage, video‑based content, workshops and projects, and virtual‑reality applications. Positive impacts highlighted are time‑ and location‑independent access, cost and time savings, greater equality of opportunity, wider audience reach and personalized learning. Negative impacts cited are participant indifference, reduced interaction, lower effectiveness compared with face‑to‑face instruction, difficulty delivering practical training, cyber‑security concerns and cheating. Participants defined digitalization as delivering education through digital tools, automating processes and enabling easy, rapid access. The conclusion notes that although digitalization in private‑sector education mirrors broader findings, face‑to‑face teaching is expected to persist. Recommendations suggest combining digital content with technologies such as VR and gamification, and aligning national education systems with private‑sector practices.

A guided diffusion model pretrained on 2+ million crystal structures and fine-tuned on 7,183 superconductors generated 200,000 candidates, which were filtered through ML/DFT for metallicity, thermodynamic and dynamical stability, yielding 773 novel candidates with DFT‑calculated Tc >5 K and Ehull <200 meV/atom. Experimental synthesis of 18 ternary candidates showed 9 superconductors above 4.2 K, but X‑ray diffraction revealed predominantly disordered BCC solid solutions rather than the predicted ordered structures, highlighting data‑sparsity artifacts and the challenge of predicting synthesizability. The pipeline achieves a ~2.3% hit rate (135× better than element‑substitution baselines and ~31× higher yield than prior generative work). Future directions include active‑learning loops and disorder‑aware screening to bridge prediction and experimental realization.

U.S. minister in Tokyo reported Japan‑China relations on 28th ultimo. The United States declined to protect Japanese archives and subjects without Chinese consent and urged Japan to withdraw troops; Japan said troops would stay until reforms enacted, denied territorial ambitions. The United States asked Japan’s reason for its presence; Japan said it responded to Chinese troops, demanded reforms, offered mediation. The chargé in Peking reported hostilities imminent and China sought British and Russian mediation. Britain asked if the United States would join an intervention; it could act only as neutral and would not join another power. Japan said its troops were to maintain order and would withdraw once order ensured. The Viceroy asked the United States to request Japan’s withdrawal.

This patent application discloses a method and apparatus for channel state information (CSI) reporting for beam operation in wireless communication systems. The method, from the UE perspective, involves configuring the UE with at least two CSI-RS (Channel State Information-Reference Signal) resources, performing measurements on those resources, generating multiple CSIs where at least one CSI corresponds to measurements on more than one CSI-RS resource, and reporting at least one of the generated CSIs. The disclosure relates to evolving wireless networks including 5G (Next Generation/Radio) technology and addresses beamforming techniques for higher frequency bands where cell coverage requires high antenna gain using larger antenna arrays. The system supports various beamforming types (digital, hybrid, analog), multiple transmission/reception points (TRPs), and different CSI reporting modes including periodic and aperiodic reporting on PUCCH and PUSCH, with CSI components comprising CQI, PMI, RI, and CRI.

Birmingham City's Maikel Kieftenbeld has won his appeal against a red card received in Saturday's 2-1 win over Bristol City. He can now play against Bolton Wanderers tomorrow, having been facing a three-match ban.

A campaign called Zimbabwe Yadzoka/Mayibuye iZimbabwe has been launched to encourage diaspora Zimbabweans to return home and register to vote in the 2018 election. Campaign leader Victor Chimhutu, based in Norway, claims Zanu PF is suppressing the diaspora vote. The campaign will target cities in Ireland, UK, Canada, Norway, and South Africa. Chimhutu also advocates for an opposition coalition to defeat Zanu PF and plans protests against President Mugabe.

Crook County Medical Services District CEO Nathan Hough announced several improvements. The nursing home earned the Women’s Choice Award as one of America’s Best for Extended Care, and an annual survey found only minor issues. A new wheelchair‑accessible, ADA‑compliant van for patient transport was purchased using a grant matched by a family donation. The district also unveiled family rooms for end‑of‑life care, funded by families of Long Term Care patients. A CT‑scanner and emergency‑department renovation backed by USDA and Sundance State Bank will begin this month, with completion targeted for September; old operating rooms will house the CT and X‑ray units, and the current X‑ray room will become a modernized trauma room, supported by a Helmsley Foundation equipment grant.

The study determines the position of publications on special education and mathematics in the literature by performing a bibliometric analysis of 487 articles retrieved from the Web of Science database covering 1980–2023. Search terms “special education and mathematics” and “special education and mathematics education” were used, with only English articles selected. The dataset comprises 120 sources, 887 keywords plus, 1,010 author keywords, 1,093 authors, and 17,813 references; the average citation count per article is 24.94 and the annual growth rate is 7.56 %. Publication growth shows a first notable increase in 2017, a dip in 2018‑2019, and a further rise in 2020; no articles appeared between 1981‑1986 and 1988‑1990. Most studies are published in special‑education journals, with the Journal of Special Education and Remedial and Special Education being the leading venues. Bouck Ec is identified as the most influential author, and the most frequently used keyword across influential articles is “mathematics”. Keyword‑trend analysis indicates that “students”, “mathematics” and “children” dominated in 2016, “instruction” in 2017 and “learning disabilities” in 2015. Co‑occurrence analysis reveals six clusters, the largest (green) centred on “students”, “mathematics” and “children”. Collaboration networks show the top‑working authors are Nese Jft, Shanley I and Elliott Sn; the strongest author pair is Fuchs Ls and Luchs D. Among countries, the USA has the highest co‑operation, followed by the United Kingdom, and universities with the most co‑operation are University of Florida, Purdue University and Vanderbilt University. The discussion notes that inclusive‑education policies, STEM initiatives and pandemic‑related learning losses have driven recent growth, emphasizing the need for greater inclusion of teachers and families, integration of technology, and stronger international and interdisciplinary collaborations. Limitations include reliance on Web of Science data and a focus on articles only.

CannabisNB, New Brunswick’s government‑run recreational marijuana retailer, will operate 20 stores in 15 communities. Age 19, under‑19 barred, product under glass, public smoking prohibited, carry limit 30 g, home storage must be locked. Sites selected by demographics, census, liquor sales and traffic.

Rent-A-Center Inc (RCII) shares rose 3.63% to $9.99. Analysts project a 52‑week price target of $10.79 (mean of 7 opinions), with a high of $15 and low of $5; the consensus target is $10.79 per Thomson Reuters. The average brokerage recommendation (ABR) is 2.5 based on 8 firms, and the industry rank by ABR is 183 of 265. Recommendations: 3 Buy, 5 Hold, 1 Underperform, 0 Sell, 0 Outperform. Both the Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier and the Breville Barista Express are $100 off ahead of Prime Day. The Ninja model is a beginner‑friendly semiautomatic with a built‑in scale, 25‑setting grinder, cold brew and drip coffee; a reviewer praised its milk steaming and espresso grinding by weight. The Breville Barista Express is a top seller known for its price, built‑in grinder, and full‑flavored espresso; a reviewer has used it for six years with no issues.

ISDA Press Report covers multiple topics: an article on liquidity considerations when negotiating ISDA Master Agreements for smaller customers, highlighting issues like cross defaults, credit events upon merger, and termination events; a Financial Times piece on Brazil's energy crisis caused by under-investment and partial deregulation; a BNA report on banking industry opposition to proposed merchant banking capital requirements; Reuters coverage of dollar and euro swap spread movements; and Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's speech on federal debt paydown implications for the economy and financial markets; and Enron's offering of a structured weather note.

SynDoc is a framework for domain-specific Visually Rich Document Understanding that combines discriminative and generative models. It uses a synthetic data generator with OCR, multi-task inquiry generation, and quality verification; an adaptively tuned discriminative "warmer" model; adaptive instruction tuning incorporating multimodal features; and recursive inferencing for iterative refinement. The framework was evaluated on four datasets (FormNLU, CORD, Ephoie, FUNSD), showing improved zero-shot performance over state-of-the-art MLLMs by integrating warmer outputs.
U.S. adults 18‑39 memory/focus issues nearly doubled 2013‑2023; cause unknown.

JAXA launched an SS-520 rocket—the world’s smallest capable of placing a micro‑satellite in orbit—from the Uchinoura Space Centre in Kagoshima, carrying a 3‑kg University of Tokyo satellite to image Earth, after a 2017 failure, testing low‑cost micro‑sat launch for private demand.

In 2015 a Chinese national, Jizhang Lu, made multiple cash deposits totaling A$3.2 million at a Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) branch on behalf of a meat‑export company called CC&B International, despite the purchases shown on receipts being fictitious. Lu was later sentenced to two years in prison after pleading guilty to money‑laundering proceeds alleged to come from an international drug syndicate. The case is cited by financial‑intelligence agency AUSTRAC in its civil lawsuit against CBA, the largest ever of its kind in Australia. AUSTRAC claims that about A$17.7 million was deposited at CBA between February and August 2015 in connection with CC&B and that the bank failed to detect nearly 54,000 suspicious transactions, constituting “serious and systemic” breaches of anti‑money‑laundering and counter‑terrorism financing rules. CBA says it will contest the lawsuit, attributing most breaches to a coding error in new ATMs while acknowledging other serious allegations. Two CC&B employees were charged with dealing in criminal proceeds; the company’s director, Ka Chun Leung, has left the country.

The lecture discusses constructing the spacetime of a compact spherical body, focusing on static spherically symmetric metrics. It introduces Schwarzschild and isotropic coordinates, derives the Schwarzschild metric by solving the vacuum Einstein equations and matching the Newtonian limit, and presents Birkhoff's theorem, which states that the exterior vacuum of any spherically symmetric body is described by the Schwarzschild metric regardless of time variations. The lecture then considers the interior solution, defining a mass function and deriving the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equation for relativistic hydrostatic equilibrium, which governs the structure of spherically symmetric static fluid bodies in general relativity.

École Élémentaire Michaëlle Jean in Binbrook and Queensdale Elementary School in Hamilton had lead levels exceeding provincial thresholds. Over the past two years, more than 640 schools and daycares provincewide failed lead tests required by 2007 legislation. Lead is a toxic metal that particularly affects fetuses and young children, causing intellectual development issues. The number of failed tests is expected to increase as new sampling rules took effect in July. One Hamilton daycare is using bottled water while another is using filters at its camp location.

The lecture addresses administrative issues with pset 2B and mentions upcoming Thanksgiving break and lectures on BARGs and final wrap-up. It recaps the progression from interactive protocols like GKR to the Kilian-Micali succinct proof system (four messages) aiming for non-interactive proofs via Fiat-Shamir paradigm. Fiat-Shamir replaces the verifier with a hash function; soundness holds in the random oracle model but was open for the standard model. A zero-knowledge protocol for Hamiltonian cycle (three messages, "half" soundness) is recalled; its parallel repetition achieves security in the random oracle model. The main result (Canetti, Lombardi, Wichs 2019) proves this parallel-repeated protocol is sound under Fiat-Shamir in the standard model using a commitment based on public-key encryption and a hash function built with fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). The hash function encrypts a function designed (in analysis) to avoid "bad" challenges, relying on semantic and circular security of FHE. This yields non-interactive zero knowledge based on lattices and generalizes to protocols like GKR for SNARGs and batch arguments. A break is taken before discussing NIZK further.

SA58 nasal spray, a broad-spectrum anti‑COVID‑19 monoclonal antibody developed by Sinovac Life Sciences, was evaluated as post‑exposure prophylaxis (PEP) in a randomized, single‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial conducted at 21 construction sites in Beijing during an Omicron BF·7 sublineage outbreak (Nov 26–Dec 9, 2022). Healthy adult workers with exposure to a laboratory‑confirmed SARS‑CoV‑2 case within 72 hours were enrolled and randomized 3:1 to receive SA58 (5 mg/mL, 1 mg per administration) or placebo, self‑administered intranasally 5–6 times daily for up to three days. The primary efficacy endpoint was laboratory‑confirmed symptomatic COVID‑19 during the case‑monitoring period (24 h after first to 24 h after last administration). Among 1,223 participants in the full analysis set, the incidence of symptomatic COVID‑19 was 0.22 per 100 person‑days in the SA58 group versus 1.17 per 100 person‑days in the placebo group, yielding a protective efficacy of 80.82% (95% CI 52.41–92.27%). SA58 also reduced the incidence of SARS‑CoV‑2 infection (RT‑PCR positive) by 61.83% (95% CI 37.50–76.69%). No severe COVID‑19 or deaths occurred. Adverse events were mild (most commonly nasal mucosal dryness, runny nose, fever, nasal congestion, headache) and did not differ significantly between groups; no serious adverse events or adverse events of special interest were reported. The intranasal route was described as less invasive and amenable to self‑administration, potentially allowing early PEP use. Limitations included early study termination due to China’s reopening, resulting in a smaller sample than planned; participants were predominantly young, healthy workers, restricting generalizability; and concurrent infection‑control measures may have influenced outcomes. The authors conclude that SA58 shows satisfactory efficacy and safety as PEP for COVID‑19 and should be further evaluated in high‑risk populations.
