TB remained the leading infectious cause of death globally (10 million cases, 1.5 million deaths in 2019). Zambia has a TB incidence of 346 per 100 000, 2.5 times the global average, with HIV co‑infection raising the risk 15–21 times. This audit examined 74 TB‑related deaths at Kitwe Teaching Hospital (KTH) from June 2018–June 2019. Patients were ≥16 years; 30 files were excluded. Most deaths were among males (67.6%), mean age 39.2 ± 11.6 years, from high‑density residential areas (83.8%), and HIV‑positive (81.1%). Common presentations included cough (41.9%), fever (40.5%), diarrhea (29.7%) and headache (21.6%). Vital signs showed MAP fell from 81.5 ± 17.4 to 75.9 ± 19.1 mmHg and pulse rate from 112.1 ± 29.7 to 94.1 ± 23.4 bpm before death. Laboratory findings included anemia (HB < 11.5 g/dL) in 39.2%, hypoalbuminemia (12.2%), renal dysfunction (creatinine > 118 µmol/L) in 10.8%, and raised liver enzymes (ALT ≥ 40 U/L 12.2%; AST ≥ 40 U/L 18.9%). Radiographic patterns included miliary TB (6.8%), cavities (2.7%) and consolidation (2.7%). The authors conclude that TB mortality is associated with male gender, age < 50 years, HIV positivity, high‑density living and hemodynamic instability, and recommend prospective studies to identify predictors and assess malignancy contribution.

The passage describes a nanosecond pulsed electric field (nsPEF) generator for tumor electrotherapy. It includes a controller, a power supply, a pulse generator, electrodes, and sensors. The pulse generator uses a Marx‑switch stack hybrid circuit with a small number of stages (≤5) and power MOSFETs to produce high‑voltage, sub‑microsecond to microsecond pulses while maintaining low impedance and high efficiency. A feedback loop measures pulse characteristics (amplitude, width, current, voltage, temperature, energy) and adjusts power‑supply and pulse‑generator control signals so that the delivered pulses match user‑specified parameters. The system can drive various loads, including suction electrodes that draw tumors into a chamber for precise nsPEF application. The passage also outlines methods in which the controller compares measured values to desired values and modifies control signals to keep parameters within acceptable limits, enabling accurate treatment of tumors by inducing apoptosis without thermal damage.

Dengue, caused by four DENV serotypes, is a major global health problem with no direct‑acting antivirals; current vaccines (CYD‑TDV and TAK‑003) provide unbalanced protection. AT‑752 is an orally administered guanosine‑nucleotide prodrug that is metabolized to the active triphosphate AT‑9010, which inhibits the DENV NS5 RNA‑dependent RNA polymerase and shows sub‑micromolar pan‑serotype activity in vitro and efficacy in a mouse model. Pre‑clinical toxicology in rats and monkeys indicated a no‑observed‑adverse‑effect level of 1000 mg/kg/day, giving a ≥40‑fold safety margin for a 250 mg human starting dose.

A first‑in‑human Phase 1, randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled study evaluated single‑ascending doses (SAD; 250–1500 mg) and multiple‑ascending doses (MAD; 1000 mg once daily, 750 mg twice daily, 750 mg three times daily) of AT‑752 in 65 healthy subjects (41 SAD, 24 MAD). Safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics (PK) and the effect of a high‑fat meal were assessed; an ethnic cohort (South/Southeast/East Asian) examined PK sensitivity.

AT‑752 was well tolerated: no serious adverse events, no discontinuations due to adverse events, and treatment‑emergent events were mild or moderate and resolved. No clinically significant changes in laboratory values, vital signs, or ECG parameters were observed.

PK results: AT‑281 (parent) was rapidly absorbed with a short plasma half‑life (~0.5 h). Metabolites AT‑551, AT‑229, and AT‑273 showed increasing half‑lives (≈2–3 h, 12–17 h, and 15–25 h, respectively). AT‑273 serves as a surrogate marker for the intracellular active AT‑9010. Plasma exposure increased dose‑proportionally for AT‑229 and greater‑than‑proportionally for AT‑281 and AT‑551; AT‑273 exposure was slightly less than dose‑proportional. A high‑fat meal reduced AT‑281, AT‑551, and AT‑229 peak concentrations but did not markedly affect total exposure; AT‑273 exposure was slightly increased. No ethnic PK differences were detected, indicating no need for dose adjustment. Renal clearance of AT‑229 and AT‑273 exceeded eGFR, suggesting active secretion.

In MAD cohorts, AT‑281 did not accumulate; AT‑273 levels rose 25–80 % with increasing dose frequency, reaching and maintaining concentrations above the in‑vitro EC90 (0.64 µM) after the 750 mg three‑times‑daily regimen.

The study demonstrates that AT‑752 is safe and well tolerated up to 1500 mg single dose and 750 mg three times daily multiple doses, exhibits no ethnic PK sensitivity, and can be taken with or without food. These results support further clinical development of AT‑752 as a dengue antiviral.

California's energy crisis in March 2001 involved negotiations to rescue nearly bankrupt utilities. The state planned to pay at least $7 billion for PG&E's transmission lines as part of rescue deals. California signed 40 long-term contracts worth approximately $40 billion for electricity over 10 years, with prices averaging $69 per megawatt hour—well above previous rates. The two main utilities, PG&E and Edison, accumulated nearly $13-14 billion in debt from soaring wholesale costs they could not pass to consumers. The state was buying roughly one-third of the power needed for the utilities through the Department of Water Resources, funding purchases with revenue bonds. Summer forecasts predicted significant power shortages with only about 60 percent of needs met through existing contracts. Multiple solutions were proposed including price caps, conservation measures, extending daylight saving time, and building new power plants. Congressional hearings explored federal intervention while utilities faced criticism for layoffs and service cuts. Municipal utilities like SMUD resisted being included in rolling blackout plans. The state also faced an estimated $90 billion infrastructure gap beyond the energy crisis.

Two oral GLP-1 drugs, orforglipron and a higher-dose oral semaglutide, have shown promise for weight loss in clinical trials, offering potential advantages over injectable versions like easier manufacturing, distribution, and no refrigeration requirements. Participants in trials lost an average of roughly 14% and 11% body weight, respectively, with side effects similar to existing GLP-1 drugs, such as nausea and vomiting, that generally subsided over time and no liver toxicity observed. Researchers hope these pills could lower costs, improve accessibility especially for marginalized populations, and be available by 2026, pending FDA approval, though long-term safety data over five to ten years is still needed.

The case examines Nissan's response to the March 11, 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, which devastated the country's automotive industry with 80% of plants suspending production. Despite damage to six production facilities and impairment of about 50 critical suppliers, Nissan demonstrated operational resilience. The company's preparedness stemmed from its 1999 near-bankruptcy experience, which fostered a risk management culture focused on early risk identification, planning, and rapid response implementation. Nissan maintained an earthquake emergency-response plan including a Global Disaster Headquarters, regular simulation training, and business continuity planning. Following the disaster, Nissan coordinated its global response through information sharing, strategic supply allocation prioritizing high-margin products, targeted production slowdown, and empowered field decision-making. The company planned to increase localized production from 70% to 90% in the Americas by 2015 and reduce Japanese components in North American factories by 50% to mitigate future disruption risks.

Ashley Leger, a paleontologist employed by Cogstone Resource Management, monitors Los Angeles Metro Purple Line extension excavations for fossils as required by California law. Since 2014, workers have uncovered Ice‑Age remains including a rabbit jaw, mastodon tooth, camel foreleg, bison vertebrae, and horse remains. The biggest find was an intact juvenile Columbian mammoth skull discovered a year after the second phase began; after a 15‑hour excavation it was moved to the La Brea Tar Pits and Museum, with both tusks attached. It weighs a few hundred pounds, is the size of an easy chair, and is one of only about 30 mammoths recovered there. The skull was named Hayden after actress Hayden Panettiere; a monitor spotted the bone while watching her TV show. Construction crews continue work nearby while paleontologists clear finds; similar fossils have been found at other urban digs, including mammoth parts and a gray whale in San Diego and an 18th‑century boat near Boston.

The passage describes enhancing the thermoelectric performance of n-type Bi2(Te,Se)3 alloys using a simple annealing treatment. Annealing at 723 K for 100 h optimizes carrier density and mobility through cation vacancy formation caused by Te(Se) volatilization while introducing atomic-scale defects that strengthen phonon scattering, reducing lattice thermal conductivity. The Bi2Te2.6Se0.4 sample achieved a peak ZT of 1.06 at 373 K and an average ZT of 0.99 between 300–423 K, with a room-temperature carrier mobility of 295.97 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ and lattice thermal conductivity of 0.48 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. This approach decouples carrier and phonon transport, offering a practical post-synthesis method for optimizing n-type Bi2Te3-based thermoelectrics for cooling applications.

This study presents a classification and mathematical model for evaluating software accessibility, focusing on users with visual impairments. The article outlines a protocol for a systematic review that aims to identify implementation determinants (barriers and facilitators), implementation strategies, and adjunctive interventions for structural interventions targeting HIV evidence‑based interventions (EBIs) in the United States. It notes that HIV disparities are driven by social and structural determinants of health and affect key populations (MSM, Black/Latino individuals, transgender women, youth, people who inject drugs), who experience unequal access to prevention (e.g., PrEP) and treatment (e.g., ART). The review addresses three research questions: (1) what determinants, strategies, and adjunctive interventions have been reported for adoption, acceptability, feasibility, appropriateness, reach, cost, sustainability, and equitable delivery; (2) what gaps exist in the literature; and (3) how structural interventions may be differentiated from implementation strategies and adjunctive interventions. The search strategy, registered with PROSPERO, includes systematic database searches from 2000‑2024 and supplemental sources from the CDC, yielding 8,098 records. Articles will be screened using natural language processing and manual review in Covidence, applying inclusion criteria that require a U.S. focus, implementation or hybrid designs, original data, behavioral/social science methods, and a structural intervention targeting social determinants of health. Data extraction will capture study design, setting, CDC priority populations, implementation outcomes (acceptability, adoption, feasibility, etc.), and intervention type, using established taxonomies (CFIR 2.0, ERIC, TDF/COM‑B). Determinants will be coded to CFIR, implementation strategies to ERIC, and adjunctive interventions to TDF/COM‑B. Analysis will involve tabulation by framework constructs, stratification by population and setting, and NLP‑assisted thematic summarization. Findings will be disseminated through two primary papers, additional qualitative manuscripts, conference presentations, and a publicly accessible literature review dashboard. The timeline anticipates completing title/abstract review in 2024, full‑text review and extraction beginning January 2025, analysis from mid‑2025 through 2026, and dissemination through fall 2026. Funding is provided by the National Institutes of Health (R24MH134305).

This study examined relationships between mentalization, attachment, and personality disorder dimensions (Criterion A and B) in 109 participants using clinical and community samples. Mentalization was assessed using self-report (RFQ) for self-mentalizing and performance-based measures (MASC) for other-mentalizing. Self-mentalizing deficits strongly predicted both self and interpersonal functioning impairments and all five maladaptive personality traits, explaining up to 55% of variance in self-functioning. Other-mentalizing only significantly predicted interpersonal functioning. Moderation analyses showed self-mentalizing buffered the relationship between attachment anxiety and both Negative Affectivity and Detachment, while other-mentalizing buffered associations between attachment avoidance and Detachment. The findings suggest self-mentalization plays a more foundational role in personality pathology than other-mentalization, and mentalization acts as a protective factor against attachment-related vulnerabilities. Clinical implications indicate prioritizing self-mentalization in psychotherapy interventions for personality disorders, as it represents the most significant predictor. Limitations include the cross-sectional design, small sample size, and heterogeneous assessment methods. The study provides support for the importance of mentalization in understanding and treating personality disorders within the DSM-5 AMPD framework.

Mod‑Cam, the first‑light and commissioning receiver for the 6 m Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST), is a 0.9 m diameter, 1.8 m long cryogenic receiver housing a 280 GHz instrument module with over 10 000 polarization‑sensitive kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs). The module uses aluminum (Al) and titanium‑nitride (TiN) lumped‑element KIDs coupled to microwave feedlines. Thermal stability of the 100 mK detector stage was measured with the stage servo‑controlled at 100 mK, yielding an RMS temperature fluctuation ΔT_RMS = 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ K over an 8‑hour period. The thermal responsivity, RT = (df₀/f₀)/dT, was determined for 2409 Al detectors (RT,Al = 1.995 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹) and 1886 TiN detectors (RT,TiN = –6.081 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹). Combining these values, the induced fractional frequency noise and equivalent optical power fluctuation ΔP_eqv were calculated: for a typical 5 pW background, Al detectors give ΔP_eqv ≈ 0.20 fW (0.004 % of the load) and TiN detectors give ΔP_eqv ≈ 0.11 fW (0.002 % of the load). The results demonstrate that the cryogenic system achieves the required temperature stability and that thermally‑induced noise is negligible relative to the photon noise floor, validating the design for background‑limited operation.

The lecture introduces MIT's Advanced Data Structures class (6.851) and focuses on temporal data structures for time travel. It covers persistence models: partial persistence (only latest version updatable, linear order), full persistence (any version updatable, tree structure), confluent persistence (versions can be combined, DAG structure), and functional persistence (nodes never modified, only new ones created). The main result discussed is that any pointer machine data structure with constant in-degree and out-degree can be made partially or fully persistent with constant amortized overhead per update (Driscoll et al., 1989). Partial persistence can be deamortized to constant worst-case slowdown (Brodle, 1997), while full persistence deamortization remains open. Confluent persistence is more challenging; Fiat and Kaplan (2003) achieved multiplicative overhead proportional to the effective depth of the version DAG, with a matching lower bound. Under the disjoint version assumption (no shared nodes), logarithmic overhead is possible (2011). Functional data structures allow persistence automatically; examples include balanced BSTs (log n via path copying) and deques (constant concatenation). Several open problems remain, including achieving constant overhead for confluent persistence and improving the log n separation between functional and optimal data structures.

Professor Noelle Selin lecture on mercury as a global pollutant and the Minamata Convention. Mercury emitted to the atmosphere lasts about half a year, mixing globally and depositing in ecosystems where it converts to methyl mercury, a neurotoxin that bioaccumulates through food chains, affecting IQ and causing cardiovascular impacts. The Minamata Convention, signed in 2013, is the first new global environmental treaty in over a decade and addresses the entire life cycle of mercury, including products, processes, artisanal and small-scale gold mining, and emissions. The lecture discusses why mercury requires international cooperation, the history of negotiations from a 2002 scientific assessment to the treaty, the roles of the US, EU, China, and developing countries, and how domestic regulations in the US and EU often lead international standards. It also covers how the treaty uses positive and negative lists to regulate mercury in products such as thermometers, batteries, lighting, and dental amalgam, and addresses the informal artisanal gold mining sector, where mercury is used to amalgamate gold, burned off, and releases mercury into the environment and food chain. The lecture highlights the complexity of international negotiations, the influence of science and stakeholder input, the capacity challenges of smaller countries, and the treaty's political and signaling importance, noting that without it mercury levels would likely increase, and that compliance mechanisms rely on shaming, capacity building, and financial assistance rather than enforcement.

A research team from the NeuroPiano Institute and Sony Computer Science Laboratories used a high‑precision non‑contact sensor system (Hackkey) to record all 88 piano keys at 1,000 fps (1 ms temporal and 0.01 mm spatial resolution) while 20 internationally renowned pianists performed with the intent of producing diverse timbres (e.g., bright/dark, light/heavy). A psychophysical experiment with 40 participants—including pianists and non‑musicians—showed that listeners consistently perceived the pianists’ intended timbres regardless of musical training, with pianists detecting differences more sensitively. Linear mixed‑effects analysis identified a limited set of key‑movement features (e.g., acceleration during escapement and hand‑synchronization deviation) that causally contributed to timbre differences. This provides the first scientific evidence that pianists can alter piano timbre through touch, resolving a question discussed since the early 20th century. The findings support evidence‑based music education, skill‑transfer, rehabilitation, and human‑interface design, and were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The work was conducted under JST Strategic Basic Research Program (CREST) and the Moonshot Research & Development Program.

Ambassador and adapter are single‑node container patterns. An ambassador isolates an application from service discovery or external routing logic; the application always connects to localhost while the ambassador introspects the environment and brokers connections. This is shown for service brokering (finding MySQL in cloud or private environments) and for experimentation, where an ambassador redirects a fraction of traffic to a beta version. The experimentation example uses nginx with IP‑based hashing and a weight parameter to send, for example, 10 % of requests to the experiment while returning production responses to users.

The adapter pattern translates heterogeneous application interfaces into a uniform interface expected by monitoring, logging, or health‑checking systems. An adapter container runs alongside an application container and adapts it to a standard format without modifying the original image. Examples include a Prometheus exporter adapting Redis to the Prometheus metrics API, Fluentd normalizing Redis slow‑query logs or Apache Storm logs, and a MySQL health‑check adapter that runs a representative query and exposes an HTTP health endpoint. Adapters enable reuse, independent versioning, and dedicated resources for each function.

Replicated load‑balanced stateless services provide redundancy and scale by running identical replicas behind a load balancer. A readiness probe tells the load balancer when a replica is ready to serve traffic. Session‑tracked services ensure that requests from the same client are routed to the same replica, typically by hashing source and destination IP addresses; application‑level session tracking (e.g., cookies) is used for external clients. The replicated pattern can be extended with a caching layer (e.g., Varnish) deployed as a sidecar or as a separate replicated tier to improve performance and reduce backend load. Caching introduces considerations for session affinity and hit‑rate optimization. The edge layer can also perform rate‑limiting and SSL termination; nginx is used for HTTPS termination, forwarding traffic to the cache and then to the application tier.

Sharded services split data or requests across multiple independent shards, each serving a subset of the overall workload. A shard router (root) distributes requests based on a sharding function—commonly a hash of a request attribute such as the path or a composite key (country code plus path). Deterministic and uniform hash functions ensure even load distribution. When the number of shards changes, a consistent‑hashing function limits the remapping of keys to only K / new_shard_count of the total, minimizing cache‑miss spikes. Shards can be replicated for fault tolerance; replicated shards allow rolling upgrades and protect against single‑node failures. Hot‑sharding dynamically moves or replicates shards to balance uneven traffic. Ambassadors (e.g., twemproxy/nutcracker) can be deployed with each application pod or as a shared routing service; trade‑offs include added latency versus reduced per‑pod complexity.

The scatter/gather pattern parallelizes computation by sending a request to multiple leaf nodes, each processing a portion of the work and returning a partial result that the root combines. A common use case is distributed document search, where term indexes are looked up on separate leaves and the root computes the intersection of results. Scatter/gather can be combined with leaf sharding so each leaf holds a disjoint data partition; the root aggregates the union of matches. The pattern improves latency for embarrassingly parallel workloads but suffers from the straggler problem: overall latency is dictated by the slowest leaf, and with many leaves the 99th‑percentile latency degrades sharply. To improve reliability and scale, each leaf shard is replicated, enabling load balancing across healthy replicas and safe rolling upgrades.

Function‑as‑a‑service (FaaS) or serverless computing executes small, stateless functions in response to events. Benefits include a short distance from code to running service, automatic scaling, and automatic restarts. Challenges arise from strong decoupling: monitoring and debugging become harder, long‑running background processing is poorly suited, and functions that require large in‑memory data incur startup latency. The cost model based on per‑request pricing can become expensive as traffic grows; alternative pricing (e.g., virtual‑machine‑based) may become more economical. The decorator pattern leverages FaaS to transform HTTP requests or responses, adding defaults or other modifications without coupling the transformation to the main service. An example uses Kubeless on Kubernetes to inject default values into incoming JSON payloads before forwarding to an API.

Overall, the passage describes a hierarchy of patterns for containerized and distributed systems: single‑node ambassador and adapter patterns, replicated and sharded multi‑node service patterns, scatter/gather for parallel computation, and event‑driven FaaS for lightweight, scalable components. Deployments typically use Kubernetes constructs such as Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, and Secrets to realize these patterns.

KaviKrishna, a nonprofit organization in Assam, India, has developed a community-based participatory action research (PAR) approach to tuberculosis (TB) control that integrates Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) with modern molecular and cellular biology methods. TB remains a major global health threat, with over 10 million active cases in 2022 and an estimated one-third of the global population harboring dormant Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB). Current TB control programs in India suffer from generalized strategies, inadequate monitoring of drug-resistant TB evolution, and limited community participation, leading to variable outcomes. To address these limitations, KaviKrishna established three units: KaviKrishna Telemedicine Care (KTC) for patient screening and monitoring, KaviKrishna Laboratory (KKL) for biomedical research, and KaviKrishna Centre of Indian Knowledge System (K-IKS) for integrating traditional practices. Central to their approach is the Indigenous Kamarupa Information Network (IKIN), a social network based on temple complexes (Namghars) in the Sualkuchi-Hajo region of Kamrup district, Assam, which serves as a platform for community engagement, TB awareness, and patient tracing. Methodologically, the project involves longitudinal TB patient follow-up in rural populations, including the Idu-Mishmi tribe in Arunachal Pradesh. Clinical samples (sputum, blood, bone marrow) are collected by trained volunteers and transported to KKL for analysis. Laboratory procedures include sputum decontamination, MTB culture on Lowenstein-Jenson medium, DNA extraction via phenol-chloroform, and species confirmation by PCR targeting the hsp65 gene to distinguish MTB from non-tuberculous mycobacteria. Drug susceptibility testing is performed using the proportion method, and MDR detection employs MASPCR for rpoB mutations. Stem cell analysis utilizes immunomagnetic sorting of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) to study MTB dormancy and reactivation. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) is conducted to identify circulating MTB lineages (Beijing, CAS/Delhi) and mutations associated with drug resistance and compensatory evolution (rpoB, rpoC). In-vivo studies using a streptomycin-dependent MTB strain (m18b) in mice demonstrate that dormant MTB can reside in MSCs and reactivate upon viral infection-induced oxidative stress. Since 2010, over 300 pulmonary TB cases have been screened and 210 patients followed up via the IKIN network. Student volunteers and local philosophers contribute to patient engagement, awareness campaigns, and graduate training programs. Collaborative research with international institutions supports capacity building and data sharing (NCBI accession PRJNA1054003). The findings suggest that dormant MTB may persist in bone marrow stem cell niches, and that stem cell reprogramming during stress could mediate reactivation and MDR evolution. The CBPR and IKS-based approach reportedly reduced stigma, improved case detection, and facilitated continuous monitoring. The authors propose that this model could be scalable for TB control in rural India and other developing regions.

The device features a multiSPI digital interface supporting various data transfer protocols between the device and host controller. Host-to-device connection topologies include single-device configurations (standard SPI or all multiSPI options) and multiple-device daisy-chain topology where devices share CONVST/CS and SCLK, with SDO-0 of each device connected to SDI of the next.

The device has three functional states: RESET (triggered by RST pin low, supporting application reset or power-on reset), ACQ (acquires analog input, supports low-power NAP mode), and CONV (conversion using internal clock, ignores further CONVST/CS transitions until complete). Transitions between states are controlled by CONVST/CS and RST signals.

A data transfer frame begins at the falling edge of CONVST/CS and ends at its rising edge. Optimal frames contain 32 SCLK cycles; shorter frames are treated as NOP for writes but valid for reads, while longer frames use the last 32 bits as command. Input command words must be 32 bits and include CLEAR_HWORD, WRITE, READ, READ_HWORD, and SET_HWORD operations. Output data word contains 16-bit conversion result with optional flags (device address, input range, AVDD alarm, input alarm, parity).

Data transfer protocols include four legacy SPI-compatible modes (SPI-00-S to SPI-11-S) selectable via SDI_MODE bits, with optional dual SDO-x (two-bit bus width) and source-synchronous (SRC) protocols using internal or external clock. The device has nine configuration registers (DEVICE_ID_REG, RST_PWRCTL_REG, SDI_CTL_REG, SDO_CTL_REG, DATAOUT_CTL_REG, RANGE_SEL_REG, ALARM_REG, ALARM_H_TH_REG, ALARM_L_TH_REG) controlling reset, protocol selection, data output, input range, and alarm thresholds.

In application, the device is a 16-bit 8-channel DAQ for industrial analog inputs, featuring programmable alarm thresholds with hysteresis and low-power modes (NAP and power-down). Power supply recommendations include decoupling AVDD and DVDD with capacitors, and PCB layout should separate analog and digital sections.

OSCAR is a one‑shot multi‑label causal discovery method for high‑dimensional event sequences. It uses two Transformer‑based density estimators (CarFormer for next events, EPredictor for next labels) to model sequences as sequential Bayesian networks. For each label Y_j it recovers the Markov Boundary (MB) by testing conditional mutual information (CMI) with a data‑driven threshold θ_j = μ + kσ. Under assumptions of causal sufficiency, bounded lagged effects and temporal precedence, CMI testing identifies the MB. The approach is fully parallelised, making its time complexity agnostic to the number of events |X| or labels |Y|, and provides a causal indicator C∈[−1,1] quantifying event influence. Evaluated on a vehicle dataset with 29 100 event types and 474 labels, OSCAR retrieved MBs with 55 % precision, 31 % recall, 40 % F1 in ~12 min, while existing local structure learning algorithms exceeded a 3‑day limit. The method delivers interpretable, deployment‑ready causal graphs for large‑scale sequential data.

The lecture discusses iterative methods for solving linear systems with large sparse matrices, where direct elimination is prohibitively expensive. A preconditioner (matrix P) is used to accelerate convergence. Key preconditioners include Jacobi (diagonal), Gauss-Seidel (triangular), SOR, and incomplete LU. Convergence depends on the spectral radius of the iteration matrix M = I - P^{-1}A. For a model problem with a tridiagonal matrix having 2 on the diagonal and -1 off-diagonal, the eigenvalues of Jacobi’s iteration matrix are 1 - cos(theta), with spectral radius approximately 1 - O(1/n^2), requiring O(n^2) iterations to reduce error. Gauss-Seidel squares the Jacobi eigenvalues, improving convergence but remaining O(n^2). Weighted Jacobi can optimize the spectral radius via a relaxation factor but still struggles with low-frequency error components. Multigrid methods are introduced as the solution to effectively handle these low-frequency components.

The study investigated preservice teachers’ views on a special‑education course delivered via distance education, focusing on course content, experienced problems, and possible solutions. A qualitative phenomenology design was used. Participants were 45 university students enrolled in a private university during the 2022‑2023 academic year; all were taking the special‑education course for the first time and participated voluntarily. Data were collected with a researcher‑developed semi‑structured interview form, which was validated by three experts and tested in a pilot session.

Demographic analysis showed that 64.4 % of participants were female and the majority were aged 22‑25 years. Regarding modality preference, 58 % stated they would prefer traditional face‑to‑face instruction, while 42 % indicated a desire for distance education. Reasons for preferring traditional teaching included perceived effectiveness, quality of instruction, and comprehensibility; distance education was valued for its flexibility in time and place but was criticized for technical problems and distraction.

On attendance requirements, 46.6 % reported that participation should be mandatory to ensure learning, and 22.2 % considered it necessary for success. Others argued that attendance need not be compulsory, citing the possibility of learning from recorded videos, lack of digital devices, and the responsibility of self‑directed learners.

When asked whether they would recommend distance education, 57.7 % gave a positive recommendation, highlighting benefits such as educational effectiveness, home‑environment comfort, and individualised learning. The remaining respondents expressed negative views, pointing to learning difficulties and systemic problems; some recommended its use only in compulsory situations.

Participants identified substantial technical and material shortcomings. 66.6 % emphasized the need for system improvement, 13.3 % called for better internet infrastructure, 11.1 % reported insufficient technical support, 6.6 % requested free internet access, and 2.2 % noted a lack of digital learning materials.

Overall, most participants were satisfied with distance education but highlighted internet connectivity and technical issues as major obstacles, stressed the importance of class participation, and recommended enhancements to the platform, infrastructure, and support services. The authors suggest further quantitative research with larger samples and additional courses to broaden the findings.

Turing’s new display pipeline adds native HDR processing and tone mapping per ITU‑R BT.2100. Enhanced NVENC encodes H.265 (HEVC) 8K at 30 fps with up to 25 % bit‑rate savings for HEVC and 15 % for H.264; NVDEC decodes HEVC 4:4:4 8/10/12‑bit and VP9 10/12‑bit HDR. Video‑encoding quality exceeds Pascal and software encoders, enabling 4K streaming.

VR headset connectivity is simplified by hardware USB‑Type‑C and the VirtualLink standard, which delivers power, display and data over a single USB‑C connector using four HBR3 DisplayPort lanes plus SuperSpeed USB 3, allowing VR on small‑form‑factor devices.

Turing replaces the old SLI bridge with second‑generation NVLink: TU102 provides two x8 links (50 GB/s per direction, 100 GB/s bidirectional) and TU104 one x8 link (25 GB/s per direction). Only two‑way SLI is supported.

Ray tracing is accelerated by dedicated RT Cores in each SM, handling BVH traversal and ray‑triangle intersection. Turing achieves >10 Giga Rays/s, roughly ten times faster than Pascal’s software‑based ray tracing.

Turing implements a hybrid rendering model that combines rasterization for primary visibility with ray tracing for reflections, refractions, shadows and ambient occlusion. Denoising reduces the number of rays needed, and BVH structures efficiently prune primitives.

NGX, powered by Turing Tensor Cores, provides AI‑based image enhancements: Deep Learning Super‑Sampling (DLSS) infers 64×‑SS quality from fewer samples, giving ~2× performance over Pascal; InPainting synthesizes content to fill gaps; AI Slow‑Mo inserts interpolated frames; AI Super Rez upscales 2×/4×/8× with higher PSNR than bicubic.

Mesh Shading introduces Task and Mesh shader stages, enabling a cooperative‑thread model, eliminating CPU draw‑call bottlenecks and supporting level‑of‑detail control, allowing hundreds of thousands of objects to be rendered in real time.

Variable Rate Shading (VRS) lets developers set shading rate per 16×16 pixel region, enabling Content Adaptive Shading, Motion Adaptive Shading and Foveated Rendering, and can increase rate for MSAA.

Texture Space Shading (TSS) decouples shading from screen‑space, storing results in a texture and sampling later, providing temporal stability and LOD‑based rate control.

Multi‑View Rendering (MVR) expands Pascal’s Simultaneous Multi‑Projection to up to four views per pass, supporting efficient stereo rendering, canted HMD panels and single‑pass cascaded shadow maps.

Turing adds Tier 3 bindless resource binding and allows multiple resource types in a single heap (Tier 2).

VR features include VirtualLink, MVR, VRS‑based foveated rendering and ray‑traced VRWorks Audio accelerated by RT Cores.

TU102 contains 13.6 B transistors, 3072 CUDA cores, 368 Tensor cores, 48 RT cores and two NVLink x8 links; TU104 has six GPCs, 48 SMs, 3072 CUDA cores, 48 RT cores, 368 Tensor cores and one NVLink x8 link (used in GeForce RTX 2080, Quadro RTX 5000, Tesla T4). TU106 has three GPCs, 36 SMs, 2304 CUDA cores, 36 RT cores, 288 Tensor cores and no NVLink (used in GeForce RTX 2070).

RTX‑OPS is a workload‑based metric combining Tensor (20 % usage), FP32 (80 %), RT (40 %) and INT32 (28 %) operations; RTX 2080 Ti achieves 78 RTX‑OPS.

Ray tracing casts rays from the camera through each pixel, intersecting primitives; BVH trees reduce primitive tests, and denoising improves image quality.

Turing enables ray‑traced shadows with correct contact hardening, ambient occlusion and reflections, eliminating limitations of screen‑space and cubemap techniques, as demonstrated in Battlefield V and Shadow of the Tomb Raider.

Overall, Turing integrates new display, encoding, VR, NVLink, ray‑tracing, AI‑enhanced rendering and advanced shading techniques to deliver real‑time hybrid rendering with greatly improved performance and visual realism.

Reversal Day refers to a day when a stock or market index changes direction after an extended up‑ or down‑trend. The two main types are Bullish Reversal Day (price rises after a downtrend, often closing above the prior day’s high) and Bearish Reversal Day (price falls after an uptrend, often closing below the prior day’s low). Reversals can be triggered by changes in market sentiment, economic conditions (interest rates, GDP, unemployment), company‑specific news, or technical factors such as overbought/oversold conditions. Indicators for spotting reversals include a change in price direction, high trading volume, moving averages, RSI, Bollinger Bands, support/resistance breaks, and divergences. Backtesting bullish reversal rules in gold (GLD) showed positive average gains (e.g., 2.02% when exiting after 24 days) with a good profit factor, whereas bearish reversal rules produced losses due to gold’s upward drift. The authors conclude that the reversal day concept has merit and advise traders to monitor trend, volume, technical indicators, and news to identify potential market turnarounds.

Cocoa futures are standardized exchange‑traded contracts to buy or sell 10 metric tons of cocoa at a pre‑agreed price on a specified future date. They trade on ICE Futures US (symbol CC) and on CME Globex (symbol CJ). Settlement is financial on CME and by physical delivery on ICE; the block minimum is 100 contracts. Contract months are March, May, July, September and December, and on ICE trading terminates the day before the last notice day (10 business days before the last business day of the delivery month).

Prices are quoted in US $ per metric ton; the minimum price fluctuation is $1/t (= $10/contract) and one contract therefore represents about $24,840 at the November 2022 price of $2,484/t. Historical data show an all‑time high of $5,379/t (July 1977) and a low of $707/t (December 2000); the highest since 1979 was $3,775/t (March 2011). Cocoa prices are driven by supply‑demand factors and exhibit seasonal patterns, performing better in summer and weaker in spring and fall.

The primary risks are leverage (e.g., 20× leverage means a 1% adverse move can wipe out an account) and low liquidity, which can cause wide spreads and difficulty exiting positions. Trading is done through a futures broker or via CFDs, and an ETF that tracks cocoa futures is the iPath Bloomberg Cocoa Subindex Total Return ETN (NIB).

Trading hours: ICE runs 9:15 AM–6:30 PM London time with pre‑ and post‑market sessions; CME Globex operates 6:00 PM–5:00 PM ET Sunday‑Friday with a 60‑minute break. Strategies typically combine technical and fundamental analysis; a back‑tested example showed a 74 % win rate and a profit factor of 2.3 over 96 trades.

Health savings accounts (HSAs) allow tax‑free contributions, investment growth, and tax‑free withdrawals for qualified medical expenses; they are only available to people enrolled in high‑deductible health plans (HDHPs). Behavioral economists note that people tend to avoid losses; a study showed that framing incentives as an upfront payment with per‑failure deductions produced higher goal adherence than a simple payment. Experts propose automatic HSA enrollment (opt‑out) similar to 401(k)s, which would increase participation but require government cost. Research shows HSA enrollees use less overall health care, yet prescription drug costs fall while emergency‑room visits rise, especially for lower‑income families, and health outcomes remain unclear. Price opacity for medical services makes it difficult to plan savings, unlike buying a house where costs are visible. Financial therapists say HSAs are useful only for those who can afford daily expenses plus an emergency fund, and that people need realistic expectations about their future health and finances.

Burnout is classified by the World Health Organization as an occupational phenomenon with a global prevalence of about 20 % and higher rates reported in sub‑Saharan Africa and Asia, especially among health‑care staff; prison officers are identified as an underserved workforce at increased risk. A quantitative cross‑sectional study was conducted at the Nsawam Medium Security Prison (NMSP) in Ghana’s Eastern Region to assess the prevalence of burnout, perceived causes, work‑environment factors, and coping strategies among prison officers (POs).

Participants were recruited using proportionate stratified random sampling. Of the 266 officers targeted, 245 questionnaires were returned and 243 were analysed (92 % response rate). Burnout was measured with the adapted 22‑item Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey (MBI‑HSS), which evaluates three dimensions: emotional exhaustion (EE), depersonalization (DP) and personal accomplishment (PA). Burnout was defined as high EE (≥ 27) or high DP (≥ 10) combined with low PA (≤ 33).

Overall burnout prevalence was 9 %. Mean scores were EE = 24.9 ± 12.5, DP = 10.6 ± 7.4, PA = 26.3 ± 10.7. By category: low EE = 25.9 %, moderate EE = 32.1 %, high EE = 42.0 %; low DP = 35.4 %, moderate DP = 32.1 %, high DP = 32.5 %; low PA = 68.7 %, moderate PA = 17.3 %, high PA = 14.0 %.

Perceived causes of burnout were irregular shifts (71.6 %), heavy workload (49.0 %), lack of training and development opportunities (47.7 %), lack of autonomy (35.8 %), and poor social status (28.0 %). Regarding the prison work environment, 56.4 % disagreed that the culture was positive and supportive; 59.7 % said their efforts were not recognized; 62.1 % reported penalties outweighed rewards. Conversely, 59.3 % felt part of a team, 74.1 % took pride in their work, and 71.2 % felt in control of their duties.

Shift allocation was significantly associated with EE (p = 0.010), with main‑shift officers showing the highest EE. Rank was significantly associated with DP (p = 0.010), junior officers having higher DP than senior officers. Logistic regression identified sex and education as significant predictors of burnout: female officers had higher odds of burnout (adjusted odds ratio = 0.31, 95 % CI 0.13–0.75, p = 0.009) and postgraduate‑educated officers had higher odds compared with diploma/certificate holders (adjusted odds ratio = 0.11, 95 % CI 0.02–0.69, p = 0.019).

The most common coping strategy was talking to colleagues (62.5 %), followed by looking forward to off‑duty days (60.1 %), talking to family (54.3 %), keeping thoughts to oneself (42.1 %), and alcohol use (29.2 %). Overall, officers used predominantly positive, socially‑oriented coping mechanisms.

The study concludes that irregular shifts, heavy workload and limited training/development opportunities are key contributors to burnout among POs. Officers experience high EE and DP with low PA; night‑shift officers show higher EE and junior officers higher DP. Implementing measures that address shift patterns, workload management and professional development could reduce burnout. The findings highlight the importance of improving the psychosocial work environment and supporting existing positive coping practices among prison officers in Ghana.

The holder in American football secures the ball for the kicker on extra points and field goals. After the snap, he catches the ball, quickly places it at the exact angle and spot the kicker prefers, and turns the laces away. Key skills are soft hands, rapid placement, consistency, and the ability to rotate the football. Any body type can serve as holder; many teams use punters, backup quarterbacks, receivers, or other players. Holders often have other responsibilities such as punting or catching. In rare fake field goal situations, the holder may throw, run, or flip the ball. Though no official stats exist for holders, their precise execution is essential, as a botched hold can determine the outcome of a game.

This memorandum provides a periodic update on international electric power sector restructuring from June-November 2000. Governments worldwide are opening generation markets to foreign investors, even where full privatization isn't planned, as they lack funds to meet growing power demands. State-owned utilities continue unbundling, and competition is being introduced at wholesale and retail levels across regions.

In Europe, the EU Directive is driving competition, with countries like France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the UK advancing liberalization through mergers, alliances, and market openings. Central and Eastern European countries are attracting capital through privatization while EU accession candidates implement reforms. Asian economies are recovering from the 1997 crisis, with governments restarting unbundling plans, though IPPs face ongoing PPA and guarantee issues. Latin American countries, affected by currency fluctuations and drought, have restarted privatizations at a slower pace. In Africa and the Middle East, governments are increasingly opening sectors to foreign investment, with regional transmission links being developed. The report includes detailed country-by-country updates and references attached exhibits.

Industrial enterprises are under pressure from geopolitical uncertainty, rising energy and raw‑material costs, supply‑chain disruptions, skilled‑labour shortages and sustainability demands, while digitalization accelerates fundamental change in manufacturing. An IDC white paper, based on a December 2021 telephone survey of 200 IT and departmental decision‑makers from large manufacturers in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, examined the use of IT‑based simulation, modelling and data analytics. Simulation and modelling replicate real processes, are supported by CAD/CAM/CAE tools and 3‑D displays (used by about two‑thirds of firms) and are increasingly linked to digital twins. The top business goal is increased innovation (named by three‑quarters of respondents), followed by faster product development, cost reduction and better decision‑making; 57 % also cite quality improvement and defect avoidance. Deployment already covers product development, production planning and quality management, with plans to reach roughly 90 % in two years. Key obstacles are data silos and the lack of a unified data foundation; respondents stress the need for a single source of truth across the value chain. About 64 % intend to invest in modern simulation, modelling and high‑performance analytics. Technologies such as virtual prototyping, IoT‑driven digital twins and AI/ML‑based analysis are expanding, and digital twins can cut development time by up to 50 % while reducing raw‑material use and CO₂ emissions. High‑performance computing (HPC) is regarded as a game changer by 81 % of all respondents and by 96 % of those already using HPC; 27 % already employ professional HPC and 39 % are piloting it. This document is a specification update for the AMD Geode CS5535 Companion Device (Silicon Revision A3) listing hardware errata. Key issues include PIC and UART failures caused by automatic clock gating remaining active during high interrupt levels or empty buffers, and PRD table alignment issues in ATAC and ACC DMA controllers where prefetching misaligned tables causes data errors. Additional bugs affect PCI signal timing (tVAL violation), ACPI S3 wake event inputs (GPIO wakeups failing), RTC CMOS RAM access (read after write errors), USB controller register stability, SMBus NEGACK status bit clearing, and GPIO atomic writes after suspend. Most resolutions recommend disabling specific automatic features (clock gating), ensuring data structure alignment (DWORD or 8-byte PRD alignment), or using software workarounds.

Uber’s nationwide panic button lets riders call 911 directly from the app, shows real‑time location, and in pilot cities (Denver, Charleston, Chattanooga, Naples, Tri‑Cities, Louisville, soon Nashville) automatically sends location and vehicle details to dispatchers.

After a loss, the speaker noted his team generated few scoring chances, fell behind early after a brief letdown following the opponent’s first goal, and despite playing evenly for most of the game, struggled on the powerplay. He emphasized the need to improve defensive coverage, generate more offense, and produce better overall performance.

In spring 1953 the United States sees a chance for a just peace after the hope of 1945 faded into fear. It describes two divergent paths: the U.S. and free nations follow principles of non‑hostility, cooperation, respect for sovereignty, and reliance on honest understanding, aiming to control arms, heal war‑torn societies, and promote prosperity. The Soviet Union instead seeks security through force and power superiority, producing an arms race, mutual suspicion and an ever‑present risk of atomic war. Free nations remain ready to welcome genuine evidence of peaceful intent. The U.S. calls on the new Soviet leadership to demonstrate sincerity by concrete deeds: an honorable armistice in Korea (immediate cease‑fire, free elections, an end to attacks on Indochina and Malaya), verifiable disarmament measures (limits on military forces and strategic materials, international control of atomic energy, prohibition of other weapons of mass destruction, with United Nations inspection), and the redirection of resources saved from disarmament toward global development—roads, schools, hospitals, and health. It stresses that only actions, not words, can prove peaceful purpose.

This study examines how digital customer experience and electronic word of mouth affect sustainable supply chain performance through brand image and supply chain image in Indonesian ICT companies. Data was collected from 315 employees involved in supply chain activities across randomly selected clusters, and analyzed using partial least square structural equation modeling. Seven hypotheses were proposed and all were supported. Digital customer experience through e-commerce and electronic word of mouth positively influence brand image, which in turn positively affects supply chain image, ultimately improving sustainable supply chain performance. The variance explained for sustainable supply chain performance was 82.3%, indicating the model effectively explains the relationships between these variables in the Indonesian ICT context.

This passage describes a hybrid gas turbine electric engine system with a motor/generator connected to the low speed spool. The engine is designed for peak efficiency during takeoff and climb but can be undersized relative to thrust requirements in those modes. During descent, the engine core is turned off or maintained at minimum temperature to prevent thermal cycling. The fan is allowed to windmill, driving the motor to generate electricity. Aircraft systems are powered by stored energy and/or windmill-generated electricity, with an electric compressor replacing conventional compressor bleed air. This configuration reduces fuel consumption and emissions during descent while maintaining aircraft system operation.

Interest rates are just below 5% on a 30‑year fixed mortgage, prompting borrowers to seek ways to boost borrowing power. Lenders evaluate the total new mortgage payment plus recurring minimum payments relative to monthly pre‑tax income; a ratio over 50% creates difficulty. Techniques to improve borrowing ability include paying off consumer debt to lower the debt‑to‑income ratio, adding a co‑signer who shares equal liability (removable only by refinance or sale), switching loan programs such as Freddie Mac to Fannie Mae or conventional to FHA, increasing the down‑payment, and changing employment before application while remaining in the same field. These options are informational and should be verified for each individual’s circumstances.

Singapore's special education evolved from a dual system under the social welfare sector pre-2004 to an inclusive approach after PM Lee Hsien Loong's 2004 vision. The government introduced Enabling Masterplans (2007-2030), ratified the UNCRPD in 2013, and increased mainstream enrollment from 2,500 (2005) to 35,500 (80% in mainstream schools). Teacher preparation expanded through programs like the 1984 Certificate in Special Education, the 1991 Diploma in Special Education, 2005 Special Needs Officers scheme (renamed SENOs in 2022), and the 2005 Certificate in Special Needs Support for mainstream teachers. Current developments include a 2020 professional development roadmap and tiered support systems. Challenges remain: special schools operate under social service agencies rather than the Ministry of Education, special educators receive lower salaries and lack undergraduate degree pathways, and options for students with higher support needs in mainstream settings are limited. Singapore's education system now shifts toward holistic development and inclusion through the "Learn for Life" movement.

The lecture discusses Homework 7 on drug diffusion from a patch into flow, requiring solutions using both COMSOL and finite volume methods. The problem involves sharp concentration gradients due to low diffusivity and high Peclet number. Professor Green explains finite volume discretization using control volumes and flux calculations, emphasizing the importance of mesh refinement and convergence verification. Numerical solver options are discussed, including fsolve, backslash, and BiCGSTAB for sparse matrices. The CFL condition (Δt·velocity/Δx < 1) is presented as necessary for stable time-dependent PDE solutions. The lecture then transitions to probability, contrasting deterministic undergraduate problems with real-world measurement fluctuations. Basic probability concepts are introduced through coin flip examples, including joint probabilities, conditional probabilities, and Bayes' theorem. Probability distributions are explained as continuous functions requiring integration over intervals, with discussion of probability density functions versus cumulative distribution functions.

D‑branes become dynamical because fluctuations of the open strings that end on them are described by massless scalar fields whose expectation values encode the brane’s position and shape. The mass (or tension) of a D‑brane is defined as the vacuum energy of all open‑string excitations living on it; this equals the tension (mass per unit volume) multiplied by the brane’s volume. In the weak‑coupling limit the tension scales as \(T_{p}\sim 1/g_{s}\,\alpha'^{-(p+1)/2}\), so the brane mass is proportional to \(1/g_{s}\).

The vacuum energy can be computed by summing world‑sheet vacuum diagrams—disks, annuli, etc.—in the Euclidean path integral. Each diagram is weighted by \(g_{s}^{-\chi}\) where the Euler number for a surface with \(h\) handles and \(b\) boundaries is \(\chi=2-2h-b\). A disk (one boundary, no handles) contributes \(g_{s}^{-1}\), an annulus (two boundaries) contributes \(g_{s}^{0}\), and higher topologies are suppressed for \(g_{s}\ll1\).

A cylinder with one boundary on each of two D‑branes represents the exchange of a massless closed string (the graviton) between them. This diagram has \(\chi=0\) and therefore contributes \(g_{s}^{0}\), confirming the \(1/g_{s}\) scaling of the brane tension. The same cylinder can be viewed as a one‑loop open‑string diagram, illustrating channel duality: the same process can be interpreted as either a tree‑level closed‑string exchange or an open‑string loop.

At low energy the massless modes on a D‑brane are a U(1) gauge field \(A_{\alpha}\) and scalar fields \(\phi^{a}\) describing transverse directions. Their effective action is the Dirac–Born–Infeld action, which combines the gauge kinetic term and the geometric (volume) term into a single square‑root form. When the field strength vanishes, the action reduces to the relativistic volume element of the embedded brane, describing the motion of a p‑dimensional object.

When \(n\) D‑branes coincide, open strings can end on any pair of branes, giving four string types (11, 22, 12, 21). Each excitation becomes a matrix‑valued field with two indices; string‑joining interactions naturally produce matrix multiplication, resulting in a U(\(n\)) symmetry. On the world‑volume this symmetry is global, but in spacetime it appears as a gauge symmetry, and the low‑energy effective theory is non‑abelian Yang–Mills. The Yang–Mills coupling satisfies \(g_{\text{YM}}^{2}\propto g_{s}\).

Separating the branes gives a vacuum expectation value to the transverse scalars, breaking the U(\(n\)) gauge symmetry (a Higgs mechanism). Formerly massless modes acquire a mass proportional to the separation, and the gauge group decomposes into a product of U(\(n_{i}\)) factors for each stack of coincident branes.

The open‑string coupling \(g_{0}\) is related to the closed‑string coupling by \(g_{0}^{2}=g_{s}\), as shown by counting boundaries in open‑string vacuum diagrams. Finally, translation invariance of the underlying Minkowski space forces the scalars \(\phi^{a}\) to be Goldstone bosons of the spontaneously broken translational symmetry.

The MSPM0 C-Series microcontrollers (MSPM0C1105, MSPM0C1106) include a Low-Frequency Sub System (LFSS) combining RTC with prescalar extension and IWDT, clocked by 32kHz LFCLK. The shared VREF module provides 1.4V/2.5V internal references for ADC/COMP up to 515ksps, with external reference support. The COMP peripheral compares two voltage inputs, supports 6 blanking sources from TIMx, wakeup from low power modes, and includes an 8-bit reference DAC. Security features include flexible firewalls and CRC-16 with custom polynomial. Communication peripherals include three UART instances (with LIN mode, DMA FIFOs, loopback), I2C (7/10-bit addressing, SMBus 3.0, up to 1Mbps), and SPI (up to 16Mbits/s, controller/peripheral modes, DMA FIFOs). Watchdog timers include IWDT (25-bit counter, 8 periods) and WWDT (8 periods, interval timer mode). RTC_B provides timekeeping with alarms, calibration for crystal offset/temperature drift, and periodic interrupts. Timers include general-purpose (TIMGx, 16-bit, QEI support) and advanced (TIMAx, 16-bit, clock doubler, PWM with dead band, fault handling) variants. Debug support uses ARM Serial Wire Debug (SWD) via DEBUGSS with mailbox communication and security features. Device factory constants in a memory-mapped FACTORY region provide read-only capability and trim data.

The Hickory Tussock Moth caterpillar, white and fluffy with black chain‑like markings and long hairs, grows to 4.5 cm and lives in trees from July to September. Its hairs are linked to a poison gland; touch can cause rash, swelling, burning, headache, nausea or allergic reaction. Wash the area, apply calamine lotion, and seek medical help for severe symptoms. Not a serious health hazard but more common.

Options trading in META is a derivatives strategy that gives investors the right to buy (call) or sell (put) an asset at a preset price on or before expiration. Traders can access options on Facebook/META, other stocks, indices, commodities and currencies, with various strikes and expirations. To start, open a trading account with a $100 minimum deposit; brokers may require higher amounts. Leverage up to 1:100 is available, amplifying both gains and losses. Margin requirements follow those for single‑stock options and depend on leverage and asset type. Orders are placed by selecting the underlying asset, option type, expiration date, strike price and number of contracts; one contract is the minimum size, and multiple contracts can be bought in a single order. Risk‑management tools include stop‑loss, take‑profit and trailing‑stop orders. Chart types (line, bar, candlestick, Renko) and technical indicators (moving averages, Bollinger Bands, MACD) aid analysis. The options chain is accessed via the “Options” tab; watch lists are created in the “Watch List” tab. Common strategies include buying calls/puts, writing covered or naked calls/puts, and using spreads, straddles or strangles. META charges no commissions, but brokers may charge fees; additional costs include financing charges, slippage and inactivity fees. Educational resources such as webinars, tutorials, video courses and a demo account help traders learn. Options carry high risk due to leverage and speculation, so investors should only risk funds they can afford to lose. Backtesting of options strategies is difficult because of multiple strikes and expirations.

The classical mean reversion strategy for the S&P 500 uses Internal Bar Strength and RSI to generate trading signals. Performance is analyzed using win rates, drawdowns, and annual returns. Inverting the parameters changes the strategy's outcomes, as shown by an equity curve.

The note traces the historical evolution of the term “unskilled” in the United States and its implications for workers and wages. In 1917 Alba Edwards formalized a six‑group occupational classification in which the first three groups were reserved for work where “mental force” dominated (professionals, proprietors, clerks) and “skill” was not applied to them. “Skill” was reserved for jobs requiring “muscular force.” The three remaining groups were labeled “skilled,” “semi‑skilled,” and “unskilled.” Unskilled occupations were defined as those requiring no special training, judgment, or manual dexterity, supplying mainly muscular strength for coarse, heavy work. The group included farm laborers, factory and building‑construction laborers, other laborers, and the servant classes. In 1930 roughly 28 % of the workforce (14 million people) were employed in these unskilled categories; African Americans were disproportionately represented (75 % of employed Black men and women versus 20 % of native‑born white and 30 % of foreign‑born white workers).

During the 20th century the meaning of “unskilled” shifted. By the 21st century government agencies and economists measured skill primarily by education and experience requirements or by job‑content analysis (routine vs. non‑routine tasks). A 2020 Social Security Administration definition described “unskilled work” as duties learned quickly with little judgment. In 2018 more than half of the U.S. labor force held jobs typically requiring a high‑school diploma or less, earning a median annual wage of $33,473. The fastest‑growing occupations through 2029—home‑health/personal‑care aides and fast‑food workers—remained low‑paid (median annual pay $25,280 and $22,740 respectively).

Three major sectors accounted for most unskilled labor: (1) farm labor, historically reliant on enslaved Africans, then sharecropping, convict leasing, and low‑wage immigrant workers; (2) factory labor, which expanded with industrialization, the assembly line, and later automation, leading to a 67 % decline in manufacturing employment between 1965 and 2020; and (3) service occupations (retail, fast food, home‑health, childcare, and gig‑platform work) that grew as household tasks were mechanized and consumer spending shifted to away‑from‑home food and services. Gig work (rideshare, delivery, micro‑task platforms) emerged in the 2000s, often paying $2–$3 per hour and using algorithmic management.

Government regulation (the Fair Labor Standards Act and the National Labor Relations Act) initially excluded agriculture, domestic work, tipped workers, and independent contractors from basic protections, leaving many unskilled workers without a minimum‑wage guarantee or the right to unionize. Union membership peaked at 34.8 % in 1954 and fell to 6.2 % by 2020; however, strikes and advocacy (e.g., the 1968 Memphis sanitation workers’ strike, the Coalition of Immokalee Workers, the National Domestic Workers Alliance) secured wage gains and new protections in several states. Some employers, such as Henry Ford’s $5‑per‑day wage in 1914 and companies practicing the “Good Jobs Strategy” (Costco, QuikTrip, In‑N‑Out), demonstrated that higher pay and job design could improve productivity and reduce turnover.

During the COVID‑19 pandemic, roughly 70 % of essential workers were in unskilled occupations, concentrated in healthcare, food production, and transportation. Their median hourly wage was about $13, and many lacked hazard pay or adequate protective equipment, underscoring the essential yet low‑paid nature of these jobs. The note concludes that the future of work will hinge on job quality rather than simply job quantity, highlighting the persistent tension between the essential role of unskilled labor and its historically low status and compensation.

The Nuclear Medicine market grew from $3500 million in 2013 to $4200 million in 2016 at a 6.27% annual growth rate and is projected to reach $5890 million by 2021. Eric Hirsch, founding CEO of EdReports, will step down at the end of the school year while the board searches for a new leader. Hirsch began as a state policy analyst and led EdReports from its 2014 launch, using an independent, Consumer‑Reports style review of instructional materials. Over 1,100 reviews have been completed, and many states and districts treat EdReports as a primary authority on curriculum decisions. The organization recently expanded to pre‑K materials and revised its scoring system to emphasize phonics, fluency and phonemic awareness, responding to criticism that reviews were slow to reflect reading‑science reforms. Alternative review services have emerged, but EdReports sees them as partners rather than competitors. Future leadership must address the role of artificial intelligence in curriculum and help teachers connect primary materials with intervention resources. Research shows many districts adopt materials without piloting them, and curriculum, teacher training and assessment can be misaligned.

The Gann Fan is a technical analysis tool developed by W.D. Gann, consisting of nine diagonal lines drawn from significant highs or lows, with the main angle at 45 degrees (the 1:1 line representing equal time and price movements). It is used to identify potential support and resistance levels based on the theory that prices move in predictable geometric patterns. Traders use the Gann Fan to analyze price movements, confirm trends, and determine entry and exit points. Additional angles include 2:1, 3:1, 4:1, 8:1, and their reciprocals. Unlike the Fibonacci fan, which relies on Fibonacci ratios, the Gann Fan is based on price-time relationships. The tool is not always accurate due to random price movements, and backtesting is recommended. Risk management techniques such as stop-loss orders and position sizing are advised when using this tool.

Cover 1 is a man‑free defense that assigns every receiver to a defender in man coverage while a free safety patrols the deep middle; a linebacker or strong safety may act as the low‑hole player, dropping to cover short‑intermediate routes over the middle. Defenses use cover 1 to stop the run, pressure the quarterback and force offenses to throw deep. Strong‑armed quarterbacks and elite wide receivers can still exploit the scheme by winning on the perimeter away from safety help. Offensive strategies to beat cover 1 focus on attacking the outside, using pick plays, double moves and routes that get receivers the ball while moving. Pick plays create natural collisions between defenders; double moves sell short routes then go deep (e.g., sluggo, stutter). Routes such as deep crossers, wheel routes and out routes help receivers gather the ball in space and gain yards after the catch. The passage provides five example plays: Ohio State’s bubble‑go, Oklahoma’s slot‑fade, Georgia’s double‑move out‑up, Oklahoma’s “Jerry Rice motion” sprint‑to‑flat, and Georgia’s scissors‑snag‑wheel combination in the red zone.

Christine Milligan was surprised when hospital staff asked her to “revoke” her daughter Cassidey Ouellete’s organ‑donation decision, even though Cassidey had signed a donor card when she received her licence at 16. Cassidey died in a car accident near Peterborough, Ont., a day before her 20th birthday, after being declared brain dead. Ontario’s Trillium Gift of Life Network allows families to override a registered donor’s wishes if the deceased later expressed regret; this happened in about 10 % of cases in 2016, down from 21 % in 2015. The agency says families are often exhausted and may need time before proceeding with donation. Trillium encourages people to discuss their donation intentions with relatives. Christine’s brother, former MPP Robert Milligan, introduced a private‑member’s bill in 2012 that would limit revocation to the donor alone and would automatically register all Ontario residents as organ donors (presumed consent) with an opt‑out option; the bill stalled when the legislature was prorogued. Trillium CEO Ronnie Gavsie says research shows no evidence that presumed consent raises donor numbers, and a 2015 poll found two‑thirds of Ontarians prefer an opt‑in system. Christine Milligan now campaigns to have the bill re‑introduced and named after her daughter.

S&P Global Platts will launch new low-sulphur marine fuel price assessments on June 1, 2017, at several Asian ports. The assessments, covering fuels with maximum 0.1 percent sulphur content, respond to growing demand and expected tighter global sulphur limits. Singapore's low-sulphur marine gasoil sales grew nearly six-fold to 1.14 million tonnes in 2016.

The passage describes three credit‑card offers reviewed by Motley Fool Money. The Wells Fargo Active Cash Card offers unlimited 2 % cash‑back on purchases, a $200 bonus after $500 spent in the first three months, a 0 % intro APR on purchases and qualifying balance transfers for 12 months (then 18.99 %–28.99 % variable), no annual fee, and up to $600 cell‑phone protection with a $25 deductible. All three cards require a Good/Excellent credit score (670–850) and approval is not guaranteed. Motley Fool Money notes that some offers appear because the site receives compensation from partners, that editorial opinions are independent, and that the service rates products for everyday finance decisions.

The passage describes the United States’ effort to correct South American misunderstandings about the Monroe Doctrine, noting that Secretary of State Root’s address at the Rio conference clarified that the US seeks only peace, respects the sovereignty and equal rights of all American republics, and aims for mutual prosperity. The speech was warmly received, praised by Argentine foreign minister Drago, and accompanied by symbolic gestures in Buenos Aires and Brazil naming a building after Monroe.
