A rogue planet named Cha 1170‑7626, 600 light‑years away in Chamaeleon constellation, was observed accreting gas and dust at 6 billion metric tons per second—fastest growth rate recorded for any planet. In late June through August its accretion rate surged to eightfold, heating its surface and surrounding disk and producing water vapor. Event mirrors rare growth bursts seen in young stars, suggesting star‑like formation. Data from 2016 indicate binge episodes. NeuroAdapter is an end-to-end brain decoding framework that conditions latent diffusion models directly on fMRI data, bypassing intermediate embedding spaces used in traditional two-stage pipelines. The method uses parcel-wise linear mapping to transform brain activity into token embeddings, integrated via cross-attention modules into a frozen Stable Diffusion model. A stochastic token dropout strategy and min-SNR loss weighting are employed during training. The approach achieves competitive performance on visual reconstruction, particularly for high-level semantic metrics, and introduces the Image-Brain BI-directional (IBBI) framework for interpretability, enabling analysis of how brain parcels contribute to and shape image generation across diffusion timesteps. Experiments on NSD, NSD-Imagery, and Deeprecon datasets demonstrate comparable or superior results to existing methods without relying on external embedding spaces.

Theresa May will ask her Cabinet at Chequers on Friday to back a “softest possible Brexit”. The plan includes the UK continuing to accept EU rules on product standards for goods and agriculture, allowing free movement of goods, while ending freedom of movement for people but offering EU citizens easier entry. The UK would collect EU import tariffs, enabling it to keep free movement of goods and sign independent trade deals. In an original proceeding under C.A.R. 21, the Colorado Supreme Court held that the petitioners (Erin Bond, a child injured when she fell from a YMCA‑owned truck, and her family) waived the psychologist‑patient privilege by claiming damages for mental suffering and psychiatric expenses in their negligence suit against YMCA. The Court found that the trial court abused its discretion by denying a protective order without balancing the petitioners’ confidentiality interest in their therapy notes against YMCA’s need for evidence to contest the mental‑damage claims. The decision emphasized the strong public‑policy protection for therapist‑patient communications and noted Dr. Vary’s affidavit establishing that disclosure would cause embarrassment, oppression, and undermine treatment. The rule was made absolute and the case remanded for the trial court to apply the proper balancing test under C.R.C.P. 26(c) and consider appropriate protective measures.

AOL Instant Messenger will shut down Dec 15, ending a service that began in 1997 and was the leading U.S. instant‑messaging app before texting, with usage declining as cell‑phone messaging and social media grew.

Earth’s total solar eclipses result from a coincidence: the Moon is about 400 times smaller than the Sun but also about 400 times closer, so it can fully cover the Sun. Mercury, Venus, Mars, and gas giants lack the necessary conditions. The Moon drifts outward roughly 1.5 inches per year; about 600 million years from now it will be too far for total eclipses.

Systems and methods for managing resources for virtual desktop instances in a cloud computing environment are described. A computing resource instance manager monitors client connections to and disconnections from virtual desktop instances and applies resource management policies to determine when to shut down underlying computing resource instances after disconnection. Storage volumes remain attached to the desktop instance data but are unmounted from the computing resource when shut down, and are reattached when the client reconnects. The service provider may develop predictive models based on historical usage patterns to anticipate connection times and optimize resource shutdown and restart timing. Policies may be specified by customer IT administrators or end users, or default policies may be applied. Detection of disconnection may occur through explicit disconnection signals or through monitoring communication channel activity for patterns indicating inactivity. The systems operate within provider networks that implement hardware virtualization, overlay networks using IP tunneling, and mapping services.

Sansa c200 is a portable media player powered by a rechargeable lithium‑ion battery installed in a compartment on the back of the device. A Hold Switch on the side locks all buttons to prevent accidental operation, and a Record button on the front starts voice or FM‑radio recording after a 2‑second press.  

The player connects to a computer via USB 2.0 and appears as a removable drive (“Sansa c200”). It supports two connection modes: MTP (default, works with Windows Media Player 10) and MSC (mass‑storage class). In MTP mode, MP3, WMA, and WAV files can be dragged to the Media folder; other file types go to the Data folder where they will not appear on the player. In MSC mode any file can be dragged to the root directory. Photos are transferred using the Sansa Media Converter (installed from the supplied CD); supported image formats are JPEG, TIFF, PNG, BMP, and GIF. Files can be deleted via the operating system’s file browser, and the player should be safely removed using the MTP icon or the Safely Remove Hardware icon on the taskbar.  

Power is turned on or off with the Power/Menu button; navigation buttons browse menus, play music, and control playback. Music can be set to repeat, shuffle, or use one of five equalizer presets (Normal, Rock, Jazz, Classic, Pop) plus a custom EQ. Songs can be added to the GoList and later cleared via the Playback settings.  

Photo mode displays stored images; a slideshow can be configured for random order, looping, and slide duration. FM radio provides auto‑scan, preset storage, and recording of broadcasts. Voice recording uses the built‑in microphone and is controlled with the Record button.  

Settings include backlight timer, display contrast, auto power‑off, USB mode selection (AutoDetect or MSC), and a factory‑reset option. The manual includes a FAQ covering file copying, supported audio formats, DRM issues, firmware updates, CD ripping, non‑supported file conversion, podcasts, and missing ID3‑tag information.  

Technical support is available at 1‑866‑726‑3475 or through the SanDisk website. The device carries a one‑year limited warranty, is not transferable, and excludes third‑party software; proof of purchase may be required. The End‑User License Agreement disclaims all warranties, limits liability, and states that the software is for use only on a single computer and may not be exported in violation of U.S. regulations.  

Disposal should follow local waste‑authority guidelines; the device must not be placed with unsorted household waste.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education is a rapidly emerging field with both benefits and challenges. Key implementation strategies include defining clear objectives, investing in infrastructure, providing faculty training, starting with pilot projects, ensuring ethical use, promoting personalized learning, leveraging predictive analytics, collaborating with EdTech providers, monitoring impact, and encouraging student involvement. Benefits include personalized learning experiences, immersive technologies, improved student engagement, intelligent tutoring systems, enhanced administrative efficiency, cost-effective education, data-driven decision-making, and increased accessibility. Limitations and challenges include high implementation costs, faculty resistance, ethical concerns about algorithmic bias, data privacy risks, technology dependence, loss of human interaction, cheating risks, and potential teacher job displacement. Responsible integration requires ethical frameworks, data privacy compliance, bias mitigation, human oversight, transparency, accessibility, and continuous evaluation. The future of AI in education promises personalized learning environments, automated administrative tasks, and immersive technologies, but success depends on thoughtful policy-making, continuous educator training, and inclusive design while addressing ethical considerations and ensuring equitable access.

The Put-Call ratio is a sentiment indicator measuring put option open interest against call option open interest on a daily basis. High readings signal fear while low readings indicate complacency. Extreme readings are sometimes used as contrarian signals, suggesting market bottoms when panic is high. The ratio can be calculated by dividing traded put options by traded call options. Backtests indicate the Put-Call ratio is inferior to other sentiment indicators like the VIX, with the author's testing showing unimpressive trading performance metrics. The ratio is available on most trading platforms and websites.

AI-based image encoding and decoding using deep neural networks (DNNs) involves AI down-scaling an original image via a first DNN before conventional encoding, transmitting AI data about the down-scaling alongside encoded image data, and at the decoder, optionally performing AI up-scaling via a second DNN based on that AI data to reconstruct a higher-resolution image. If the first image was not AI down-scaled or the second DNN is unavailable, the decoder outputs the directly decoded image, possibly with legacy or display-side up-scaling. The first and second DNNs are jointly trained based on quality loss, with multiple DNN setting options corresponding to different up-scaling targets. AI data includes resolution differences, codec types, bitrates, and encoding parameters to determine up-scaling and DNN settings.

During the lecture the instructor reviews the analogy between the large‑N expansion of gauge theories and string scattering amplitudes: both have a topological expansion in powers of 1/N, with single‑trace operators corresponding to string states and Feynman diagrams interpreted as discretizations of worldsheet surfaces. He explains why directly matching a Yang–Mills theory to a string theory is difficult: the string action is unknown, and only at strong coupling do highly complicated Feynman diagrams approximate smooth surfaces, a regime that is not tractable. Simpler examples such as matrix integrals and matrix quantum mechanics illustrate the idea and show that the correspondence works in low dimensions.

The lecturer then discusses extensions that include quark fields, which introduce boundaries on the surfaces and open strings. He points out that ordinary string theory in four‑dimensional Minkowski space is inconsistent; consistency requires 26 (pure) or 10 (superstring) dimensions. To describe a large‑N gauge theory one therefore needs extra dimensions. Imposing the gauge theory’s spacetime symmetries forces the metric to factor as a(z) ημν dx^μdx^ν, with the extra coordinate z. If the gauge theory is scale invariant, the function must be R/z, giving a space that is Anti‑de Sitter (AdS) in one higher dimension.

The lecturer reviews the historical development: ‘t Hooft’s large‑N insight, the 1974 realization that string theory contains gravity, Wilson’s lattice QCD, the late‑1980s matrix‑model work, ‘t Hooft’s holographic principle, Polchinski’s D‑branes, and Maldacena’s 1997 conjecture linking a conformal gauge theory to string theory on AdS, later clarified by Witten as an explicit realization of holography.

Finally, the Polyakov (or Nambu‑Goto) action for a string is introduced; its re‑writing shows that quantizing a string is equivalent to quantizing two‑dimensional gravity coupled to D scalar fields. The lecture concludes with a plan to study closed‑ and open‑string spectra and the physics of D‑branes to derive the gauge‑gravity duality.

The invention describes methods and systems for driving light sources in a near‑eye display by adjusting luminance according to the user’s eye gaze. A display controller determines a maximum luminance location based on the field of view of the user’s eye, typically the center of the field of view or the region of the fovea, using eye‑tracking. Light sources closer to this location are driven to higher luminance for a given input display value, while sources farther away receive lower luminance. The display can be partitioned into zones, each with its own relationship between input values and luminance; peripheral zones have smaller luminance ranges than a central zone. Light sources may be, for example, organic light‑emitting diodes (OLEDs), active‑matrix OLEDs, or micro‑LEDs. By reducing luminance in peripheral zones where human visual sensitivity is low, power consumption can be lowered (e.g., reductions of about 5–40 %) with minimal impact on perceived image quality. The controller can include a composition engine, a timing controller, and drivers to generate a luminance map and individually drive each source. Instructions for performing the method are stored on a non‑transitory machine‑readable storage medium.

The PGA848 has a linear operating input range within 3V of either supply and maintains common-mode rejection. It is typically used to drive a 16-bit, 1MSPS SAR ADC (ADS8860), accepting single-ended or differential inputs. The circuit uses ±15V for the input stage and 5.3V for the output stage, with the REF6250 as the voltage reference. The PGA output is referenced to a midscale voltage generated by a precision voltage divider and buffered by an OPA192 op amp configured with dual feedback for stability. Three filters are employed: an input EMI/RFI filter, a feedback filter using CFB with the PGA’s internal resistors (nominal cutoff 318kHz), and a charge reservoir filter at the ADC inputs. The nominal -3dB bandwidth is 318kHz, with -0.1dB flatness to 41kHz. Power supplies should be ±15V nominal, with outputs clamped to input-stage levels; voltages above 40V damage the device. Layout guidelines emphasize symmetrical input paths, bypass capacitors, trace separation, and minimizing leakage and thermal effects. Simulation tools like TINA-TI and PSpice are available for design verification. Support resources include TI E2E forums and documentation update notifications.

In mild Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients aged 50-74 years with CSF biomarker-confirmed diagnosis, APOE4 carriers (n=33) with the BCHE-K variant (n=11) had a mean age-at-diagnosis 6.4 years earlier than BCHE-K noncarriers (n=22), with similar findings for age-at-baseline. No significant effect of BCHE-K was observed in APOE4 noncarriers (n=12). APOE4 carriers with BCHE-K showed slightly higher amyloid and tau accumulations compared to those without BCHE-K, despite being over 6 years younger at baseline. APOE4 homozygotes with BCHE-K exhibited the highest amyloid pathology, lowest tau and neurodegenerative pathology, and lowest glial activation markers (YKL-40). The APOE4/BCHE-K combination was associated with a limbic-amnestic phenotype. Multiple regression analyses indicated amyloid accumulation associated with APOE4 carrier status, larger brain ventricle volume, less synaptic injury (Ng), and less tau (p-tau181). Tau pathophysiology was associated with higher neuroaxonal damage (NfL), more synaptic injury (Ng), and higher glial activation (YKL-40). The findings suggest that BCHE-K modifies AD prognosis in APOE4 carriers under 75 years, with functional glial activation potentially mediating the effects of both APOE4 and BCHE-K on early AD phenotype. The study was cross-sectional with a small sample size (n=45) and limited to patients under 75 years.

The lecture discusses FIR filter structures, including direct form and transposed forms derived from the difference equation, and notes that parallel forms do not apply to FIR systems due to lack of poles. It emphasizes exploiting linear phase symmetry in FIR systems to reduce multiplications by half, showing how symmetry allows combining symmetric coefficients into a single summation with N/2 unique coefficients while retaining the same number of delays. The lecture then introduces a frequency sampling structure derived by expressing the system function in terms of discrete Fourier transform coefficients, resulting in a cascade of a term (1 – z⁻ᴺ) with a parallel combination of first-order poles at roots of unity that cancel zeros, and discusses its advantages in sparse frequency sample scenarios and shared hardware for filter banks. Finally, it addresses practical implementation issues such as finite register length effects, specifically parameter quantization sensitivity, showing that direct form structures are most sensitive to coefficient quantization while cascade and parallel forms are less sensitive, and that second-order sections can be implemented in direct form or coupled form, with each imposing different grid constraints on achievable pole locations due to quantization of coefficients like r² and 2r cos θ versus r cos θ and r sin θ.

The ultralight backpacking movement originated from a 1994 Backpacker magazine article by Mark Jenkins that described shedding most of his gear on a long trip across Europe and Africa, an idea that resonated with many hikers. In that article Jenkins defined the approach as carrying only what you are wearing, a down jacket, and a few items, and the article is widely credited with launching the ultralight movement. Today ultralight is commonly defined by base weight (all gear excluding what is worn and consumables) of 10 lb or less; “super‑ultralight” targets 5 lb or less, while “lightweight” stays at 15 lb or less. The author, who has kept a base weight of 10 lb for over a decade, suggests that the most effective way to lighten a pack is to bring less, evaluating each item by whether it is needed for warmth, comfort, food, or safety. He recommends ruthlessly cutting unnecessary items such as extra stuff sacks, and focusing on the three heaviest components: the backpack, sleep system, and shelter. He advises starting with the shelter and sleep system, then choosing a pack that fits, and trying “cowboy camping” (sleeping under a tarp or open sky) to learn personal comfort needs. He notes that quilts can replace sleeping bags for many conditions, and that flexibility—such as not eating where you camp—reduces food‑odor issues and makes breaking camp easier. The author also mentions that a tick‑borne Lyme disease infection has made him more selective about tarp camping locations. Ultimately, ultralight backpacking is described as a philosophy of reducing everything that interferes with enjoying the outdoors, achieved through continual experimentation and by shedding items that are not truly needed.

This study uses US vital statistics from 2014–2020 to examine excess mortality for cancer and other chronic conditions during the COVID-19 pandemic. The researchers modeled weekly excess mortality for 10 conditions, including six cancer types (all-cause, colorectal, breast, pancreatic, lung, hematological), at national and state levels (New York, California, Texas), using both underlying cause (UC) and multiple cause (MC) mortality data.

The study identified three COVID-19 waves in 2020: spring (April), summer (July), and winter (through December). Nationally, UC cancer deaths declined in spring 2020, while MC cancer deaths increased across all waves, resulting in 12,000 excess cancer deaths in 2020—a 2% elevation over baseline. Hematological cancer showed the largest relative increase (5%, 3100 deaths), while pancreatic and lung cancer showed no excess. In contrast, diabetes and Alzheimer’s experienced substantial excess mortality correlated with COVID-19 waves, with MC elevations of 39% and 31%, respectively.

State-level analysis revealed that New York’s intense spring wave was associated with an 8% rise in MC cancer mortality, varying by cancer type (pancreatic and lung ≤2%; colorectal, hematological, breast 8–15%). California and Texas showed less pronounced changes, within ±6%, not statistically significant.

The researchers developed a demographic model to project excess mortality under the null hypothesis that cancer is not a COVID-19 risk factor, considering age, population size, and baseline risk. Under the null, the model projected a 7% elevation for all cancers, 1–2% for highly fatal cancers (pancreatic, lung), and 6–14% for less fatal cancers (colorectal, breast). Observed elevations were consistent with these projections. For diabetes and Alzheimer’s, model projections (28% and 46%, respectively) aligned with observed excess mortality (39% and 31%).

The study concludes that cancer mortality showed at most a modest elevation during the pandemic, likely due to competing risks from cancer itself rather than immunosuppression. Hematological cancers showed more pronounced increases, consistent with previous cohort studies. The findings emphasize the importance of using multiple cause-of-death records to account for coding changes and competing risks.

The United States experienced an unusually early, severe RSV surge in autumn 2022. Researchers sequenced RSV genomes from 105 diagnostic specimens from Massachusetts patients, generating 54 near-complete and 23 partial genomes. Genomic analysis revealed the surge was driven by multiple lineages of RSV-A (91%) and RSV-B (9%), belonging to genotypes GA2.3.5 and GB5.0.5a respectively. RSV-A genomes came from at least 10 distinct lineages with common ancestors dating to 2014-2017, while RSV-B lineages traced to 2019. Some lineages were shared with Washington state samples. The genetic divergence was consistent with normal evolutionary rates, unlike the accelerated evolution seen in SARS-CoV-2 variants. The findings indicate the surge was caused by multiple pre-existing viral lineages rather than a single highly transmissible variant, and non-viral factors including pandemic-related immunity changes warrant investigation.

M. de Martens notes that no government may search or arrest foreign ships on the high seas except when piracy is suspected. Russian authorities seized the whaling bark Cape Horn Pigeon 125 mi from the nearest Russian land and 84 mi from Japanese territory while she was on the high seas engaged in lawful whaling. A Russian commission later acknowledged that the vessel had not entered Russian waters, found no ground for confiscation, returned her and admitted the seizure was a misunderstanding, yet the indemnity offered was inadequate. The owners claimed $45,000 for loss of the voyage, calculating the loss by averaging past catches, and cited precedent allowing recovery of lost profits from similar unlawful detentions.

Environmental education is a process aimed at fostering environmental awareness, values, and responsible behavior to address environmental crises such as global warming and natural disasters. The need for global cooperation emerged after the 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm and was reinforced by the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, which adopted Agenda 21 emphasizing sustainable development. In 1975, UNEP and UNESCO launched the International Environmental Education Workshop in Belgrade, outlining objectives including awareness, knowledge, attitude, skills, participation, and evaluation ability. The Belgrade Charter established guiding principles: consideration of natural and human-made environments, continuous lifelong learning, interdisciplinary approach, emphasis on participation, global perspective with regional consideration, focus on current and future situations, and consideration of developmental impacts.

Environmental education components include developing sensitivity and awareness, providing understanding of environmental fundamentals, cultivating supportive values, developing problem-solving skills, encouraging active involvement, and instilling evaluation abilities. The environment encompasses natural and man-made elements, classified into biotic and abiotic components. Environmental knowledge is categorized into natural resources, social environment, environmental technology, and waste/pollution. Environmental properties include uniqueness, interdependence, dependence on other elements, integration into ecosystems, chain reactions, varied resilience and vulnerability, and temporal changes.

Environmental education is implemented through formal and non-formal education, emphasizing integrated learning and outdoor experiences to promote behavioral changes. Sustainable development is defined as meeting present needs without compromising future generations, with principles of balance in economic growth, fair distribution, and quality of life, along with improvement, meeting present needs without harming future potential, and starting with local efforts. Guidelines for sustainable environmental development include reducing energy consumption, minimizing waste, conserving natural resources and environmental quality, and utilizing clean technologies. Successful examples include the Collaborative Learning Project for Community Development and the Huai Sai development project in Thailand, demonstrating the role of environmental education in achieving sustainable environmental, economic, and social outcomes. Natural capital accounting projects in Thailand, in cooperation with UNEP, also support sustainable landscapes.

The passage emphasizes interdisciplinary music education's role in enhancing cognitive, linguistic, and emotional skills through STEAM integration. A case study of a music department student identifies gaps in basic music education and recommends practical courses (e.g., Orff, Kodály), drama, material design, and preparatory classes to improve teaching. The authors advocate for educational policies that support interdisciplinary music education for comprehensive student development.

Russia has cultivated ties with Western far‑right activists to spread a narrative of Western chaos and present itself as an alternative global power. A new book by Anton Shekhovtsov, “Tango Noir: Russia and the Western Far Right,” traces this strategy from Soviet‑era efforts to a 2008 watershed when Moscow launched a full‑scale information war after the Georgia conflict. Shekhovtsov identifies three main tactics: “nudge propaganda” using fringe activists, “narrative laundering” that disguises fake news as mainstream discourse, and selective sourcing that amplifies far‑right themes such as the 2013 Stockholm riots. The book describes a network of “operators” under Putin’s inner court—sympathetic foreign groups, far‑right activists, think‑tanks, loyal oligarchs, diplomatic missions and United Russia officials—that have tried to influence politics in Austria, Italy, France and Germany. Shekhovtsov concludes that Kremlin interventions have largely failed, especially in France, but have made inroads in Germany. He warns that emerging evidence of Russian paramilitary support to European far‑right groups could become a more potent weapon of disruption.

The first procedure is a native, stackless assembler routine that initializes the processor and cache system to create a pre‑memory stack region, dividing it among cores, mapping it to global address space and setting the MTRRs. It checks protected mode, configures SS:ESP appropriately, creates a UEFI_SEC_PEI_HAND_OFF structure in the stack frame, and returns status codes (SUCCESS, WARNING with stack re‑entry, or FATAL for unknown family); registers EAX, ECX, EDX, EDI, ESI (and DS, ES in 16‑bit mode) are destroyed while EBX is preserved for use as a return address. The second procedure returns the processor and cache system to a non‑stack‑enabled state after main memory is available, disabling CAR mode without changing MCRR settings, and must be run on all cores.

SATA SSDs can require more power than some computers provide; if unrecognized, disconnect other USB devices. New research from Yale's Budget Lab and the Brookings Institution found no evidence of "discernible disruption" to U.S. jobs since ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, with most occupational changes already underway before widespread AI adoption. Entry-level workers face challenges, though researchers attribute this to broader labor market dynamics rather than direct AI impact. The passage describes SOS defensive tactics for low post disruptions, including Post Front, Base Go, Go Top, Go Wing, Hold, and YoYo. Each tactic involves specific defender rotations to double team, front, or deny post passes, with right and left side variations.

The Gold Overnight Trading Strategy involves buying gold futures or gold miners ETF at the market close and selling at the next day's open to capture overnight price changes caused by global factors like interest rates and political events. Backtests show small average daily gains for assets like GDX (0.12%) and GLD (0.04%), but these are often not tradable due to low profitability. The strategy carries high risk and volatility due to influences like economic conditions and market sentiment. After two decades of backtesting, the authors conclude gold and commodities are harder to trade than stocks, with strategies tending to break down over time. They offer trading plans, risk management steps, and psychological guidance, and mention having strategies in incubation with varying performance. The authors also note that overnight edges are more consistent in stock markets.

The Office of the Historian at the U.S. Department of State released an ebook edition of the “Foreign Relations of the United States” (FRUS) series, offering a portable, searchable version with bookmarking and note‑taking features that works offline. The edition strives to preserve the content of the printed volumes; page numbers are represented using document numbers for citation, and older volumes append bracketed document numbers to page references. The passage also lists Senate Executive Documents concerning U.S.–Hawaiian relations, including President Benjamin Harrison’s February 1893 messages transmitting a draft 1854 treaty with Hawaii and a report on U.S.–Hawaiian correspondence from 1820 to 1893.

Enron made a $35 million purchase in March from an entity run by officer Michael Kopper, part of complex transactions that kept hundreds of millions in debt off its balance sheet. The company faces a formal SEC investigation into its dealings with partnerships run by former CFO Andrew Fastow. Short seller James Chanos detected red flags in Enron's filings and began shorting the stock. Enron's auditor Arthur Andersen may face scrutiny over the clarity of financial disclosures. The AFL-CIO is calling for corporate governance reforms. Enron may need to sell assets including power plants and pipelines to restore investor confidence. The company's Indian unit (Dabhol Power) has served an asset transfer notice to Maharashtra State Electricity Board due to payment defaults. Enron is also in talks to sell stakes in assets including a Korean gas joint venture.

The minister of foreign affairs told Major Wodehouse that the finance minister’s action was approved by the cabinet and that claimants were remanded to the courts. In June 1881 Blaine instructed the U.S. minister that the Hawaiian government could not grant privileges reserved for the United States under the 1875 treaty without violating it, and warned the U.S. would support Hawaii against undue external pressure. In December 1881 Blaine declared that the United States viewed the Hawaiian Islands as key to American Pacific dominance and would seek an “American solution” if benevolent neutrality proved impossible. In 1883 the United States declined to join a Hawaiian protest against British and French annexations in Polynesia, noting its distant interest. The reciprocity treaty was renewed by a convention signed 6 December 1884, extending the agreement for seven years and granting the United States exclusive rights to develop Pearl River Harbor as a coaling and repair station (Article II). Ratification was delayed until November 1887 because of opposition from American sugar interests and Britain. In 1884 a cable project proposed by the Australasian Cable Syndicate received a Hawaiian subsidy, but landing rights and British protests over exclusive privileges were raised. A U.S. cable survey was conducted by the USS Albatross in 1891‑92.

Rapid response to a stroke can prevent lasting damage. The American Stroke Association recommends the FAST acronym: Face drooping (ask to smile), Arm weakness (inability to raise both arms), Speech difficulty (slurred or unclear speech), and Time to call 911. Even if symptoms are brief, dial emergency services and note symptom onset. A simpler alternative mnemonic is S.T.R., representing Smile, Talk, and Raise both arms. Sources: American Stroke Association, Berkeley Wellness.

Sara Zaske's daughter Sophia, who rarely wanted a phone in Germany, asked for one after moving to California where classmates owned smartphones. Germany has about 51% of children 6‑13 with a mobile phone, while Europe has 46% of children 9‑16 owning a smartphone; restrictions vary by country. United States has 45% of children 10‑12 with a smartphone, 22% get a service plan around age 10, and 42% of children 8 have a tablet. South Korea shows highest ownership: 72% of children 11‑12 own a smartphone and spend 5.4 hours daily. Ownership rises in Taiwan (45% at 11 years to 71% at 15) and grew Malawi, Ghana and South Africa between 2007‑2014 (Malawi 0.6%→8.4%; Ghana 2.4%→16.2%; South Africa 21%→50.8%). In Australia median age for first phone is 8 years. American Academy of Pediatrics says no universally correct age and recommends limiting children under 5 to one hour of screen time daily, avoiding digital media for infants except video‑chatting, monitoring content, and keeping screens out of bedtime and meals.

A film about a Frenchman who froze his wife notes that freezing solidifies tissues. A London teenager was cryopreserved after grandparents paid £37,000 to send her body to the US. Celebrities including Simon Cowell, Peter Thiel, Larry King have expressed interest. Scientists dispute revival; the passage criticises cryogenic firms for exploiting fear of death.

Beignet, a nutria mascot raised by South Louisiana Wetlands Discovery Center director Jonathan Foret, was presented on Groundhog Day and World Wetlands Day. He didn't see his shadow, predicting a mild hurricane season. Nutria are invasive, requiring a permit.

Robin Chase, co‑founder of Zipcar, grew up abroad with a diplomat father and an artist mother who taught her flexibility and respect for all people. After studying at the American College in Paris and Wellesley College, she worked at a public‑health consulting firm and decided to attend MIT Sloan, where she overcame a low GMAT math score and mastered finance. In September 1999 she learned about car‑sharing from Antje Danielson and, with Danielson, incorporated Zipcar in January 2000, naming it after market‑testing strangers’ reactions. Chase built a small team including Roy Russell, Stephen Oakley, Larry Slotnick and later hired Keefer Welch as president, but fired him after three months. She developed a simple wireless‑ready car‑access system using MIT engineering students, leased Volkswagens, secured parking through a city RFP and obtained insurance. The pricing model featured a $300 security deposit, a $50 annual fee, hourly ($4.50–$7.00) and per‑mile ($0.40) rates and a daily cap of $44 for up to 125 miles. Zipcar launched in June 2000 with four cars and gained press coverage; by mid‑September it had about 430 members and was adding 35 new members per week. In October, with 10 cars and a pending $1.3 million funding round, Chase analyzed usage data and discovered car utilization was only 22 % (far below the 40 % forecast) and revenue per trip was roughly half the projection. She traced the shortfall to the daily‑rate component, which accounted for 50 % of revenue, and concluded that a 20 % price increase was required to break even, a change that would affect members who had already paid deposits and annual fees. Team members raised concerns about a potential backlash and the timing with the Series A close, but Chase, advised by her brother Mark and others, decided to raise the daily rate. The case illustrates how early financial miscalculations forced rapid pricing adjustments while the company navigated fundraising in a post‑dot‑com bust environment.

The passage outlines U.S. positions on post-war settlements. Alsace-Lorraine's return to France is highly desirable but contingent on France's willingness to fight. Poland should be independent and democratic with boundaries based on national and economic factors, adequate sea access, and government left to Poles, requiring a democratic foundation to ensure stability against internal divisions and external pressures.

The TPS7H500x-SP is a radiation-hardness-assured current mode PWM controller family for space-grade DC-DC converters, supporting switching frequencies up to 2 MHz with three operational modes (internal oscillator, external synchronization, and primary-secondary) and peak current mode control. The controllers use a transconductance error amplifier (1800 µA/V transconductance, 10,000 V/V DC gain) with output voltage programmed via resistor divider to a 0.613 V reference. Soft start is controlled by a capacitor on the SS pin, with synchronous rectifier outputs activating when SS reaches 1 V. Primary switching outputs (OUTA/OUTB) and synchronous rectifier outputs (SRA/SRB) each provide ~150-mA peak current, requiring external gate drivers. Dead time is programmable (8 ns minimum, 50 ns fixed for TPS7H5003-SP), and leading edge blank time is also programmable. The devices support duty cycle limits of 50%, 75%, or 100% via the DCL pin configuration, and include pulse skipping mode for high-frequency operation. Current sense via CS_ILIM pin triggers hiccup mode at 1.05 V threshold, while external fault protection is available through the FAULT pin. Thermal shutdown occurs at 175°C with restart at 160°C. The controllers operate from 4-14 V input and support multiple topologies including buck, flyback, forward, push-pull, and full-bridge. Layout guidelines emphasize separating analog and power grounds, minimizing switching loop areas, and proper capacitor placement.

The passage describes a method and system for performing incremental or differential backups of virtual machines in cloud or network computing environments that do not natively support change‑block tracking (CBT). In such environments (e.g., OpenStack), the disclosed technique captures images of a virtual machine disk at two points in time, compares the images to identify which blocks have changed, generates a map of the changed block locations, loads a copy of the disk at a virtual server agent, and uses the map to extract and back up only the changed blocks. The information management system architecture comprises a storage manager that coordinates operations, data agents running on client computing devices to process primary data, and media agents running on secondary storage computing devices to manage secondary copies. Primary data is stored on primary storage devices and secondary copies are stored on secondary storage devices. The system supports various backup operations including full, incremental, differential, synthetic full, snapshot, replication, archive, and deduplication, as well as information lifecycle management and hierarchical storage management. Data agents can be specialized for specific applications (e.g., Microsoft Exchange, SQL Server, SharePoint) and media agents maintain indexes of stored secondary copies. The architecture is scalable, supporting multiple client computing devices, secondary storage computing devices, and media agents, with load balancing and failover capabilities. Information management policies define parameters and rules for automated execution of backup and restore operations. The described CBT method enables differential and incremental backups in cloud architectures that lack native API functionality for CBT, and can work with virtual disk formats such as QCOW2.

This protocol outlines a three‑arm, parallel randomized controlled trial evaluating a digital mindfulness‑based psychoeducation program (Digital‑MindCAN) for cancer survivors in Singapore. Adults aged 21–65 who finished curative cancer treatment 2 weeks to 2 years after diagnosis, without severe mental illness, pregnancy, or severe medical conditions, will be recruited from a tertiary cancer centre and randomly assigned (1:1:1) to: (i) Digital‑MindCAN plus standard care, (ii) Palouse Mindfulness (an 8‑week internet‑based MBSR program) plus standard care, or (iii) a wait‑list control. Target sample size is 150 participants (50 per group). The Digital‑MindCAN intervention consists of eight weekly 90‑minute real‑time video sessions that combine cancer‑specific psychoeducation (stress related to symptoms, treatment side‑effects, thoughts, emotions, relationships) with mindfulness practice (breathing, body scan, PAIN management, loving‑kindness, etc.). Participants also perform 10–30 minutes of home practice daily and record it in a Mindfulness Practice Diary. The Palouse Mindfulness program covers general stress reduction without cancer‑specific content, using the same schedule and duration. Primary outcomes are objective stress (skin temperature, heart rate, SpO2) and subjective stress. Secondary outcomes encompass psychological well‑being, perceived relaxation, mindfulness, resilience, depression, and anxiety. Data are collected via self‑report questionnaires at baseline, after the fourth session, and after the eighth session, with physiological measures taken pre‑ and post‑each session; focus‑group interviews will be conducted after the final session. Randomisation uses a computer‑generated list concealed until consent, and blinding of participants and assessors is limited but physiological measures mitigate detection bias. Analysis will include ANCOVA with baseline scores as covariates, repeated‑measures ANOVA for physiological variables, and intent‑to‑treat with multiple imputation for missing data. Qualitative data will be analysed using a realist evaluation framework. Ethical approval was obtained from the NHG Domain Specific Review Board; participants provide written informed consent and receive an honorarium. Positive findings could support integrating Digital‑MindCAN into standard cancer care as a digital mindfulness option.

The study investigated preschool teachers' views on sensory education and their classroom practices. A phenomenological qualitative design was used, and 20 teachers were selected by maximum‑diversity sampling from different school types (kindergarten, nursery school, practice kindergarten, private kindergarten) and settlements (village, district, town). Data were collected with a semi‑structured interview form and analyzed by content analysis, producing 81 codes organized into nine categories and three main themes.

The first theme, “importance of sensory education,” comprised categories on the importance of sensory education, its impact on children's developmental areas, and how to support sensory education. Teachers reported that sensory education is essential in early childhood, contributes to cognitive, language, social‑emotional, and self‑care development, and should be integrated into daily routines, enriched environments, and family cooperation.

The second theme, “relationship with the preschool education program,” included categories on the inclusion of sensory education in the program, its place in daily planning, evaluation of sensory activities, and family participation. Teachers indicated that the 2013 preschool program contains outcomes and indicators related to the senses but does not explicitly state “sensory education.” They described implementing sensory activities (visual, auditory, tactile, musical, dramatic, experimental, and play‑based) in daily routines and evaluating them through observation, development forms, and feedback. Family involvement was addressed via communication, seminars, and home activities.

The third theme, “challenges and limitations,” covered the physical and equipment facilities of schools and classrooms and teachers' self‑efficacy perceptions. Participants reported insufficient sensory materials and inadequate physical conditions, and expressed varying confidence in applying sensory education, with almost all indicating a need for further training.

The discussion noted that teachers recognized the benefits of sensory education for children's development but sometimes confused the terms “sense” and “emotion” and commonly referred to only five senses. Recommendations for practice include providing in‑service training for teachers, interdisciplinary support from occupational therapists, equipping classrooms with sensory materials, integrating sensory education into undergraduate teacher preparation, and preparing sample activities in collaboration with therapists and teachers.

Stanford researchers engineered E. coli to secrete a sticky protein under blue light, allowing them to pattern bacterial biofilms by illuminating selected areas. Reported in PNAS (Mar. 19), the technique, called biofilm lithography, achieves 25 µm resolution—about one‑quarter a grain of table salt. Bacteria attach to lit regions, forming patterns from polka dots to circuits. Compared with inkjet printing or chemical pre‑patterning, biofilm lithography is faster, simpler, higher‑resolution. Sharp patterns indicated many cells are weakly bound to the surface, hopping on and off. The method could aid studies of bacterial community dynamics, synthetic microbial systems, and applications such as metabolic biosynthesis, distributed biocomputation and conductive biofilm circuits. Researchers are now extending it to pattern multiple bacterial strains and explore antibiotic‑resistance sharing. Funding: Stanford Bio‑X, NSERC Canada, American Cancer Society.

Higher‑education projects (HEPs) established by Russian academics who emigrated after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine were examined to understand how they shape identity linked to their homeland. The study followed four initiatives that differ in institutionalisation (from informal online courses to accredited on‑campus programmes) and used phenomenological semi‑structured interviews with project leaders together with discourse analysis of public materials. Findings are organised around three self‑conceptualisation narratives. First, HEPs present themselves as a “safe haven,” providing infrastructural support (positions, scholarships, visa help) and forming informal therapeutic communities that allow fleeing scholars and students to preserve professional and national identity. Second, they act as spaces of preservation, seeking to maintain academic heritage (schools of thought, Russian‑language teaching, liberal‑arts model) while engaging with international partners for reconceptualisation, though changes to the exported heritage remain limited. Third, HEPs practice “hope‑making praxis,” shifting from passive anticipation of return to active, future‑oriented work that fosters democratic values and builds hope for an “educated European Russia.” The conclusion notes that HEPs simultaneously serve as sanctuaries, preserve collective academic legacy, and generate hopeful agency, while urging further scrutiny of biases, colonial influences, and gaps between stated goals and everyday practice.

TB is the leading infectious cause of death globally, with 10.6 million cases and 1.3 million deaths in 2022. Undernutrition is the leading risk factor for TB, contributing at least 2.2 million cases. The RATIONS randomized trial demonstrated that nutritional supplementation reduced TB incidence by 40% and mortality by 35% among household contacts of persons with TB in India.

This study developed a Markov model to assess cost-effectiveness of a RATIONS-style intervention from India's governmental and societal perspectives. The intervention provides household contacts a food basket containing micronutrients, rice, and lentils for 6 months ($13/month), plus supplemental nutrition for TB patients during treatment. Model parameters came from the RATIONS trial conducted in Jharkhand, India.

Per 100,000 household contacts over lifetime, the RATIONS intervention reduced TB incidence (6,749 vs 7,718 cases) and TB mortality (906 vs 1,529 deaths) compared to usual care. The intervention averted 13,775 DALYs. From the healthcare perspective, costs were $3.93 million (intervention) vs $0.76 million (usual care), with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of $229 per DALY averted. From the societal perspective, costs were $7.76 million vs $5.24 million, with an ICER of $184 per DALY averted. Both estimates fall below India's willingness-to-pay threshold of $550 per DALY averted.

Sensitivity analyses showed the intervention remains cost-effective across wide ranges of supplement costs and effect sizes, including at the lowest estimated risk reductions (15% for both incidence and mortality). The intervention would be cost-effective as long as supplement costs remain below $75-100 per recipient over 6 months. Probabilistic analysis found the intervention preferred in over 99% of simulations at the threshold willingness-to-pay.

The study concluded that a RATIONS-style nutritional intervention would be cost-effective for populations with high dual burden of TB and undernutrition in India, driving substantial reductions in TB incidence and mortality among household contacts.

The lecture introduces dynamic optimality for binary search trees (BSTs), asking whether one BST can match the performance of any other BST for any access sequence. The BST model permits pointer navigation and rotations, with searches assumed successful and without insertions or deletions. While the worst-case lower bound is Ω(log n), dynamic optimality seeks good amortized performance for all sequences. Specific properties such as sequential access, dynamic finger, entropy, working set, and unified bounds characterize scenarios where costs below log n are achievable. Whether any BST achieves the unified property or constant competitive dynamic optimality remains open; splay trees are conjectured to be dynamically optimal but this is unproven. A geometric view models access sequences as point sets in space-time, where valid BST executions correspond to point sets satisfying that every rectangle spanned by two points contains another point. The offline optimal problem is to minimally augment a point set to satisfy this property, approximable within log log n. A greedy algorithm based on this view can be implemented online using split trees.

The lecture explains that putting a CFT on a sphere at finite temperature gives richer physics than on flat space because the sphere provides a scale, so temperature is relevant via the dimensionless product rT. The gravity dual can be thermal AdS, a small black hole, or a big black hole. The small black hole has negative specific heat and is unstable; the big black hole has positive specific heat and dominates at high temperature. Below a minimum temperature only thermal AdS exists; at a critical temperature Tc > T_min a first‑order Hawking‑Page transition occurs: for T < Tc the thermal AdS (free energy ≈ 0) dominates, and for T > Tc the big black hole (negative free energy ∝ N²) dominates. The Euclidean action of thermal AdS is zero relative to pure AdS, while black‑hole actions scale as N². A toy model of N² free harmonic oscillators with an SU(N) singlet constraint reproduces the same transition: at low temperature only low‑energy states (order N⁰) contribute, and at high temperature the exponentially large density of order N² states dominates, giving the Hawking‑Page phase change.

In Cape Breton, Dale Capstick and her husband have been dealing with nightly appearances of large Eratigena atrica (giant house spiders) since August, spotting about three dozen and killing roughly 30. A neighbour, Charles Andrews, also captured a specimen that later died and shrank. Calum Ewing, a biologist at the Nova Scotia Museum, confirmed the species, noting that the spiders have bodies 10–18 mm long and leg spans up to 10 cm, are harmless, native to western Europe and first recorded in Nova Scotia in the mid‑1990s. The spiders, often called “bathtub spiders,” build non‑sticky funnel webs and are fast predators that require a substantial insect population to thrive; if the prey disappears, the spiders die or leave, and an exterminator can resolve persistent infestations.

He co‑created AutoInvest.ca, a tool that compares all‑in costs of robo‑advisors using different pricing models; the Advanced Filters tab is recommended, and the site receives affiliate commissions. Robertson also offers an online course, Practical Index Investing for Canadians, with step‑by‑step videos for Tangerine, TD Direct Investing and Questrade. The Ask the Spud segment reviews Vanguard’s new asset‑allocation ETFs (one‑fund portfolios with a 0.22 % management fee). It outlines trade‑offs: portfolio size affects dollar impact of fee cuts; switching from TD e‑Series saves <$2 per $10 000 per month, from Tangerine ~$7 per $10 000 per month. HPE introduced the Edgeline Services Platform and two software‑defined OT apps – the Edgeline Data Aggregation App and the Edgeline Address Translation App – at its Discover 2017 conference. The platform runs IoT applications at the edge (factories, refineries, vehicles, cities) rather than in traditional data centers. The Data Aggregation App consolidates data from PLCs, SCADA and other OT devices; the Address Translation App routes network address translations across sub‑networks using software‑defined configuration. ESA has inaugurated a 35‑metre deep‑space antenna, called New Norcia 3, at its New Norcia ground station in Western Australia. The fourth antenna in ESA’s Estrack network, it features cryogenically cooled receivers (≈‑263 °C) and a 20 kW transmitter, enabling communication with spacecraft billions of kilometres away. The antenna is scheduled to become operational in 2026 and will support current ESA missions (Juice, Solar Orbiter, BepiColombo, Mars Express, Hera, Euclid, ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter) and future missions (Plato, Envision, Ariel, Ramses, Vigil). Construction cost was €62.3 million, with €3 million contributed by the Australian Space Agency. European industry (Thales Alenia Space, Schwartz Hautmont) led the build, with involvement of Australian firms (TIAM Solutions, Thales Australia, Fredon, Westforce Construction). The station is operated locally by CSIRO and complements ESA’s antennas in Argentina and Spain. The new antenna can also support other agencies (NASA, JAXA, ISRO) and will provide data‑download capacity for decades, reinforcing Europe’s deep‑space communication independence.

Researchers at UCL and Imperial College London discovered that last‑resort polymyxin antibiotics kill Gram‑negative bacteria by forcing the cells to rapidly produce and shed their outer membrane armor. High‑resolution atomic‑force microscopy showed bumps and bulges appearing within minutes, followed by massive armor loss that creates gaps allowing the drug to enter and destroy the cell. This lethal process occurs only when bacteria are metabolically active; dormant cells keep armor production turned off and survive the treatment. Adding a food source such as glucose awakens dormant cells, restoring polymyxin susceptibility after about 15 minutes. The findings suggest combining polymyxins with agents that stimulate armor production or rouse sleeping bacteria could improve therapy.

Card initialization begins after the bus is activated. The host sends CMD8 to verify voltage compatibility and enable expanded ACMD41 functionality. The host repeatedly issues ACMD41 with the HCS (Host Capacity Support) bit set according to its capacity and monitors the busy bit in the OCR. Initialization must complete within one second; cards that do not set the busy bit after this timeout are considered incompatible and are moved to the Inactive state. When the card returns ready, the response includes the CCS (Card Capacity Status) field: CCS = 0 indicates a Standard‑Capacity SD Memory Card and CCS = 1 indicates an SDHC or SDXC card. After the first ready response, the host issues CMD2 (ALL_SEND_CID) to obtain the card’s unique identification (CID) and then CMD3 (SEND_RELATIVE_ADDR) to assign a shorter relative card address (RCA) for future addressing.

For UHS‑I cards, the host sets S18R in the ACMD41 argument to request 1.8 V signaling. The card responds with S18A; if S18A = 1 the host sends CMD11 to perform the voltage‑switch sequence. After the switch, tuning of the sampling point is performed by repeatedly issuing CMD19 (Send Tuning Block) up to 40 times within 150 ms. The host may use CMD6 (Switch Function) to select bus speed modes, command‑system extensions, driver strength, and power‑limit settings. CMD6 operates in two modes: mode 0 queries supported functions and maximum power, mode 1 switches the selected function; a function is only changed when it is not busy.

In data‑transfer mode the host selects a card with CMD7, retrieves its CSD using CMD9, optionally configures driver stages with CMD4, and then performs block reads (CMD17, CMD18) and writes (CMD24, CMD25). All block transfers are protected by a CRC and may be aborted with CMD12. A card signals busy by pulling DAT0 low; write buffering allows the next block to be sent while the previous one is being programmed, but CSD, write‑protect, and erase operations do not support buffering. Erase operations use CMD32, CMD33, and CMD38; variants include discard (CMD38 = 00000001h) and full‑user‑area logical erase (FULE) (CMD38 = 00000002h). Write protection can be mechanical, internal, or password based. Password‑based lock/unlock is performed with CMD42, which carries the operation mode, password length, and optional password data. A card locked by a password accepts only commands of class 0, ACMD41, CMD16, and lock‑card commands; all other commands are illegal. Card Ownership Protection (COP) adds a Force‑Erase Password (FEP) register; when FEP is set, a COP unlock (CMD42[1Fh]) is required before other CMD42 functions, and force erase with FEP is disabled while FEP is cleared.

High‑Speed mode (25 MB/s) is optional and selected via CMD6 (function 1 in the Access‑Mode group). CMD8 (Send Interface Condition) is used in the Idle state to confirm voltage support and to enable expansion of ACMD41. SDSC cards use byte addressing and variable block length, while SDHC/SDXC cards use fixed 512‑byte block addressing; partial and misaligned accesses are disabled for the latter. Bus width can be changed with ACMD6 only when the card is unlocked.

Cordle v. General Hugh Mercer Corp., 325 S.E.2d 111 (W.Va. 1984). Three at‑will employees (Deborah J. Cordle, Brenda G. Billings, Brenda L. Hall) of a Holiday Inn were terminated on October 12 1982 after refusing a polygraph test they had agreed to take in January 1981. They sued for wrongful termination, and the Circuit Court of Mercer County denied the employer’s motion to dismiss, treating it as summary judgment, and certified two questions to the Supreme Court of Appeals: (A) whether terminating the employees for refusing the polygraph violated a substantial public policy of West Virginia, and (B) whether the existence of public policy is a question of law for the court. The Supreme Court held that determining public policy is a matter of law and that terminating at‑will employees for refusing a polygraph test contravenes West Virginia public policy, reasoning that the State recognizes a legally protected interest in individual privacy. The court affirmed the circuit court and remanded the case for further proceedings. Two justices dissented, asserting that no pre‑existing public policy prohibited such a discharge and that applying the newly articulated rule retroactively was unfair and unnecessary.

The device is a 16‑bit SAR ADC that supports both single‑ended and differential inputs, bipolar or unipolar ranges, and provides a straight‑binary output; its full‑scale range equals the difference between positive and negative full‑scale input voltages, and the LSB size is FSR⁄2¹⁶ (for VREF = 4.096 V, LSB values are listed in Table 6‑4). Alarm functionality is provided on the ALARM/SDO‑1/GPO pin and is enabled by setting the SDO1_CONFIG bits; the device monitors an input alarm (user‑programmable high and low thresholds with hysteresis) and an AVDD alarm (fixed thresholds of 4.7 V low and 5.3 V high). Each alarm has an active flag (cleared at the end of conversion) and a tripped flag (cleared after reading ALARM_REG); alarm flags can be read via the pin, internal registers, or appended to the data output. The device operates in three functional states—RESET (active‑low RST that can be configured as an application or power‑on reset), ACQ (acquires the analog input and supports a low‑power NAP mode), and CONV (conversion begins on the rising edge of CONVST/CS and ignores further transitions until conversion completes)—with the conversion time varying within specified limits. Communication uses a multiSPI interface that presents the device as a 32‑bit input‑output shift register; host‑to‑device topologies include a single‑device configuration (all multiSPI options), a minimum‑pin standard SPI connection, and a daisy‑chain of multiple devices sharing CONVST/CS and SCLK, where an optimal data‑transfer frame contains 32 × N SCLK edges for N devices and throughput scales with the number of devices. A data‑transfer frame starts on the falling edge of CONVST/CS and ends on its rising edge; the host supplies SCLK to shift data in and out, and if the SCLK count equals 32 the frame is treated as an optimal command word, short frames (<32 clocks) invalidate writes, and long frames (>32 clocks) use the last 32 bits as the command. Programming uses nine configuration registers (addresses 00h–2Bh): DEVICE_ID_REG (00h), RST_PWRCTL_REG (04h), SDI_CTL_REG (08h), SDO_CTL_REG (0Ch), DATAOUT_CTL_REG (10h), RANGE_SEL_REG (14h), ALARM_REG (20h), ALARM_H_TH_REG (24h), and ALARM_L_TH_REG (28h), controlling reset/power‑down, SPI protocol selection, output modes, alarm thresholds, input range selection, and alarm flags. Output data is determined by the previous command and the DATA_VAL bits, and the DATAOUT_CTL_REG register can append device address, range flags, alarm flags, and parity bits to the conversion result. The device supports four legacy SPI protocols (SPI‑00‑S, SPI‑01‑S, SPI‑10‑S, SPI‑11‑S) for configuration, and read operations can use single‑SDO‑x, dual‑SDO‑x (halving SCLK cycles), or a source‑synchronous (SRC) mode with internal or external clocking. The application section describes the ADS868xW as a fully integrated 16‑bit SAR ADC with analog front‑end, precision reference, PGA, and over‑voltage protection; an example 8‑channel PLC analog input module combines the ADS8681W with a MUX36D08 multiplexer for fast 5 µs settling, programmable voltage/current ranges, and alarm monitoring; an NTC‑thermistor temperature‑monitoring example illustrates how user‑programmable alarm thresholds and hysteresis prevent false triggers. Power‑supply recommendations include separate AVDD and DVDD rails, decoupling AVDD with ≥10 µF and 1 µF capacitors and DVDD with a ≥10 µF capacitor close to the pin, and noting that decoupling improves PSRR. Low‑power modes are NAP (enabled via the NAP_EN bit and exited on a falling CONVST/CS edge) and power‑down (PWRDN bit, which powers down analog blocks while retaining registers and leaving the interface active). PCB layout guidelines advise separating analog and digital sections, routing analog signals on one layer and digital on another, placing bypass caps very close to supply pins, using low‑ESR caps for the REFCAP pin, and decoupling the REFIO pin with ≥4.7 µF when the internal reference is used. Support resources include TI E2E forums, related datasheets (OPA320, SN6501, TPS7A49, ISO764xFM), trademark notices (multiSPI, TI E2E), and ESD handling cautions; mechanical, packaging, and orderable information completes the document.

MARY CAROLYN FINE v. EDWARD T. DENNY (May 28, 1952). Parents had two children, Lynda and Edward. In 1946 mother went to Nevada, obtained divorce awarding Lynda to her and purportedly awarding Edward to the father; both later remarried. Father had exclusive custody of Edward 1946‑1949. In June 1949 mother sued for custody, kept Edward until August 1950 when court ordered return to father pending trial. On Feb. 8, 1951 trial court denied mother’s request and confirmed father’s custody. Mother appealed, arguing Civil Code §138 favors mother for tender‑year child when parents equally fit. Appellate court held child’s best interest and stability with father outweighed statutory preference, affirming judgment.

Professor announces schedule: no class Monday, Monday class Tuesday, quiz Wednesday night, TA review Wednesday at 3:00. He begins a lecture on ODE‑IVPs, explaining that an ODE involves derivatives with respect to a single variable and that an initial value problem gives all conditions at a single t. He shows conversion to first‑order form dy/dt = f(y) for MATLAB solvers, which expect f(t,y). A solver outputs a time vector and corresponding y matrix for plotting.

The lecture reviews numerical integration. The Forward Euler scheme (y_{n+1}=y_n+dt f(y_n)) is the discrete analogue of the rectangle rule; its per‑step error is O(dt^2) but total error scales as O(dt). Higher‑order methods—midpoint, trapezoid, Runge‑Kutta—estimate the average of f over the step and reduce total error to O(dt^2) or better.

He analyzes error propagation: each step multiplies the error by the matrix I+dt J (J Jacobian of the update function). A method is numerically stable only if the norm of this matrix stays ≤1. Even when the original ODE is stable (negative eigenvalues), an unsuitable method can make the norm >1, as shown by solving dy/dt = –2y with Forward Euler and dt=1, which produces oscillations unless dt<0.5.

The lecture references textbook derivations of stability criteria and assigns homework 4, in which students must implement their own ODE solver.

The paper presents an MDA‑driven framework for digital business process modeling that combines three components: a static domain model (entities, actors, resources), a workflow model (process activities and orchestration), and a value model (value exchanges between parties). Business rules are expressed in controlled natural languages (e.g., ACE, SBVR) and translated into logic‑based formalisms such as Discourse Representation Structures, OWL DL, and SWRL to enable automated reasoning. The work stresses the need for hybrid reasoning that integrates closed‑world Horn‑rule inference with open‑world description‑logic reasoning, and addresses modal interpretations of rules (alethic and deontic) using operators such as necessary, possible, obligatory, permitted, and forbidden. For process flow, graphical notations like BPMN and UML Activity diagrams are used, with formal semantics provided by Petri nets, π‑calculus, or temporal logics (LTL, CTL). Declarative representations support consistency checking, data export, and annotation of process models. The value model can be represented graphically (e.g., e³‑value) or in logic‑based formalisms (Prolog‑style FOL), allowing profitability calculations and a‑priori evaluation of collaborations. Relations among the three models are examined through static, semi‑dynamic, and dynamic consistency checks, employing cross‑checking mechanisms and monitoring based on log files. The authors conclude that multi‑faceted business process models require diverse inference techniques and that open issues remain in detecting critical areas and representing stakeholder motivations.

Digital storytelling in African higher education: a qualitative document analysis. Education is a fundamental human right, yet access to quality education remains problematic in Africa, with sub-Saharan enrollment at only 6%. Digital storytelling combines traditional narrative with multimedia tools to create personal stories using text, graphics, sound, and video. The seven essential elements include point of view, dramatic question, emotional content, voice, soundtrack, economy, and pacing. The process involves pre-production (narrative creation and emotional positioning), production (visualization and audio recording), and post-production phases (assembly and distribution). Benefits include improved digital and media literacy, enhanced creativity, problem-solving skills, engagement, and critical thinking. Digital storytelling promotes empowerment, cultural enrichment, and transformative learning experiences while fostering community building among diverse student populations. Research from multiple African countries (South Africa, Nigeria, Egypt, Tanzania, Uganda, Kenya) using qualitative methodologies examined digital storytelling in pre-service teacher training, geography education, language learning, and cultural preservation. Findings indicate positive impacts on oral performance, map-reading skills, reflective capabilities, and higher-order thinking. Challenges include resource shortages, insufficient digital equipment, inconsistent electricity, and time constraints due to rigid curricula. Emphasis should be placed on narrative content rather than technology itself when integrating digital storytelling into assessments. Digital storytelling serves as both an educational tool and a bridge between traditional oral knowledge transmission and modern technology.

AMO physics is defined by its community of researchers and by its building blocks—atoms, molecules and photons (including electromagnetic fields). Historically the field studied gases of isolated particles and two‑particle collisions; it now focuses on few‑body and many‑body quantum systems, entanglement and overlap with condensed‑matter physics. It is characterized by low‑energy quantum physics and by the goal of controlling nature: first internal states (optical pumping, Nobel 1966), then external motion (laser cooling, Bose‑Einstein condensation), and finally single‑quantum‑system control (single atoms, photons and ions). Technological advances—solid‑state lasers, femtosecond pulses, frequency combs (Nobel 2005) and high‑finesse cavities—have driven rapid growth, reshaping paradigms from laser spectroscopy through magneto‑optical traps to ultracold fermions and entanglement studies. Current frontiers include quantum‑information‑related entanglement, topological states and micro‑mechanical oscillators. The MIT graduate course 8.422 covers QED from first principles, light‑atom interaction, spontaneous emission and open‑system density‑matrix formalism, mechanical forces of light, single‑photon physics, quantum gates and many‑body physics of quantum gases, while omitting high‑energy collisions, advanced atomic structure and high‑intensity lasers. Course logistics include ten problem sets, a term paper, TAs from several MIT groups and a website (cua.mit.edu/8.422). As an illustrative system the lecture uses atoms in an optical standing wave: the dipole interaction creates a periodic potential; deep lattices enable magic‑wavelength optical clocks (≈10⁻¹⁷ accuracy) and isolated atoms, while shallow lattices permit tunneling, Bloch states and a Mott‑insulator transition for bosons or a metal‑to‑Mott crossover for fermions. Pulsed optical lattices act as beam splitters for atom interferometers, measure dynamic structure factors of interacting many‑body systems and connect precision measurement with many‑body physics.

University of Utah scientists, including Sin‑Mei Wu (first author), used a dense network of 133 portable seismometers to map the near‑surface geology of Old Faithful. The study, published in Geophysical Research Letters, reveals that the geyser’s hydrothermal reservoir is roughly 200 m in diameter and holds about 300 000 m³ (79 million gal) of water, while each eruption releases only ~30 m³ (≈8 000 gal). Seismic recordings show 60‑minute bursts of tremor separated by ~30‑minute quiet periods; the eruption occurs at the end of the tremor after collapsing bubbles generate the shaking. The researchers exploited ambient ground vibration and hydrothermal sources as seismic signals, and the data indicate an anomalous underground feature west of Old Faithful that scatters waves—identified as the reservoir. Permanent seismometers (30 units) and low‑cost (<$2 000) instruments were employed. Future work includes additional surveys, temperature‑related studies, earthquake‑wave predictions, and similar analysis in Norris Geyser Basin.

Secretary Stettinius emphasized that delegations should approach the general conference with open minds, avoid formal positions, and keep Dumbarton Oaks proposals informal to allow modifications. Discussions addressed objections to the name “United Nations” and the inclusion of specific principles such as treaty respect, juridical equality and territorial integrity. The term “United Nations” originated from a 1941 joint declaration by President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill. During early 1945 Stettinius arranged travel to the Yalta Conference and to a meeting of Foreign Ministers in Mexico City. He instructed U.S. embassies to warn six Latin American associated nations that failure to declare war on the Axis could exclude them from the initial United Nations Conference. Preparations for the Big‑Three meeting included a ten‑point binder and policy guidance for the U.S. delegation, with a plan to start the conference machinery if the President resolved pending issues. The British accepted the compromise voting formula, but Roosevelt indicated the U.S. would likely accept a Russian unanimity requirement while expecting the Soviets to drop their proposal for seventeen votes. The Yalta Conference was the first chief‑of‑state meeting attended by a Secretary of State.

Ronald L. Johnson appealed the denial of his habeas petition, challenging the admission of his confession at a 1964 Massachusetts trial for first‑degree murder, armed robbery and related offenses. The confession was obtained about 8½ hours after his arrest following a high‑speed chase, during which he suffered head and other injuries. He was interrogated at 5:50 a.m. for roughly 40 minutes without Miranda warnings, while many officers were present and after several line‑ups in which he was identified as the shooter. At the time of arrest Johnson was 29, had a sixth‑grade education and an IQ of 86. Prior police encounters showed he was not easily intimidated and he resisted and cursed at officers during booking.

The trial court admitted the confession, finding it voluntary. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court affirmed, and a later cert petition was dismissed. Johnson’s federal habeas petition raised three claims: (1) the trial court failed to consider the totality of circumstances required by Procunier v. Atchley; (2) the Lego v. Twomey burden‑of‑proof standard applies retroactively; and (3) the confession was involuntary as a matter of law.

The First Circuit found it unnecessary to rule on the first two issues. Performing an independent “totality of the circumstances” review, the court concluded that the confession was voluntary even under the Lego standard. Factors such as Johnson’s prior police experience, his lack of physical abuse, his ability to resist and question line‑up witnesses, and the absence of promises or threats showed his will was not overborne. The confession was therefore admissible.

The court affirmed the district court’s denial of the writ.

Healthy Davis Together (HDT) and its Yolo County expansion (HYT) provided free saliva‑based PCR testing and limited rapid antigen testing from November 2020 to June 2022, grouping the pandemic into four variant‑defined periods (Pre‑Delta, Delta, Omicron, Post‑Omicron). The program performed 770,165 tests for 89,924 unique residents, reaching 41.1 % of the Yolo County population and 78.4 % of Davis residents. Daily testing rates per 100 000 rose from 422 (Pre‑Delta) to 746 (Delta), 895 (Omicron) and fell to 435 (Post‑Omicron). Omicron had the highest daily test volume and accounted for 50.8 % of all positive cases. Participation declined after Omicron; new tester enrollment fell from 39,819 in Pre‑Delta to 2,788 in Post‑Omicron. Frequent testers (multiple tests within ≤15 days) peaked at 39.7 % during Omicron. Across all periods, frequent testers were predominantly female (≈59 %), aged 19‑34 (≈40 %) and White (≈52 %). Women composed a larger share of tests and more frequent testing than men. Testing coverage exceeded 25 % for all race/ethnic and age groups under 85 years, with the lowest coverage in those >85 years. The program combined free testing, targeted communication, PPE distribution, community partnerships and economic support. Post‑Omicron declines were linked to pandemic fatigue, vaccine availability, at‑home testing and waning trust. The data illustrate how variant‑driven surges, demographic factors and public‑health messaging shaped community testing behavior.
